HOW TO USE THIS BANK

This is a combined study bank for the 15 subject slots in Semesters I, II and III shown by the supplied University of Madras BCA course books. It is designed for answer-writing practice, not as a prediction of the next examination.
Evidence labels
• PYQ-backed means the topic or question form appears in the supplied previous-year papers. The paper code and year range are identified in the relevant subject section.
• Textbook-based model means it is included because it appears in the supplied syllabus or textbook, but no matching PYQ paper was present in the uploaded PYQ archive.

• Legacy-paper caution means an older paper asks about a text or topic that does not appear in the supplied semester textbook syllabus. Verify it with the current examination notice or tutor before spending revision time on it.
What was inspected
The uploaded PYQ ZIP contained 110 PDF entries. After exact duplicate files were removed, 87 unique question-paper PDFs remained. They cover eight theory-paper series:
Semester | Subject / paper series | Unique papers
I | Fundamentals of Digital Computers – UCC1A | 12
I | English – UEB1A | 10
I | Mathematics I – URC1A | 12
II | Programming in C – UCC2A | 11
II | English – UEB2A | 11
II | Mathematics II – URC2A | 11
III | Numerical and Statistical Methods – UCC3C | 10
III | Financial Accounting – UNC3A | 10

The uploaded textbook ZIP contained 16 course-book PDFs. It also supplies material for Communicative English I and II, PC Software Lab, Programming in C Lab, Programming in C++ and Data Structures, Microprocessors and its Applications, and Programming in C++ using Data Structures Lab. No matching PYQ PDFs for those seven subject areas were found in the PYQ archive. Questions in those sections are therefore clearly marked textbook-based model questions, not verified past-paper questions.
Common theory-paper structure in the supplied papers
The supplied theory papers generally state three hours and 75 marks, with this recurring structure:
• Part / Section A: 10 × 2 = 20 marks; answer any ten.
• Part / Section B: 5 × 5 = 25 marks; answer any five.
• Part / Section C: 3 × 10 = 30 marks; answer any three.
Follow the exact instructions printed on the question paper you receive. The format above describes the uploaded papers; it is not a guarantee that a future paper cannot change.
How to write for marks
2 marks: Write a definition, formula, key distinction or one correct example. Do not write an essay.
5 marks: Give a short introduction, four to six explained points or a worked method, and a concluding sentence. For numerical questions, show the formula, substitution and answer.

10 marks: Use a clear heading, definition, diagram/table/formula where relevant, ordered explanation, worked example or application, and a short conclusion. In literature answers, discuss the theme and events rather than retelling without analysis.
Honest priority guide

“High priority” means the topic appears repeatedly in the supplied papers or is central to the official syllabus. It does not mean that the topic is certain to appear. Prepare the complete syllabus, then use the priority guide to decide what to revise first.

blocks.subject: Fundamentals of Digital Computers

blocks.text: 1. Fundamentals of computers: characteristics, computer languages, operating systems and generations.
blocks.subject: Fundamentals of Digital Computers

blocks.text: 2. Number systems: conversions, complements, binary codes, binary logic, logic gates and truth tables.
blocks.subject: Fundamentals of Digital Computers

blocks.text: 3. Boolean algebra: axioms/laws, truth-table simplification, Karnaugh maps up to five variables and McCluskey tabulation.
blocks.subject: Fundamentals of Digital Computers

blocks.text: 4. Sequential logic: RS, JK, D and T flip-flops; registers; shift registers; ripple and synchronous counters; counter design.
blocks.subject: Fundamentals of Digital Computers

blocks.text: 5. Combinational and programmable logic: adders, subtractors, decoders, encoders, multiplexers, demultiplexers, ROM and PLA.
blocks.subject: Fundamentals of Digital Computers

blocks.text: PYQ recurrence map
blocks.subject: Fundamentals of Digital Computers

blocks.text: The supplied UCC1A papers repeatedly ask about number systems and complements, ASCII/EBCDIC/BCD, logic gates, Boolean laws, K-maps, universal gates, adders, decoders/encoders, multiplexers, flip-flops, registers and counters. These form the first revision block. The question bank below combines repeated question forms instead of reproducing duplicate wording from every sitting.
blocks.subject: Fundamentals of Digital Computers

blocks.text: PART A – 2-MARK QUESTIONS WITH MODEL ANSWERS
blocks.subject: Fundamentals of Digital Computers

blocks.text: 1. What are the characteristics of a computer?
blocks.subject: Fundamentals of Digital Computers

blocks.text: A computer has high speed, accuracy, diligence, storage capacity, versatility and automation. It performs operations according to instructions supplied by a program. Its output depends on the correctness of data and instructions.
blocks.subject: Fundamentals of Digital Computers

blocks.text: 2. What is an operating system?
blocks.subject: Fundamentals of Digital Computers

blocks.text: An operating system is system software that manages computer hardware and software resources and provides services for application programs. It acts as an interface between the user/programs and the hardware.
blocks.subject: Fundamentals of Digital Computers

blocks.text: 3. What is a computer language?
blocks.subject: Fundamentals of Digital Computers

blocks.text: A computer language is a formal set of symbols, rules and instructions used to communicate operations to a computer. The textbook distinguishes machine language, assembly language and high-level language.
blocks.subject: Fundamentals of Digital Computers

blocks.text: 4. What is a number system?
blocks.subject: Fundamentals of Digital Computers

blocks.text: A number system is a method of representing numbers using a set of symbols and a base (radix). Common positional systems are decimal (base 10), binary (base 2), octal (base 8) and hexadecimal (base 16).
blocks.subject: Fundamentals of Digital Computers

blocks.text: 5. Define binary number.
blocks.subject: Fundamentals of Digital Computers

blocks.text: A binary number is a number represented using only the digits 0 and 1. Each digit position has a weight that is a power of 2.
blocks.subject: Fundamentals of Digital Computers

blocks.text: 6. What is a complement?
blocks.subject: Fundamentals of Digital Computers

blocks.text: A complement is a number representation used to simplify subtraction and signed-number operations. In base 2, the 1's complement is obtained by changing 0 to 1 and 1 to 0; the 2's complement is obtained by adding 1 to the 1's complement.
blocks.subject: Fundamentals of Digital Computers

blocks.text: 7. Expand ASCII, EBCDIC and BCD.
blocks.subject: Fundamentals of Digital Computers

blocks.text: ASCII – American Standard Code for Information Interchange. EBCDIC – Extended Binary Coded Decimal Interchange Code. BCD – Binary Coded Decimal.
blocks.subject: Fundamentals of Digital Computers

blocks.text: 8. What is a logic gate?
blocks.subject: Fundamentals of Digital Computers

blocks.text: A logic gate is an electronic circuit that performs a Boolean operation on one or more binary inputs and produces a binary output.
blocks.subject: Fundamentals of Digital Computers

blocks.text: 9. What are universal gates?
blocks.subject: Fundamentals of Digital Computers

blocks.text: NAND and NOR are called universal gates because any Boolean function or basic logic gate can be implemented using only NAND gates or only NOR gates.
blocks.subject: Fundamentals of Digital Computers

blocks.text: 10. State De Morgan's theorems.
blocks.subject: Fundamentals of Digital Computers

blocks.text: 11. What is a Karnaugh map (K-map)?
blocks.subject: Fundamentals of Digital Computers

blocks.text: A Karnaugh map is a graphical method of simplifying Boolean expressions. Adjacent cells represent minterms that differ in one variable; groups of 1s are combined to obtain a simplified expression.
blocks.subject: Fundamentals of Digital Computers

blocks.text: 12. Define minterm and maxterm.
blocks.subject: Fundamentals of Digital Computers

blocks.text: A minterm is a product term containing every variable exactly once, either complemented or uncomplemented. A maxterm is a sum term containing every variable exactly once.
blocks.subject: Fundamentals of Digital Computers

blocks.text: 13. What is a flip-flop?
blocks.subject: Fundamentals of Digital Computers

blocks.text: A flip-flop is a bistable sequential circuit that stores one bit of information. Its output depends on the present inputs and the previously stored state.
blocks.subject: Fundamentals of Digital Computers

blocks.text: 14. What is a register?
blocks.subject: Fundamentals of Digital Computers

blocks.text: A register is a group of flip-flops used to store a multi-bit binary word. A shift register can move stored bits left or right under clock control.
blocks.subject: Fundamentals of Digital Computers

blocks.text: 15. What is a counter?
blocks.subject: Fundamentals of Digital Computers

blocks.text: A counter is a sequential circuit that moves through a specified sequence of binary states in response to clock pulses.
blocks.subject: Fundamentals of Digital Computers

blocks.text: 16. Differentiate encoder and decoder.
blocks.subject: Fundamentals of Digital Computers

blocks.text: An encoder converts one active input among many into a coded binary output. A decoder accepts a coded input and activates the corresponding output line.
blocks.subject: Fundamentals of Digital Computers

blocks.text: 17. What is a multiplexer?
blocks.subject: Fundamentals of Digital Computers

blocks.text: A multiplexer (MUX) is a data selector. It selects one of several input lines and connects the selected input to a single output using select lines.
blocks.subject: Fundamentals of Digital Computers

blocks.text: 18. What is a demultiplexer?
blocks.subject: Fundamentals of Digital Computers

blocks.text: A demultiplexer (DEMUX) routes one input to one of several output lines according to the select-line combination.
blocks.subject: Fundamentals of Digital Computers

blocks.text: 19. What is ROM?
blocks.subject: Fundamentals of Digital Computers

blocks.text: Read Only Memory (ROM) is a memory device in which stored information is read during normal operation. It can be used to implement fixed logic functions.
blocks.subject: Fundamentals of Digital Computers

blocks.text: 20. What is PLA?
blocks.subject: Fundamentals of Digital Computers

blocks.text: A Programmable Logic Array (PLA) is a programmable logic device with programmable AND and OR arrays used to implement Boolean functions in sum-of-products form.
blocks.subject: Fundamentals of Digital Computers

blocks.text: 21. Define half adder.
blocks.subject: Fundamentals of Digital Computers

blocks.text: A half adder adds two one-bit binary inputs and produces Sum and Carry outputs. Its equations are S=A⊕ B and C=AB.
blocks.subject: Fundamentals of Digital Computers

blocks.text: 22. Define full adder.
blocks.subject: Fundamentals of Digital Computers

blocks.text: A full adder adds three one-bit inputs (A, B and carry-in) and produces Sum and carry-out. It can be constructed from two half adders and an OR gate.
blocks.subject: Fundamentals of Digital Computers

blocks.text: 23. What is a ripple counter?
blocks.subject: Fundamentals of Digital Computers

blocks.text: A ripple counter is an asynchronous counter in which the output of one flip-flop drives the clock input of the next flip-flop. The change propagates through the stages.
blocks.subject: Fundamentals of Digital Computers

blocks.text: 24. What is a synchronous counter?
blocks.subject: Fundamentals of Digital Computers

blocks.text: A synchronous counter applies the same clock pulse to all flip-flops. The required state changes are controlled by combinational logic, so the stages change together.
blocks.subject: Fundamentals of Digital Computers

blocks.text: 25. What is an ALU?
blocks.subject: Fundamentals of Digital Computers

blocks.text: An Arithmetic Logic Unit performs arithmetic operations such as addition and subtraction and logical operations such as AND, OR and comparison within a processor.
blocks.subject: Fundamentals of Digital Computers

blocks.text: PART B – 5-MARK QUESTIONS WITH MODEL ANSWERS
blocks.subject: Fundamentals of Digital Computers

blocks.text: 1. Explain the number systems with examples.
blocks.subject: Fundamentals of Digital Computers

blocks.text: A positional number system assigns a weight to each digit according to its position and base. The four systems used in digital computers are:
blocks.subject: Fundamentals of Digital Computers

blocks.text: • Decimal: base 10; digits 0–9. Example: 347_(10).
blocks.subject: Fundamentals of Digital Computers

blocks.text: • Binary: base 2; digits 0 and 1. Example: 1011_2=11_(10).
blocks.subject: Fundamentals of Digital Computers

blocks.text: • Octal: base 8; digits 0–7. Example: 17_8=15_(10).
blocks.subject: Fundamentals of Digital Computers

blocks.text: • Hexadecimal: base 16; digits 0–9 and A–F. Example: 1F_(16)=31_(10).
blocks.subject: Fundamentals of Digital Computers

blocks.text: To convert a positional number to decimal, multiply each digit by its place value and add. To convert a positive decimal integer to another base, repeatedly divide by the new base and read the remainders from bottom to top. Binary-to-octal conversion groups bits in threes; binary-to-hexadecimal conversion groups bits in fours.
blocks.subject: Fundamentals of Digital Computers

blocks.text: 2. Explain 1's complement and 2's complement with an example.
blocks.subject: Fundamentals of Digital Computers

blocks.text: For the 8-bit binary number 00010110:
blocks.subject: Fundamentals of Digital Computers

blocks.text: • 1's complement: invert every bit → 11101001.
blocks.subject: Fundamentals of Digital Computers

blocks.text: • 2's complement: add 1 to the 1's complement → 11101010.
blocks.subject: Fundamentals of Digital Computers

blocks.text: The 2's-complement representation is commonly used for signed binary arithmetic. To obtain the negative of a binary number in a fixed width, invert all bits and add one. Keep the chosen bit width consistent; changing the width changes the represented bit pattern.
blocks.subject: Fundamentals of Digital Computers

blocks.text: 3. Explain basic laws of Boolean algebra.
blocks.subject: Fundamentals of Digital Computers

blocks.text: For binary variables A, B and C, the principal laws are:
blocks.subject: Fundamentals of Digital Computers

blocks.text: • Identity: A+0=A, A·1=A.
blocks.subject: Fundamentals of Digital Computers

blocks.text: • Null / domination: A+1=1, A·0=0.
blocks.subject: Fundamentals of Digital Computers

blocks.text: • Idempotent: A+A=A, AA=A.
blocks.subject: Fundamentals of Digital Computers

blocks.text: • Complement: A+A'=1, AA'=0.
blocks.subject: Fundamentals of Digital Computers

blocks.text: • Commutative: A+B=B+A, AB=BA.
blocks.subject: Fundamentals of Digital Computers

blocks.text: • Associative: (A+B)+C=A+(B+C); (AB)C=A(BC).
blocks.subject: Fundamentals of Digital Computers

blocks.text: • Distributive: A(B+C)=AB+AC; A+BC=(A+B)(A+C).
blocks.subject: Fundamentals of Digital Computers

blocks.text: • Absorption: A+AB=A, A(A+B)=A.
blocks.subject: Fundamentals of Digital Computers

blocks.text: These laws are used to simplify logic expressions and reduce the number of gates in a circuit.
blocks.subject: Fundamentals of Digital Computers

blocks.text: 4. Explain the NOR gate as a universal gate.
blocks.subject: Fundamentals of Digital Computers

blocks.text: A NOR gate gives Y=(A+B)'. By connecting inputs appropriately, it can implement NOT, OR and AND:
blocks.subject: Fundamentals of Digital Computers

blocks.text: • NOT: A' = A\ NOR\ A.
blocks.subject: Fundamentals of Digital Computers

blocks.text: • OR: A+B=(A\ NOR\ B)\ NOR\ (A\ NOR\ B).
blocks.subject: Fundamentals of Digital Computers

blocks.text: • AND: AB=(A\ NOR\ A)\ NOR\ (B\ NOR\ B).
blocks.subject: Fundamentals of Digital Computers

blocks.text: Since NOT, OR and AND are sufficient to build any Boolean expression, NOR is a universal gate. NAND is also universal.
blocks.subject: Fundamentals of Digital Computers

blocks.text: 5. Explain a half adder and full adder.
blocks.subject: Fundamentals of Digital Computers

blocks.text: A half adder has two inputs A and B. Its truth table is:
blocks.subject: Fundamentals of Digital Computers

blocks.text: A | B | Sum | Carry
blocks.subject: Fundamentals of Digital Computers

blocks.text: Equations: S=A⊕ B, C=AB. A half adder cannot accept a carry from a previous stage. A full adder has A, B and carry-in C_(in); it produces S=A⊕ B⊕ C_(in) and C_(out)=AB+AC_(in)+BC_(in). Full adders are connected to build multi-bit adders.
blocks.subject: Fundamentals of Digital Computers

blocks.text: 6. Explain an encoder and a decoder.
blocks.subject: Fundamentals of Digital Computers

blocks.text: An encoder has multiple input lines and fewer output lines. For a simple 4-to-2 encoder, one active input is represented by a two-bit code. A decoder performs the reverse operation: a two-bit input can activate one of four output lines. Encoders are used in keypads and priority coding; decoders are used in address selection, display systems and instruction decoding. State any assumptions about active-high/active-low inputs when drawing the circuit.
blocks.subject: Fundamentals of Digital Computers

blocks.text: 7. Explain a multiplexer.
blocks.subject: Fundamentals of Digital Computers

blocks.text: A 4-to-1 multiplexer has four data inputs I_0,I_1,I_2,I_3, two select inputs S_1,S_0, and one output Y. The select combination chooses the corresponding input: 00 selects I_0, 01 selects I_1, 10 selects I_2, and 11 selects I_3. Its Boolean expression is:
blocks.subject: Fundamentals of Digital Computers

blocks.text: Multiplexers are used for data routing, channel selection and implementing Boolean functions.
blocks.subject: Fundamentals of Digital Computers

blocks.text: 8. Explain a shift register and its uses.
blocks.subject: Fundamentals of Digital Computers

blocks.text: A shift register is a set of flip-flops connected so that each clock pulse transfers data from one stage to the next. The common types are serial-in serial-out, serial-in parallel-out, parallel-in serial-out and parallel-in parallel-out. Shift registers are used for serial/parallel conversion, temporary data storage, delay circuits and sequence generation.
blocks.subject: Fundamentals of Digital Computers

blocks.text: PART C – 10-MARK QUESTIONS WITH MODEL ANSWERS
blocks.subject: Fundamentals of Digital Computers

blocks.text: 1. Explain the basic logic gates with truth tables.
blocks.subject: Fundamentals of Digital Computers

blocks.text: Logic gates implement Boolean operations. A NOT gate has one input and produces its complement. AND produces 1 only when all inputs are 1. OR produces 1 when at least one input is 1. NAND is the complement of AND; NOR is the complement of OR. XOR produces 1 when the inputs differ; XNOR produces 1 when the inputs are equal.
blocks.subject: Fundamentals of Digital Computers

blocks.text: A | B | AND | OR | NAND | NOR | XOR | XNOR
blocks.subject: Fundamentals of Digital Computers

blocks.text: For a NOT gate: A=0 gives output 1 and A=1 gives output 0. NAND and NOR are universal gates because the basic operations can be implemented using only one of these gate types. In an exam, draw the standard symbols and label each input and output clearly.
blocks.subject: Fundamentals of Digital Computers

blocks.text: 2. Explain K-map simplification and solve a typical Boolean function.
blocks.subject: Fundamentals of Digital Computers

blocks.text: A K-map places minterms in Gray-code order so that adjacent cells differ in one variable. Enter 1 in the cells corresponding to the listed minterms; group adjacent 1s in powers of two (1, 2, 4, 8, ...). Make the largest possible groups, allow wrap-around adjacency and overlap when useful, and ensure every 1 is covered. Each group removes the variables that change within it; the remaining literals form a product term. Add the product terms to obtain the simplified SOP expression.
blocks.subject: Fundamentals of Digital Computers

blocks.text: For a four-variable function, use a 4 × 4 map with row and column order 00, 01, 11, 10. For a three-variable function, use a 2 × 4 map. Do not use ordinary binary order 00, 01, 10, 11 around a K-map edge; Gray-code order is essential. The uploaded papers repeatedly require 3- and 4-variable K-map reductions, including expressions in A, B, C, D or W, X, Y, Z. In a numerical exam answer, show the minterm placement, the marked groups and the final reduced expression.
blocks.subject: Fundamentals of Digital Computers

blocks.text: 3. Explain flip-flops, registers and counters.
blocks.subject: Fundamentals of Digital Computers

blocks.text: A flip-flop is a one-bit storage element. The SR (RS) flip-flop has Set and Reset inputs; the JK flip-flop removes the invalid SR condition and toggles when J=K=1; the D flip-flop transfers D to Q on the active clock; the T flip-flop toggles when T=1. A register is a group of flip-flops. A shift register shifts a stored word left or right. A counter is a sequential circuit that advances through a state sequence.
blocks.subject: Fundamentals of Digital Computers

blocks.text: Counters may be asynchronous (ripple) or synchronous. In a ripple counter, each stage is triggered by the preceding stage and propagation delay accumulates. In a synchronous counter, all flip-flops receive a common clock and combinational logic decides which stages toggle. A 3-bit binary counter has eight states, from 000 through 111, then returns to 000. In the examination, include the state table, clock/logic diagram and a short explanation of operation.
blocks.subject: Fundamentals of Digital Computers

blocks.text: 4. Describe the design and functions of an arithmetic logic unit.
blocks.subject: Fundamentals of Digital Computers

blocks.text: An ALU is the part of a digital system that performs arithmetic and logical operations. Its inputs are binary operands and control signals. A typical ALU may support addition, subtraction, increment, decrement, AND, OR, XOR and complement. The selection/control lines determine which operation is performed. The ALU uses adders, logic gates, multiplexers and internal registers. Status outputs may include carry, zero, sign and overflow indications. The ALU works with the control unit, which decodes instructions and directs data movement. Thus, the ALU performs the actual arithmetic/logical processing while the control unit coordinates the system.
blocks.subject: Fundamentals of Digital Computers

blocks.text: 1. Define the forward difference operator.
blocks.subject: Mathematics I

blocks.text: For equally spaced arguments, Δ y_r=y_(r+1)-y_r. It is the difference between the next value and the current value.
blocks.subject: Mathematics I

blocks.text: 2. Define the backward difference operator.
blocks.subject: Mathematics I

blocks.text: ∇ y_r=y_r-y_(r-1). It is the difference between the current value and the preceding value.
blocks.subject: Mathematics I

blocks.text: 3. State the relation between E and Δ.
blocks.subject: Mathematics I

blocks.text: E=1+Δ, where E is the shift operator.
blocks.subject: Mathematics I

blocks.text: 4. State the relation between E and ∇.
blocks.subject: Mathematics I

blocks.text: ∇=1-E^(-1), equivalently E^(-1)=1-∇.
blocks.subject: Mathematics I

blocks.text: 5. What is an orthogonal matrix?
blocks.subject: Mathematics I

blocks.text: A square matrix A is orthogonal if A^TA=I. Its transpose is its inverse: A^(-1)=A^T.
blocks.subject: Mathematics I

blocks.text: 6. Define Hermitian matrix.
blocks.subject: Mathematics I

blocks.text: A complex square matrix A is Hermitian if A^=A, where A^ is the conjugate transpose.
blocks.subject: Mathematics I

blocks.text: 7. Define skew-Hermitian matrix.
blocks.subject: Mathematics I

blocks.text: A complex square matrix A is skew-Hermitian if A^*=-A.
blocks.subject: Mathematics I

blocks.text: 8. What is an eigenvalue?
blocks.subject: Mathematics I

blocks.text: A scalar λ is an eigenvalue of A if there is a non-zero vector x such that Ax=λ x. The vector x is an eigenvector.
blocks.subject: Mathematics I

blocks.text: 9. State the Cayley–Hamilton theorem.
blocks.subject: Mathematics I

blocks.text: Every square matrix satisfies its own characteristic equation. If the characteristic polynomial is p(λ), then p(A)=0.
blocks.subject: Mathematics I

blocks.text: 10. State Newton–Raphson formula.
blocks.subject: Mathematics I

blocks.text: 11. Write Newton's forward interpolation formula.
blocks.subject: Mathematics I

blocks.text: 12. Write Lagrange's interpolation formula.
blocks.subject: Mathematics I

blocks.text: 13. State Leibnitz theorem.
blocks.subject: Mathematics I

blocks.text: For the nth derivative of a product, D^n(uv)=Σ_(r=0)^(n)C(n,r)u^((n-r))v^((r)).
blocks.subject: Mathematics I

blocks.text: 14. Define Jacobian.
blocks.subject: Mathematics I

blocks.text: For functions u and v of x and y, the Jacobian is ∂(u,v)/∂(x,y)=u_xv_y-u_yv_x.
blocks.subject: Mathematics I

blocks.text: 15. Define radius of curvature for y=f(x).
blocks.subject: Mathematics I

blocks.text: 16. Define reciprocal equation.
blocks.subject: Mathematics I

blocks.text: A polynomial equation is reciprocal when its coefficients are symmetric from the two ends (or have the corresponding alternating symmetry), allowing transformations using x+1/x or x-1/x.
blocks.subject: Mathematics I

blocks.text: 17. Give the expansion of log(1+x), for |x|<1.
blocks.subject: Mathematics I

blocks.text: 18. Give the expansion of (1+x)^(-2), for |x|<1.
blocks.subject: Mathematics I

blocks.text: PART B – 5-MARK QUESTIONS WITH MODEL ANSWERS
blocks.subject: Mathematics I

blocks.text: 1. Construct a forward difference table and explain its use.
blocks.subject: Mathematics I

blocks.text: For equally spaced x-values, list the corresponding y-values in the first column. Compute first differences by subtracting each y-value from the next; repeat the operation to obtain second, third and higher differences. The table is triangular. Forward differences are used when the required x-value is near the beginning of the table. Backward differences are preferred near the end. Check that the x-interval h is constant before using Newton's equal-interval formulas.
blocks.subject: Mathematics I

blocks.text: 2. Explain Newton–Raphson method.
blocks.subject: Mathematics I

blocks.text: To find a root of f(x)=0, choose an initial approximation x_0. Draw the tangent to the curve at (x_0,f(x_0)); its x-intercept gives the next approximation. Repeat:
blocks.subject: Mathematics I

blocks.text: Stop when successive values agree to the required decimal places or when the error is within the specified tolerance. The method can converge rapidly when the starting value is suitable and the derivative is not zero near the root. It may fail or converge to a different root if the initial approximation is poor.
blocks.subject: Mathematics I

blocks.text: 3. Explain how to test whether a matrix is orthogonal.
blocks.subject: Mathematics I

blocks.text: For a real square matrix A, find its transpose A^T, multiply A^TA, and check whether the result is the identity matrix. If it is, A is orthogonal and A^(-1)=A^T. Another check is that the rows (or columns) form mutually perpendicular unit vectors. Show the multiplication; simply writing “orthogonal” without verification is insufficient for a proof question.
blocks.subject: Mathematics I

blocks.text: 4. Find eigenvalues of a 2 × 2 matrix.
blocks.subject: Mathematics I

blocks.text: For A=[a b; c d], solve |A-λ I|=0:
blocks.subject: Mathematics I

blocks.text: Expand the determinant to obtain a quadratic equation. Solve it for λ. For each eigenvalue, solve (A-λ I)x=0 to obtain an eigenvector. Verify by substituting into Ax=λ x.
blocks.subject: Mathematics I

blocks.text: 5. Explain the transformation of roots.
blocks.subject: Mathematics I

blocks.text: If α is a root of f(x)=0 and the required new root is α+k, substitute x-k for x in the original polynomial to obtain the equation whose roots are increased by k. To decrease roots by k, substitute x+k. To form an equation with roots multiplied by k, use the corresponding scaling substitution and clear denominators. Always state the transformation and simplify the polynomial carefully.
blocks.subject: Mathematics I

blocks.text: 6. Explain logarithm of a complex number.
blocks.subject: Mathematics I

blocks.text: Let z=x+iy=re^(iθ), where r=√(x^2+y^2) and θ=arg z. Then
blocks.subject: Mathematics I

blocks.text: log z=ln r+i(θ+2nπ), n∈Z.
blocks.subject: Mathematics I

blocks.text: The principal value uses the principal argument. For example, 1+i has modulus √2 and principal argument π/4, so its principal logarithm is (ln 2)/2+iπ/4.
blocks.subject: Mathematics I

blocks.text: PART C – 10-MARK QUESTIONS WITH MODEL ANSWERS
blocks.subject: Mathematics I

blocks.text: 1. Explain Newton's forward and backward interpolation formulas.
blocks.subject: Mathematics I

blocks.text: Interpolation estimates a value between known tabulated values. For equal intervals h, construct a difference table. When x is near the beginning, use Newton's forward formula with u=(x-x_0)/h:
blocks.subject: Mathematics I

blocks.text: When x is near the end, use Newton's backward formula with u=(x-x_n)/h:
blocks.subject: Mathematics I

blocks.text: Procedure: verify equal spacing, prepare the difference table, calculate u, substitute the relevant leading differences, and simplify. Use only as many terms as the data accuracy supports. If intervals are unequal, use Lagrange interpolation.
blocks.subject: Mathematics I

blocks.text: 2. State and apply the Cayley–Hamilton theorem to find an inverse.
blocks.subject: Mathematics I

blocks.text: First form the characteristic equation |A-λ I|=0. Write the resulting polynomial as p(λ)=0. By Cayley–Hamilton, replace λ by A to obtain p(A)=0. If the constant term is non-zero and A is non-singular, rearrange this matrix equation to isolate A inverse. For a 2 × 2 matrix, if A^2-tA+dI=0, then A(A-tI)+dI=0, so A^(-1)=(tI-A)/d. Here t is the trace and d is the determinant. Always verify the result by multiplying A by the proposed inverse.
blocks.subject: Mathematics I

blocks.text: 3. Explain eigenvalues and eigenvectors with the procedure.
blocks.subject: Mathematics I

blocks.text: For a square matrix A, an eigenvalue λ and corresponding non-zero eigenvector X satisfy AX=λ X. Rearranging gives (A-λ I)X=0. A non-trivial solution exists only when |A-λ I|=0, which is the characteristic equation. Solve it for eigenvalues. Substitute each eigenvalue into (A-λ I)X=0 and solve the resulting homogeneous equations for an eigenvector. Eigenvalues describe scaling factors of the matrix transformation along special directions; eigenvectors identify those directions.
blocks.subject: Mathematics I

blocks.text: 4. Explain maxima and minima of a function of two variables.
blocks.subject: Mathematics I

blocks.text: For a differentiable function z=f(x,y), first find stationary points by solving f_x=0 and f_y=0. Then compute A=f_(xx), B=f_(xy) and C=f_(yy) at each stationary point. Let D=AC-B^2. If D>0 and A>0, there is a local minimum; if D>0 and A<0, there is a local maximum; if D<0, the point is a saddle; if D=0, the test is inconclusive. For a constrained extremum with condition g(x,y)=0, use Lagrange multipliers: solve ∇ f=λ∇ g together with the constraint.
blocks.subject: Mathematics I

blocks.text: 5. Explain successive differentiation and Leibnitz theorem.
blocks.subject: Mathematics I

blocks.text: Successive differentiation means differentiating a function repeatedly to obtain second, third and higher derivatives. For products, Leibnitz theorem gives the nth derivative without expanding every term independently:
blocks.subject: Mathematics I

blocks.text: D^n(uv)=uD^nv+n(Du)D^(n-1)v+(n(n-1))/(2!)D^2uD^(n-2)v+…+vD^nu.
blocks.subject: Mathematics I

blocks.text: The general coefficient is binomial: binom nr. In applications, prepare a derivative table for u and v, multiply diagonally with the binomial coefficients, and add the terms.
blocks.subject: Mathematics I

blocks.subject: English I

blocks.text: Textbook: SFEN11 – First Year English
blocks.subject: English I

blocks.text: PYQ series: UEB1A (10 unique papers, 2019–2025)
blocks.subject: English I

blocks.subject: English I

blocks.subject: English I

blocks.text: • Unit III – Poetry: “The Pulley or the Gift of God”; “La Belle Dame Sans Merci”; “The Night of the Scorpion”; “The Death of the Bird”.
blocks.subject: English I

blocks.text: • Unit IV – Short stories: “Mrs. Packletide’s Tiger”; “A Snake in the Grass”; “Three Questions”; “The Gift of the Magi”.
blocks.subject: English I

blocks.text: • Unit V – Grammar and sound: tenses/aspect, primary and modal auxiliaries, negatives, yes/no and wh-questions, tag questions, sentence completion, common errors, synonyms, antonyms, word classes; sounds, stress, strong/weak forms, intonation and voice modulation.
blocks.subject: English I

blocks.text: PART A – 2-MARK GRAMMAR BANK WITH ANSWERS
blocks.subject: English I

blocks.text: 1. Contracted forms
blocks.subject: English I

blocks.text: • You are → you're.
blocks.subject: English I

blocks.text: • Must not → mustn't.
blocks.subject: English I

blocks.text: • I am → I'm.
blocks.subject: English I

blocks.text: • He has → he's (context determines whether it means “he is” or “he has”).
blocks.subject: English I

blocks.text: • I would / I had → I'd (context determines the expansion).
blocks.subject: English I

blocks.text: 2. Introductory “there” and “it”
blocks.subject: English I

blocks.text: • Many lodges are near the station. → There are many lodges near the station.
blocks.subject: English I

blocks.text: • A lot of noise was in the street. → There was a lot of noise in the street.
blocks.subject: English I

blocks.text: • My ambition is to become a pilot. → It is my ambition to become a pilot.
blocks.subject: English I

blocks.text: Use “there” to introduce existence or presence. Use introductory “it” for an impersonal subject or to postpone a clause/infinitive phrase.
blocks.subject: English I

blocks.text: 3. Articles
blocks.subject: English I

blocks.text: • “a” before a consonant sound: a university, a book.
blocks.subject: English I

blocks.text: • “an” before a vowel sound: an honest man, an apple.
blocks.subject: English I

blocks.text: • “the” for a particular or already identified person/thing, unique reference, or a superlative.
blocks.subject: English I

blocks.text: Example: “He gave a one-hundred-rupee note to an honest boy.” (“one” begins with a /w/ sound; “honest” begins with a silent h and a vowel sound.)
blocks.subject: English I

blocks.text: 4. Prepositions
blocks.subject: English I

blocks.text: • married to; explain to someone; write with a pencil; arrive at a place / arrive in a city or country; on a date; in a month or year; between two people; among more than two.
blocks.subject: English I

blocks.text: 5. Negative sentences
blocks.subject: English I

blocks.text: • I practise the violin every morning. → I do not practise the violin every morning.
blocks.subject: English I

blocks.text: • She sang the song. → She did not sing the song. (After did not, use the base form.)
blocks.subject: English I

blocks.text: 6. Yes/no and wh-questions
blocks.subject: English I

blocks.text: • She sang the song very well. → Did she sing the song very well? / How did she sing the song?
blocks.subject: English I

blocks.text: • I am going home now. → Are you going home now? / Where are you going now?
blocks.subject: English I

blocks.text: • He has gone home. → Has he gone home? / Where has he gone?
blocks.subject: English I

blocks.text: 7. Reported speech
blocks.subject: English I

blocks.text: Direct: He said, “I know a better restaurant.”
blocks.subject: English I

blocks.text: Indirect: He said that he knew a better restaurant.
blocks.subject: English I

blocks.text: For a past reporting verb, adjust pronouns and tense where required; change time/place expressions when the context demands it. Questions are reported using “asked” and statement word order, not question word order.
blocks.subject: English I

blocks.text: 8. Synonyms and antonyms
blocks.subject: English I

blocks.text: Synonyms have similar meanings; antonyms have opposite meanings. Examples: valiant – brave; obvious – clear; wet – dry; sharp – blunt; gain – loss. Choose a word that fits the sentence, not merely one with a similar dictionary meaning.
blocks.subject: English I

blocks.text: 9. Adjectival forms
blocks.subject: English I

blocks.text: Examples: silence → silent; laugh → laughable; resist → irresistible; quarrel → quarrelsome; beauty → beautiful. Check spelling changes before adding the suffix.
blocks.subject: English I

blocks.text: 10. Sentence stress and word stress
blocks.subject: English I

blocks.text: In ordinary speech, content words (nouns, main verbs, adjectives and adverbs) usually carry stronger stress than grammatical words (articles, prepositions, auxiliaries) unless the speaker contrasts or emphasizes them. Mark stress clearly; do not confuse word stress with sentence stress.
blocks.subject: English I

blocks.text: 11. Strong and weak forms
blocks.subject: English I

blocks.text: Function words often have a strong form when emphasized or spoken alone and a weak form in connected speech. For example, “can” is usually weak in “I can do it” but strong in “Yes, I CAN.” The exact sound depends on the sentence and accent.
blocks.subject: English I

blocks.text: PART B – 5-MARK LITERATURE ANSWERS
blocks.subject: English I

blocks.text: 1. “Competition Matters” – the importance of a genuine winner.
blocks.subject: English I

blocks.text: Suzanne Sievert questions the practice of declaring every child a winner merely to protect children from disappointment. When judges give the same ribbon to every participant, the excitement and purpose of a contest are weakened. Through her experience with a game that was abandoned after everyone was allowed to win, she explains that competition is linked with motivation. A fair contest teaches children to accept both success and failure. A child who loses can learn from mistakes, practise and try again. The lesson is not that winning is everything; it is that honest competition, sportsmanship and resilience help children develop. The author argues that children should be supported while they learn to handle defeat, rather than being protected from every loss.
blocks.subject: English I

blocks.text: 2. “A Personal Crisis May Change History” – Kalam's message.
blocks.subject: English I

blocks.text: Dr. A.P.J. Abdul Kalam explains that a personal insult or crisis can become a turning point when a person responds with courage and empathy. He recalls how Mahatma Gandhi experienced racial discrimination in South Africa. Instead of returning to India in defeat, Gandhi decided to oppose injustice through non-violent action. Nelson Mandela later continued the struggle against apartheid and endured imprisonment before helping bring political change. The lesson presents adversity as a test of character. A person may surrender to anger or despair, or may transform humiliation into a commitment to justice. Kalam's central message is that courage, perseverance and concern for others can change both individual lives and history.
blocks.subject: English I

blocks.text: 3. “Why Preserve Biodiversity?” – three reasons.
blocks.subject: English I

blocks.text: Prof. D. Balasubramanian gives ethical/aesthetic, utilitarian and ecological reasons for conserving biodiversity. First, living beings have value and beauty; humans have a responsibility to protect other life forms and preserve them for future generations. Second, human beings depend on biodiversity for food, medicine, materials and other useful resources. Many crops and medicines have their origins in wild plants and microorganisms. Third, ecosystems depend on the interaction of many species. When species disappear or habitats are damaged, ecological balance and the services that support human life are threatened. The lesson asks readers to recognise that biodiversity is not merely a collection of attractive animals; it is the foundation of healthy ecosystems and human well-being.
blocks.subject: English I

blocks.text: 4. “My Greatest Olympic Prize” – Jesse Owens and Luz Long.
blocks.subject: English I

blocks.text: Jesse Owens describes how his friendship with the German athlete Luz Long became more valuable than a medal. During the long-jump competition at the Berlin Olympics, Owens was struggling with his attempts. Long, who was his rival and a leading competitor, gave him friendly advice that helped him qualify. Their sportsmanship challenged racial prejudice and demonstrated respect beyond national or political divisions. Long congratulated Owens after his victory, and the two athletes walked together in front of the crowd. Owens says his greatest Olympic prize was not a gold medal but the friendship of Luz Long. The story celebrates fair play, courage and human dignity.
blocks.subject: English I

blocks.text: 5. “If You Are Wrong, Admit It” – Dale Carnegie's advice.
blocks.subject: English I

blocks.text: The lesson explains that defending an obvious mistake creates unnecessary conflict, while admitting it can reduce hostility. A person who accepts responsibility shows honesty and self-respect. Carnegie uses examples to show that people who do not search for excuses can win cooperation and forgiveness. Admission should be clear and sincere; it should not be followed by blame-shifting. The practical lesson is to acknowledge an error promptly, correct it where possible and learn from it. This approach protects relationships and makes problem-solving easier.
blocks.subject: English I

blocks.text: 6. “Monday Morning” – Tom Sawyer's behaviour.
blocks.subject: English I

blocks.text: Mark Twain presents Tom Sawyer as an imaginative and mischievous boy who dislikes going to school. On Monday morning he invents several excuses to remain at home, hoping that a supposed illness will persuade Aunt Polly. He first complains about a toe, then remembers a loose tooth and attempts to make his condition appear serious. His brother Sid and sister Mary react differently, and Aunt Polly tries to discover whether Tom is genuinely ill. The humour arises from Tom's elaborate pretence and the contrast between his clever excuses and the simple truth that he wants to avoid school. The episode shows childhood mischief and the comic gap between a child's imagination and adult experience.
blocks.subject: English I

blocks.text: 7. “The Unexpected” – the value of surprise and observation.
blocks.subject: English I

blocks.text: Robert Lynd uses everyday experiences to show that life is full of unexpected incidents. People often plan their actions and assume that events will follow a predictable path, but ordinary encounters can change the direction of a day. The essay encourages readers to observe carefully and remain open to surprise. Its title is appropriate because the incidents discussed reveal that the unexpected is not always extraordinary; it may arise from common experiences that people overlook. A good answer should refer to the particular examples in the prescribed lesson and explain how they support the author's observation.
blocks.subject: English I

blocks.text: 8. “The Pulley” – the gift of God.
blocks.subject: English I

blocks.text: George Herbert imagines God pouring blessings upon Man: strength, beauty, wisdom, honour and pleasure. God withholds one blessing – rest – so that human beings will not become completely satisfied with worldly gifts. Their weariness and dissatisfaction will turn their thoughts towards God. The pulley is a metaphor for this spiritual movement: the absence of rest draws humanity back to its Creator. The poem suggests that material blessings alone cannot provide complete fulfilment; spiritual connection is essential.
blocks.subject: English I

blocks.text: 9. “The Night of the Scorpion” – the mother's selfless love.
blocks.subject: English I

blocks.text: Nissim Ezekiel describes an Indian village scene after a scorpion stings a mother. The villagers gather, pray, chant and try to explain the suffering through traditional beliefs. The father, who is more rational and experimental, tries different remedies. The mother endures pain for many hours. When the pain finally subsides, she does not complain about her suffering; instead, she is thankful that the scorpion stung her rather than her children. Her final reaction reveals selfless maternal love. The poem also presents the contrast between superstition, community sympathy and rational responses without reducing the village scene to a single judgement.
blocks.subject: English I

blocks.text: 10. “The Death of the Bird” – central idea.
blocks.subject: English I

blocks.text: A.D. Hope presents the death of a bird as a serious event rather than a trivial occurrence. The poem uses the bird's death to reflect on the vulnerability of life and the relationship between individual existence and the natural world. A strong answer should identify the images used in the poem, explain the contrast between life and death, and connect the bird's fate to the poem's wider meditation on mortality. Avoid writing only “the bird died”; explain how the poet makes the event meaningful.
blocks.subject: English I

blocks.text: 11. “Three Questions” – Tolstoy's moral.
blocks.subject: English I

blocks.text: In Leo Tolstoy's story, a king seeks answers to three questions: the right time to begin an action, the most important people to work with, and the most important thing to do. He believes that correct answers will help him govern wisely. Through his meeting with a wounded man and a hermit, he learns that the most important time is the present, the most important person is the one with whom he is engaged at that moment, and the most important action is to do good to that person. The story teaches mindfulness, kindness and responsibility. Its lesson is that moral action cannot be postponed to an imaginary perfect time.
blocks.subject: English I

blocks.text: 12. “A Snake in the Grass” – the search for the snake.
blocks.subject: English I

blocks.text: R.K. Narayan's story presents the anxiety and confusion caused by the report of a snake in a household. The family members react differently, and the search exposes their fears and assumptions. The episode uses humour and suspense to show how a small incident can reveal human behaviour. In an exam answer, describe the search, the reactions of the people involved and the way the story resolves the situation. Support the explanation with the particular details and ending given in the textbook.
blocks.subject: English I

blocks.text: PART C – 10-MARK MODEL ANSWERS / ESSAY PLANS
blocks.subject: English I

blocks.text: 1. “The Night of the Scorpion” as a pen portrait of an Indian village.
blocks.subject: English I

blocks.text: The poem presents a village through the community's response to a mother's suffering. After a scorpion stings her, neighbours come to the house with concern. They gather around her and try to relieve her pain through prayers, chants and traditional explanations. Their actions reveal a collective belief system in which suffering is linked to fate, karma and the movement of the scorpion. The poem does not present the villagers simply as cruel or foolish; they are anxious and wish to help, but their response is shaped by tradition.
blocks.subject: English I

blocks.text: The father offers a contrast. He uses a more practical approach and tries remedies to reduce the poison's effect. His actions show a desire to act through observation and experiment. The mother's children watch the adults and experience the fear of the situation. The household becomes a small picture of the wider village: faith, superstition, scientific thinking, neighbourly concern and family love exist together.
blocks.subject: English I

blocks.text: The poem's most powerful moment comes when the mother, after enduring the pain, says she is thankful that the scorpion stung her rather than her children. This final statement shifts the focus from the village's explanations to the mother's love. Her gratitude is not for the pain itself but for the fact that her children were spared. Through ordinary details, Ezekiel creates a memorable portrait of village life and reveals the strength of maternal affection.
blocks.subject: English I

blocks.text: 2. “La Belle Dame Sans Merci” – critical appreciation.
blocks.subject: English I

blocks.text: John Keats's ballad tells of a knight who has been left pale, weak and alone. A speaker meets him in a desolate landscape and asks why he wanders there. The knight explains that he met a mysterious and beautiful woman, described as a “faery's child”. He was captivated by her beauty and followed her to an enchanted place. She fed him, sang to him and lulled him to sleep. During sleep he dreamed of pale kings, princes and warriors who warned that the beautiful lady had him in her power. When he awoke, he found himself alone on the cold hillside.
blocks.subject: English I

blocks.text: The poem explores enchantment, desire, isolation and the destructive power of an unattainable ideal. The lady is never fully explained; her mystery contributes to the poem's romantic atmosphere. The autumnal landscape – with withered sedge, fading colour and lack of birds – reflects the knight's physical and emotional decline. Keats uses ballad form, repetition, simple dialogue and vivid imagery to create a haunting mood. The ending remains unresolved: the knight is still waiting, and the reader is left to consider whether the lady is supernatural, deceptive or a projection of desire. The title, meaning “the beautiful lady without mercy”, captures the central tension between beauty and suffering.
blocks.subject: English I

blocks.text: 3. “Three Questions” – character and moral analysis.
blocks.subject: English I

blocks.text: The king's search begins with a practical wish to rule effectively. He believes that knowing the right time, the right people and the right action will prevent mistakes. The answers offered by advisers are contradictory, so he visits a hermit who is known for wisdom. The hermit does not give him a lecture; instead, he involves him in work. The king helps the hermit dig, then cares for a wounded man who arrives seeking revenge.
blocks.subject: English I

blocks.text: By helping the wounded man, the king saves his life and prevents further violence. The man becomes grateful and asks forgiveness. The king then understands that moral wisdom is revealed through action rather than abstract discussion. The present moment is the only time over which a person has control; the person currently with us is the person who needs our attention; and doing good is the most important action. The story teaches compassion, presence of mind and forgiveness. Its simple plot carries a universal lesson about ethical responsibility.
blocks.subject: English I

blocks.text: 4. “Mrs. Packletide's Tiger” as social satire.
blocks.subject: English I

blocks.text: Saki satirises social vanity and the desire for public admiration. Mrs. Packletide arranges a tiger hunt not because she needs to protect herself or her community, but because she wishes to outshine Loona Bimberton. The hunt is carefully staged and becomes a social performance. The old tiger, the villagers, the paid arrangement and the unexpected death of the goat expose the artificial nature of the achievement. Mrs. Packletide's supposed courage is not genuine bravery; it is a constructed spectacle intended to produce newspaper attention and social prestige.
blocks.subject: English I

blocks.text: The story's humour depends on irony. A large reward is offered, but the outcome is not the heroic event that the spectators imagine. Miss Mebbin discovers the truth and uses it for personal gain, showing that greed and manipulation operate beneath polite social manners. Mrs. Packletide is eventually forced to pay for silence. The title directs attention to her, but the plot also exposes the society that values publicity more than truth. Saki's light tone makes the criticism sharp: status-seeking can turn even a hunting expedition into a ridiculous performance.
blocks.subject: English I

blocks.text: 5. “The Gift of the Magi” – love and sacrifice.
blocks.subject: English I

blocks.text: O. Henry's story centres on Della and Jim, a young married couple with very little money but deep affection for each other. Della wants to buy Jim a meaningful Christmas gift and sells her beautiful long hair to obtain the money. Jim, unknown to her, sells his treasured watch to buy combs for Della's hair. When they exchange gifts, both discover that the objects they purchased cannot be used immediately: the combs are for hair that has been cut, and the watch chain is for a watch that has been sold.
blocks.subject: English I

blocks.text: The apparent failure of the gifts becomes the story's emotional success. Each spouse has sacrificed something personally valuable to make the other happy. Their gifts are materially useless for the moment, but they reveal generosity, trust and unselfish love. The title refers to the Magi, the wise men who brought gifts to the infant Jesus. The narrator suggests that Della and Jim are wise because they understand the spirit of giving. O. Henry uses situational irony and a surprising ending to show that love is measured not by the price of a gift but by the sacrifice behind it.
blocks.subject: English I
