blocks.text: SEMESTER II
SUBJECT 4 – PROGRAMMING IN C
blocks.subject: Programming in C

blocks.text: Textbook: SUCA104 – Programming in C
blocks.subject: Programming in C

blocks.text: PYQ series: UCC2A (11 unique papers, 2019–2025)
blocks.subject: Programming in C

blocks.text: Syllabus map
blocks.subject: Programming in C

blocks.text: 1. Character set, identifiers, keywords, data types, constants, variables, declarations, expressions and statements.
blocks.subject: Programming in C

blocks.text: 2. Operators and library functions; input/output functions; decision making; while, do-while and for loops; nested control structures; switch, break, continue, goto and comma operator.
blocks.subject: Programming in C

blocks.text: 3. Functions, prototypes, arguments, recursion and storage classes; multiple-file programs.
blocks.subject: Programming in C

blocks.text: 4. Arrays, multidimensional arrays, strings, structures, user-defined types, self-referential structures, unions and bitwise operations.
blocks.subject: Programming in C

blocks.text: 5. Pointers, pointer operations, pointers with arrays/structures/functions and file handling.
blocks.subject: Programming in C

blocks.text: PART A – 2-MARK QUESTIONS WITH MODEL ANSWERS
blocks.subject: Programming in C

blocks.text: 1. What is an identifier?
blocks.subject: Programming in C

blocks.text: An identifier is a user-defined name given to a program element such as a variable, function or array. It may contain letters, digits and underscores, but it must not begin with a digit and must not be a C keyword.
blocks.subject: Programming in C

blocks.text: 2. What is a keyword?
blocks.subject: Programming in C

blocks.text: A keyword is a reserved word with a predefined meaning in C, such as int, if, return, while and struct. A keyword cannot be used as an ordinary identifier.
blocks.subject: Programming in C

blocks.text: 3. What is a token?
blocks.subject: Programming in C

blocks.text: A token is the smallest individual unit recognised by the compiler. C tokens include keywords, identifiers, constants, string literals, operators and punctuators.
blocks.subject: Programming in C

blocks.text: 4. Define data type.
blocks.subject: Programming in C

blocks.text: A data type specifies the kind of value a variable can store, its storage requirements and the operations permitted on it. Examples include char, int, float, double and derived/user-defined types.
blocks.subject: Programming in C

blocks.text: 5. What is a constant?
blocks.subject: Programming in C

blocks.text: A constant is a value that does not change during program execution. Examples include integer constants (25), floating constants (3.14), character constants ('A') and string literals ("BCA").
blocks.subject: Programming in C

blocks.text: 6. What is a variable?
blocks.subject: Programming in C

blocks.text: A variable is a named memory location whose value may change during program execution. It must be declared with a data type before use.
blocks.subject: Programming in C

blocks.text: 7. What is an expression?
blocks.subject: Programming in C

blocks.text: An expression is a combination of operands and operators that is evaluated to produce a value, for example a + b * 2.
blocks.subject: Programming in C

blocks.text: 8. What is a relational operator?
blocks.subject: Programming in C

blocks.text: A relational operator compares two values and produces a true/false result represented as 1 or 0 in C. Examples: <, >, <=, >=, == and !=.
blocks.subject: Programming in C

blocks.text: 9. What is a bitwise operator?
blocks.subject: Programming in C

blocks.text: A bitwise operator acts on individual bits of integer operands. C provides &, |, ^, ~, << and >>.
blocks.subject: Programming in C

blocks.text: 10. What is a jumping statement?
blocks.subject: Programming in C

blocks.text: A jumping statement transfers control from the normal sequential flow. C jumping statements include break, continue, goto and return.
blocks.subject: Programming in C

blocks.text: 11. Write the syntax of a while loop.
blocks.subject: Programming in C

blocks.text: while (condition) { statements; }
blocks.subject: Programming in C

blocks.text: The condition is tested before each iteration; the loop may execute zero times.
blocks.subject: Programming in C

blocks.text: 12. Differentiate while and do-while.
blocks.subject: Programming in C

blocks.text: A while loop tests the condition before the body, so it may execute zero times. A do-while loop tests the condition after the body, so it executes at least once.
blocks.subject: Programming in C

blocks.text: 13. What is a function prototype?
blocks.subject: Programming in C

blocks.text: A function prototype declares a function's name, return type and parameter types before it is called. Example: int add(int, int);.
blocks.subject: Programming in C

blocks.text: 14. What is recursion?
blocks.subject: Programming in C

blocks.text: Recursion is a technique in which a function calls itself to solve a smaller form of the same problem. A correct recursive function must have a base condition to stop further calls.
blocks.subject: Programming in C

blocks.text: 15. What is a library function?
blocks.subject: Programming in C

blocks.text: A library function is a predefined function supplied by the C standard library, such as printf, scanf, sqrt, strlen and strcmp.
blocks.subject: Programming in C

blocks.text: 16. What is a storage class?
blocks.subject: Programming in C

blocks.text: A storage class specifies the scope, lifetime and linkage/storage behaviour of an identifier. The textbook discusses automatic, external, static and register variables.
blocks.subject: Programming in C

blocks.text: 17. What is an array?
blocks.subject: Programming in C

blocks.text: An array is a collection of elements of the same data type stored in consecutive memory locations and accessed using an index. In C, array indexing starts at 0.
blocks.subject: Programming in C

blocks.text: 18. What is a string?
blocks.subject: Programming in C

blocks.text: A C string is an array of characters terminated by the null character \0.
blocks.subject: Programming in C

blocks.text: 19. What is a structure?
blocks.subject: Programming in C

blocks.text: A structure is a user-defined data type that groups related variables, possibly of different data types, under one name.
blocks.subject: Programming in C

blocks.text: 20. What is a union?
blocks.subject: Programming in C

blocks.text: A union is a user-defined data type in which all members share the same memory area. The size is sufficient for its largest member, subject to alignment.
blocks.subject: Programming in C

blocks.text: 21. What is a pointer?
blocks.subject: Programming in C

blocks.text: A pointer is a variable that stores the address of another object. The address-of operator & obtains an address and the dereference operator * accesses the pointed-to object.
blocks.subject: Programming in C

blocks.text: 22. What is EOF?
blocks.subject: Programming in C

blocks.text: EOF is the end-of-file indicator used by C input functions to signal that no more input characters are available from a stream.
blocks.subject: Programming in C

blocks.text: 23. How do you open and close a file?
blocks.subject: Programming in C

blocks.text: Open a file using fopen() and close it using fclose(). Example: FILE *fp = fopen("data.txt", "r"); followed later by fclose(fp);. Always check whether fopen returned NULL.
blocks.subject: Programming in C

blocks.text: 24. What is a preprocessor directive?
blocks.subject: Programming in C

blocks.text: A preprocessor directive begins with # and is processed before compilation. Examples include #include, #define, #if and #ifdef.
blocks.subject: Programming in C

blocks.text: 25. What is an inline function?
blocks.subject: Programming in C

blocks.text: In standard C, inline is a function specifier that suggests inline substitution to the compiler; it does not guarantee that the compiler will replace every call with the function body. The exact support depends on the C standard and compiler.
blocks.subject: Programming in C

blocks.text: PART B – 5-MARK QUESTIONS WITH MODEL ANSWERS
blocks.subject: Programming in C

blocks.text: 1. Explain the basic data types in C.
blocks.subject: Programming in C

blocks.text: The basic C data types include:
blocks.subject: Programming in C

blocks.text: • char: stores a character or small integer value.
blocks.subject: Programming in C

blocks.text: • int: stores integer values.
blocks.subject: Programming in C

blocks.text: • float: stores single-precision floating-point values.
blocks.subject: Programming in C

blocks.text: • double: stores double-precision floating-point values.
blocks.subject: Programming in C

blocks.text: • void: represents no value or an unspecified type in suitable declarations.
blocks.subject: Programming in C

blocks.text: Type modifiers such as signed, unsigned, short and long modify certain integer types. Exact sizes are implementation-dependent, so use sizeof(type) rather than assuming the same size on every platform. A variable declaration specifies the type and name, for example int count;.
blocks.subject: Programming in C

blocks.text: 2. Explain the categories of operators in C with examples.
blocks.subject: Programming in C

blocks.text: Arithmetic: + - * / %; relational: < > <= >= == !=; logical: && || !; assignment: = += -= *=; increment/decrement: ++ --; conditional: ?:; bitwise: & | ^ ~ << >>; and other operators such as sizeof, comma, address-of &, dereference * and member access ./->. Parentheses should be used to make complex expressions clear. Remember that = assigns a value, while == tests equality.
blocks.subject: Programming in C

blocks.text: 3. Explain input and output statements.
blocks.subject: Programming in C

blocks.text: The standard formatted input/output functions are scanf() and printf(), declared in <stdio.h>. Example:
blocks.subject: Programming in C

blocks.text: #include <stdio.h> int main(void) { int age; printf("Enter age: "); if (scanf("%d", &age) != 1) return 1; printf("Age = %d\n", age); return 0; }
blocks.subject: Programming in C

blocks.text: scanf uses the address of a variable for most conversions. Format specifiers must match the argument type. Other character/string functions include getchar, putchar, fgets and puts. Prefer fgets over unsafe unbounded string input.
blocks.subject: Programming in C

blocks.text: 4. Explain decision-making statements.
blocks.subject: Programming in C

blocks.text: The if statement executes a block when a condition is true. if-else selects between two alternatives. Nested if statements test several related conditions. An else-if ladder handles multiple choices. A switch statement selects a matching case based on an integral expression; break prevents unintended fall-through. Use braces to make the block structure clear.
blocks.subject: Programming in C

blocks.text: 5. Explain looping statements.
blocks.subject: Programming in C

blocks.text: C provides while, do-while and for loops. A while loop tests before execution and is useful when the number of iterations is not known. A do-while loop executes the body at least once. A for loop combines initialization, condition and update in one line and is suitable for counter-controlled repetition. break exits the loop; continue skips to the next iteration.
blocks.subject: Programming in C

blocks.text: 6. Explain storage classes.
blocks.subject: Programming in C

blocks.text: • Automatic: ordinary local variables; normally created when the block is entered and destroyed when it is exited.
blocks.subject: Programming in C

blocks.text: • Register: requests that the implementation keep the variable in a fast-access register if possible; the request may be ignored.
blocks.subject: Programming in C

blocks.text: • Static: retains its value for the entire program execution. A local static variable retains its value between function calls; a file-scope static object has internal linkage.
blocks.subject: Programming in C

blocks.text: • External: an object declared with extern refers to a definition with external linkage, potentially located in another source file.
blocks.subject: Programming in C

blocks.text: For a 5-mark answer, compare scope, lifetime and linkage separately; do not say that every extern declaration allocates storage.
blocks.subject: Programming in C

blocks.text: 7. Explain arrays and two-dimensional arrays.
blocks.subject: Programming in C

blocks.text: An array stores same-type elements in consecutive memory locations. Example: int a[5]; declares five integers with valid indexes 0–4. A two-dimensional array is an array of arrays, commonly used for matrices. Example: int m[2][3]; stores two rows and three columns. Access an element using m[i][j]. C stores multidimensional arrays in row-major order. Always ensure that indexes remain within bounds.
blocks.subject: Programming in C

blocks.text: 8. Explain structures and unions.
blocks.subject: Programming in C

blocks.text: A structure stores separate members, each with its own storage. Example: struct Student int roll; char name[30]; float mark; ;. Members are accessed using the dot operator, and a pointer to a structure uses ->. A union stores different members in shared memory, so writing one member may change the interpretation of the others. A structure is suitable for records whose fields must coexist; a union is useful when only one of several representations is needed at a time.
blocks.subject: Programming in C

blocks.text: 9. Explain pointer operations.
blocks.subject: Programming in C

blocks.text: A pointer is declared using *, for example int *p;. The address-of operator assigns an object's address: p=&x;. Dereferencing *p accesses the object. Pointer arithmetic such as p+1 advances by one element of the pointed-to type, not one byte. Pointers can be passed to functions to allow a function to modify caller-owned objects. Only perform arithmetic within an array object (or one past its end); dereferencing invalid pointers causes undefined behaviour.
blocks.subject: Programming in C

blocks.text: 10. Explain file handling in C.
blocks.subject: Programming in C

blocks.text: File handling uses the FILE type and functions from <stdio.h>. Common steps are:
blocks.subject: Programming in C

blocks.text: 1. Declare a file pointer: FILE *fp;.
blocks.subject: Programming in C

blocks.text: 2. Open: fp=fopen("data.txt","w");.
blocks.subject: Programming in C

blocks.text: 3. Check for failure: if(fp==NULL) ... .
blocks.subject: Programming in C

blocks.text: 4. Read or write using functions such as fprintf, fscanf, fputs, fgets, fgetc or fputc.
blocks.subject: Programming in C

blocks.text: 5. Close using fclose(fp);.
blocks.subject: Programming in C

blocks.text: Common modes include r (read), w (create/overwrite for writing), a (append), and corresponding + modes for update. Binary modes use b where required by the implementation. Always close an opened file and handle errors.
blocks.subject: Programming in C

blocks.text: PART C – 10-MARK QUESTIONS WITH MODEL ANSWERS
blocks.subject: Programming in C

blocks.text: 1. Write a C program to find the factorial of a positive integer. Explain it.
blocks.subject: Programming in C

blocks.text: #include <stdio.h> int main(void) { int n, i; unsigned long long fact = 1; printf("Enter a non-negative integer: "); if (scanf("%d", &n) != 1 || n < 0 || n > 20) { printf("Invalid input (enter 0 to 20)\n"); return 1; } for (i = 1; i <= n; ++i) { fact *= (unsigned long long)i; } printf("Factorial = %llu\n", fact); return 0; }
blocks.subject: Programming in C

blocks.text: The program reads n, rejects invalid or negative input, initializes the result to 1 and multiplies it by every integer from 1 to n. The result for 0 is 1 because the loop does not execute. The chosen integer type has a limited range; very large factorials overflow.
blocks.subject: Programming in C

blocks.text: Sample output
blocks.subject: Programming in C

blocks.text: Enter a non-negative integer: 5 Factorial = 120
blocks.subject: Programming in C

blocks.text: 2. Write a C program to generate the Fibonacci series.
blocks.subject: Programming in C

blocks.text: #include <stdio.h> int main(void) { int n, i; unsigned long long a = 0, b = 1, next; printf("Enter number of terms: "); if (scanf("%d", &n) != 1 || n < 0 || n > 93) { printf("Invalid input (enter 0 to 93)\n"); return 1; } for (i = 0; i < n; ++i) { printf("%llu ", a); next = a + b; a = b; b = next; } printf("\n"); return 0; }
blocks.subject: Programming in C

blocks.text: The first two terms are 0 and 1. Every later term is the sum of the previous two. The loop updates the pair after printing the current term. As with factorial, the data type imposes a maximum safe term size.
blocks.subject: Programming in C

blocks.text: 3. Write a C program for matrix multiplication.
blocks.subject: Programming in C
Programming in C

blocks.text: Multiplication is possible only when the number of columns of A equals the number of rows of B. The result has r1 rows and c2 columns. Each output element is the sum of products across a row of A and a column of B.
blocks.subject: Programming in C

blocks.text: 4. Explain recursion with a factorial function.
blocks.subject: Programming in C

blocks.text: #include <stdio.h> unsigned long long factorial(int n) { if (n <= 1) return 1; /* base case */ return (unsigned long long)n * factorial(n - 1); } int main(void) { int n; printf("Enter n (0 to 20): "); if (scanf("%d", &n) != 1 || n < 0 || n > 20) { printf("Enter an integer from 0 to 20.\n"); return 1; } printf("Factorial = %llu\n", factorial(n)); return 0; }
blocks.subject: Programming in C

blocks.text: The base case stops the recursion. For n greater than 1, the function reduces the problem to factorial(n−1). Every call uses stack memory; an absent or incorrect base case can cause unbounded recursion and stack exhaustion.
blocks.subject: Programming in C

blocks.text: 5. Explain local and global variables.
blocks.subject: Programming in C

blocks.text: A local variable is declared inside a function or block and is normally accessible only within that scope. Its ordinary automatic lifetime ends when the block is exited. A global (file-scope) variable is declared outside all functions and can be accessed by functions in that file subject to its linkage and declarations. A local variable can hide a global variable with the same name. Use parameters and return values for clear data flow; avoid unnecessary global state. Static local variables retain their value between calls but remain block-scoped.
blocks.subject: Programming in C

blocks.text: 6. Explain arrays, structures, pointers and files as advanced C features.
blocks.subject: Programming in C

blocks.text: Arrays store collections of same-type values; structures group different fields; pointers store addresses and allow indirect access; files preserve data beyond program execution. These concepts can be combined. An array of structures can represent a group of student records. A pointer can pass a structure to a function efficiently. File functions can store and retrieve those records. A good answer includes a small syntax example for each concept and explains how the concepts work together.
blocks.subject: Programming in C

blocks.text: COMMON C PROGRAMMING EXAM ERRORS
blocks.subject: Programming in C

blocks.text: • Missing & in scanf for ordinary scalar variables.
blocks.subject: Programming in C

blocks.text: • Using = instead of == in a condition.
blocks.subject: Programming in C

blocks.text: • Writing i <= n when an array has only indexes 0 to n−1.
blocks.subject: Programming in C

blocks.text: • Forgetting break in a switch when fall-through is not intended.
blocks.subject: Programming in C

blocks.text: • Forgetting the terminating condition in recursion.
blocks.subject: Programming in C

blocks.text: • Using an uninitialized pointer or dereferencing NULL.
blocks.subject: Programming in C

blocks.text: • Forgetting to check fopen() for NULL.
blocks.subject: Programming in C

blocks.text: • Using void main() in place of the standard int main(void) form.
blocks.subject: Programming in C

blocks.text: SUBJECT 5 – MATHEMATICS II
blocks.subject: Mathematics II

blocks.text: Textbook: SUCA106 – Mathematics II
blocks.subject: Mathematics II

blocks.text: PYQ series: URC2A (11 unique papers, 2019–2025)
blocks.subject: Mathematics II

blocks.text: Syllabus map
blocks.subject: Mathematics II

blocks.text: • Integral calculus: Bernoulli's formula and reduction formulae for powers of sine and cosine; Fourier series and half-range sine/cosine series.
blocks.subject: Mathematics II

blocks.text: • Differential equations: second-order non-homogeneous ordinary differential equations with constant coefficients; formation and solution of partial differential equations; Lagrange's linear equation.
blocks.subject: Mathematics II

blocks.text: • Laplace transforms: standard transforms, properties, inverse transforms and applications to linear differential equations up to second order.
blocks.subject: Mathematics II

blocks.text: • Vector differentiation: scalar/vector point functions, nabla operator, gradient, divergence, curl, solenoidal and irrotational fields, identities.
blocks.subject: Mathematics II

blocks.text: • Vector integration: line, surface and volume integrals; Gauss, Stokes and Green's theorems (statements and simple applications; proofs are not required in the course outline).
blocks.subject: Mathematics II

blocks.text: PART A – 2-MARK FORMULAS AND DEFINITIONS
blocks.subject: Mathematics II

blocks.text: 1. Define Laplace transform.
blocks.subject: Mathematics II

blocks.text: F(s) = ∫₀^∞ e^(−st) f(t) dt
blocks.subject: Mathematics II

blocks.text: 2. Write the transform of 1 and t.
blocks.subject: Mathematics II

blocks.text: L[1] = 1/s and L[t] = 1/s², for suitable real part of s.
blocks.subject: Mathematics II

blocks.text: 3. Write the transform of e^(at).
blocks.subject: Mathematics II

blocks.text: L[e^(at)] = 1/(s − a), for Re(s) > a.
blocks.subject: Mathematics II

blocks.text: 4. State the first shifting property.
blocks.subject: Mathematics II

blocks.text: If L[f(t)] = F(s), then L[e^(at) f(t)] = F(s − a).
blocks.subject: Mathematics II

blocks.text: 5. State the transform of a derivative.
blocks.subject: Mathematics II

blocks.text: L[f′(t)] = sF(s) − f(0). Also L[f″(t)] = s²F(s) − s f(0) − f′(0).
blocks.subject: Mathematics II

blocks.text: 6. Define gradient.
blocks.subject: Mathematics II

blocks.text: For scalar field φ, ∇φ = i(∂φ/∂x) + j(∂φ/∂y) + k(∂φ/∂z). It points in the direction of greatest increase of the scalar field.
blocks.subject: Mathematics II

blocks.text: 7. Define divergence.
blocks.subject: Mathematics II

blocks.text: For vector field F = Pi + Qj + Rk, ∇·F = ∂P/∂x + ∂Q/∂y + ∂R/∂z.
blocks.subject: Mathematics II

blocks.text: 8. Define curl.
blocks.subject: Mathematics II

blocks.text: ∇×F is the curl of a vector field and measures its local rotational tendency.
blocks.subject: Mathematics II

blocks.text: 9. Define solenoidal field.
blocks.subject: Mathematics II

blocks.text: A vector field is solenoidal if its divergence is zero: ∇·F = 0.
blocks.subject: Mathematics II

blocks.text: 10. Define irrotational field.
blocks.subject: Mathematics II

blocks.text: A vector field is irrotational if its curl is zero: ∇×F = 0.
blocks.subject: Mathematics II

blocks.text: 11. What is a Fourier series?
blocks.subject: Mathematics II

blocks.text: A Fourier series represents a suitable periodic function as a sum of sine and cosine terms.
blocks.subject: Mathematics II

blocks.text: 12. What is a partial differential equation (PDE)?
blocks.subject: Mathematics II

blocks.text: A PDE is an equation involving an unknown function of two or more independent variables and its partial derivatives.
blocks.subject: Mathematics II

blocks.text: 13. State the standard second-order linear ODE form.
blocks.subject: Mathematics II

blocks.text: ay''+by'+cy=X, where a, b and c are constants and X is a specified function of the independent variable.
blocks.subject: Mathematics II

blocks.text: 14. State Bernoulli's formula for integration by parts (repeated form).
blocks.subject: Mathematics II

blocks.text: For repeated integration by parts, the successive derivatives of one function are paired with successive integrals of the other with alternating signs. Write the actual derivative/integral sequence for the specific question; do not substitute a memorised unrelated reduction formula.
blocks.subject: Mathematics II

blocks.text: 15. State Green's theorem.
blocks.subject: Mathematics II

blocks.text: For a suitably smooth positively oriented simple closed curve C bounding region R in the plane, ∮C (P dx + Q dy) = ∬R (∂Q/∂x − ∂P/∂y) dA.
blocks.subject: Mathematics II

blocks.text: 16. State Gauss divergence theorem.
blocks.subject: Mathematics II

blocks.text: The outward flux through a closed surface equals the volume integral of the divergence over the enclosed volume: ∬S F·n dS = ∭V (∇·F) dV.
blocks.subject: Mathematics II

blocks.text: 17. State Stokes' theorem.
blocks.subject: Mathematics II

blocks.text: The circulation around a positively oriented boundary curve equals the surface integral of the curl: ∮C F·dr = ∬S (∇×F)·n dS.
blocks.subject: Mathematics II

blocks.text: PART B – 5-MARK QUESTIONS WITH MODEL ANSWERS
blocks.subject: Mathematics II

blocks.text: 1. Explain the reduction formula for powers of sine.
blocks.subject: Mathematics II

blocks.text: A reduction formula expresses an integral involving sin^n x in terms of a similar integral with a lower power. A standard form is:
blocks.subject: Mathematics II

blocks.text: Iₙ = ∫₀^(π/2) sinⁿ(x) dx = ((n − 1)/n) Iₙ₋₂, for n ≥ 2.
blocks.subject: Mathematics II

blocks.text: The initial values are I_0=π/2 and I_1=1. Repeated application reduces the exponent by two until an initial value is reached. For even n, the result is a product of even/odd factors multiplied by π/2; for odd n, it is a product of odd/even factors. Show the reduction step and the base case in a full solution.
blocks.subject: Mathematics II

blocks.text: 2. Explain Fourier series expansion.
blocks.subject: Mathematics II

blocks.text: For a periodic function of period 2π satisfying the required piecewise smoothness conditions, the Fourier series is:
blocks.subject: Mathematics II

blocks.text: f(x) ~ a₀/2 + Σ[n = 1 to ∞] (aₙ cos(nx) + bₙ sin(nx)).
blocks.subject: Mathematics II

blocks.text: where
blocks.subject: Mathematics II

blocks.text: a₀ = (1/π) ∫₋π^π f(x) dx; aₙ = (1/π) ∫₋π^π f(x) cos(nx) dx; bₙ = (1/π) ∫₋π^π f(x) sin(nx) dx.
blocks.subject: Mathematics II

blocks.text: Use symmetry to simplify: an even function has only cosine terms; an odd function has only sine terms. In half-range expansions on 0 to L, extend the function as even for a cosine series or odd for a sine series.
blocks.subject: Mathematics II

blocks.text: 3. Explain the method for solving a second-order linear ODE with constant coefficients.
blocks.subject: Mathematics II

blocks.text: Write the equation as ay''+by'+cy=X. First solve the complementary function by forming the auxiliary equation am^2+bm+c=0. Depending on the roots, write the complementary function: distinct real roots give C_1e^(m_1x)+C_2e^(m_2x); repeated roots give (C_1+C_2x)e^(mx); complex roots α±iβ give e^(α x)(C_1cosβ x+C_2sinβ x). Then find a particular integral for X using the applicable method. The complete solution is CF + PI. Finally apply given initial/boundary conditions to find constants.
blocks.subject: Mathematics II

blocks.text: 4. Explain Laplace transform solution of a differential equation.
blocks.subject: Mathematics II

blocks.text: Take the Laplace transform of every term. Use derivative formulas to include initial values. The resulting equation is algebraic in F(s). Solve for F(s), decompose into standard forms or partial fractions, and take the inverse Laplace transform. Verify that the resulting function satisfies the differential equation and initial conditions. For exam answers, show the initial-value substitutions explicitly.
blocks.subject: Mathematics II

blocks.text: 5. Explain gradient, divergence and curl.
blocks.subject: Mathematics II

blocks.text: The nabla operator is ∇ = i(∂/∂x) + j(∂/∂y) + k(∂/∂z). For a scalar field φ, the gradient ∇φ is a vector. For a vector field F, divergence ∇·F is a scalar and curl ∇×F is a vector. A field with zero divergence is solenoidal; one with zero curl is irrotational. These operators are used to describe spatial rates of change, sources/sinks and rotation.
blocks.subject: Mathematics II

blocks.text: PART C – 10-MARK QUESTIONS WITH MODEL ANSWERS
blocks.subject: Mathematics II

blocks.text: 1. Solve a linear differential equation using Laplace transforms – standard procedure.
blocks.subject: Mathematics II

blocks.text: Given a second-order equation such as y″ + ay′ + by = g(t), with initial values y(0) and y′(0), take the transform of both sides:
blocks.subject: Mathematics II

blocks.text: Collect Y(s):
blocks.subject: Mathematics II

blocks.text: Factor the denominator when possible and use partial fractions. Apply inverse transforms to obtain y(t). In a specific exam problem, substitute the supplied coefficients, forcing function and initial values before partial fraction decomposition. A complete answer must show the transformed equation, Y(s), partial fractions and inverse transform.
blocks.subject: Mathematics II

blocks.text: 2. Explain vector differentiation with examples.
blocks.subject: Mathematics II

blocks.text: For a scalar field φ(x,y,z), its gradient gives the direction and rate of maximum increase. For vector field F = Pi + Qj + Rk, divergence is ∂P/∂x + ∂Q/∂y + ∂R/∂z, and curl is:
blocks.subject: Mathematics II

blocks.text: A vector field is solenoidal when divergence is zero and irrotational when curl is zero. For an exam question, calculate the partial derivatives separately, substitute them into the operator and simplify each component. If asked to verify an identity, show the components on both sides rather than asserting the result.
blocks.subject: Mathematics II

blocks.text: 3. Explain Fourier series and half-range expansions.
blocks.subject: Mathematics II

blocks.text: Fourier series represent periodic functions using sine and cosine components. For a function defined on (−L,L), the full series is:
blocks.subject: Mathematics II

blocks.text: f(x) ~ a₀/2 + Σ[n = 1 to ∞] [aₙ cos(nπx/L) + bₙ sin(nπx/L)].
blocks.subject: Mathematics II

blocks.text: with coefficients calculated over (−L,L). If the function is even, all sine coefficients vanish; if odd, all cosine coefficients including the constant term vanish. For a function defined only on (0,L), an even extension gives the half-range cosine series and an odd extension gives the half-range sine series. In the solution, write the required coefficient formulas, use symmetry, evaluate the integrals and present the resulting series.
blocks.subject: Mathematics II

blocks.text: 4. Explain Gauss, Stokes and Green's integral theorems.
blocks.subject: Mathematics II

blocks.text: Green's theorem converts a line integral around a plane curve to a double integral over its enclosed region. Gauss's theorem converts outward flux through a closed surface into a volume integral of divergence. Stokes' theorem converts circulation around a boundary curve into a surface integral of curl. All three theorems relate an integral over a boundary to an integral over the region/surface/volume it bounds. Before applying a theorem, identify the domain, orientation, normal direction and smoothness conditions. Choose the theorem that changes the given integral into the simpler form.
blocks.subject: Mathematics II

blocks.text: • Unit V – Communicative grammar: framing questions, common errors, word building, prefixes and suffixes.
blocks.subject: English II

blocks.text: PART A – 2-MARK GRAMMAR BANK WITH ANSWERS
blocks.subject: English II

blocks.text: 1. What are synonyms and antonyms?
blocks.subject: English II

blocks.text: Synonyms are words with similar meanings; antonyms are words with opposite meanings. Example: “rapid” is a synonym of “quick”; “ancient” is an antonym of “modern”.
blocks.subject: English II

blocks.text: 2. What are homophones?
blocks.subject: English II

blocks.text: Homophones are words that sound alike but have different meanings and often different spellings, such as “right” and “write”.
blocks.subject: English II

blocks.text: 3. What are prefixes and suffixes?
blocks.subject: English II

blocks.text: A prefix is added at the beginning of a word (kind → unkind). A suffix is added at the end (teach → teacher; happy → happiness).
blocks.subject: English II

blocks.text: 4. Form two words with the prefix “mis-”.
blocks.subject: English II

blocks.text: Misunderstand, misbehave. The prefix often conveys a wrong or incorrect action.
blocks.subject: English II

blocks.text: 5. Form two words with the suffix “-ship”.
blocks.subject: English II

blocks.text: Friendship, leadership. The suffix can form nouns describing a state, condition or relationship.
blocks.subject: English II

blocks.text: 6. Choose the correct preposition.
blocks.subject: English II

blocks.text: • Columbus crossed the Atlantic Ocean in 1492.
blocks.subject: English II

blocks.text: • His birthday is on 10 February.
blocks.subject: English II

blocks.text: • The postmaster was a young man from Calcutta.
blocks.subject: English II

blocks.text: 7. Correct the error: “I did not went there.”
blocks.subject: English II

blocks.text: “I did not go there.” After auxiliary “did”, use the base form of the main verb.
blocks.subject: English II

blocks.text: 8. Correct the error: “The cat was sitting besides the stove.”
blocks.subject: English II

blocks.text: “The cat was sitting beside the stove.” “Beside” means next to. “Besides” usually means in addition to.
blocks.subject: English II

blocks.text: 9. Choose the correct connective.
blocks.subject: English II

blocks.text: Use a connector according to the logical relation: “although” for contrast; “because” for reason; “therefore” for result; “nevertheless” for contrast despite a previous statement.
blocks.subject: English II

blocks.text: 10. Use “either” correctly.
blocks.subject: English II

blocks.text: “He doesn't like coffee or tea. He doesn't like milk either.” Use “either” in a negative addition; “too” is normally used in affirmative additions.
blocks.subject: English II

blocks.text: 11. Change a sentence into passive voice.
blocks.subject: English II

blocks.text: Active: The rain forced us to remain indoors.
blocks.subject: English II

blocks.text: Passive: We were forced to remain indoors by the rain.
blocks.subject: English II

blocks.text: 12. Frame a yes/no question.
blocks.subject: English II

blocks.text: Statement: The postmaster has left.
blocks.subject: English II

blocks.text: Question: Has the postmaster left?
blocks.subject: English II

blocks.text: 13. Frame a wh-question.
blocks.subject: English II

blocks.text: Statement: The postmaster came from Calcutta.
blocks.subject: English II

blocks.text: Question: Where did the postmaster come from?
blocks.subject: English II

blocks.text: 14. Identify a sentence pattern.
blocks.subject: English II

blocks.text: “My daughter eats an apple every day” follows Subject–Verb–Object–Adverbial (SVOA) in a common school-level analysis. “We buy flowers from the florist” also has Subject–Verb–Object followed by a prepositional phrase. Identify the object and any complement/adverbial requested by the question.
blocks.subject: English II

blocks.text: 15. What is a phrasal verb?
blocks.subject: English II

blocks.text: A phrasal verb is a verb combined with an adverb or preposition to form a meaning that may differ from the verb alone. Examples: “blow out” candles; “break in” to enter by force; “turn down” an offer; “throw away” something unwanted.
blocks.subject: English II

blocks.text: PART B – 5-MARK LITERATURE ANSWERS
blocks.subject: English II

blocks.text: 1. “The Refugee” – central theme.
blocks.subject: English II

blocks.text: K.A. Abbas's story presents the human consequences of displacement and communal conflict. The refugee is not merely a person who has crossed a geographical boundary; he or she has lost a home, security, familiar relationships and a sense of belonging. The story encourages readers to look beyond labels and recognise the suffering of ordinary people caught in political and social violence. A strong answer should explain the situation of the central character, the treatment received, and how the story presents compassion and human dignity.
blocks.subject: English II

blocks.text: 2. “The Lion and the Lamb” – the contrast in the story.
blocks.subject: English II

blocks.text: Leonard Clark's story places apparently opposite qualities beside each other. The title suggests a contrast between strength and gentleness. The circumstances involving the lion and the people around it reveal how fear, courage and compassion influence human response. In an exam answer, explain the incident that brings the lion into the story, how the people react, and what the title suggests. Use the episode and conclusion given in the prescribed text rather than adding events not found there.
blocks.subject: English II

blocks.text: 3. “The Lady or the Tiger?” – the dilemma.
blocks.subject: English II

blocks.text: Frank R. Stockton's story describes a semi-barbaric king who uses a public arena to decide the fate of an accused person. The accused must choose between two doors: one conceals a tiger and the other a woman whom he must marry. The king's daughter loves the young man and discovers which door hides the lady. She must decide whether to direct him towards life with another woman or towards death by the tiger. The ending leaves the choice unresolved, forcing readers to consider jealousy, love and human nature. The ambiguity is the central strength of the story.
blocks.subject: English II

blocks.text: 4. “The Sky is the Limit” – Kalpana Chawla's message.
blocks.subject: English II

blocks.text: Kalpana Chawla's account presents determination, curiosity and hard work as the foundations of achievement. Her journey from an interest in flying to a career in aerospace and space exploration demonstrates that ambitious goals can be pursued through education and perseverance. The phrase “the sky is the limit” expresses the belief that people should not restrict their dreams because of their background or present circumstances. A good answer should discuss the stages of her journey described in the lesson and connect them to the message of self-confidence and disciplined effort.
blocks.subject: English II

blocks.text: 5. “The Solitary Reaper” – beauty of the countryside.
blocks.subject: English II

blocks.text: William Wordsworth describes a young woman working alone in a field and singing as she reaps grain. Her voice fills the valley and affects the traveller who hears it. The poet compares the song to the calls of birds in distant landscapes, suggesting that its beauty is beyond ordinary description. He cannot understand every word, but the melody remains with him after he leaves. The poem celebrates rural life, the power of music and the emotional force of nature. The reaper's song becomes a memory that the poet carries in his heart.
blocks.subject: English II

blocks.text: 6. “Gift” – Alice Walker's poem.
blocks.subject: English II

blocks.text: Alice Walker's poem reflects on identity, history and the meaning of a gift. The speaker rejects a sentimental or self-congratulatory gesture that ignores the history of racial injustice. The poem challenges the idea that a gift can erase wrongdoing or substitute for genuine understanding. A good answer should explain the speaker's response to the proposed gift and show how the poem questions power, memory and moral responsibility.
blocks.subject: English II

blocks.text: 7. “O What is that Sound” – the movement of soldiers.
blocks.subject: English II

blocks.text: W.H. Auden structures the poem as a dialogue in which one speaker hears a sound and asks about it, while the other tries to explain the approach of soldiers. The repeated questions build suspense and fear. The soldiers' movement gradually becomes more threatening as they come closer. The poem moves from uncertainty to recognition of danger and betrayal. The sound represents the arrival of violence and the collapse of security. Discuss how repetition and dialogue create the atmosphere.
blocks.subject: English II

blocks.text: 8. “Ode to the West Wind” – destroyer and preserver.
blocks.subject: English II

blocks.text: P.B. Shelley addresses the West Wind as a powerful force of nature. It destroys dead leaves and carries seeds to the earth, where they remain until spring. It is therefore both destroyer and preserver: it removes the old but protects the possibility of new life. The wind also becomes a symbol of poetic and political change. Shelley asks the wind to spread his thoughts and help bring renewal. The poem moves from natural imagery to the poet's personal hopes for transformation.
blocks.subject: English II

blocks.text: 9. “The Fortune-Teller” – irony.
blocks.subject: English II

blocks.text: Karel Čapek's story explores the gap between what people believe and what actually happens. The fortune-teller's prediction influences the actions and expectations of the characters, but the final outcome exposes the irony of attempting to control life through prediction. The story uses coincidence, misunderstanding and reversal to make readers question certainty. A good answer should connect the exact prediction and ending in the prescribed text to the theme of irony.
blocks.subject: English II

blocks.text: 10. “The Postmaster” – friendship and separation.
blocks.subject: English II

blocks.text: Rabindranath Tagore's story centres on the relationship between a young postmaster and Ratan, an orphaned village girl who works in his household. The postmaster teaches her to read and shares memories of his family. Ratan begins to imagine that she belongs to his family, while he gradually becomes attached to her presence. When he falls ill, Ratan nurses him. Later, he decides to leave the village. Ratan hopes that he will take her with him, but he does not. Their unequal expectations reveal how affection can be deep for one person and temporary for another. The story ends in separation and quiet sadness.
blocks.subject: English II

blocks.text: 11. “The Model Millionaire” – Alan Trevor.
blocks.subject: English II

blocks.text: Alan Trevor is an artist who uses a beggar as a model for a painting. Hughie Erskine, a kind but financially unsuccessful young man, visits Trevor's studio and gives the supposed beggar money. Trevor later reveals that the model is actually Baron Hausberg, a wealthy man. Alan is practical, observant and amused by Hughie's generosity. His role exposes the difference between outward appearance and actual status. The story uses the painter's knowledge to create irony and bring about the happy ending.
blocks.subject: English II

blocks.text: 12. “The Dying Detective” – Holmes's plan.
blocks.subject: English II

blocks.text: In Arthur Conan Doyle's story, Sherlock Holmes appears dangerously ill, causing Dr. Watson to fear for his life. Holmes's strange behaviour is part of a plan to expose Culverton Smith, a suspected criminal. Watson is drawn into the deception without knowing the full truth. When Smith arrives, Holmes reveals that the illness was staged to make the suspect confess or reveal himself. The story shows Holmes's intelligence, self-control and ability to use psychological pressure as part of an investigation.
blocks.subject: English II

blocks.text: 13. “The Death Trap” – Prince Dimitri's strategy.
blocks.subject: English II

blocks.text: Saki's one-act play presents Prince Dimitri as a man who recognises that conspirators are preparing to kill him. Although he is trapped by political circumstances, he uses intelligence and careful planning to turn their plot against them. The prince's actions demonstrate that helplessness can be challenged through wit. The title is appropriate because the trap intended for the prince also becomes a trap for the disloyal conspirators. The play combines suspense, political intrigue and irony.
blocks.subject: English II

blocks.text: 14. “The Dear Departed” – satire on greed.
blocks.subject: English II

blocks.text: Stanley Houghton's play exposes the selfishness of family members who appear concerned about an elderly relative but are actually interested in his possessions. The daughters argue over household property and make arrangements as though their father has died. When Abel Merryweather reveals that he is alive and intends to change his will, their hypocrisy becomes clear. His decision to marry Mrs. Shorrocks and leave the house exposes the greed and lack of affection shown by his daughters. The play uses humour to criticise materialism and false family loyalty.
blocks.subject: English II

blocks.text: 15. “The Sheriff's Kitchen” – Robin Hood and his companions.
blocks.subject: English II

blocks.text: Ronald Gow's play draws on the Robin Hood tradition. Robin Hood's companions use disguise, courage and teamwork to overcome the Sheriff's authority and rescue their leader. Little John plays an important role in the rescue by using the opportunity created by the Sheriff's arrangements. The play celebrates loyalty, resourcefulness and resistance to unjust power. In an answer, describe the steps of the rescue and explain the contribution of the characters as shown in the textbook.
blocks.subject: English II

blocks.text: 16. “The Anniversary” – comic situations.
blocks.subject: English II

blocks.text: Anton Chekhov's play presents the disorder that arises during a bank anniversary celebration. The manager is preoccupied with the event and the people around him, while interruptions and misunderstandings prevent the proceedings from running smoothly. The humour comes from the contrast between the formal importance of the occasion and the ridiculous behaviour of the characters. The play satirises bureaucracy, self-importance and the gap between public praise and actual competence.
blocks.subject: English II

blocks.text: PART C – 10-MARK MODEL ANSWERS / ESSAY PLANS
blocks.subject: English II

blocks.text: 1. “The Postmaster” – friendship and separation.
blocks.subject: English II

blocks.text: Tagore's “The Postmaster” presents a relationship between two people whose needs and expectations are not equal. The postmaster is transferred to a remote village and feels lonely because he has no companions there. Ratan, an orphaned village girl, works for him and gradually becomes his close companion. In the evenings, he asks about her family and shares memories of his own home. He also teaches her to read. These ordinary conversations create a bond that Ratan begins to understand as a family relationship.
blocks.subject: English II

blocks.text: When the postmaster becomes ill, Ratan cares for him with devotion. Her affection becomes stronger because she sees him as someone who has given her attention and education. However, the postmaster's attachment is limited by his homesickness and his desire to return to the city. When he resigns and prepares to leave, Ratan hopes that he will take her with him. He does not. He offers money, but money cannot replace the relationship she hoped to preserve.
blocks.subject: English II

blocks.text: The story is moving because it shows how affection can be experienced differently by two people. For the postmaster, the village relationship is a temporary comfort; for Ratan, it has become a source of belonging. The departure therefore creates emotional separation. Tagore does not make the story sentimental through dramatic events; he uses quiet conversation and everyday kindness to reveal loneliness, attachment and the pain of unfulfilled expectations.
blocks.subject: English II

blocks.text: 2. “The Dear Departed” as a comedy with a social message.
blocks.subject: English II

blocks.text: Stanley Houghton's “The Dear Departed” uses comic misunderstanding to expose the greed of two daughters. Mrs. Slater and Mrs. Jordan believe that their father, Abel Merryweather, has died. Instead of expressing genuine grief, they immediately discuss his possessions and argue over who should have particular pieces of furniture. Their behaviour reveals that their concern is financial rather than emotional.
blocks.subject: English II

blocks.text: The situation becomes more comic when Abel appears alive. He discovers that his daughters have already begun dividing his belongings and making arrangements without confirming his death. He recognises their hypocrisy and decides to take control of his own future. He announces his intention to marry Mrs. Shorrocks and make arrangements for his will. His decision shocks the daughters because they realise that they may lose the inheritance they expected.
blocks.subject: English II

blocks.text: The humour arises from dramatic irony, selfish dialogue and the sudden reversal of power. Abel is not a helpless old man; he can make decisions for himself. The play criticises materialism, false affection and the neglect of elderly parents. Its message is that family relationships should be based on care and respect, not on the expectation of property or money.
blocks.subject: English II

blocks.text: 3. “Ode to the West Wind” – the wind as a symbol of renewal.
blocks.subject: English II

blocks.text: Shelley addresses the West Wind as a powerful force that moves through the natural world. In autumn, it drives dead leaves away like ghosts and carries seeds to the earth. These seeds lie dormant through winter but later grow into new life. The wind destroys what is dead and preserves what may become new. This dual role explains the phrase “destroyer and preserver”.
blocks.subject: English II

blocks.text: The poet then turns from the external world to his own condition. He wishes he could move with the freedom and force of the wind. He feels burdened by personal suffering and asks the wind to lift him. In the final section, he asks the West Wind to scatter his words across the world so that his thoughts may inspire change. Nature becomes a symbol for political and spiritual renewal.
blocks.subject: English II

blocks.text: The poem uses apostrophe, personification, natural imagery and repeated invocations. The wind is not only a weather force; it represents revolutionary energy, poetic inspiration and the hope that a period of difficulty may be followed by renewal. The closing question about spring suggests optimism after hardship.
blocks.subject: English II

blocks.text: 4. “The Refugee” – prepare a full answer from the prescribed narrative.
blocks.subject: English II

blocks.text: For a 10-mark response, begin with the refugee's displacement and loss of home. Explain the social or political circumstances that force the person to leave, the treatment encountered in the new place, and the emotional effects of separation. Then discuss the human response shown in the story: fear, dignity, compassion, prejudice or solidarity, depending on the specific episode in the textbook. Conclude with the lesson's central concern for humanity and the suffering of ordinary people caught in conflict. Use the names and incidents exactly as they appear in the supplied lesson; do not invent details.
blocks.subject: English II

blocks.text: 5. “The Lady or the Tiger?” – explain the unresolved ending.
blocks.subject: English II

blocks.text: The story places the princess in a painful moral conflict. The young man she loves must choose one of two doors. One door will release a tiger and kill him; the other will lead him to a woman and a forced marriage. The princess has secretly discovered which door contains which fate. Her decision is complicated by love and jealousy. If she directs him to the lady, he lives but marries another woman. If she sends him to the tiger, he dies but cannot belong to anyone else. The story ends without revealing which door she indicates. This uncertainty is deliberate: it forces the reader to consider whether love is generous or possessive and whether jealousy can overcome affection. The open ending is the story's central literary device.
blocks.subject: English II

blocks.text: LEGACY-PAPER CAUTION – “ARMS AND THE MAN”
blocks.subject: English II

blocks.text: Some older UEB2A papers in the uploaded archive ask questions about “Arms and the Man”, Bluntschli and Sergius. These items are not listed in the supplied SFEN12 syllabus.
