blocks.text: SUBJECT 7 – COMMUNICATIVE ENGLISH I: SPEAKING SKILLS
blocks.subject: Communicative English I: Speaking Skills

blocks.text: Textbook: SFCE11 – Communicative English, Semester I, Paper I
blocks.subject: Communicative English I: Speaking Skills

blocks.text: Evidence status: Textbook-based model questions. No matching Communicative English I PYQ paper was present in the uploaded PYQ archive.
blocks.subject: Communicative English I: Speaking Skills

blocks.text: Syllabus map
blocks.subject: Communicative English I: Speaking Skills

blocks.text: The course book identifies six units: (1) introduction to phonetics, pronunciation and neutral-accent training; (2) practising conversations and effective business conversations; (3) speaking in interviews; (4) team communication, group discussions and giving instructions; (5) presentations, lectures, speeches, business presentations, extempore/JAM speaking and hosting events; and (6) speaking skills and non-verbal communication. Its scheme of lessons includes Speaking Skills, Non-Verbal Communication, Introduction to Phonetics, Business Conversations, Speaking in Interviews, Group Discussion and Panel Discussion, Giving Instructions, Making Presentation, Hosting Events and Business Presentations.
blocks.subject: Communicative English I: Speaking Skills

blocks.text: PART A – 2-MARK QUESTIONS WITH MODEL ANSWERS
blocks.subject: Communicative English I: Speaking Skills

blocks.text: 1. What are the four basic language skills?
blocks.subject: Communicative English I: Speaking Skills

blocks.text: The four basic language skills are listening, speaking, reading and writing. Listening and reading are generally receptive skills; speaking and writing are productive skills.
blocks.subject: Communicative English I: Speaking Skills

blocks.text: 2. Define speaking skill.
blocks.subject: Communicative English I: Speaking Skills

blocks.text: Speaking is the ability to express ideas, information, feelings and opinions orally in a clear and meaningful way. Effective speaking requires suitable vocabulary, pronunciation, fluency and awareness of the listener.
blocks.subject: Communicative English I: Speaking Skills

blocks.text: 3. What is phonetics?
blocks.subject: Communicative English I: Speaking Skills

blocks.text: Phonetics is the study of speech sounds: how they are produced by the speech organs, how they travel as sound waves and how they are heard. In this course it supports pronunciation and intelligibility.
blocks.subject: Communicative English I: Speaking Skills

blocks.text: 4. What is a neutral accent?
blocks.subject: Communicative English I: Speaking Skills

blocks.text: A neutral accent is a clear and easily understood way of pronouncing words that avoids unnecessarily strong regional features. The aim is intelligibility, not imitation of a particular nationality.
blocks.subject: Communicative English I: Speaking Skills

blocks.text: 5. What is non-verbal communication?
blocks.subject: Communicative English I: Speaking Skills

blocks.text: Non-verbal communication is the exchange of meaning without relying only on spoken or written words. It includes facial expressions, gestures, posture, eye contact, physical distance and voice qualities.
blocks.subject: Communicative English I: Speaking Skills

blocks.text: 6. What is a business conversation?
blocks.subject: Communicative English I: Speaking Skills

blocks.text: A business conversation is a purposeful exchange of information in a professional context, such as discussing a service, arranging a meeting, negotiating a point or responding to a customer. It should be polite, focused and clear.
blocks.subject: Communicative English I: Speaking Skills

blocks.text: 7. What is a group discussion?
blocks.subject: Communicative English I: Speaking Skills

blocks.text: A group discussion is a structured exchange of views among several participants on a given topic. Participants are expected to contribute relevant ideas, listen to others, support points and maintain respectful turn-taking.
blocks.subject: Communicative English I: Speaking Skills

blocks.text: 8. What is a panel discussion?
blocks.subject: Communicative English I: Speaking Skills

blocks.text: A panel discussion is a discussion in which a small group of speakers share different views on a subject before an audience, usually under the guidance of a moderator.
blocks.subject: Communicative English I: Speaking Skills

blocks.text: 9. What is extempore speaking?
blocks.subject: Communicative English I: Speaking Skills

blocks.text: Extempore speaking is speaking on a topic with little or no preparation time. The speaker must organise ideas quickly and present them in a logical sequence.
blocks.subject: Communicative English I: Speaking Skills

blocks.text: 10. What is a Just-a-Minute (JAM) speech?
blocks.subject: Communicative English I: Speaking Skills

blocks.text: A JAM speech is a short, usually one-minute talk on a given topic. It tests clarity, fluency, relevance and the ability to organise thoughts within a strict time limit.
blocks.subject: Communicative English I: Speaking Skills

blocks.text: PART B – 5-MARK MODEL ANSWERS
blocks.subject: Communicative English I: Speaking Skills

blocks.text: 1. Explain the importance of speaking skills.
blocks.subject: Communicative English I: Speaking Skills

blocks.text: Speaking allows people to exchange information, build relationships, ask questions and express opinions. In education it helps students participate in discussions and presentations. In employment it supports interviews, teamwork, customer service and professional meetings. Good speaking is not merely speaking loudly or using difficult words. It requires clear pronunciation, appropriate vocabulary, a logical sequence, suitable tone and awareness of the audience. A speaker should also listen to responses and adjust the message when necessary. Regular practice improves fluency and confidence.
blocks.subject: Communicative English I: Speaking Skills

blocks.text: 2. Explain the main elements of non-verbal communication.
blocks.subject: Communicative English I: Speaking Skills

blocks.text: • Facial expression: communicates emotions such as interest, surprise or concern.
blocks.subject: Communicative English I: Speaking Skills

blocks.text: • Eye contact: can show attention and confidence, but should be culturally appropriate and not become staring.
blocks.subject: Communicative English I: Speaking Skills

blocks.text: • Gesture: hand and arm movements can support or clarify ideas.
blocks.subject: Communicative English I: Speaking Skills

blocks.text: • Posture: an open, balanced posture can suggest confidence and attention.
blocks.subject: Communicative English I: Speaking Skills

blocks.text: • Appearance and distance: dress and physical distance affect professional impressions.
blocks.subject: Communicative English I: Speaking Skills

blocks.text: • Voice qualities: tone, pace, volume and pauses influence how spoken words are understood.
blocks.subject: Communicative English I: Speaking Skills

blocks.text: Non-verbal signals should support the spoken message. They must be interpreted in context rather than assuming that one gesture always has one fixed meaning.
blocks.subject: Communicative English I: Speaking Skills

blocks.text: 3. Describe the structure of an effective business conversation.
blocks.subject: Communicative English I: Speaking Skills

blocks.text: Begin with a polite greeting and introduce yourself or your organisation. State the purpose of the conversation briefly. Ask clear questions and listen without interrupting. Provide relevant information in simple language and confirm that the other person has understood. If there is a problem, acknowledge it and discuss practical options. Before ending, summarise decisions, responsibilities and dates. Close politely. A professional conversation avoids slang, unnecessary personal comments, aggressive language and vague promises.
blocks.subject: Communicative English I: Speaking Skills

blocks.text: 4. How should a candidate prepare for an interview?
blocks.subject: Communicative English I: Speaking Skills

blocks.text: The candidate should learn about the organisation and the role, review the qualifications and experience relevant to the job, and prepare examples of skills or achievements. They should plan a short self-introduction and practise answers to common questions such as strengths, weaknesses and career goals. On the day, they should arrive on time, dress appropriately, greet the panel politely and listen to each question. Answers should be honest, relevant and concise. The candidate may ask one or two thoughtful questions at the end and thank the interviewers.
blocks.subject: Communicative English I: Speaking Skills

blocks.text: 5. State the rules for effective group discussion.
blocks.subject: Communicative English I: Speaking Skills

blocks.text: Understand the topic before speaking. Begin with a clear point rather than repeating the question. Contribute relevant facts, examples or reasoning. Listen carefully and do not interrupt. Disagree with an idea politely instead of attacking the speaker. Invite quieter participants when appropriate and avoid dominating the discussion. Keep the conversation connected to the topic, manage time and help the group reach a balanced conclusion. Good participation is judged by quality, listening and cooperation, not by the number of times a person speaks.
blocks.subject: Communicative English I: Speaking Skills

blocks.text: 6. Explain the steps in giving clear instructions.
blocks.subject: Communicative English I: Speaking Skills

blocks.text: First identify the purpose and the people who must follow the instructions. Arrange the actions in the correct order. Use short, direct sentences and familiar words. Give one action at a time, using sequence markers such as first, next, then and finally. Mention warnings or safety points before the relevant action. Demonstrate or provide an example when the task is difficult. Ask the listener to repeat the important steps or invite questions to confirm understanding.
blocks.subject: Communicative English I: Speaking Skills

blocks.text: 7. Describe the structure of a good presentation.
blocks.subject: Communicative English I: Speaking Skills

blocks.text: A presentation should have an introduction, a body and a conclusion. The introduction greets the audience, introduces the topic and explains the purpose. The body presents two to four main points in a logical order, supported by examples, evidence or visuals. The conclusion summarises the message and gives a final recommendation or takeaway. The speaker should use readable slides, maintain appropriate eye contact, speak at a measured pace, avoid reading every word from the screen and leave time for questions.
blocks.subject: Communicative English I: Speaking Skills

blocks.text: PART C – 10-MARK MODEL ANSWERS / PRACTICAL SPEAKING TASKS
blocks.subject: Communicative English I: Speaking Skills

blocks.text: 1. Explain how to make an effective business presentation.
blocks.subject: Communicative English I: Speaking Skills

blocks.text: An effective business presentation communicates a specific message to a professional audience. Preparation begins by identifying the audience, purpose and expected outcome. The speaker should decide whether the aim is to inform, persuade, report progress or recommend a decision. Next, collect relevant information and arrange it into a clear structure. The opening should gain attention, introduce the subject and state the objective. The main body should contain a small number of connected points, supported by accurate figures, examples or demonstrations. The conclusion should restate the main message and identify the action required.
blocks.subject: Communicative English I: Speaking Skills

blocks.text: Visual aids should be simple. Each slide should contain one main idea, readable text and only useful images or charts. The presenter should not turn slides into a script. Rehearse the presentation, check timing and test the equipment. During delivery, stand confidently, use natural gestures, maintain suitable eye contact and vary the voice to maintain attention. Listen to questions fully and answer honestly. When a question cannot be answered, say so and offer to verify it rather than inventing a response. A good presentation is judged by clarity, relevance, accuracy and audience understanding.
blocks.subject: Communicative English I: Speaking Skills

blocks.text: 2. Discuss the importance of team communication and group discussion.
blocks.subject: Communicative English I: Speaking Skills

blocks.text: Team communication allows members to exchange information, coordinate tasks, identify difficulties and make decisions. A group discussion is useful because participants contribute different knowledge and experiences. It can improve problem-solving when members listen to one another and evaluate ideas fairly. To participate effectively, a student should understand the topic, make a relevant opening point, support ideas with examples, listen actively and respond to previous speakers. The student should avoid interrupting, repeating points, making personal remarks or speaking only to impress the evaluator. A moderator or chairperson should introduce the topic, explain time limits, encourage balanced participation and summarise the result. The group should aim for a reasoned conclusion, even when full agreement is not possible. Team communication succeeds when members respect each other and remain focused on the shared objective.
blocks.subject: Communicative English I: Speaking Skills

blocks.text: 3. Model interview: “Tell me about yourself.”
blocks.subject: Communicative English I: Speaking Skills

blocks.text: Sample answer for practice; replace the bracketed details with your own true information:
blocks.subject: Communicative English I: Speaking Skills

blocks.text: “Good morning. My name is [name]. I am pursuing a Bachelor of Computer Applications. I have studied subjects such as programming, computer fundamentals and mathematics. I am interested in [relevant field] and have practised [one real project or skill]. I consider my strengths to be [two genuine strengths], and I am working to improve [one skill]. I am applying for this position because it matches my interest in [role-related area], and I would like to learn while contributing responsibly to the team. Thank you for the opportunity.”
blocks.subject: Communicative English I: Speaking Skills

blocks.text: A good answer is brief, truthful and related to the position. Do not memorise claims that are not true.
blocks.subject: Communicative English I: Speaking Skills

blocks.text: 4. Prepare a short event-hosting script.
blocks.subject: Communicative English I: Speaking Skills

blocks.text: “Good morning to our respected chief guest, distinguished guests, teachers and dear students. It is my pleasure to welcome you to [name of event], organised by [institution or department]. Today we have gathered to [state the purpose in one sentence]. We are honoured by the presence of [guest's name and designation, if confirmed]. I request everyone to take their seats as we begin the programme. May I now invite [speaker's name] to deliver the welcome address. Thank you.”
blocks.subject: Communicative English I: Speaking Skills

blocks.text: A host should verify names, titles, programme order and pronunciation before the event. Use a warm but formal tone and speak slowly enough for the audience to follow.
blocks.subject: Communicative English I: Speaking Skills

blocks.text: QUICK REVISION – COMMUNICATIVE ENGLISH I
blocks.subject: Communicative English I: Speaking Skills

blocks.text: • Practise vowel/consonant pronunciation and clear word stress; intelligibility matters more than imitating an accent.
blocks.subject: Communicative English I: Speaking Skills

blocks.text: • Memorise the structure of a business conversation, interview, group discussion, instruction sequence and presentation.
blocks.subject: Communicative English I: Speaking Skills

blocks.text: • Review facial expression, eye contact, gesture, posture, proxemics and voice qualities.
blocks.subject: Communicative English I: Speaking Skills

blocks.text: • Practise one 60-second JAM speech daily on a familiar topic.
blocks.subject: Communicative English I: Speaking Skills

blocks.text: • Record one practice answer, listen to it and improve clarity, pace and filler words.
blocks.subject: Communicative English I: Speaking Skills

blocks.text: SUBJECT 8 – PC SOFTWARE LAB
blocks.subject: PC Software Lab

blocks.text: Textbook: SUCA102 – Practical I: PC Software Lab, Semester I
blocks.subject: PC Software Lab

blocks.text: Evidence status: Textbook-based practical bank. No matching PC Software Lab PYQ paper was present in the uploaded archive. Menu names may vary by Microsoft Office version; follow the version available in the examination lab.
blocks.subject: PC Software Lab

blocks.text: SYLLABUS MAP
blocks.subject: PC Software Lab

blocks.text: MS Word: text manipulation; numbering and bullets; headers and footers; spell check; Find and Replace; text formatting; picture insertion and alignment; document creation using templates; creating templates; mail merge; copying text and pictures from Excel.
blocks.subject: PC Software Lab

blocks.text: MS Excel: cell editing; formulae and built-in functions; file manipulation; sorting numbers and alphabets; worksheet preparation; charts/graphs; AutoFormat.
blocks.subject: PC Software Lab

blocks.text: PowerPoint: inserting clip art and pictures; animation/frame movement; new slides; organisation charts; presentation wizards; design templates.
blocks.subject: PC Software Lab

blocks.text: PART A – 2-MARK QUESTIONS WITH MODEL ANSWERS
blocks.subject: PC Software Lab

blocks.text: 1. What is a word processor?
blocks.subject: PC Software Lab

blocks.text: A word processor is application software used to create, edit, format, save and print text documents. Microsoft Word is an example.
blocks.subject: PC Software Lab

blocks.text: 2. What is mail merge?
blocks.subject: PC Software Lab

blocks.text: Mail merge combines a main document with a data source containing records such as names and addresses. It produces a separate personalised document or label for each record.
blocks.subject: PC Software Lab

blocks.text: 3. What is the difference between a header and a footer?
blocks.subject: PC Software Lab

blocks.text: A header appears in the top margin of a page; a footer appears in the bottom margin. They commonly contain page numbers, titles, dates or other repeated information.
blocks.subject: PC Software Lab

blocks.text: 4. What is Find and Replace?
blocks.subject: PC Software Lab

blocks.text: Find locates specified text in a document. Replace changes the selected occurrence or all matching occurrences to new text.
blocks.subject: PC Software Lab

blocks.text: 5. What is a cell in Excel?
blocks.subject: PC Software Lab

blocks.text: A cell is the intersection of a row and a column in a worksheet. It is identified by a cell address such as A1 or C5.
blocks.subject: PC Software Lab

blocks.text: 6. What is a formula in Excel?
blocks.subject: PC Software Lab

blocks.text: A formula is an expression used to calculate a result in a worksheet. It normally begins with an equals sign, for example =A1+B1.
blocks.subject: PC Software Lab

blocks.text: 7. What is a chart in Excel?
blocks.subject: PC Software Lab

blocks.text: A chart is a graphical representation of worksheet data. It helps users compare values and identify patterns.
blocks.subject: PC Software Lab

blocks.text: 8. What is a PowerPoint slide?
blocks.subject: PC Software Lab

blocks.text: A slide is an individual page of a presentation. It can contain text, pictures, charts, shapes, audio, video or other objects.
blocks.subject: PC Software Lab

blocks.text: 9. What is a design template?
blocks.subject: PC Software Lab

blocks.text: A design template is a predefined presentation design containing coordinated colours, fonts, backgrounds and layout styles.
blocks.subject: PC Software Lab

blocks.text: 10. What is an organisation chart?
blocks.subject: PC Software Lab

blocks.text: An organisation chart is a diagram showing the reporting relationships or hierarchy of positions within an organisation.
blocks.subject: PC Software Lab

blocks.text: PART B – 5-MARK MODEL ANSWERS
blocks.subject: PC Software Lab

blocks.text: 1. Explain the procedure for creating and formatting a Word document.
blocks.subject: PC Software Lab

blocks.text: 1. Open Microsoft Word and choose a blank document or a suitable template.
blocks.subject: PC Software Lab

blocks.text: 2. Type the required text and save the file with a meaningful name.
blocks.subject: PC Software Lab

blocks.text: 3. Select text and apply font type, size, bold, italic, underline and alignment as required.
blocks.subject: PC Software Lab

blocks.text: 4. Use paragraph spacing, indentation and line spacing to make the document readable.
blocks.subject: PC Software Lab

blocks.text: 5. Apply bullets or numbering to lists and use styles for headings.
blocks.subject: PC Software Lab

blocks.text: 6. Insert a header/footer or page number when required.
blocks.subject: PC Software Lab

blocks.text: 7. Run spelling/grammar checks, use Print Preview and save the final version.
blocks.subject: PC Software Lab

blocks.text: Always check page breaks, margins and alignment before printing or submitting.
blocks.subject: PC Software Lab

blocks.text: 2. Explain how to perform mail merge in Word.
blocks.subject: PC Software Lab

blocks.text: Create the main document containing the common text, such as a letter. Open the Mailings tab and start Mail Merge, selecting the required document type. Choose or create a recipient list/data source, for example an Excel table with columns for name, address and other fields. Insert merge fields at the correct places in the letter. Preview the records to check that the fields are mapped correctly. Finish and Merge to create individual documents, print them or send them by the supported method. Check spelling and records before producing the final batch.
blocks.subject: PC Software Lab

blocks.text: 3. Explain common Excel functions with examples.
blocks.subject: PC Software Lab

blocks.text: • =SUM(B2:B6) adds the values in B2 through B6.
blocks.subject: PC Software Lab

blocks.text: • =AVERAGE(B2:B6) calculates their arithmetic mean.
blocks.subject: PC Software Lab

blocks.text: • =MAX(B2:B6) returns the largest value.
blocks.subject: PC Software Lab

blocks.text: • =MIN(B2:B6) returns the smallest value.
blocks.subject: PC Software Lab

blocks.text: • =COUNT(B2:B6) counts cells containing numbers.
blocks.subject: PC Software Lab

blocks.text: • =IF(C2>=50,"Pass","Fail") returns one result when the condition is true and another when it is false.
blocks.subject: PC Software Lab

blocks.text: The exact formula separators may depend on regional settings. Check the result using the sample data.
blocks.subject: PC Software Lab

blocks.text: 4. Explain sorting and chart creation in Excel.
blocks.subject: PC Software Lab

blocks.text: Select the full data range, including headings. Use the Sort command and choose the column to sort by. Select ascending or descending order and confirm that the data has headers. Check that entire rows move together; sorting only one column may separate records and corrupt the table. To create a chart, select the required labels and values, choose Insert Chart and select a suitable type such as column, bar, line or pie. Add a meaningful chart title and axis labels where appropriate. Verify that the chart uses the correct data range.
blocks.subject: PC Software Lab

blocks.text: 5. Explain how to create a PowerPoint presentation.
blocks.subject: PC Software Lab

blocks.text: Open PowerPoint and choose a blank presentation or design template. Add a title slide and insert further slides using an appropriate layout. Add concise text, pictures or diagrams. Use a consistent font and colour scheme. Insert an organisation chart when the task requires a hierarchy. Add animations or transitions only when asked; keep them controlled and consistent. Run the slide show from the beginning, check text size and sequence, and save the presentation in the required format.
blocks.subject: PC Software Lab

blocks.text: PART C – 10-MARK PRACTICAL TASKS / MODEL PROCEDURES
blocks.subject: PC Software Lab

blocks.text: 1. Word practical: prepare a formal invitation letter with mail merge.
blocks.subject: PC Software Lab

blocks.text: Task: Create a one-page invitation letter to multiple recipients using an Excel recipient list.
blocks.subject: PC Software Lab

blocks.text: Procedure:
blocks.subject: PC Software Lab

blocks.text: 1. Create an Excel workbook with clear headings such as Name, Address, City and EventDate. Enter one recipient per row and save it.
blocks.subject: PC Software Lab

blocks.text: 2. Open Word and type the common letter. Leave spaces for personal information.
blocks.subject: PC Software Lab

blocks.text: 3. Select Mailings → Start Mail Merge → Letters (wording may vary by version).
blocks.subject: PC Software Lab

blocks.text: 4. Select Recipients → Use an Existing List and choose the Excel workbook and correct sheet.
blocks.subject: PC Software Lab

blocks.text: 5. Place the cursor where the recipient name should appear and insert the Name merge field. Insert address fields in the correct positions.
blocks.subject: PC Software Lab

blocks.text: 6. Preview each record and confirm that no field is blank or shifted.
blocks.subject: PC Software Lab

blocks.text: 7. Finish and Merge to create the merged letters.
blocks.subject: PC Software Lab

blocks.text: 8. Save the main document and the merged output.
blocks.subject: PC Software Lab

blocks.text: Check: Recipient names and addresses must match the spreadsheet rows. Do not share the data source outside the practical task.
blocks.subject: PC Software Lab

blocks.text: 2. Excel practical: prepare a student mark sheet.
blocks.subject: PC Software Lab

blocks.text: Create columns: Roll Number, Name, Subject 1, Subject 2, Subject 3, Total, Average and Result. Enter the marks. In F2 use =SUM(C2:E2). In G2 use =AVERAGE(C2:E2). In H2 use =IF(G2>=40,"Pass","Fail") if the stated pass criterion is a 40% average; use the threshold given in the question instead of assuming one. Copy formulas down for all students. Format headings, borders and numeric cells. Sort by Total from largest to smallest without separating rows. Select Name and Total and insert a column chart. Save the workbook and verify a sample row manually.
blocks.subject: PC Software Lab

blocks.text: 3. PowerPoint practical: prepare an organisation presentation.
blocks.subject: PC Software Lab

blocks.text: Create a title slide with the organisation name. Add a slide describing its purpose. Insert an organisation chart with the top position and subordinate departments. Add a slide for each department's role. Use relevant pictures or icons only when they clarify the content. Apply one design template and consistent layouts. Add limited animations if required. Start Slide Show and check sequence, readability and alignment. Save the presentation with a clear file name.
blocks.subject: PC Software Lab

blocks.text: 4. Shortcuts and troubleshooting.
blocks.subject: PC Software Lab

blocks.text: • Ctrl+S: save; Ctrl+C: copy; Ctrl+V: paste; Ctrl+X: cut; Ctrl+Z: undo; Ctrl+F: find; Ctrl+H: replace in many Office versions.
blocks.subject: PC Software Lab

blocks.text: • If a formula shows as text, check whether the cell is formatted as Text and whether the formula begins with =.
blocks.subject: PC Software Lab

blocks.text: • If Excel sorting separates names from marks, undo immediately and sort the entire table range.
blocks.subject: PC Software Lab

blocks.text: • If a picture moves unexpectedly in Word, check text-wrapping and anchor/layout settings.
blocks.subject: PC Software Lab

blocks.text: • If a slide looks crowded, reduce text and use a clearer layout rather than shrinking all text excessively.
blocks.subject: PC Software Lab

blocks.subject: PC Software Lab

blocks.subject: PC Software Lab

blocks.subject: PC Software Lab

blocks.text: SEMESTER II – ADDITIONAL SUBJECTS
SUBJECT 9 – COMMUNICATIVE ENGLISH II: LISTENING SKILLS
blocks.subject: Communicative English II: Listening Skills

blocks.text: Textbook: SFCE12 – Listening Skills, Semester II, Paper II
blocks.subject: Communicative English II: Listening Skills

blocks.text: Evidence status: Textbook-based model questions. No matching Listening Skills PYQ paper was present in the uploaded archive.
blocks.subject: Communicative English II: Listening Skills

blocks.text: SYLLABUS MAP
blocks.subject: Communicative English II: Listening Skills

blocks.text: Unit 1: introduction to listening – active and passive listening, barriers to effective listening, improving active listening and identifying foreign accents. Unit 2: listening to announcements and decoding instructions. Unit 3: listening to lectures, speeches, news bulletins and audio-video materials, with note-taking. Unit 4: listening to stories and answering analytical questions. Unit 5: listening for leadership and professional interpersonal communication.
blocks.subject: Communicative English II: Listening Skills

blocks.text: PART A – 2-MARK QUESTIONS WITH MODEL ANSWERS
blocks.subject: Communicative English II: Listening Skills

blocks.text: 1. Distinguish hearing from listening.
blocks.subject: Communicative English II: Listening Skills

blocks.text: Hearing is the physical reception of sound. Listening is an active mental process in which the listener pays attention, interprets meaning and responds to what is heard.
blocks.subject: Communicative English II: Listening Skills

blocks.text: 2. What is active listening?
blocks.subject: Communicative English II: Listening Skills

blocks.text: Active listening means concentrating on the speaker, understanding the message, noticing important details and responding appropriately. It includes asking relevant questions and confirming understanding.
blocks.subject: Communicative English II: Listening Skills

blocks.text: 3. What is passive listening?
blocks.subject: Communicative English II: Listening Skills

blocks.text: Passive listening occurs when a person receives sound with limited attention or involvement. The listener may hear the words without carefully analysing or remembering the message.
blocks.subject: Communicative English II: Listening Skills

blocks.text: 4. State two barriers to effective listening.
blocks.subject: Communicative English II: Listening Skills

blocks.text: Noise and distraction are two barriers. Other barriers include bias, lack of interest, unfamiliar vocabulary, fast speech and emotional reactions.
blocks.subject: Communicative English II: Listening Skills

blocks.text: 5. What is note-taking?
blocks.subject: Communicative English II: Listening Skills

blocks.text: Note-taking is recording key information while listening or reading. Good notes use keywords, short phrases, headings and symbols rather than attempting to write every word.
blocks.subject: Communicative English II: Listening Skills

blocks.text: 6. What is an announcement?
blocks.subject: Communicative English II: Listening Skills

blocks.text: An announcement is a short public message that communicates information such as a change, instruction, warning, event or service update to a group of people.
blocks.subject: Communicative English II: Listening Skills

blocks.text: 7. What is a foreign accent?
blocks.subject: Communicative English II: Listening Skills

blocks.text: A foreign accent is a pronunciation pattern influenced by a speaker's first language or speech community. Listeners should focus on context, key words and meaning rather than judging the accent.
blocks.subject: Communicative English II: Listening Skills

blocks.text: 8. What is a news bulletin?
blocks.subject: Communicative English II: Listening Skills

blocks.text: A news bulletin is a short organised broadcast containing reports about current events. It commonly presents the main facts, including who, what, when, where, why and how.
blocks.subject: Communicative English II: Listening Skills

blocks.text: 9. Define listening comprehension.
blocks.subject: Communicative English II: Listening Skills

blocks.text: Listening comprehension is the ability to understand spoken language, identify main ideas and details, infer meaning and respond to questions about what was heard.
blocks.subject: Communicative English II: Listening Skills

blocks.text: 10. How does listening support leadership?
blocks.subject: Communicative English II: Listening Skills

blocks.text: Listening helps leaders understand concerns, collect information, build trust, resolve conflict and make better decisions. It shows respect for team members.
blocks.subject: Communicative English II: Listening Skills

blocks.text: PART B – 5-MARK MODEL ANSWERS
blocks.subject: Communicative English II: Listening Skills

blocks.text: 1. Explain the difference between active and passive listening.
blocks.subject: Communicative English II: Listening Skills

blocks.text: Active listening involves purposeful attention. The listener focuses on the speaker, identifies the main idea, notices supporting details, asks questions and provides feedback. Passive listening involves receiving sound without strong concentration or response. For example, listening carefully to a manager's instructions and writing down deadlines is active listening. Having a radio playing in the background without concentrating is passive listening. Active listening improves learning, safety and teamwork because it reduces misunderstanding. The listener can improve it by removing distractions, maintaining suitable eye contact, avoiding interruption and summarising the message.
blocks.subject: Communicative English II: Listening Skills

blocks.text: 2. Explain the barriers to effective listening and ways to overcome them.
blocks.subject: Communicative English II: Listening Skills

blocks.text: Noise, poor audio quality, unfamiliar accents, rapid speech, difficult vocabulary, distraction, prejudice and emotional stress can prevent understanding. Listeners can reduce physical noise, choose a suitable place, keep devices aside and concentrate on the speaker. They should listen for the main idea before focusing on every detail, use context to understand unfamiliar words and ask for clarification when necessary. Taking notes helps retain important information. The listener should also avoid forming an opinion before the speaker finishes.
blocks.subject: Communicative English II: Listening Skills

blocks.text: 3. How should a student listen to and decode announcements?
blocks.subject: Communicative English II: Listening Skills

blocks.text: Identify the type of announcement first: a warning, instruction, schedule change, invitation or information message. Listen for names, dates, times, locations, amounts, deadlines and required actions. Note negations such as not, except or unless, because they change the meaning. Follow the sequence of instructions and distinguish confirmed information from optional advice. If a critical detail is unclear, ask for repetition or consult the official written notice. Do not guess a time or location from incomplete information.
blocks.subject: Communicative English II: Listening Skills

blocks.text: 4. Explain an effective note-taking method for lectures and speeches.
blocks.subject: Communicative English II: Listening Skills

blocks.text: Before listening, write the topic and date. During the lecture, record headings, main points, definitions, names, dates, formulae and examples. Use abbreviations and symbols consistently. Leave spaces to add details later. Do not attempt to copy every sentence, because this can prevent attention to the speaker. After the lecture, organise the notes into headings and add a short summary. Check unclear names or figures against the source material. The result should preserve the central message and important supporting details.
blocks.subject: Communicative English II: Listening Skills

blocks.text: 5. Explain how listening can support leadership in a professional setting.
blocks.subject: Communicative English II: Listening Skills

blocks.text: A leader needs to understand employee concerns, customer feedback, risks and different viewpoints. Active listening encourages people to speak honestly and builds trust. It also helps the leader identify the real cause of a problem instead of responding only to the first complaint. A leader should allow the speaker to finish, ask neutral questions, paraphrase key points and confirm next steps. Listening does not require agreeing with every opinion; it requires understanding before making a decision. In a meeting, the leader can summarise agreed actions, owners and deadlines to ensure follow-through.
blocks.subject: Communicative English II: Listening Skills

blocks.text: PART C – 10-MARK MODEL ANSWERS / LISTENING PRACTICE
blocks.subject: Communicative English II: Listening Skills

blocks.text: 1. Discuss the process of effective listening.
blocks.subject: Communicative English II: Listening Skills

blocks.text: Effective listening begins before the speaker starts. The listener should be physically prepared, reduce distractions and have a clear purpose for listening. During the message, attention should remain on the speaker. The listener should identify the topic, main idea and supporting details. Tone, stress and pauses may signal emphasis or emotion. The listener should interpret unfamiliar words through context, but should not invent meaning when a critical point is unclear. Relevant facts such as dates, amounts, names, instructions and warnings should be written down.
blocks.subject: Communicative English II: Listening Skills

blocks.text: After listening, the listener should organise the information and check understanding. A short summary in the listener's own words can reveal missing details. Questions should be specific and respectful. In a professional environment, the listener should record decisions, assigned responsibilities and deadlines. Effective listening is therefore an active cycle of attention, interpretation, memory, evaluation and response. It improves accuracy, relationships and decision-making.
blocks.subject: Communicative English II: Listening Skills

blocks.text: 2. Model note-taking from a short announcement.
blocks.subject: Communicative English II: Listening Skills

blocks.text: Practice announcement: “Attention passengers. Train 12680 scheduled to depart from Platform 2 at 5:30 p.m. will now depart from Platform 4 at 5:50 p.m. Passengers requiring assistance should contact the station help desk.”
blocks.subject: Communicative English II: Listening Skills

blocks.text: Good notes: Service: Train 12680. Original platform/time: Platform 2, 5:30 p.m. Revised platform/time: Platform 4, 5:50 p.m. Action: Passengers needing assistance → station help desk.
blocks.subject: Communicative English II: Listening Skills

blocks.text: Comprehension answers: (a) Train number: 12680. (b) New platform: 4. (c) New departure time: 5:50 p.m. (d) Help point: station help desk.
blocks.subject: Communicative English II: Listening Skills

blocks.text: This shows why listeners must distinguish changed information from earlier information.
blocks.subject: Communicative English II: Listening Skills

blocks.text: 3. Explain how to listen to stories and answer analytical questions.
blocks.subject: Communicative English II: Listening Skills

blocks.text: A listener should identify the setting, main characters and central problem. Next, follow the order of events and note the decisions that influence the plot. Pay attention to changes in tone, repeated ideas and details that may foreshadow later events. Distinguish what a character says from what the narrator reveals. After listening, identify the conflict, turning point and outcome. Analytical answers should go beyond retelling: explain why a character acts, what a particular event changes and what theme the story communicates. Support the answer with details actually heard in the story. If the listener is uncertain about a name or event, it should be checked rather than invented.

blocks.text: SUBJECT 10 – PROGRAMMING IN C LAB
blocks.subject: Programming in C Lab

blocks.text: Textbook: SUCA105 – Practical II: Programming in C Lab, Semester II
blocks.subject: Programming in C Lab

blocks.text: Evidence status: Textbook-based practical bank. No matching Programming in C Lab PYQ paper was present in the uploaded PYQ archive. Programs below are standard C implementations of the practical exercises listed in the supplied course book. Compile using a C compiler; the textbook may use older compiler conventions.
blocks.subject: Programming in C Lab

blocks.text: SYLLABUS MAP
blocks.subject: Programming in C Lab

blocks.text: The book lists: summation of sine, cosine and exponential series; string operations (count vowels/consonants/words/white spaces, reverse, palindrome, substring detection/count/removal, find/replace); recursion (nPr, nCr, GCD, Fibonacci, maximum/minimum and Towers of Hanoi); matrix operations (addition, subtraction, multiplication, transpose, trace, determinant and inverse); sorting/searching (including insertion sort; the continuation of the exercise list includes search routines).
blocks.subject: Programming in C Lab

blocks.text: PART A – 2-MARK QUESTIONS WITH MODEL ANSWERS
blocks.subject: Programming in C Lab

blocks.text: 1. What is a series expansion?
blocks.subject: Programming in C Lab

blocks.text: A series expansion represents a function as a sum of terms. For example, the Maclaurin expansion of sin x is x − x³/3! + x⁵/5! − …, where x is in radians.
blocks.subject: Programming in C Lab

blocks.text: 2. What is recursion?
blocks.subject: Programming in C Lab

blocks.text: Recursion is a programming technique in which a function calls itself to solve a smaller instance of the same problem. A recursive function must contain a base case to stop further calls.
blocks.subject: Programming in C Lab

blocks.text: 3. Define a palindrome string.
blocks.subject: Programming in C Lab

blocks.text: A palindrome is a string that reads the same forwards and backwards, such as level or madam.
blocks.subject: Programming in C Lab

blocks.text: 4. What is a substring?
blocks.subject: Programming in C Lab

blocks.text: A substring is a contiguous sequence of characters occurring within a larger string.
blocks.subject: Programming in C Lab

blocks.text: 5. What is nPr?
blocks.subject: Programming in C Lab

blocks.text: The number of permutations of r objects selected from n distinct objects is nPr = n!/(n−r)!, for 0 ≤ r ≤ n.
blocks.subject: Programming in C Lab

blocks.text: 6. What is nCr?
blocks.subject: Programming in C Lab

blocks.text: The number of combinations of r objects selected from n distinct objects is nCr = n!/[r!(n−r)!].
blocks.subject: Programming in C Lab

blocks.text: 7. Define a square matrix.
blocks.subject: Programming in C Lab

blocks.text: A square matrix has the same number of rows and columns. Its order is n × n.
blocks.subject: Programming in C Lab

blocks.text: 8. What is insertion sort?
blocks.subject: Programming in C Lab

blocks.text: Insertion sort builds a sorted part of an array by taking each next element and inserting it into its correct position among the elements already processed.
blocks.subject: Programming in C Lab

blocks.text: 9. What is linear search?
blocks.subject: Programming in C Lab

blocks.text: Linear search checks each element sequentially until the target is found or the list ends. It works on both sorted and unsorted arrays.
blocks.subject: Programming in C Lab

blocks.text: 10. What is binary search?
blocks.subject: Programming in C Lab

blocks.text: Binary search repeatedly compares the target with the middle element and halves the search interval. The array must be sorted before binary search is used.
blocks.subject: Programming in C Lab

blocks.text: PART B – 5-MARK MODEL ANSWERS
blocks.subject: Programming in C Lab

blocks.text: 1. Explain the Maclaurin series for sin x, cos x and eˣ.
blocks.subject: Programming in C Lab

blocks.text: For x measured in radians:
blocks.subject: Programming in C Lab

blocks.text: • sin x = x − x³/3! + x⁵/5! − x⁷/7! + …
blocks.subject: Programming in C Lab

blocks.text: A program calculates a finite number of terms and compares the sum with the corresponding library function from <math.h>. Accuracy normally improves as more terms are included for values within a suitable range, but floating-point error and overflow can affect results.
blocks.subject: Programming in C Lab

blocks.text: 2. Explain the algorithm to count vowels, consonants, words and white spaces.
blocks.subject: Programming in C Lab

blocks.text: Read a full line of text. Visit each character using a loop. Convert alphabetic characters to a common case before checking whether they are a, e, i, o or u. Count other alphabetic characters as consonants. Count white-space characters separately. Count a word when a non-space character follows the start of the line or a whitespace character. Ignore repeated spaces when counting words. The program should use a character-classification function or an explicit condition to avoid treating punctuation as a consonant.
blocks.subject: Programming in C Lab

blocks.text: 3. Explain recursive calculation of GCD.
blocks.subject: Programming in C Lab

blocks.text: The Euclidean algorithm uses GCD(a, b) = GCD(b, a mod b), with the base case GCD(a, 0) = |a|. Each recursive call reduces the second argument until it becomes zero. The algorithm is efficient and avoids prime factorisation. Inputs should be integers; handle negative values by converting them to absolute values.
blocks.subject: Programming in C Lab

blocks.text: 4. Explain the Tower of Hanoi algorithm.
blocks.subject: Programming in C Lab

blocks.text: To move n disks from source A to destination C using auxiliary B: (1) move n−1 disks from A to B using C; (2) move the largest disk from A to C; (3) move n−1 disks from B to C using A. The base case is one disk, which is moved directly. The recurrence is T(n) = 2T(n−1) + 1, so the minimum number of moves is 2ⁿ − 1.
blocks.subject: Programming in C Lab

blocks.text: 5. Distinguish linear and binary search.
blocks.subject: Programming in C Lab

blocks.text: Feature | Linear search | Binary search
blocks.subject: Programming in C Lab

blocks.text: Data order | Any order | Must be sorted
blocks.subject: Programming in C Lab

blocks.text: Method | Checks sequentially | Repeatedly halves range
blocks.subject: Programming in C Lab

blocks.text: Best case | First item | Middle item
blocks.subject: Programming in C Lab

blocks.text: Worst-case time | O(n) | O(log n)
blocks.subject: Programming in C Lab

blocks.text: Use | Small or unsorted data | Larger sorted data
blocks.subject: Programming in C Lab

blocks.text: PART C – 10-MARK PRACTICAL PROGRAMS WITH MODEL SOLUTIONS
blocks.subject: Programming in C Lab

blocks.text: 1. C program to check whether a string is a palindrome.
blocks.subject: Programming in C Lab
Programming in C Lab

blocks.text: Explanation: fgets reads a complete line. The newline is removed. Two indices compare characters from opposite ends. isalnum ignores spaces and punctuation, while tolower makes the comparison case-insensitive. For a strict character-by-character practical, remove the isalnum/tolower calls and compare the original characters exactly.
blocks.subject: Programming in C Lab

blocks.text: 2. C program to calculate GCD recursively.
blocks.subject: Programming in C Lab

blocks.text: #include <stdio.h> #include <stdlib.h> int gcd(int a, int b) { if (b == 0) return abs(a); return gcd(b, a % b); } int main(void) { int a, b; printf("Enter two integers: "); if (scanf("%d %d", &a, &b) != 2) return 1; printf("GCD = %d\n", gcd(a, b)); return 0; }
blocks.subject: Programming in C Lab

blocks.text: Sample: Input 48 18 gives GCD = 6. The base case stops recursion when the remainder becomes zero.
blocks.subject: Programming in C Lab

blocks.text: 3. C program to generate the Fibonacci sequence using recursion.
blocks.subject: Programming in C Lab

blocks.text: #include <stdio.h> long long fib(int n) { if (n == 0) return 0; if (n == 1) return 1; return fib(n - 1) + fib(n - 2); } int main(void) { int n, i; printf("Number of terms (1 to 40): "); if (scanf("%d", &n) != 1 || n < 1 || n > 40) return 1; for (i = 0; i < n; i++) printf("%lld ", fib(i)); printf("\n"); return 0; }
blocks.subject: Programming in C Lab

blocks.text: Sample: For 7 terms: 0 1 1 2 3 5 8. This simple recursive method is easy to understand but repeats calculations and becomes slow for large n. A loop or memoisation is more efficient; use the form requested by the examiner.
blocks.subject: Programming in C Lab

blocks.text: 4. C program for matrix multiplication (two 2 × 2 matrices).
blocks.subject: Programming in C Lab
Programming in C Lab

blocks.text: Explanation: Each result element is the sum of products from a row of A and a column of B. Matrix multiplication is possible only when the number of columns of A equals the number of rows of B.
blocks.subject: Programming in C Lab

blocks.text: 5. C program for insertion sort.
blocks.subject: Programming in C Lab

blocks.text: #include <stdio.h> int main(void) { int a[100], n, i, j, key; printf("Enter number of elements (1-100): "); if (scanf("%d", &n) != 1 || n < 1 || n > 100) return 1; printf("Enter %d integers: ", n); for (i = 0; i < n; i++) scanf("%d", &a[i]); for (i = 1; i < n; i++) { key = a[i]; j = i - 1; while (j >= 0 && a[j] > key) { a[j + 1] = a[j]; j--; } a[j + 1] = key; } printf("Sorted: "); for (i = 0; i < n; i++) printf("%d ", a[i]); printf("\n"); return 0; }
blocks.subject: Programming in C Lab

blocks.text: Sample: Input 5 and 9 3 7 1 4 gives 1 3 4 7 9. The sorted prefix grows by one element in each pass.
blocks.subject: Programming in C Lab

blocks.text: 6. C program for sine series and comparison with the library function.
blocks.subject: Programming in C Lab
Programming in C Lab

blocks.text: Explanation: The next term is obtained from the previous term using the ratio −x²/[(2k)(2k+1)]. sin() and fabs() are declared in <math.h>. Some compilers require linking the math library. The input x must be in radians.
blocks.subject: Programming in C Lab

blocks.text: LAB VIVA QUESTIONS
blocks.subject: Programming in C Lab

blocks.text: 1. Why is a base case required in recursion? To stop recursive calls and prevent infinite recursion/stack overflow.
blocks.subject: Programming in C Lab

blocks.text: 2. Why must binary search use sorted data? Because it decides which half can be discarded by comparing the middle value.
blocks.subject: Programming in C Lab

blocks.text: 3. What is the condition for multiplying matrices A and B? Columns in A must equal rows in B.
blocks.subject: Programming in C Lab

blocks.text: 4. What is the difference between `strlen` and `sizeof`? strlen counts characters before the null terminator; sizeof returns the storage size in bytes of an object or type.
blocks.subject: Programming in C Lab

blocks.text: 5. Why use `fgets` for a line? It can read spaces in a line, unlike %s, which stops at whitespace.
blocks.subject: Programming in C Lab

blocks.text: 6. What is the role of `<math.h>`? It declares common mathematical functions such as sin, cos, exp and sqrt.
blocks.subject: Programming in C Lab

blocks.text: SEMESTER III
SUBJECT 11 – PROGRAMMING IN C++ AND DATA STRUCTURES
blocks.subject: Programming in C++ and Data Structures

blocks.text: Textbooks: SUCA201A and SUCA201B – Programming in C++ and Data Structures, Volumes I and II
blocks.subject: Programming in C++ and Data Structures

blocks.text: Evidence status: Textbook-based model bank. No matching C++/Data Structures theory PYQ paper was present in the uploaded archive. Questions and answers below follow the supplied syllabus.
blocks.subject: Programming in C++ and Data Structures

blocks.text: SYLLABUS MAP
blocks.subject: Programming in C++ and Data Structures

blocks.text: The supplied two-volume course book covers: C++ tokens, keywords, identifiers, variables, operators, manipulators, expressions and control structures; pointers and functions; function prototypes, parameter passing, return values, inline, friend and virtual functions; classes and objects; constructors and destructors; function/operator overloading and type conversion; inheritance; pointers, virtual functions and polymorphism; console I/O; file streams; command-line arguments; primitive/composite data types; asymptotic notation; arrays and ordered lists; stacks and their applications; infix-to-postfix conversion; recursion and maze problems; queues and circular queues; singly and doubly linked lists; polynomial representation/addition; trees and traversals; graphs, hashing, graph traversal and Dijkstra's shortest-path algorithm.
blocks.subject: Programming in C++ and Data Structures

blocks.text: PART A – 2-MARK QUESTIONS WITH MODEL ANSWERS
blocks.subject: Programming in C++ and Data Structures

blocks.text: 1. What is object-oriented programming?
blocks.subject: Programming in C++ and Data Structures

blocks.text: Object-oriented programming (OOP) is a programming approach that organises a program around objects containing data and functions. Its central ideas include encapsulation, abstraction, inheritance and polymorphism.
blocks.subject: Programming in C++ and Data Structures

blocks.text: 2. Define a class and an object.
blocks.subject: Programming in C++ and Data Structures

blocks.text: A class is a user-defined type that specifies data members and member functions. An object is an instance of a class that has its own state and can use the class's operations.
blocks.subject: Programming in C++ and Data Structures

blocks.text: 3. What is encapsulation?
blocks.subject: Programming in C++ and Data Structures

blocks.text: Encapsulation combines data and the functions that operate on it in one unit, usually a class. Access control helps protect the internal state from unauthorised modification.
blocks.subject: Programming in C++ and Data Structures

blocks.text: 4. What is abstraction?
blocks.subject: Programming in C++ and Data Structures

blocks.text: Abstraction presents essential features and hides unnecessary implementation details. A user can operate an object through its public interface without knowing the internal code.
blocks.subject: Programming in C++ and Data Structures

blocks.text: 5. What is a constructor?
blocks.subject: Programming in C++ and Data Structures

blocks.text: A constructor is a special member function called automatically when an object is created. It has the same name as its class and no return type. It is used to initialise the object.
blocks.subject: Programming in C++ and Data Structures

blocks.text: 6. What is a destructor?
blocks.subject: Programming in C++ and Data Structures

blocks.text: A destructor is a special member function called when an object is destroyed. Its name is the class name preceded by ~; it has no return type and no parameters.
blocks.subject: Programming in C++ and Data Structures

blocks.text: 7. What is inheritance?
blocks.subject: Programming in C++ and Data Structures

blocks.text: Inheritance is the mechanism by which a new class derives data and functions from an existing class. It supports reuse and extension of class behaviour.
blocks.subject: Programming in C++ and Data Structures

blocks.text: 8. Define polymorphism.
blocks.subject: Programming in C++ and Data Structures

blocks.text: Polymorphism means “many forms”. In C++, function/operator overloading provides compile-time polymorphism, while virtual functions support run-time polymorphism through base-class pointers or references.
blocks.subject: Programming in C++ and Data Structures

blocks.text: 9. What is function overloading?
blocks.subject: Programming in C++ and Data Structures

blocks.text: Function overloading allows multiple functions to have the same name but different parameter lists. The compiler selects the appropriate function from the call's arguments.
blocks.subject: Programming in C++ and Data Structures

blocks.text: 10. What is operator overloading?
blocks.subject: Programming in C++ and Data Structures

blocks.text: Operator overloading gives an existing C++ operator a defined meaning for a user-defined type. It must preserve understandable usage and cannot change an operator's precedence or number of operands.
blocks.subject: Programming in C++ and Data Structures

blocks.text: 11. What is a virtual function?
blocks.subject: Programming in C++ and Data Structures

blocks.text: A virtual function is a base-class member function declared with virtual so that an overridden function can be selected at run time through a base pointer or reference.
blocks.subject: Programming in C++ and Data Structures

blocks.text: 12. What is a data structure?
blocks.subject: Programming in C++ and Data Structures

blocks.text: A data structure is a way of organising and storing data so that operations such as access, insertion, deletion and searching can be performed efficiently.
blocks.subject: Programming in C++ and Data Structures

blocks.text: 13. Define a stack.
blocks.subject: Programming in C++ and Data Structures

blocks.text: A stack is a linear data structure that follows Last In, First Out (LIFO). Insertion is called push and deletion is called pop.
blocks.subject: Programming in C++ and Data Structures

blocks.text: 14. Define a queue.
blocks.subject: Programming in C++ and Data Structures

blocks.text: A queue is a linear data structure that usually follows First In, First Out (FIFO). Insertion takes place at the rear and deletion at the front.
blocks.subject: Programming in C++ and Data Structures

blocks.text: 15. What is a linked list?
blocks.subject: Programming in C++ and Data Structures

blocks.text: A linked list is a dynamic collection of nodes. Each node contains data and one or more links to other nodes. Nodes need not occupy consecutive memory locations.
blocks.subject: Programming in C++ and Data Structures

blocks.text: 16. What is a binary tree?
blocks.subject: Programming in C++ and Data Structures

blocks.text: A binary tree is a tree in which each node has at most two children, commonly called the left and right child.
blocks.subject: Programming in C++ and Data Structures

blocks.text: 17. What is a graph?
blocks.subject: Programming in C++ and Data Structures

blocks.text: A graph is a structure consisting of vertices (nodes) and edges connecting pairs of vertices. Edges may be directed or undirected and may carry weights.
blocks.subject: Programming in C++ and Data Structures

blocks.text: 18. What is hashing?
blocks.subject: Programming in C++ and Data Structures

blocks.text: Hashing uses a hash function to map a key to an index in a table. A collision occurs when different keys map to the same index; a collision-resolution method is then required.
blocks.subject: Programming in C++ and Data Structures

blocks.text: 19. What is Big-O notation?
blocks.subject: Programming in C++ and Data Structures

blocks.text: Big-O notation describes an asymptotic upper bound on an algorithm's growth rate, commonly used to express how time or space requirements increase with input size.
blocks.subject: Programming in C++ and Data Structures

blocks.text: 20. What is Dijkstra's algorithm?
blocks.subject: Programming in C++ and Data Structures

blocks.text: Dijkstra's algorithm finds shortest-path distances from a source vertex in a weighted graph with non-negative edge weights.
blocks.subject: Programming in C++ and Data Structures

blocks.text: PART B – 5-MARK MODEL ANSWERS
blocks.subject: Programming in C++ and Data Structures

blocks.text: 1. Explain the basic features of object-oriented programming.
blocks.subject: Programming in C++ and Data Structures

blocks.text: • Class and object: a class defines a type; an object is an instance.
blocks.subject: Programming in C++ and Data Structures

blocks.text: • Encapsulation: data and related functions are placed together, with access controlled by private, protected and public.
blocks.subject: Programming in C++ and Data Structures

blocks.text: • Abstraction: the public interface exposes required operations while implementation details remain hidden.
blocks.subject: Programming in C++ and Data Structures

blocks.text: • Inheritance: a derived class can reuse and extend a base class.
blocks.subject: Programming in C++ and Data Structures

blocks.text: • Polymorphism: one interface can represent different implementations, through overloading or virtual functions.
blocks.subject: Programming in C++ and Data Structures

blocks.text: These features support modular design and code reuse, but they do not automatically make a program correct; classes must still be designed carefully.
blocks.subject: Programming in C++ and Data Structures

blocks.text: 2. Distinguish function overloading and function overriding.
blocks.subject: Programming in C++ and Data Structures

blocks.text: Function overloading | Function overriding
blocks.subject: Programming in C++ and Data Structures

blocks.text: Same function name with different parameter lists | Derived class supplies a new implementation of a base virtual function
blocks.subject: Programming in C++ and Data Structures

blocks.text: Usually resolved at compile time | Supports run-time dispatch through virtual functions
blocks.subject: Programming in C++ and Data Structures

blocks.text: Can occur in one class or scope | Requires inheritance and compatible function signature
blocks.subject: Programming in C++ and Data Structures

blocks.text: Return type alone cannot distinguish overloads | Return type must be compatible; covariant returns are permitted in specific class-pointer/reference cases
blocks.subject: Programming in C++ and Data Structures

blocks.text: 3. Explain the types of constructors.
blocks.subject: Programming in C++ and Data Structures

blocks.text: A default constructor can be called without arguments and initialises an object with default values. A parameterised constructor accepts arguments to initialise an object with specified values. A copy constructor creates an object from another object of the same class, usually with a reference parameter such as const ClassName&. C++ also supports move constructors in modern standards, though the course's foundational treatment may focus on default, parameterised and copy constructors. A constructor may be overloaded to provide several initialisation forms.
blocks.subject: Programming in C++ and Data Structures

blocks.text: 4. Explain inheritance and its common forms.
blocks.subject: Programming in C++ and Data Structures

blocks.text: Single inheritance derives one class from one base class. Multilevel inheritance forms a chain in which a derived class becomes the base of another class. Multiple inheritance derives one class from more than one base class. Hierarchical inheritance has several derived classes sharing one base class. Hybrid inheritance combines two or more inheritance patterns. Inheritance should model a genuine “is-a” relationship and access specifiers determine which inherited members are available to derived classes and outside code.
blocks.subject: Programming in C++ and Data Structures

blocks.text: 5. Explain stack operations and applications.
blocks.subject: Programming in C++ and Data Structures

blocks.text: A stack maintains a top position. Push inserts an item at the top; pop removes the top item; peek returns the top item without removing it. An array implementation must check overflow before push and underflow before pop. A linked implementation allocates and frees nodes dynamically. Applications include function-call management, recursion, bracket matching, expression conversion, postfix evaluation, undo operations and depth-first search.
blocks.subject: Programming in C++ and Data Structures

blocks.text: 6. Explain the operations on a queue and circular queue.
blocks.subject: Programming in C++ and Data Structures

blocks.text: A queue inserts at the rear and removes from the front. In a simple array queue, front and rear indices track the ends. Deletions may leave unused spaces at the beginning. A circular queue treats the array as circular and wraps an index using modulo arithmetic. It reuses freed positions. Empty/full conditions must be defined carefully; one common design keeps a count, making empty count == 0 and full count == capacity.
blocks.subject: Programming in C++ and Data Structures

blocks.text: 7. Explain singly and doubly linked lists.
blocks.subject: Programming in C++ and Data Structures

blocks.text: A singly linked list node contains data and a pointer to the next node. Traversal proceeds in one direction. Insertion at the beginning is efficient because only the head pointer changes; insertion at an arbitrary position requires locating the preceding node. A doubly linked list stores both prev and next pointers, allowing traversal in both directions. It uses more memory but simplifies some deletion and reverse-traversal operations. In both forms, pointers must be updated carefully and deleted nodes must be released.
blocks.subject: Programming in C++ and Data Structures

blocks.text: 8. Explain tree traversals.
blocks.subject: Programming in C++ and Data Structures

blocks.text: For a binary tree, preorder traversal visits Root–Left–Right; inorder visits Left–Root–Right; postorder visits Left–Right–Root. In a binary search tree, inorder traversal visits keys in sorted order. Preorder is useful for recording/copying a tree structure, while postorder is useful when child subtrees must be processed before the parent, such as deletion or expression evaluation.
blocks.subject: Programming in C++ and Data Structures

blocks.text: 9. Explain graph traversal using DFS and BFS.
blocks.subject: Programming in C++ and Data Structures

blocks.text: Depth First Search (DFS) explores one path as far as possible before backtracking. It can be implemented recursively or with a stack. Breadth First Search (BFS) explores vertices level by level using a queue. Both mark visited vertices to avoid repeatedly visiting them. For an adjacency-list representation, each traversal takes O(V+E) time, where V is the number of vertices and E the number of edges.
blocks.subject: Programming in C++ and Data Structures

blocks.text: 10. Explain hashing and collision resolution.
blocks.subject: Programming in C++ and Data Structures

blocks.text: A hash function converts a key into a table index. When different keys produce the same index, a collision occurs. Separate chaining stores colliding items in a list or bucket at that index. Open addressing stores items in the table itself by searching for another position, using methods such as linear probing, quadratic probing or double hashing. A good hash function distributes keys evenly and keeps the load factor manageable.
blocks.subject: Programming in C++ and Data Structures

blocks.text: PART C – 10-MARK MODEL ANSWERS / PROGRAMS
blocks.subject: Programming in C++ and Data Structures

blocks.text: 1. C++ program demonstrating a class, object and constructor.
blocks.subject: Programming in C++ and Data Structures

blocks.text: #include <iostream> #include <string> using namespace std; class Student { private: int rollNo; string name; public: Student(int r, const string& n) : rollNo(r), name(n) {} void display() const { cout << "Roll number: " << rollNo << '\n'; cout << "Name: " << name << '\n'; } }; int main() { Student s1(101, "Anu"); s1.display(); return 0; }
blocks.subject: Programming in C++ and Data Structures

blocks.text: Explanation: Student is a class. rollNo and name are private data members. The public constructor initialises them when s1 is created. display() is a member function. The object s1 calls that function. The program uses standard C++ headers and can be compiled with a modern C++ compiler.
blocks.subject: Programming in C++ and Data Structures

blocks.text: 2. C++ program demonstrating inheritance and run-time polymorphism.
blocks.subject: Programming in C++ and Data Structures

blocks.text: #include <iostream> using namespace std; class Shape { public: virtual double area() const = 0; virtual ~Shape() = default; }; class Rectangle : public Shape { double length, breadth; public: Rectangle(double l, double b) : length(l), breadth(b) {} double area() const override { return length * breadth; } }; class Circle : public Shape { double radius; public: explicit Circle(double r) : radius(r) {} double area() const override { return 3.141592653589793 * radius * radius; } }; int main() { Rectangle r(5, 4); Circle c(3); Shape* shapes[] = {&r, &c}; for (Shape* s : shapes) cout << s->area() << '\n'; return 0; }
blocks.subject: Programming in C++ and Data Structures

blocks.text: Explanation: Rectangle and Circle inherit from Shape. The pure virtual area() makes Shape an abstract class. The call through a base-class pointer is resolved at run time and executes the appropriate derived implementation. The virtual destructor allows safe destruction through a base pointer.
blocks.subject: Programming in C++ and Data Structures

blocks.text: 3. Explain conversion of infix expression to postfix using a stack.
blocks.subject: Programming in C++ and Data Structures

blocks.text: Infix notation places operators between operands, as in A + B * C. Postfix notation places operators after their operands, as in A B C * +. Scan the infix expression from left to right. Output operands immediately. Push opening parentheses. When an operator appears, pop operators of higher precedence (and equal precedence when the operator is left-associative) before pushing the new operator. When a closing parenthesis appears, pop until the matching opening parenthesis. At the end, pop all remaining operators. For A+B*C, multiplication has higher precedence, so the postfix form is ABC*+. For (A+B)*C, the result is AB+C*. Mention that exponentiation is commonly right-associative and should be handled separately if included.
blocks.subject: Programming in C++ and Data Structures

blocks.text: 4. Explain Dijkstra's shortest-path algorithm.
blocks.subject: Programming in C++ and Data Structures

blocks.text: Assign distance zero to the source and infinity to every other vertex. Mark all vertices unvisited. Repeatedly select the unvisited vertex with the smallest tentative distance. For every adjacent vertex, test whether the route through the selected vertex is shorter; if so, update its tentative distance and predecessor. Mark the selected vertex visited. Continue until all reachable vertices are processed or the required destination is finalised. The predecessor links reconstruct the path. Dijkstra's algorithm assumes non-negative edge weights; it is not suitable for graphs containing negative-weight edges. A simple array implementation is O(V²), while a priority-queue implementation with adjacency lists is typically O((V+E) log V).
blocks.subject: Programming in C++ and Data Structures

blocks.text: 5. Explain asymptotic notations with examples.
blocks.subject: Programming in C++ and Data Structures

blocks.text: Big-O, O(f(n)), gives an asymptotic upper bound; Big-Omega, Ω(f(n)), gives a lower bound; Big-Theta, Θ(f(n)), gives a tight asymptotic bound when both upper and lower bounds match. A single loop over n elements is O(n). Two nested loops each running n times are O(n²). Binary search halves the interval at each step and is O(log n). Asymptotic notation ignores constant factors and lower-order terms, so 3n²+5n+2 is Θ(n²). It helps compare algorithm growth for large inputs.
blocks.subject: Programming in C++ and Data Structures

blocks.text: IMPORTANT PROGRAMMING POINTS
blocks.subject: Programming in C++ and Data Structures

blocks.text: • Use #include <iostream> and using namespace std; for standard C++ examples. Older textbook listings may use compiler-specific headers such as iostream.h and conio.h; those are not portable to modern compilers.

blocks.text: • A constructor has no return type. A destructor has no return type or parameters.
blocks.subject: Programming in C++ and Data Structures

blocks.text: • private members are not directly accessible outside the class.
blocks.subject: Programming in C++ and Data Structures

blocks.text: • A virtual function should be overridden with a compatible signature; use override in modern C++.
blocks.subject: Programming in C++ and Data Structures

blocks.text: • Never pop an empty stack or delete from an empty queue.
blocks.subject: Programming in C++ and Data Structures

blocks.text: • Mark graph vertices visited to avoid infinite traversal in cyclic graphs.
blocks.subject: Programming in C++ and Data Structures

blocks.text: • For algorithm questions, state the input assumptions, data structure used and time complexity where relevant.
