blocks.text: A. 2-MARK QUESTIONS WITH ANSWERS
blocks.subject: Programming in C++ and Data Structures

blocks.text: 1. Define object-oriented programming.
blocks.subject: Programming in C++ and Data Structures

blocks.text: Answer: Object-oriented programming organises a program around objects that combine data and functions. Its main concepts include classes, objects, encapsulation, abstraction, inheritance and polymorphism.
blocks.subject: Programming in C++ and Data Structures

blocks.text: 2. Distinguish class and object.
blocks.subject: Programming in C++ and Data Structures

blocks.text: Answer: A class is a user-defined blueprint/type that defines data members and functions. An object is an instance of that class created during program execution.
blocks.subject: Programming in C++ and Data Structures

blocks.text: 3. What is a constructor?
blocks.subject: Programming in C++ and Data Structures

blocks.text: Answer: A constructor is a special member function called when an object is initialised. It has the same name as the class and no return type.
blocks.subject: Programming in C++ and Data Structures

blocks.text: 4. What is a destructor?
blocks.subject: Programming in C++ and Data Structures

blocks.text: Answer: A destructor is a special member function called when an object's lifetime ends. Its name is the class name preceded by a tilde and it has no return type or parameters.
blocks.subject: Programming in C++ and Data Structures

blocks.text: 5. Define inheritance.
blocks.subject: Programming in C++ and Data Structures

blocks.text: Answer: Inheritance allows a derived class to acquire accessible members of a base class and add or modify its own features.
blocks.subject: Programming in C++ and Data Structures

blocks.text: 6. What is polymorphism?
blocks.subject: Programming in C++ and Data Structures

blocks.text: Answer: Polymorphism allows one interface or name to represent different behaviours. In C++, function/operator overloading supports compile-time polymorphism and virtual functions support run-time polymorphism.
blocks.subject: Programming in C++ and Data Structures

blocks.text: 7. Define stack.
blocks.subject: Programming in C++ and Data Structures

blocks.text: Answer: A stack is a linear data structure that follows LIFO: the last inserted item is the first removed.
blocks.subject: Programming in C++ and Data Structures

blocks.text: 8. Define queue.
blocks.subject: Programming in C++ and Data Structures

blocks.text: Answer: A queue is a linear data structure that follows FIFO: the first inserted item is the first removed.
blocks.subject: Programming in C++ and Data Structures

blocks.text: 9. What is a linked list?
blocks.subject: Programming in C++ and Data Structures

blocks.text: Answer: A linked list is a collection of nodes where each node stores data and one or more links to other nodes.
blocks.subject: Programming in C++ and Data Structures

blocks.text: 10. Define hashing.
blocks.subject: Programming in C++ and Data Structures

blocks.text: Answer: Hashing uses a hash function to map a key to an index in a hash table. A collision occurs when different keys map to the same index.
blocks.subject: Programming in C++ and Data Structures

blocks.text: B. 5-MARK QUESTIONS WITH ANSWERS
blocks.subject: Programming in C++ and Data Structures

blocks.text: 1. Explain the basic concepts of OOP.
blocks.subject: Programming in C++ and Data Structures

blocks.text: Answer:
blocks.subject: Programming in C++ and Data Structures

blocks.text: • Class: blueprint for objects.
blocks.subject: Programming in C++ and Data Structures

blocks.text: • Object: instance of a class with state and behaviour.
blocks.subject: Programming in C++ and Data Structures

blocks.text: • Encapsulation: combining data and member functions and controlling access.
blocks.subject: Programming in C++ and Data Structures

blocks.text: • Abstraction: showing essential features and hiding implementation details.
blocks.subject: Programming in C++ and Data Structures

blocks.text: • Inheritance: deriving a class from another class for reuse and extension.
blocks.subject: Programming in C++ and Data Structures

blocks.text: • Polymorphism: allowing an interface to have different behaviours.
blocks.subject: Programming in C++ and Data Structures

blocks.text: These concepts help organise complex programs and support reuse and maintenance.
blocks.subject: Programming in C++ and Data Structures

blocks.text: 2. Explain constructors and destructors.
blocks.subject: Programming in C++ and Data Structures

blocks.text: Answer:
blocks.subject: Programming in C++ and Data Structures

blocks.text: A constructor initialises an object when it is created. It has the class name and no return type. Constructors may be default, parameterised or copy constructors; they can be overloaded. A destructor uses the class name preceded by ~ and is called when the object is destroyed. It is used to release resources owned by the object. The textbook also discusses the this pointer and constructor conversion.
blocks.subject: Programming in C++ and Data Structures

blocks.text: 3. Explain the types of inheritance.
blocks.subject: Programming in C++ and Data Structures

blocks.text: Answer:
blocks.subject: Programming in C++ and Data Structures

blocks.text: • Single: one derived class has one base class.
blocks.subject: Programming in C++ and Data Structures

blocks.text: • Multilevel: inheritance occurs in a chain.
blocks.subject: Programming in C++ and Data Structures

blocks.text: • Multiple: one derived class inherits from more than one base class.
blocks.subject: Programming in C++ and Data Structures

blocks.text: • Hierarchical: multiple derived classes share one base class.
blocks.subject: Programming in C++ and Data Structures

blocks.text: • Hybrid: a combination of two or more forms.
blocks.subject: Programming in C++ and Data Structures

blocks.text: Draw a simple diagram for each form in a 5-mark answer.
blocks.subject: Programming in C++ and Data Structures

blocks.text: 4. Explain stack and queue operations.
blocks.subject: Programming in C++ and Data Structures

blocks.text: Answer:
blocks.subject: Programming in C++ and Data Structures

blocks.text: Stack operations include PUSH (insert at top), POP (remove top), PEEK/TOP (inspect top), and empty/full checks. Stack follows LIFO. Queue operations include ENQUEUE (insert at rear) and DEQUEUE (remove from front); queue follows FIFO. Both can be implemented using arrays or linked nodes. Array implementations need overflow/underflow checks; linked implementations need pointer management.
blocks.subject: Programming in C++ and Data Structures

blocks.text: 5. Explain binary tree traversals.
blocks.subject: Programming in C++ and Data Structures

blocks.text: Answer:
blocks.subject: Programming in C++ and Data Structures

blocks.text: Preorder visits Root–Left–Right (NLR). Inorder visits Left–Root–Right (LNR). Postorder visits Left–Right–Root (LRN). Use the same tree and show the visiting sequence. In a binary search tree, inorder traversal produces keys in sorted order when the tree satisfies the BST property.
blocks.subject: Programming in C++ and Data Structures

blocks.text: C. 10-MARK QUESTIONS WITH ANSWERS
blocks.subject: Programming in C++ and Data Structures

blocks.text: 1. Explain classes, objects, encapsulation and inheritance with a C++ example.
blocks.subject: Programming in C++ and Data Structures

blocks.text: Answer:
blocks.subject: Programming in C++ and Data Structures

blocks.text: A class defines data and functions; an object is an instance. Encapsulation keeps data and related operations together and uses access specifiers to control access. Inheritance derives a new class from an existing class. Example:
blocks.subject: Programming in C++ and Data Structures
Programming in C++ and Data Structures

blocks.text: The class Student inherits the protected name member and public setName function from Person. Private mark is accessed through public member functions. In the examination, explain the access specifiers and state the output.
blocks.subject: Programming in C++ and Data Structures

blocks.text: 2. Explain polymorphism and virtual functions.
blocks.subject: Programming in C++ and Data Structures

blocks.text: Answer:
blocks.subject: Programming in C++ and Data Structures

blocks.text: Polymorphism means one interface can represent different behaviours. Compile-time polymorphism is achieved through function overloading and operator overloading. Run-time polymorphism is achieved through inheritance and virtual functions. A derived class overrides a virtual function of the base class. When the function is called through a base-class pointer or reference, the derived version is selected at run time. A complete answer should include a base class, derived class, virtual declaration, overriding function and output demonstrating dynamic binding.
blocks.subject: Programming in C++ and Data Structures

blocks.text: 3. Explain linked lists, stacks and queues with operations and applications.
blocks.subject: Programming in C++ and Data Structures

blocks.text: Answer:
blocks.subject: Programming in C++ and Data Structures

blocks.text: A linked list uses nodes containing data and links. In a singly linked list each node points to the next node; in a doubly linked list each node points to both previous and next nodes. Basic operations include creation, traversal, searching, insertion, deletion and updating. A stack follows LIFO and supports PUSH/POP; applications include recursion and expression conversion. A queue follows FIFO and supports enqueue/dequeue; applications include scheduling and buffering. For full marks draw node structures and show pointer updates for insertion/deletion.
blocks.subject: Programming in C++ and Data Structures

blocks.text: 4. Explain graph traversal and Dijkstra's shortest-path algorithm.
blocks.subject: Programming in C++ and Data Structures

blocks.text: Answer:
blocks.subject: Programming in C++ and Data Structures

blocks.text: A graph contains vertices and edges and may be directed/undirected and weighted/unweighted. It can be represented using an adjacency matrix or adjacency list. DFS explores deeply before backtracking and uses recursion or a stack. BFS visits level by level using a queue. Both use a visited marker. Dijkstra's algorithm finds shortest paths from a source in a weighted graph with non-negative edge weights. Initialise source distance to zero and others to infinity; repeatedly select the unprocessed vertex with smallest tentative distance; relax its outgoing edges; mark it processed; continue until required vertices are processed.
blocks.subject: Programming in C++ and Data Structures

blocks.text: D. ADDITIONAL PRACTICE QUESTIONS
blocks.subject: Programming in C++ and Data Structures

blocks.text: 1. Distinguish data abstraction and data encapsulation. 2. Explain reference variables and C++ operators. 3. Define inline, friend and virtual functions. 4. Explain operator overloading and type conversions. 5. Describe file-stream classes and file error handling. 6. Explain asymptotic notation O, Ω and Θ. 7. Convert an infix expression to postfix using a stack. 8. Explain circular queues and their conditions. 9. Explain polynomial representation and addition using linked lists. 10. Explain hashing and collision handling. 11. Solve a tree traversal problem. 12. Apply DFS and BFS to a given graph.
blocks.subject: Programming in C++ and Data Structures

blocks.text: SUBJECT 12 – MICROPROCESSORS AND ITS APPLICATIONS (SUCA202)
blocks.subject: Microprocessors and its Applications

blocks.text: Core Paper VI | 8085 microprocessor
blocks.subject: Microprocessors and its Applications

blocks.text: A. 2-MARK QUESTIONS WITH ANSWERS
blocks.subject: Microprocessors and its Applications

blocks.text: 1. Define a microprocessor.
blocks.subject: Microprocessors and its Applications

blocks.text: Answer: A microprocessor is a programmable, clock-driven, register-based electronic device that reads instructions, processes binary data and produces results.
blocks.subject: Microprocessors and its Applications

blocks.text: 2. State the word length of the 8085.
blocks.subject: Microprocessors and its Applications

blocks.text: Answer: The 8085 is an 8-bit microprocessor.
blocks.subject: Microprocessors and its Applications

blocks.text: 3. How many address lines does the 8085 have?
blocks.subject: Microprocessors and its Applications

blocks.text: Answer: It has 16 address lines and can address 2^16 = 65,536 locations (64 KB).
blocks.subject: Microprocessors and its Applications

blocks.text: 4. What is the function of the Program Counter?
blocks.subject: Microprocessors and its Applications

blocks.text: Answer: The Program Counter holds the address of the next instruction to be fetched/executed.
blocks.subject: Microprocessors and its Applications

blocks.text: 5. What is the function of the Stack Pointer?
blocks.subject: Microprocessors and its Applications

blocks.text: Answer: The Stack Pointer holds the address of the top of the stack in memory.
blocks.subject: Microprocessors and its Applications

blocks.text: 6. Name the 8085 flags.
blocks.subject: Microprocessors and its Applications

blocks.text: Answer: Sign (S), Zero (Z), Auxiliary Carry (AC), Parity (P) and Carry (CY).
blocks.subject: Microprocessors and its Applications

blocks.text: 7. What is ALE?
blocks.subject: Microprocessors and its Applications

blocks.text: Answer: Address Latch Enable is a control signal used to latch the low-order address that shares the multiplexed AD7–AD0 lines.
blocks.subject: Microprocessors and its Applications

blocks.text: 8. Define an interrupt.
blocks.subject: Microprocessors and its Applications

blocks.text: Answer: An interrupt is a signal/event that causes the processor to suspend its normal sequence and execute an interrupt service routine, then normally resume the interrupted program.
blocks.subject: Microprocessors and its Applications

blocks.text: B. 5-MARK QUESTIONS WITH ANSWERS
blocks.subject: Microprocessors and its Applications

blocks.text: 1. Explain the three bus groups in a microprocessor system.
blocks.subject: Microprocessors and its Applications

blocks.text: Answer:
blocks.subject: Microprocessors and its Applications

blocks.text: The address bus carries the address of the memory or I/O location. It is generally unidirectional from the processor to the addressed unit. The data bus carries instructions/data and is bidirectional. The control bus carries signals coordinating read, write and other operations. Together they enable communication among CPU, memory and I/O devices.
blocks.subject: Microprocessors and its Applications

blocks.text: 2. Explain the main registers of 8085.
blocks.subject: Microprocessors and its Applications

blocks.text: Answer:
blocks.subject: Microprocessors and its Applications

blocks.text: The accumulator is used in many arithmetic and logical operations. B, C, D, E, H and L are general-purpose registers and may form selected register pairs. The Program Counter stores the next instruction address. The Stack Pointer points to the top of the stack. The flag register stores status conditions such as sign, zero, auxiliary carry, parity and carry. Draw the architecture/register diagram where required.
blocks.subject: Microprocessors and its Applications

blocks.text: 3. Explain 8085 addressing modes.
blocks.subject: Microprocessors and its Applications

blocks.text: Answer:
blocks.subject: Microprocessors and its Applications

blocks.text: • Immediate: operand is part of instruction, e.g. MVI A, 32H.
blocks.subject: Microprocessors and its Applications

blocks.text: • Register: operand is in a register, e.g. MOV A,B.
blocks.subject: Microprocessors and its Applications

blocks.text: • Direct: the memory address is specified, e.g. LDA 2050H.
blocks.subject: Microprocessors and its Applications

blocks.text: • Register indirect: a register pair holds the address, e.g. MOV A,M (HL points to the memory location).
blocks.subject: Microprocessors and its Applications

blocks.text: • Implied: operand is implied by the instruction, e.g. CMA operates on the accumulator.
blocks.subject: Microprocessors and its Applications

blocks.text: 4. Explain CALL and RET instructions.
blocks.subject: Microprocessors and its Applications

blocks.text: Answer:
blocks.subject: Microprocessors and its Applications

blocks.text: CALL transfers program control to a subroutine and saves the return address on the stack. RET returns to the saved address. The Stack Pointer is used to manage the return address. Conditional CALL/return instructions act according to the specified flag condition. Track stack operations and addresses carefully.
blocks.subject: Microprocessors and its Applications

blocks.text: C. 10-MARK QUESTIONS WITH ANSWERS
blocks.subject: Microprocessors and its Applications

blocks.text: 1. Explain the architecture and operation of the 8085 microprocessor.
blocks.subject: Microprocessors and its Applications

blocks.text: Answer:
blocks.subject: Microprocessors and its Applications

blocks.text: The 8085 is an 8-bit microprocessor with an 8-bit data bus and 16-bit address bus. Its address capacity is 64 KB. The architecture includes the accumulator, general-purpose registers, temporary registers, flag register, Program Counter, Stack Pointer, instruction register/decoder, timing and control unit, and arithmetic and logic unit. The multiplexed AD7–AD0 lines carry low-order address during the first part of a machine cycle and data later; ALE is used to latch the low-order address. A15–A8 carry the high-order address. Explain the function of each block and label the architecture diagram.
blocks.subject: Microprocessors and its Applications

blocks.text: 2. Explain the instruction set and addressing modes of 8085.
blocks.subject: Microprocessors and its Applications

blocks.text: Answer:
blocks.subject: Microprocessors and its Applications

blocks.text: The instruction set is the collection of instructions understood by the processor. Main groups include data transfer, arithmetic, logical, branching/control transfer and machine/control instructions. Examples include MOV/MVI/LXI for data transfer; ADD/SUB/INR/DCR for arithmetic; ANA/ORA/XRA/CMA/CMP for logical operations; JMP/JZ/JNZ/CALL/RET for program control; and HLT/NOP/EI/DI for control. Addressing modes include immediate, register, direct, register indirect and implied. For each instruction, verify opcode, number of bytes and flag effects in the official instruction table.
blocks.subject: Microprocessors and its Applications

blocks.text: 3. Write an 8085 program to add two 8-bit numbers stored at 2050H and 2051H and store the sum and carry at 2052H and 2053H. Answer (illustrative 8085 routine):
blocks.subject: Microprocessors and its Applications

blocks.text:
LXI H,2050H
        MOV A,M
        INX H
        ADD M
        MVI C,00H
        JNC SKIP
        MVI C,01H
SKIP:   INX H
        MOV M,A
        INX H
        MOV M,C
        HLT
blocks.subject: Microprocessors and its Applications

blocks.text: Explanation: HL points to the first operand. The first value is loaded into A. The second is added. C is cleared and set to 1 if carry is generated. The sum is stored at 2052H and carry byte at 2053H. Confirm the assembler syntax and required convention used by the study centre.
blocks.subject: Microprocessors and its Applications

blocks.text: 4. Explain 8085 interrupts and DMA.
blocks.subject: Microprocessors and its Applications

blocks.text: Answer:
blocks.subject: Microprocessors and its Applications

blocks.text: An interrupt diverts the processor to an interrupt service routine. The standard 8085 interrupts include TRAP, RST 7.5, RST 6.5, RST 5.5 and INTR. Explain priority, maskability, vector addresses and triggering as shown in the official textbook. TRAP is the highest-priority non-maskable interrupt in the standard 8085 description. DMA (Direct Memory Access) transfers data between an I/O device and memory with reduced direct CPU involvement. A DMA controller requests bus control, performs the transfer and releases the bus. Include the handshake/bus-control sequence from the prescribed text.
blocks.subject: Microprocessors and its Applications

blocks.text: D. ADDITIONAL PRACTICE
blocks.subject: Microprocessors and its Applications

blocks.text: 1. Draw and explain the 8085 pin diagram. 2. Explain ALE, RD, WR, IO/M, SID and SOD signals. 3. Write assembly programs for multi-byte addition and subtraction. 4. Explain BCD, binary, hexadecimal and ASCII code conversion. 5. Explain a modulo-10 counter and time-delay routine. 6. Explain seven-segment LED code conversion. 7. Distinguish direct (isolated) I/O and memory-mapped I/O. 8. Explain RAM/ROM interfacing and address decoding.
blocks.subject: Microprocessors and its Applications

blocks.text: SUBJECT 13 – NUMERICAL AND STATISTICAL METHODS (SUCA203)
blocks.subject: Numerical and Statistical Methods

blocks.text: Core Paper VII | Five syllabus units
blocks.subject: Numerical and Statistical Methods

blocks.text: A. 2-MARK QUESTIONS WITH ANSWERS
blocks.subject: Numerical and Statistical Methods

blocks.text: 1. Define absolute error.
blocks.subject: Numerical and Statistical Methods

blocks.text: Answer: Absolute error is the absolute difference between the true value and the approximate value: |true value − approximate value|.
blocks.subject: Numerical and Statistical Methods

blocks.text: 2. State the bisection formula.
blocks.subject: Numerical and Statistical Methods

blocks.text: Answer: The midpoint of an interval [a,b] is c=(a+b)/2. Retain the subinterval with a sign change when f is continuous.
blocks.subject: Numerical and Statistical Methods

blocks.text: 3. State the Newton-Raphson formula.
blocks.subject: Numerical and Statistical Methods

blocks.text: Answer: x_(n+1)=x_n−f(x_n)/f'(x_n).
blocks.subject: Numerical and Statistical Methods

blocks.text: 4. State Simpson's 1/3 rule.
blocks.subject: Numerical and Statistical Methods

blocks.text: Answer: For an even number of equal subintervals, I≈h/3[y₀+y_n+4(sum of odd-index interior ordinates)+2(sum of even-index interior ordinates)].
blocks.subject: Numerical and Statistical Methods

blocks.text: 5. Define arithmetic mean.
blocks.subject: Numerical and Statistical Methods

blocks.text: Answer: Arithmetic mean is the sum of observations divided by the number of observations. For frequency data, mean=Σfx/Σf.
blocks.subject: Numerical and Statistical Methods

blocks.text: 6. Define variance.
blocks.subject: Numerical and Statistical Methods

blocks.text: Answer: Variance measures the average squared deviation from the mean. Population variance is σ²=Σ(x−μ)²/N; sample variance commonly uses s²=Σ(x−x̄)²/(n−1).
blocks.subject: Numerical and Statistical Methods

blocks.text: 7. State the binomial probability formula.
blocks.subject: Numerical and Statistical Methods

blocks.text: Answer: P(X=x)=nCx p^x(1−p)^(n−x), where n is number of independent trials and p is constant probability of success.
blocks.subject: Numerical and Statistical Methods

blocks.text: 8. What is correlation?
blocks.subject: Numerical and Statistical Methods

blocks.text: Answer: Correlation measures the direction and strength of association between variables. It does not by itself prove causation.
blocks.subject: Numerical and Statistical Methods

blocks.text: B. 5-MARK QUESTIONS WITH ANSWERS
blocks.subject: Numerical and Statistical Methods

blocks.text: 1. Explain the bisection method.
blocks.subject: Numerical and Statistical Methods

blocks.text: Answer:
blocks.subject: Numerical and Statistical Methods

blocks.text: For continuous f on [a,b], start with f(a) and f(b) of opposite signs. Compute c=(a+b)/2. If f(c)=0, c is a root. Otherwise retain the half interval in which the sign change occurs. Repeat until the interval width or root error is within the required tolerance. Bisection is reliable under the sign-change condition but converges relatively slowly.
blocks.subject: Numerical and Statistical Methods

blocks.text: 2. Explain Gauss elimination and Gauss-Jordan methods.
blocks.subject: Numerical and Statistical Methods

blocks.text: Answer:
blocks.subject: Numerical and Statistical Methods

blocks.text: Gauss elimination transforms the augmented matrix into upper triangular form using elementary row operations, then obtains the unknowns by back substitution. Gauss-Jordan continues row operations until the coefficient matrix becomes the identity matrix, so the solution is read directly from the right-hand column. Partial or complete pivoting may be used to reduce numerical difficulties. Show all row operations.
blocks.subject: Numerical and Statistical Methods

blocks.text: 3. Explain trapezoidal, Simpson's 1/3 and Simpson's 3/8 rules.
blocks.subject: Numerical and Statistical Methods

blocks.text: Answer:
blocks.subject: Numerical and Statistical Methods

blocks.text: Trapezoidal rule approximates the area under a curve by trapezia: I≈h/2[y₀+y_n+2Σ(interior y)]. Simpson's 1/3 rule fits parabolic arcs and requires an even number of subintervals: I≈h/3[y₀+y_n+4Σ odd ordinates+2Σ even ordinates]. Simpson's 3/8 rule requires the number of subintervals to be a multiple of three: I≈3h/8[y₀+y_n+3Σ ordinates not multiple of 3+2Σ ordinates whose index is a multiple of 3].
blocks.subject: Numerical and Statistical Methods

blocks.text: 4. Explain the binomial and Poisson distributions.
blocks.subject: Numerical and Statistical Methods

blocks.text: Answer:
blocks.subject: Numerical and Statistical Methods

blocks.text: The binomial distribution models the number of successes in a fixed number of independent trials with constant success probability p. Its mean is np and variance np(1−p). The Poisson distribution models counts over a fixed interval under a stable event rate λ: P(X=x)=e^(−λ)λ^x/x!, with mean and variance λ. Identify the conditions before selecting a distribution.
blocks.subject: Numerical and Statistical Methods

blocks.text: C. 10-MARK QUESTIONS WITH ANSWERS
blocks.subject: Numerical and Statistical Methods

blocks.text: 1. Find an approximate root of x²−2=0 using bisection on [1,2] for three iterations.
blocks.subject: Numerical and Statistical Methods

blocks.text: Answer:
blocks.subject: Numerical and Statistical Methods

blocks.text: f(x)=x²−2. f(1)=−1 and f(2)=2, so a root is bracketed. Iteration 1: c₁=(1+2)/2=1.5. f(1.5)=0.25, so interval becomes [1,1.5]. Iteration 2: c₂=(1+1.5)/2=1.25. f(1.25)=−0.4375, so interval becomes [1.25,1.5]. Iteration 3: c₃=(1.25+1.5)/2=1.375. f(1.375)=−0.109375, so interval becomes [1.375,1.5]. After three iterations the root is bracketed in [1.375,1.5]. Continue the process for greater accuracy. The exact root is √2≈1.4142, but the three-iteration interval is the answer requested by this exercise.
blocks.subject: Numerical and Statistical Methods

blocks.text: 2. Explain mean, median, mode and standard deviation for frequency data.
blocks.subject: Numerical and Statistical Methods

blocks.text: Answer:
blocks.subject: Numerical and Statistical Methods

blocks.text: For a frequency distribution with class midpoint x and frequency f, arithmetic mean is x̄=Σfx/Σf. Median is the central value; for grouped continuous data use Median=L+[(N/2−cf)/f_m]h, where L is the lower boundary of the median class, cf is cumulative frequency before that class, f_m is its frequency and h is class width. The modal class has the highest frequency; Mode=L+[(f₁−f₀)/(2f₁−f₀−f₂)]h. Standard deviation is the positive square root of variance. For population data σ²=Σf(x−μ)²/N. Show the frequency table and all required columns.
blocks.subject: Numerical and Statistical Methods

blocks.text: 3. Explain tests of significance and the chi-square test.
blocks.subject: Numerical and Statistical Methods

blocks.text: Answer:
blocks.subject: Numerical and Statistical Methods

blocks.text: A significance test evaluates evidence about a population claim. State the null hypothesis H₀ and alternative H₁, choose a significance level α, identify the test statistic and assumptions, calculate it, compare with a critical value or p-value, and state the conclusion in context. A Type I error rejects a true H₀; a Type II error fails to reject a false H₀. The Pearson chi-square statistic is χ²=Σ(O−E)²/E, where O is observed frequency and E is expected frequency. It is used in goodness-of-fit and contingency-table/independence analysis. For an r×c independence table, df=(r−1)(c−1). Check expected-frequency conditions and use the correct degrees of freedom.
blocks.subject: Numerical and Statistical Methods

blocks.text: D. ADDITIONAL NUMERICAL PRACTICE
blocks.subject: Numerical and Statistical Methods

blocks.text: 1. Solve roots by Regula Falsi, Newton-Raphson, Secant, Muller's and Bairstow's methods. 2. Solve simultaneous equations by inverse matrix, Gauss-Jordan, LU and Gauss-Seidel methods. 3. Apply Romberg integration. 4. Solve first-order ODEs using Euler, Taylor, RK2, RK4 and predictor-corrector methods. 5. Construct frequency distributions and diagrams. 6. Calculate mean, median, mode, GM, HM, range, mean deviation, variance, standard deviation, moments, skewness and kurtosis. 7. Solve conditional probability, expectation, binomial, Poisson and hypergeometric problems. 8. Calculate Pearson, Spearman, multiple and partial correlation; fit regression lines. 9. Solve chi-square, t-test and F-test problems.
blocks.subject: Numerical and Statistical Methods

blocks.text: SUBJECT 14 – PROGRAMMING IN C++ USING DATA STRUCTURES LAB (SUCA204)
blocks.subject: C++ Data Structures Lab

blocks.text: Core Paper VIII | Practical III
blocks.subject: C++ Data Structures Lab

blocks.text: A. 2-MARK QUESTIONS WITH ANSWERS
blocks.subject: C++ Data Structures Lab

blocks.text: 1. What is stack overflow?
blocks.subject: C++ Data Structures Lab

blocks.text: Answer: Stack overflow occurs when an insertion is attempted on a full stack in a bounded array implementation.
blocks.subject: C++ Data Structures Lab

blocks.text: 2. What is stack underflow?
blocks.subject: C++ Data Structures Lab

blocks.text: Answer: Stack underflow occurs when POP is attempted on an empty stack.
blocks.subject: C++ Data Structures Lab

blocks.text: 3. What is postfix notation?
blocks.subject: C++ Data Structures Lab

blocks.text: Answer: Postfix notation places an operator after its operands. For example, infix A+B is written AB+ in postfix form.
blocks.subject: C++ Data Structures Lab

blocks.text: 4. Why is a queue called FIFO?
blocks.subject: C++ Data Structures Lab

blocks.text: Answer: Because the first item inserted is the first item removed.
blocks.subject: C++ Data Structures Lab

blocks.text: 5. What is DFS?
blocks.subject: C++ Data Structures Lab

blocks.text: Answer: Depth First Search explores a graph along one path as deeply as possible before backtracking. It can be implemented using recursion or a stack.
blocks.subject: C++ Data Structures Lab

blocks.text: 6. What is BFS?
blocks.subject: C++ Data Structures Lab

blocks.text: Answer: Breadth First Search visits vertices level by level and commonly uses a queue.
blocks.subject: C++ Data Structures Lab

blocks.text: B. 5-MARK QUESTIONS WITH ANSWERS
blocks.subject: C++ Data Structures Lab

blocks.text: 1. Explain PUSH and POP operations using an array stack.
blocks.subject: C++ Data Structures Lab

blocks.text: Answer:
blocks.subject: C++ Data Structures Lab

blocks.text: Maintain top=-1 for an empty stack. PUSH checks whether top equals capacity−1. If full, report overflow; otherwise increment top and store the value. POP checks whether top equals −1. If empty, report underflow; otherwise read data[top] and decrement top. Both operations take constant time in a standard array implementation.
blocks.subject: C++ Data Structures Lab

blocks.text: 2. Explain infix-to-postfix conversion.
blocks.subject: C++ Data Structures Lab

blocks.text: Answer:
blocks.subject: C++ Data Structures Lab

blocks.text: Scan the expression from left to right. Send operands directly to the output. Push opening brackets. For an operator, pop operators of higher precedence (and equal precedence where associativity requires) before pushing it. On a closing bracket, pop until the matching opening bracket. At the end, pop the remaining operators. Show the stack and output after each symbol.
blocks.subject: C++ Data Structures Lab

blocks.text: 3. Explain DFS and BFS.
blocks.subject: C++ Data Structures Lab

blocks.text: Answer:
blocks.subject: C++ Data Structures Lab

blocks.text: DFS marks a vertex visited, explores an unvisited neighbour recursively or using a stack, and backtracks when no unvisited neighbour remains. BFS marks the start vertex, enqueues it, then repeatedly dequeues a vertex and enqueues each unvisited neighbour. Both require visited tracking and can be extended to disconnected graphs by starting another traversal at each unvisited vertex.
blocks.subject: C++ Data Structures Lab

blocks.text: C. 10-MARK PRACTICAL QUESTIONS WITH ANSWERS
blocks.subject: C++ Data Structures Lab

blocks.text: 1. Write a C++ program to implement a stack using an array.
blocks.subject: C++ Data Structures Lab

blocks.text: Answer:
blocks.subject: C++ Data Structures Lab
C++ Data Structures Lab

blocks.text: Output: 20. Explain top initialisation, overflow check, insertion and removal.
blocks.subject: C++ Data Structures Lab

blocks.text: 2. Explain polynomial addition using linked representation.
blocks.subject: C++ Data Structures Lab

blocks.text: Answer:
blocks.subject: C++ Data Structures Lab

blocks.text: Represent each term as a node containing coefficient, exponent and next pointer. Keep terms in descending exponent order. Compare the current terms of two polynomials. If exponents match, add coefficients and append the combined term. If one exponent is greater, copy that term and advance its pointer. Continue until one list ends, then append the remaining terms. Remove zero-coefficient terms if required. Draw the node structure and show one example.
blocks.subject: C++ Data Structures Lab

blocks.text: 3. Explain binary tree traversals and graph searching practicals.
blocks.subject: C++ Data Structures Lab

blocks.text: Answer:
blocks.subject: C++ Data Structures Lab

blocks.text: For a linked binary tree, each node contains data, left pointer and right pointer. Preorder is Root–Left–Right, Inorder is Left–Root–Right and Postorder is Left–Right–Root. For graphs, DFS uses recursion/stack; BFS uses a queue. Mark vertices visited, process neighbours in the required order and include all components if the graph is disconnected. Show the sample graph/tree and resulting sequence.
blocks.subject: C++ Data Structures Lab

blocks.text: SUBJECT 15 – FINANCIAL ACCOUNTING (SUCA205)
blocks.subject: Financial Accounting

blocks.text: Non-Major Elective I | Five syllabus units; six textbook lessons
blocks.subject: Financial Accounting

blocks.text: A. 2-MARK QUESTIONS WITH ANSWERS
blocks.subject: Financial Accounting

blocks.text: 1. Define accounting.
blocks.subject: Financial Accounting

blocks.text: Answer: Accounting is the process of identifying, measuring, recording, classifying, summarising and communicating economic information to users for informed decisions.
blocks.subject: Financial Accounting

blocks.text: 2. State the accounting equation.
blocks.subject: Financial Accounting

blocks.text: Answer: Assets = Liabilities + Owner's Equity (Capital).
blocks.subject: Financial Accounting

blocks.text: 3. State the three traditional classes of accounts.
blocks.subject: Financial Accounting

blocks.text: Answer: Personal accounts, real accounts and nominal accounts.
blocks.subject: Financial Accounting

blocks.text: 4. What is a Journal?
blocks.subject: Financial Accounting

blocks.text: Answer: A Journal is the chronological book of original entry in which transactions are first recorded with debit and credit aspects and a narration.
blocks.subject: Financial Accounting

blocks.text: 5. What is a Ledger?
blocks.subject: Financial Accounting

blocks.text: Answer: A Ledger is the principal book of accounts containing separate accounts to which transactions are posted from the Journal or subsidiary books.
blocks.subject: Financial Accounting

blocks.text: 6. Define Trial Balance.
blocks.subject: Financial Accounting

blocks.text: Answer: A Trial Balance is a statement of ledger balances on a particular date, prepared to check the arithmetical agreement of debit and credit balances.
blocks.subject: Financial Accounting

blocks.text: 7. Define depreciation.
blocks.subject: Financial Accounting

blocks.text: Answer: Depreciation is the gradual and continuing reduction in the value/book amount of a fixed asset due to use, passage of time, obsolescence or other causes.
blocks.subject: Financial Accounting

blocks.text: 8. Define Single Entry System.
blocks.subject: Financial Accounting

blocks.text: Answer: Single Entry System is an incomplete method of bookkeeping in which both aspects of every transaction are not recorded systematically.
blocks.subject: Financial Accounting

blocks.text: B. 5-MARK QUESTIONS WITH ANSWERS
blocks.subject: Financial Accounting

blocks.text: 1. Explain the objectives of accounting.
blocks.subject: Financial Accounting

blocks.text: Answer:
blocks.subject: Financial Accounting

blocks.text: Accounting maintains systematic records of financial transactions, helps ascertain profit or loss, shows financial position, provides information to investors/creditors/managers and other users, and supports planning and control. It helps users make investment, credit and business decisions. The accounting process identifies, measures, records, classifies, summarises and communicates economic events.
blocks.subject: Financial Accounting

blocks.text: 2. Explain the rules of debit and credit.
blocks.subject: Financial Accounting

blocks.text: Answer:
blocks.subject: Financial Accounting

blocks.text: Traditional rules:
blocks.subject: Financial Accounting

blocks.text: • Personal Account: Debit the receiver; Credit the giver.
blocks.subject: Financial Accounting

blocks.text: • Real Account: Debit what comes in; Credit what goes out.
blocks.subject: Financial Accounting

blocks.text: • Nominal Account: Debit expenses and losses; Credit incomes and gains.
blocks.subject: Financial Accounting

blocks.text: Under the accounting-equation approach, increases in assets and expenses are debits; increases in liabilities, capital and revenue are credits. Decreases are the reverse. Every transaction must have equal debit and credit amounts.
blocks.subject: Financial Accounting

blocks.text: 3. Explain the purpose of Trading Account, Profit and Loss Account and Balance Sheet.
blocks.subject: Financial Accounting

blocks.text: Answer:
blocks.subject: Financial Accounting

blocks.text: Trading Account determines gross profit/loss from buying and selling goods. Profit and Loss Account determines net profit/loss after indirect expenses and other incomes. Balance Sheet shows assets, liabilities and capital on a particular date. Together, they summarise the operating result and financial position of a sole-trading concern.
blocks.subject: Financial Accounting

blocks.text: 4. Distinguish Straight Line and Written Down Value depreciation.
blocks.subject: Financial Accounting

blocks.text: Answer:
blocks.subject: Financial Accounting

blocks.text: Straight Line Method charges a fixed amount each year, calculated on original cost less residual value over useful life. Written Down Value Method charges a fixed percentage on the opening reduced book value, so the annual amount normally decreases over time. SLM uses original cost as its base; WDV uses the opening WDV.
blocks.subject: Financial Accounting

blocks.text: 5. Explain the Statement of Affairs method.
blocks.subject: Financial Accounting

blocks.text: Answer:
blocks.subject: Financial Accounting

blocks.text: Prepare Statement of Affairs at the beginning and end of the period. Capital equals assets minus outside liabilities. Then calculate profit: Closing Capital + Drawings − Additional Capital − Opening Capital. Drawings are added back because they reduce closing capital; additional capital is deducted because it is not earned profit.
blocks.subject: Financial Accounting

blocks.text: C. 10-MARK QUESTIONS WITH ANSWERS
blocks.subject: Financial Accounting

blocks.text: 1. Journalise the following transactions: started business with cash Rs.50,000; purchased furniture for cash Rs.5,000; purchased goods on credit from Ravi Rs.8,000; paid salary Rs.2,000.
blocks.subject: Financial Accounting

blocks.text: Answer:
blocks.subject: Financial Accounting

blocks.text: 1. Cash A/c Dr. 50,000 To Capital A/c 50,000 (Being business started with cash.) 2. Furniture A/c Dr. 5,000 To Cash A/c 5,000 (Being furniture purchased for cash.) 3. Purchases A/c Dr. 8,000 To Ravi A/c 8,000 (Being goods purchased on credit.) 4. Salary A/c Dr. 2,000 To Cash A/c 2,000 (Being salary paid.) Note: furniture is a fixed asset, not goods purchased for resale; therefore debit Furniture A/c, not Purchases A/c.
blocks.subject: Financial Accounting

blocks.text: 2. Prepare the key calculations for Final Accounts from the following data: Net Sales Rs.1,00,000; Opening Stock Rs.10,000; Net Purchases Rs.60,000; Direct Wages Rs.5,000; Closing Stock Rs.15,000; Indirect Expenses Rs.12,000; Other Income Rs.2,000.
blocks.subject: Financial Accounting

blocks.text: Answer:
blocks.subject: Financial Accounting

blocks.text: Cost of Goods Sold = Opening Stock + Net Purchases + Direct Wages − Closing Stock = 10,000 + 60,000 + 5,000 − 15,000 = Rs.60,000. Gross Profit = Net Sales − Cost of Goods Sold = 1,00,000 − 60,000 = Rs.40,000. Net Profit = Gross Profit + Other Income − Indirect Expenses = 40,000 + 2,000 − 12,000 = Rs.30,000. In the full answer, prepare Trading A/c, Profit and Loss A/c and Balance Sheet in the format prescribed by the textbook. Apply all adjustments with their two effects.
blocks.subject: Financial Accounting

blocks.text: 3. Calculate depreciation under Straight Line Method and Written Down Value Method.
blocks.subject: Financial Accounting

blocks.text: Answer:
blocks.subject: Financial Accounting

blocks.text: Given cost Rs.25,000, residual value Rs.5,000, useful life 10 years: SLM annual depreciation = (25,000−5,000)/10 = Rs.2,000. SLM rate = 2,000/25,000×100 = 8% of original cost. For WDV at 10%: Year 1: 25,000×10%=2,500; closing WDV=22,500. Year 2: 22,500×10%=2,250; closing WDV=20,250. Year 3: 20,250×10%=2,025; closing WDV=18,225. Clearly state which method is used. For part-year acquisition or disposal, apply the time fraction specified in the question.
blocks.subject: Financial Accounting

blocks.text: 4. Explain Departmental Accounts and interdepartmental transfers.
blocks.subject: Financial Accounting

blocks.text: Answer:
blocks.subject: Financial Accounting

blocks.text: Departmental accounts prepare separate Trading and Profit and Loss Accounts for departments to determine their individual results and compare performance. Direct expenses are charged to the department that incurs them. Common expenses are apportioned using a suitable basis such as floor area, machine value, meter readings, wages, sales or time spent by a manager. Where departments transfer goods at selling price, closing stock may contain unrealised internal profit. A stock reserve is created to remove that unrealised profit from the business's overall result. Expenses that cannot be allocated reliably may be shown in a General P&L Account as the textbook directs.
blocks.subject: Financial Accounting

blocks.text: D. ACCOUNTING PRACTICE / NUMERICAL PRIORITIES
blocks.subject: Financial Accounting

blocks.text: 1. Journalise transactions using personal, real and nominal account rules. 2. Post entries to Ledger accounts and balance them. 3. Prepare a Trial Balance. 4. Prepare single-, two- and three-column Cash Books. 5. Prepare Trading A/c, P&L A/c and Balance Sheet with closing stock, outstanding/prepaid expenses, accrued income, income received in advance, depreciation, bad debts and provisions. 6. Apportion common departmental expenses using the basis supplied. 7. Calculate stock reserve on unsold interdepartmental transfers. 8. Prepare Machinery/Asset Account under SLM and WDV, including part-year acquisition/disposal. 9. Calculate profit by Statement of Affairs method.
blocks.subject: Financial Accounting

blocks.text: E. IMPORTANT SYLLABUS NOTE
blocks.subject: Financial Accounting

blocks.text: The SUCA205 printed syllabus states that Single Entry numerical problems are on the Statement of Affairs method only. The textbook also explains a Conversion Method, but prioritise Statement of Affairs calculations for numerical practice unless the official examination instructions state otherwise.
blocks.subject: Financial Accounting
