blocks.text: SUBJECT 1 – FUNDAMENTALS OF DIGITAL COMPUTERS (SUCA101)
blocks.subject: Fundamentals of Digital Computers

blocks.text: UNIT I – FUNDAMENTALS OF COMPUTERS
blocks.subject: Fundamentals of Digital Computers

blocks.text: 2-MARK QUESTIONS
blocks.subject: Fundamentals of Digital Computers

blocks.text: 1. What are the three basic units of a computer system?
blocks.subject: Fundamentals of Digital Computers

blocks.text: Answer: The basic units are the Input Unit, Central Processing Unit (CPU) and Output Unit. The CPU performs processing and control; memory/storage supports the system.
blocks.subject: Fundamentals of Digital Computers

blocks.text: 2. What is the function of the Arithmetic Logic Unit?
blocks.subject: Fundamentals of Digital Computers

blocks.text: Answer: The ALU performs arithmetic operations such as addition and subtraction and logical operations such as AND, OR, NOT and comparison.
blocks.subject: Fundamentals of Digital Computers

blocks.text: 3. What is a control unit?
blocks.subject: Fundamentals of Digital Computers

blocks.text: Answer: The Control Unit directs and coordinates computer operations. It interprets instructions and issues control signals to other units.
blocks.subject: Fundamentals of Digital Computers

blocks.text: 4. What is machine language?
blocks.subject: Fundamentals of Digital Computers

blocks.text: Answer: Machine language is the binary-coded instruction language directly understood and executed by the processor.
blocks.subject: Fundamentals of Digital Computers

blocks.text: 5. What is an assembler?
blocks.subject: Fundamentals of Digital Computers

blocks.text: Answer: An assembler translates an assembly-language program written with mnemonics into machine code.
blocks.subject: Fundamentals of Digital Computers

blocks.text: 5-MARK QUESTIONS
blocks.subject: Fundamentals of Digital Computers

blocks.text: 1. Distinguish system software and application software.
blocks.subject: Fundamentals of Digital Computers

blocks.text: Answer: System software manages computer resources and provides the platform for other programs. Examples include operating systems, language translators and system utilities. Application software performs user-oriented tasks such as word processing, spreadsheet calculation and accounting. System software supports general system operation; application software solves a particular user problem.
blocks.subject: Fundamentals of Digital Computers

blocks.text: 2. Explain the main functions of an operating system.
blocks.subject: Fundamentals of Digital Computers

blocks.text: Answer: The operating system manages processes, memory, files and input/output devices. It schedules CPU time, allocates memory, organises files, controls peripheral access, provides a user interface and supports security and user permissions. These services allow application programs to use hardware without directly controlling every device operation.
blocks.subject: Fundamentals of Digital Computers

blocks.text: 3. Compare machine, assembly and high-level languages.
blocks.subject: Fundamentals of Digital Computers

blocks.text: Answer: Machine language uses binary codes and is directly executed by the processor. Assembly language uses mnemonic instructions and symbolic addresses and is translated by an assembler. High-level languages use more human-readable statements and are translated by a compiler or interpreter. Machine language is hardware-dependent; high-level languages generally offer better portability and readability.
blocks.subject: Fundamentals of Digital Computers

blocks.text: 10-MARK QUESTIONS
blocks.subject: Fundamentals of Digital Computers

blocks.text: 1. Explain computer generations and the development of computer technology.
blocks.subject: Fundamentals of Digital Computers

blocks.text: Answer: The textbook organises computer development into generations based on the major electronic technology used. First-generation systems used vacuum tubes; second-generation systems used transistors; third-generation systems used integrated circuits; fourth-generation systems used microprocessors. Fifth-generation descriptions commonly refer to advanced processing and artificial-intelligence-oriented systems. In an examination answer, use the exact dates, examples and characteristics appearing in the official lesson. Compare generations by size, speed, reliability, heat/power, cost and programming facilities. Conclude that successive generations increased processing capability while reducing physical size and improving reliability.
blocks.subject: Fundamentals of Digital Computers

blocks.text: 2. Explain the functions and types of operating systems.
blocks.subject: Fundamentals of Digital Computers

blocks.text: Answer: An operating system acts as an intermediary between user/application programs and hardware. Its functions include process scheduling, memory allocation, file-system management, device control, input/output coordination, security and interface services. Types described in computer textbooks include batch systems, multiprogramming systems, time-sharing systems, multiprocessing systems and real-time systems. A batch system processes groups of jobs; a time-sharing system shares CPU time among users/tasks; multiprogramming keeps several jobs available to improve CPU utilisation; multiprocessing uses more than one processor; and real-time systems are designed to respond within specified timing constraints. Add the textbook's classifications and examples.
blocks.subject: Fundamentals of Digital Computers

blocks.text: UNIT II – NUMBER SYSTEMS, ARITHMETIC, COMPLEMENTS, CODES AND GATES
blocks.subject: Fundamentals of Digital Computers

blocks.text: 2-MARK QUESTIONS WITH ANSWERS
blocks.subject: Fundamentals of Digital Computers

blocks.text: 1. Convert (245)10 into binary.
blocks.subject: Fundamentals of Digital Computers

blocks.text: Answer: Repeated division by 2 gives remainders 1,0,1,0,1,1,1,1 when read upwards. Therefore (245)10 = (11110101)2.
blocks.subject: Fundamentals of Digital Computers

blocks.text: 2. Convert (7B)16 into decimal.
blocks.subject: Fundamentals of Digital Computers

blocks.text: 3. Convert (110101.101)2 into decimal.
blocks.subject: Fundamentals of Digital Computers

blocks.text: Answer: Integer part = 32+16+4+1 = 53. Fractional part = 1/2 + 0/4 + 1/8 = 0.625. Total = 53.625.
blocks.subject: Fundamentals of Digital Computers

blocks.text: 4. State the binary addition rule for 1+1.
blocks.subject: Fundamentals of Digital Computers

blocks.text: Answer: 1+1 = 10 in binary; write 0 and carry 1 to the next column.
blocks.subject: Fundamentals of Digital Computers

blocks.text: 5. What is BCD?
blocks.subject: Fundamentals of Digital Computers

blocks.text: Answer: Binary Coded Decimal represents each decimal digit separately using a four-bit binary code. For example, decimal 59 is represented as 0101 1001 in 8421 BCD.
blocks.subject: Fundamentals of Digital Computers

blocks.text: 6. What is Gray code?
blocks.subject: Fundamentals of Digital Computers

blocks.text: Answer: Gray code is a non-weighted code in which two successive code words differ in only one bit. It reduces ambiguity during transitions.
blocks.subject: Fundamentals of Digital Computers

blocks.text: 7. Why are complements used in digital arithmetic?
blocks.subject: Fundamentals of Digital Computers

blocks.text: Answer: Complements simplify subtraction and the representation of negative numbers in digital systems by converting subtraction into addition-based procedures.
blocks.subject: Fundamentals of Digital Computers

blocks.text: 5-MARK QUESTIONS WITH ANSWERS
blocks.subject: Fundamentals of Digital Computers

blocks.text: 1. Explain decimal-to-binary conversion with an example.
blocks.subject: Fundamentals of Digital Computers

blocks.text: Answer: Divide the decimal integer repeatedly by 2, record each remainder, and read the remainders from bottom to top. Example: 25÷2=12 r1; 12÷2=6 r0; 6÷2=3 r0; 3÷2=1 r1; 1÷2=0 r1. Hence (25)10=(11001)2. For a fraction, repeatedly multiply the fractional part by 2 and record the integer parts in order.
blocks.subject: Fundamentals of Digital Computers

blocks.text: 2. Explain 1's complement and 2's complement.
blocks.subject: Fundamentals of Digital Computers

blocks.text: Answer: 1's complement is obtained by changing all 0s to 1s and 1s to 0s. 2's complement is obtained by adding 1 to the 1's complement. Example in 8 bits: 00010110 becomes 11101001 in 1's complement and 11101010 in 2's complement. The bit width must remain fixed during the operation.
blocks.subject: Fundamentals of Digital Computers

blocks.text: 3. Explain BCD addition.
blocks.subject: Fundamentals of Digital Computers

blocks.text: Answer: Add the four-bit BCD digits as binary. If a digit result exceeds 1001 (9), or a carry is generated from the four-bit digit, add 0110 (decimal 6) to correct the digit. Propagate any carry to the next decimal digit. In the examination, show each nibble and the correction step.
blocks.subject: Fundamentals of Digital Computers

blocks.text: 4. Explain universal gates.
blocks.subject: Fundamentals of Digital Computers

blocks.text: Answer: NAND and NOR are called universal gates because any Boolean function can be implemented using only NAND gates or only NOR gates. NOT is obtained by joining the inputs of a NAND/NOR gate; AND/OR can then be formed using De Morgan's laws and combinations of these gates.
blocks.subject: Fundamentals of Digital Computers

blocks.text: 10-MARK QUESTIONS WITH ANSWERS
blocks.subject: Fundamentals of Digital Computers

blocks.text: 1. Explain number-system conversion methods and solve examples.
blocks.subject: Fundamentals of Digital Computers

blocks.text: Answer: A positional number is expanded as a sum of digit×base-power terms. To convert a base-b number to decimal, multiply each digit by its positional weight and add. To convert a decimal integer to base-b, repeatedly divide by b and read remainders upwards. To convert fractions, repeatedly multiply the fraction by the target base. Binary-to-octal conversion groups bits in threes; binary-to-hexadecimal groups bits in fours. Examples: (245)10=(11110101)2; (7B)16=(123)10; (110101.101)2=(53.625)10. Always show the base as a subscript and preserve the radix point.
blocks.subject: Fundamentals of Digital Computers

blocks.text: 2. Explain logic gates with truth tables and applications.
blocks.subject: Fundamentals of Digital Computers

blocks.text: Answer: AND gives 1 only when all inputs are 1; OR gives 1 when at least one input is 1; NOT complements one input. NAND and NOR are complements of AND and OR. XOR gives 1 when two inputs differ; XNOR gives 1 when they are equal. Draw symbols and truth tables for every gate. Mention that gates are building blocks for arithmetic circuits, control circuits, comparison and data selection.
blocks.subject: Fundamentals of Digital Computers

blocks.text: UNIT III – BOOLEAN ALGEBRA AND SIMPLIFICATION
blocks.subject: Fundamentals of Digital Computers

blocks.text: 2-MARK QUESTIONS
blocks.subject: Fundamentals of Digital Computers

blocks.text: 1. State the identity laws of Boolean algebra.
blocks.subject: Fundamentals of Digital Computers

blocks.text: Answer: A+0=A and A·1=A.
blocks.subject: Fundamentals of Digital Computers

blocks.text: 2. State the absorption laws.
blocks.subject: Fundamentals of Digital Computers

blocks.text: Answer: A+AB=A and A(A+B)=A.
blocks.subject: Fundamentals of Digital Computers

blocks.text: 3. What is a minterm?
blocks.subject: Fundamentals of Digital Computers

blocks.text: Answer: A minterm is a product term containing every variable exactly once, either complemented or uncomplemented. It is 1 for exactly one input combination.
blocks.subject: Fundamentals of Digital Computers

blocks.text: 4. What is a maxterm?
blocks.subject: Fundamentals of Digital Computers

blocks.text: Answer: A maxterm is a sum term containing every variable exactly once. It is 0 for exactly one input combination.
blocks.subject: Fundamentals of Digital Computers

blocks.text: 5. What is a prime implicant?
blocks.subject: Fundamentals of Digital Computers

blocks.text: Answer: A prime implicant is a product term that cannot be combined further to eliminate another variable while remaining an implicant of the function.
blocks.subject: Fundamentals of Digital Computers

blocks.text: 5-MARK QUESTIONS
blocks.subject: Fundamentals of Digital Computers

blocks.text: 1. Explain the principal laws of Boolean algebra.
blocks.subject: Fundamentals of Digital Computers

blocks.text: Answer: Identity, null, idempotent, complement, involution, commutative, associative, distributive, absorption and De Morgan's laws are used to simplify expressions. Write each law in both OR and AND forms where applicable. For example, A+A'=1, AA'=0, A+AB=A, and (A+B)'=A'B'.
blocks.subject: Fundamentals of Digital Computers

blocks.text: 2. Explain the steps in K-map simplification.
blocks.subject: Fundamentals of Digital Computers

blocks.text: Answer: Draw a K-map for the number of variables, label rows/columns in Gray-code order, enter the function's minterms, group adjacent 1s in powers of two, form the largest groups possible, allow edge wrap-around and overlapping when useful, then write the variables that remain constant in each group. Verify the resulting expression with the original truth table.
blocks.subject: Fundamentals of Digital Computers

blocks.text: 3. Describe the tabulation method.
blocks.subject: Fundamentals of Digital Computers

blocks.text: Answer: List minterms in binary and group them by the number of 1s. Compare terms from neighbouring groups and combine terms differing in one bit. Repeat until no further combinations are possible. Uncombined terms are prime implicants. Prepare a prime-implicant chart and choose essential prime implicants plus any additional terms needed to cover all minterms.
blocks.subject: Fundamentals of Digital Computers

blocks.text: 10-MARK QUESTIONS
blocks.subject: Fundamentals of Digital Computers

blocks.text: 1. Simplify F(A,B,C)=Σm(1,3,5,7) using a K-map.
blocks.subject: Fundamentals of Digital Computers

blocks.text: Answer: Write the three-variable K-map and enter 1 in cells 1, 3, 5 and 7. These four cells form one group of four. In the corresponding binary minterms, C=1 throughout while A and B vary. Therefore the simplified function is F=C. In a university answer, draw the map, mark the group and show the variable that remains constant.
blocks.subject: Fundamentals of Digital Computers

blocks.text: 2. Explain the McCluskey tabulation method with its stages.
blocks.subject: Fundamentals of Digital Computers

blocks.text: Answer: The method is a systematic Boolean minimisation procedure. Convert minterms to binary; group by number of 1s; compare adjacent groups; combine terms that differ in one bit by replacing the differing bit with a dash; mark terms that have been combined; repeat the process; collect prime implicants; form the prime-implicant chart; identify essential prime implicants and select the minimum cover. Demonstrate each stage with the example used in the textbook.
blocks.subject: Fundamentals of Digital Computers

blocks.text: UNIT IV – SEQUENTIAL LOGIC
blocks.subject: Fundamentals of Digital Computers

blocks.text: 2-MARK QUESTIONS
blocks.subject: Fundamentals of Digital Computers

blocks.text: 1. What is a sequential circuit?
blocks.subject: Fundamentals of Digital Computers

blocks.text: Answer: A sequential circuit is a logic circuit whose output depends on current inputs and the stored previous state.
blocks.subject: Fundamentals of Digital Computers

blocks.text: 2. What is the race-around condition in a JK flip-flop?
blocks.subject: Fundamentals of Digital Computers

blocks.text: Answer: In a level-triggered JK flip-flop, when J=K=1 and the clock pulse is too wide, the output may toggle repeatedly during one clock pulse. Master-slave or edge-triggered designs avoid this problem.
blocks.subject: Fundamentals of Digital Computers

blocks.text: 3. What is a shift register?
blocks.subject: Fundamentals of Digital Computers

blocks.text: Answer: A shift register is a group of flip-flops that stores binary data and shifts the stored bits left or right when clock pulses are applied.
blocks.subject: Fundamentals of Digital Computers

blocks.text: 4. Distinguish asynchronous and synchronous counters.
blocks.subject: Fundamentals of Digital Computers

blocks.text: Answer: In an asynchronous counter, the output of one flip-flop clocks the next stage. In a synchronous counter, all flip-flops receive a common clock.
blocks.subject: Fundamentals of Digital Computers

blocks.text: 5. How many flip-flops are required for a MOD-16 counter?
blocks.subject: Fundamentals of Digital Computers

blocks.text: Answer: Four flip-flops are required because 2^4=16 states.
blocks.subject: Fundamentals of Digital Computers

blocks.text: 5-MARK QUESTIONS
blocks.subject: Fundamentals of Digital Computers

blocks.text: 1. Explain the operation of RS and JK flip-flops.
blocks.subject: Fundamentals of Digital Computers

blocks.text: Answer: An RS flip-flop has Set and Reset inputs that control the stored bit; one input combination may be invalid or restricted depending on the gate implementation. A JK flip-flop has J and K inputs. J=0,K=0 holds; J=0,K=1 resets; J=1,K=0 sets; J=1,K=1 toggles at the active clock event. Draw the textbook truth/characteristic tables.
blocks.subject: Fundamentals of Digital Computers

blocks.text: 2. Explain registers and their types.
blocks.subject: Fundamentals of Digital Computers

blocks.text: Answer: A register stores a group of binary bits using flip-flops. Shift-register forms include serial-in serial-out, serial-in parallel-out, parallel-in serial-out and parallel-in parallel-out. Explain the data-entry method, direction of shifting and output form for each type with a labelled diagram.
blocks.subject: Fundamentals of Digital Computers

blocks.text: 3. Explain ripple and synchronous counters.
blocks.subject: Fundamentals of Digital Computers

blocks.text: Answer: A ripple counter uses the output of one flip-flop to trigger the next, so propagation delay accumulates. A synchronous counter applies the clock simultaneously to all flip-flops, with combinational logic determining the next state. Synchronous designs are generally faster but require more logic.
blocks.subject: Fundamentals of Digital Computers

blocks.text: 10-MARK QUESTIONS
blocks.subject: Fundamentals of Digital Computers

blocks.text: 1. Explain RS, JK, D and T flip-flops with truth tables.
blocks.subject: Fundamentals of Digital Computers

blocks.text: Answer: Begin with the meaning of a bistable storage element. For each flip-flop, describe input signals, clock behaviour, next-state operation, truth table and characteristic equation. RS: set/reset control; JK: hold, reset, set and toggle; D: next state equals D at the active clock; T: hold when T=0 and toggle when T=1. Use the clock convention and forbidden-state notation shown in SUCA101. Include circuit symbols and applications.
blocks.subject: Fundamentals of Digital Computers

blocks.text: 2. Explain the design procedure for a synchronous counter.
blocks.subject: Fundamentals of Digital Computers

blocks.text: Answer: Specify the required counting sequence, determine the number of states and minimum flip-flops, assign binary state codes, construct the present-state/next-state table, select the flip-flop type, derive excitation requirements, simplify the input equations using Boolean algebra or K-map, draw the logic circuit and verify the sequence. Discuss unused states and recovery behaviour if covered by the question.
blocks.subject: Fundamentals of Digital Computers

blocks.text: UNIT V – COMBINATIONAL CIRCUITS, ROM AND PLA
blocks.subject: Fundamentals of Digital Computers

blocks.text: 2-MARK QUESTIONS
blocks.subject: Fundamentals of Digital Computers

blocks.text: 1. Define a decoder.
blocks.subject: Fundamentals of Digital Computers

blocks.text: Answer: A decoder is a combinational circuit that converts an n-bit input code into one of up to 2^n output lines, normally activating the line corresponding to the input code.
blocks.subject: Fundamentals of Digital Computers

blocks.text: 2. Define an encoder.
blocks.subject: Fundamentals of Digital Computers

blocks.text: Answer: An encoder converts an active input line into a coded binary output. Its operation normally assumes only one input is active unless it is a priority encoder.
blocks.subject: Fundamentals of Digital Computers

blocks.text: 3. What is a demultiplexer?
blocks.subject: Fundamentals of Digital Computers

blocks.text: Answer: A demultiplexer routes one input signal to one of several output lines according to selection inputs.
blocks.subject: Fundamentals of Digital Computers

blocks.text: 4. What is ROM?
blocks.subject: Fundamentals of Digital Computers

blocks.text: Answer: Read Only Memory is a memory device used to store data or logic patterns that can be read by the system.
blocks.subject: Fundamentals of Digital Computers

blocks.text: 5. What is a PLA?
blocks.subject: Fundamentals of Digital Computers

blocks.text: Answer: A Programmable Logic Array is a programmable logic device used to implement Boolean functions through programmable logic structures.
blocks.subject: Fundamentals of Digital Computers

blocks.text: 5-MARK QUESTIONS
blocks.subject: Fundamentals of Digital Computers

blocks.text: 1. Distinguish MUX and DEMUX.
blocks.subject: Fundamentals of Digital Computers

blocks.text: Answer: A multiplexer selects one of many inputs and sends it to a single output. A demultiplexer takes one input and routes it to one of many outputs. A MUX is many-to-one; a DEMUX is one-to-many. Selection lines choose the path. Draw a 4:1 MUX and 1:4 DEMUX for illustration.
blocks.subject: Fundamentals of Digital Computers

blocks.text: 2. Explain half subtractor and full subtractor.
blocks.subject: Fundamentals of Digital Computers

blocks.text: Answer: A half subtractor subtracts B from A and generates Difference and Borrow. Difference = A XOR B; Borrow = A'B. A full subtractor subtracts B and borrow-in Bin from A. Difference = A XOR B XOR Bin; Borrow-out = A'B + A'Bin + BBin. Include truth tables and logic diagrams.
blocks.subject: Fundamentals of Digital Computers

blocks.text: 3. Compare ROM and PLA.
blocks.subject: Fundamentals of Digital Computers

blocks.text: Answer: ROM stores a fixed pattern and uses address inputs to select output words; a logic function can be implemented by storing its truth-table outputs. PLA has programmable AND and OR structures and can implement selected sum-of-products expressions. State the structures and design method shown in the textbook.
blocks.subject: Fundamentals of Digital Computers

blocks.text: 10-MARK QUESTIONS
blocks.subject: Fundamentals of Digital Computers

blocks.text: 1. Explain adders and subtractors with equations and truth tables.
blocks.subject: Fundamentals of Digital Computers

blocks.text: Answer: A half adder adds two bits: Sum=A XOR B; Carry=AB. A full adder adds A, B and Cin: Sum=A XOR B XOR Cin; Cout=AB+ACin+BCin. A half subtractor has Difference=A XOR B and Borrow=A'B. A full subtractor has Difference=A XOR B XOR Bin and Borrow=A'B+A'Bin+BBin. Draw truth tables, symbols and logic diagrams. Mention that full adders/subtractors support multi-bit arithmetic when connected in stages.
blocks.subject: Fundamentals of Digital Computers

blocks.text: 2. Explain the design of a combinational logic circuit using a decoder or multiplexer.
blocks.subject: Fundamentals of Digital Computers

blocks.text: Answer: Express the required function as a truth table or minterm list. For decoder implementation, apply the variables to decoder inputs and combine the required output lines with an OR gate. For a MUX implementation, choose select variables and assign each data input as 0, 1, a variable or its complement according to the truth table. Draw the circuit and verify each output combination. Use the exact design method demonstrated in the official lesson.
blocks.subject: Fundamentals of Digital Computers

blocks.text: SUBJECT 2 – PC SOFTWARE LAB (SUCA102)
blocks.subject: PC Software Lab

blocks.text: WORD PROCESSING – ADDITIONAL QUESTIONS
blocks.subject: PC Software Lab

blocks.text: 2-MARK QUESTIONS
blocks.subject: PC Software Lab

blocks.text: 1. What is word wrapping?
blocks.subject: PC Software Lab

blocks.text: Answer: Word wrapping automatically moves text to the next line when it reaches the right margin, without requiring the user to press Enter at the end of each line.
blocks.subject: PC Software Lab

blocks.text: 2. What is Find and Replace?
blocks.subject: PC Software Lab

blocks.text: Answer: Find searches a document for specified text; Replace substitutes the matched text with new text. Review replacements carefully before applying them to the entire document.
blocks.subject: PC Software Lab

blocks.text: 3. What is a template?
blocks.subject: PC Software Lab

blocks.text: Answer: A template is a reusable document design containing predefined page layout, styles and formatting. It helps create consistent documents.
blocks.subject: PC Software Lab

blocks.text: 4. What is text alignment?
blocks.subject: PC Software Lab

blocks.text: Answer: Text alignment determines how text is positioned between the left and right margins. Common settings are left, centre, right and justified.
blocks.subject: PC Software Lab

blocks.text: 5. What are merge fields?
blocks.subject: PC Software Lab

blocks.text: Answer: Merge fields are placeholders in a mail-merge main document that are replaced with corresponding data-source values for each recipient.
blocks.subject: PC Software Lab

blocks.text: 5-MARK PRACTICAL QUESTIONS
blocks.subject: PC Software Lab

blocks.text: 1. Give the steps to insert and format a picture in Word.
blocks.subject: PC Software Lab

blocks.text: Answer: Open the document; place the cursor; choose Insert/Picture; select the image; insert it; resize proportionally using a corner handle; select an appropriate text-wrapping option; align the image; add a caption if required; save the document. Check that the picture does not obscure text.
blocks.subject: PC Software Lab

blocks.text: 2. Explain Mail Merge.
blocks.subject: PC Software Lab

blocks.text: Answer: Prepare the main document containing common text; create/select the recipient data source; connect it to the document; insert merge fields; preview each record; complete the merge; inspect the generated letters/labels and save or print the final output. The main document provides common content, the data source contains variable records and merge fields identify where the variable values appear.
blocks.subject: PC Software Lab

blocks.text: EXCEL – ADDITIONAL QUESTIONS
blocks.subject: PC Software Lab

blocks.text: 2-MARK QUESTIONS
blocks.subject: PC Software Lab

blocks.text: 1. What is a worksheet?
blocks.subject: PC Software Lab

blocks.text: Answer: A worksheet is a grid of rows and columns inside an Excel workbook.
blocks.subject: PC Software Lab

blocks.text: 2. What is a formula?
blocks.subject: PC Software Lab

blocks.text: Answer: A formula is an expression entered in a cell to calculate a result. It normally begins with an equal sign (=).
blocks.subject: PC Software Lab

blocks.text: 3. What is a range?
blocks.subject: PC Software Lab

blocks.text: Answer: A range is a group of selected cells, for example A1:A10.
blocks.subject: PC Software Lab

blocks.text: 4. What does SUM(A1:A5) do?
blocks.subject: PC Software Lab

blocks.text: Answer: It adds the numeric values in cells A1 through A5.
blocks.subject: PC Software Lab

blocks.text: 5. What is sorting?
blocks.subject: PC Software Lab

blocks.text: Answer: Sorting arranges rows based on one or more selected fields, such as numeric values in ascending order or names alphabetically.
blocks.subject: PC Software Lab

blocks.text: 5-MARK PRACTICAL QUESTIONS
blocks.subject: PC Software Lab

blocks.text: 1. Explain how to create a chart in Excel.
blocks.subject: PC Software Lab

blocks.text: Answer: Enter data with clear headings; select the complete data range; choose Insert and a suitable chart type; insert the chart; add a chart title and axis titles/labels; check the data series; adjust layout and formatting; save the workbook. Use a column/bar chart for category comparisons and a line chart where a trend over an ordered axis is relevant.
blocks.subject: PC Software Lab

blocks.text: 2. Explain sorting safely in Excel.
blocks.subject: PC Software Lab

blocks.text: Answer: Select the entire data table, not only one column; open Sort; identify whether the first row contains headers; choose the field; choose ascending or descending order; apply; verify that each row's data remains together. Sorting only one column can separate values from their associated records.
blocks.subject: PC Software Lab

blocks.text: 10-MARK PRACTICAL SCENARIO
blocks.subject: PC Software Lab

blocks.text: A company keeps employee names, department, salary and attendance. Describe how to create a worksheet, calculate total salary, sort by department/name and create a chart.
blocks.subject: PC Software Lab

blocks.text: Answer: Enter the headings in row 1 and one employee per subsequent row. Use a formula such as =SUM(C2:C20) for a salary total if salary is in column C. Use cell formatting, borders and appropriate number formats. Select the entire table and sort by department, then name. Select department and total salary data and insert a suitable chart. Add titles and labels, verify values, set print area and save the workbook. Use actual cell references based on the worksheet layout.
blocks.subject: PC Software Lab

blocks.text: POWERPOINT – ADDITIONAL QUESTIONS
blocks.subject: PC Software Lab

blocks.text: 2-MARK QUESTIONS
blocks.subject: PC Software Lab

blocks.text: 1. What is a slide layout?
blocks.subject: PC Software Lab

blocks.text: Answer: A slide layout is a predefined arrangement of placeholders for titles, text, pictures, charts or other content.
blocks.subject: PC Software Lab

blocks.text: 2. What is a design template?
blocks.subject: PC Software Lab

blocks.text: Answer: A design template is a presentation theme or prepared design that provides consistent colours, fonts and backgrounds.
blocks.subject: PC Software Lab

blocks.text: 3. What is an organisation chart?
blocks.subject: PC Software Lab

blocks.text: Answer: An organisation chart is a diagram showing roles and reporting relationships within an organisation.
blocks.subject: PC Software Lab

blocks.text: 5-MARK QUESTION
blocks.subject: PC Software Lab

blocks.text: Explain the steps to prepare a presentation using a design template.
blocks.subject: PC Software Lab

blocks.text: Answer: Open PowerPoint; create a new presentation; select a design template/theme; add slides using suitable layouts; enter concise content; insert relevant pictures/charts; maintain font and colour consistency; review slide order and spelling; run Slide Show; save the file. Avoid overcrowding slides and keep text readable.
blocks.subject: PC Software Lab

blocks.text: 10-MARK PRACTICAL QUESTION
blocks.subject: PC Software Lab

blocks.text: Prepare a short presentation on a college department with a title slide, introduction, organisation chart, services and conclusion.
blocks.subject: PC Software Lab

blocks.text: Answer: Create a title slide; add an introduction slide; add a department profile; insert an organisation chart showing head/coordinators/staff; add services or activities; use a consistent theme; add appropriate images; use transitions/animations only as required; proofread; run the presentation and save. Use a logical sequence and avoid excessive text.
blocks.subject: PC Software Lab

blocks.text: SUBJECT 3 – MATHEMATICS I (SUCA103)
blocks.subject: Mathematics I

blocks.text: UNIT I – ALGEBRA AND NUMERICAL METHODS
blocks.subject: Mathematics I

blocks.text: 2-MARK QUESTIONS
blocks.subject: Mathematics I

blocks.text: 1. Define a proper rational fraction.
blocks.subject: Mathematics I

blocks.text: Answer: A rational fraction is proper when the degree of the numerator is less than the degree of the denominator.
blocks.subject: Mathematics I

blocks.text: 2. What is a partial fraction?
blocks.subject: Mathematics I

blocks.text: Answer: A partial-fraction decomposition expresses a rational function as a sum of simpler rational fractions whose denominators are factors of the original denominator.
blocks.subject: Mathematics I

blocks.text: 3. Define the forward difference operator.
blocks.subject: Mathematics I

blocks.text: Answer: For equally spaced values with step h, Δy_x = y_(x+h) − y_x.
blocks.subject: Mathematics I

blocks.text: 4. Define the backward difference operator.
blocks.subject: Mathematics I

blocks.text: Answer: ∇y_x = y_x − y_(x−h).
blocks.subject: Mathematics I

blocks.text: 5. State the relation between E and Δ.
blocks.subject: Mathematics I

blocks.text: Answer: E = 1 + Δ.
blocks.subject: Mathematics I

blocks.text: 6. State the Newton-Raphson formula.
blocks.subject: Mathematics I

blocks.text: Answer: x_(n+1)=x_n−f(x_n)/f'(x_n).
blocks.subject: Mathematics I

blocks.text: 7. What is interpolation?
blocks.subject: Mathematics I

blocks.text: Answer: Interpolation estimates an unknown value of a function within the range of known data points.
blocks.subject: Mathematics I

blocks.text: 5-MARK QUESTIONS
blocks.subject: Mathematics I

blocks.text: 1. Explain the construction of a forward difference table.
blocks.subject: Mathematics I

blocks.text: Answer: List equally spaced x-values and their function values. Subtract consecutive y-values to obtain first differences. Repeat the subtraction on each difference column to obtain second, third and higher differences. Align each difference with the appropriate starting point. Check arithmetic because the table is used in interpolation.
blocks.subject: Mathematics I

blocks.text: 2. Distinguish Newton forward and backward interpolation.
blocks.subject: Mathematics I

blocks.text: Answer: Newton forward interpolation is suited to estimating a value near the beginning of an equally spaced table and uses forward differences. Newton backward interpolation is suited to a value near the end and uses backward differences. Forward uses u=(x−x0)/h and terms u(u−1), u(u−1)(u−2), etc.; backward uses u=(x−xn)/h and terms u(u+1), u(u+1)(u+2), etc.
blocks.subject: Mathematics I

blocks.text: 3. Explain Lagrange interpolation.
blocks.subject: Mathematics I

blocks.text: Answer: Lagrange interpolation constructs a polynomial through distinct data points without requiring equal spacing. For points (xi,yi), P(x)=Σ yi Li(x), where Li(x)=Π(j≠i)(x−xj)/(xi−xj). Form each basis polynomial, multiply by the corresponding yi, add and substitute the required x.
blocks.subject: Mathematics I

blocks.text: 10-MARK SOLVED PROBLEMS
blocks.subject: Mathematics I

blocks.text: 1. Use Newton-Raphson to approximate √2 by solving x²−2=0, starting x0=1.5.
blocks.subject: Mathematics I

blocks.text: Answer: f(x)=x²−2 and f'(x)=2x. Formula x_(n+1)=x_n−(x_n²−2)/(2x_n)=(x_n+2/x_n)/2.
blocks.subject: Mathematics I

blocks.text: 2. Use Newton forward interpolation for x=1.5 from the following data: x=0,1,2,3; y=1,2,5,10.
blocks.subject: Mathematics I

blocks.text: Answer: h=1, x0=0, u=(1.5−0)/1=1.5. Values y0=1, y1=2, y2=5, y3=10. First differences: 1,3,5. Second differences: 2,2. Third difference: 0. Newton forward: y=y0+uΔy0+[u(u−1)/2!]Δ²y0. Substitute: y=1+1.5(1)+[1.5(0.5)/2](2)=1+1.5+0.75=3.25. The interpolated value is 3.25.
blocks.subject: Mathematics I

blocks.text: 3. Find the eigenvalues of A=[[2,0],[0,3]].
blocks.subject: Mathematics I

blocks.text: Answer: |A−λI|=|(2−λ) 0; 0 (3−λ)|=(2−λ)(3−λ)=0. Hence λ=2 or λ=3. For λ=2, an eigenvector is [1,0]^T; for λ=3, an eigenvector is [0,1]^T.
blocks.subject: Mathematics I

blocks.text: UNIT II – MATRICES
blocks.subject: Mathematics I

blocks.text: 2-MARK QUESTIONS
blocks.subject: Mathematics I

blocks.text: 1. Define a symmetric matrix.
blocks.subject: Mathematics I

blocks.text: Answer: A square matrix A is symmetric if A^T=A.
blocks.subject: Mathematics I

blocks.text: 2. Define a skew-symmetric matrix.
blocks.subject: Mathematics I

blocks.text: Answer: A square matrix A is skew-symmetric if A^T=−A.
blocks.subject: Mathematics I

blocks.text: 3. Define an orthogonal matrix.
blocks.subject: Mathematics I

blocks.text: Answer: A real square matrix A is orthogonal if A^T A=I; therefore A^−1=A^T.
blocks.subject: Mathematics I

blocks.text: 4. Define a Hermitian matrix.
blocks.subject: Mathematics I

blocks.text: Answer: A complex square matrix is Hermitian if its conjugate transpose equals the matrix: A*=A.
blocks.subject: Mathematics I

blocks.text: 5. Define eigenvalue and eigenvector.
blocks.subject: Mathematics I

blocks.text: Answer: A non-zero vector X is an eigenvector of A corresponding to λ if AX=λX. The scalar λ is the eigenvalue.
blocks.subject: Mathematics I

blocks.text: 5-MARK QUESTIONS
blocks.subject: Mathematics I

blocks.text: 1. Explain how eigenvalues are obtained.
blocks.subject: Mathematics I

blocks.text: Answer: Start with AX=λX; rearrange to (A−λI)X=0. For a non-zero eigenvector, the determinant must vanish: |A−λI|=0. Expand and solve the characteristic equation for λ. Substitute each eigenvalue into (A−λI)X=0 to find a corresponding eigenvector.
blocks.subject: Mathematics I

blocks.text: 2. State and explain the Cayley-Hamilton theorem.
blocks.subject: Mathematics I

blocks.text: Answer: The Cayley-Hamilton theorem states that every square matrix satisfies its own characteristic equation. If the characteristic polynomial is p(λ), then p(A)=0. The syllabus asks for the theorem without proof, verification and computation of inverse using the theorem.
blocks.subject: Mathematics I

blocks.text: 10-MARK QUESTION
blocks.subject: Mathematics I

blocks.text: Explain the different special matrices and their defining conditions.
blocks.subject: Mathematics I

blocks.text: Answer: A symmetric matrix satisfies A^T=A; a skew-symmetric matrix satisfies A^T=−A; an orthogonal matrix satisfies A^T A=I; a Hermitian matrix satisfies A*=A; a skew-Hermitian matrix satisfies A*=−A; and a unitary matrix satisfies A*A=I. Define transpose and conjugate transpose, state the conditions and provide a small example for each if time permits. Do not confuse real transpose with complex conjugate transpose.
blocks.subject: Mathematics I

blocks.text: UNIT III – THEORY OF EQUATIONS
blocks.subject: Mathematics I

blocks.text: 2-MARK QUESTIONS
blocks.subject: Mathematics I

blocks.text: 1. What is a polynomial equation?
blocks.subject: Mathematics I

blocks.text: Answer: An equation of the form a_nx^n+a_(n−1)x^(n−1)+...+a_1x+a_0=0, with a_n≠0, is a polynomial equation of degree n.
blocks.subject: Mathematics I

blocks.text: 2. What are conjugate roots?
blocks.subject: Mathematics I

blocks.text: Answer: For a polynomial with real coefficients, non-real complex roots occur in conjugate pairs a+bi and a−bi.
blocks.subject: Mathematics I

blocks.text: 3. State the sum and product of roots for ax²+bx+c=0.
blocks.subject: Mathematics I

blocks.text: Answer: If the roots are α and β, α+β=−b/a and αβ=c/a.
blocks.subject: Mathematics I

blocks.text: 4. What is a reciprocal equation?
blocks.subject: Mathematics I

blocks.text: Answer: A reciprocal equation has coefficients arranged symmetrically or anti-symmetrically as described in the textbook, allowing a suitable substitution to reduce its degree.
blocks.subject: Mathematics I

blocks.text: 5-MARK QUESTIONS
blocks.subject: Mathematics I

blocks.text: 1. Explain symmetric functions of roots for a cubic equation.
blocks.subject: Mathematics I

blocks.text: Answer: For ax³+bx²+cx+d=0 with roots α,β,γ: α+β+γ=−b/a; αβ+βγ+γα=c/a; αβγ=−d/a. These relations connect combinations of roots with polynomial coefficients.
blocks.subject: Mathematics I

blocks.text: 2. Explain transformation of an equation when each root is increased by a constant k.
blocks.subject: Mathematics I

blocks.text: Answer: If x is an original root and the new root is y=x+k, substitute x=y−k into the original polynomial, expand and collect powers of y. The resulting equation has roots shifted by k. If roots are decreased by k, use x=y+k. Check the direction of substitution before expanding.
blocks.subject: Mathematics I

blocks.text: 10-MARK QUESTION
blocks.subject: Mathematics I

blocks.text: Describe methods for finding approximate roots and explain Newton's method.
blocks.subject: Mathematics I

blocks.text: Answer: The syllabus includes Newton's method for approximate roots. Define f(x)=0 and its derivative. Choose an initial approximation x0 and calculate x_(n+1)=x_n−f(x_n)/f'(x_n). Repeat until the required accuracy is achieved. Explain that a poor initial value, a derivative near zero or divergence can cause difficulty. Use one worked example, such as x²−2=0, and show iterations.
blocks.subject: Mathematics I

blocks.text: UNIT IV – TRIGONOMETRY
blocks.subject: Mathematics I

blocks.text: 2-MARK QUESTIONS
blocks.subject: Mathematics I

blocks.text: 1. State the power series for sin x.
blocks.subject: Mathematics I

blocks.text: Answer: sin x=x−x³/3!+x⁵/5!−x⁷/7!+... for x in radians.
blocks.subject: Mathematics I

blocks.text: 2. State the power series for cos x.
blocks.subject: Mathematics I

blocks.text: Answer: cos x=1−x²/2!+x⁴/4!−x⁶/6!+... for x in radians.
blocks.subject: Mathematics I

blocks.text: 3. Define sinh x and cosh x.
blocks.subject: Mathematics I

blocks.text: Answer: sinh x=(e^x−e^(−x))/2 and cosh x=(e^x+e^(−x))/2.
blocks.subject: Mathematics I

blocks.text: 4. State a basic hyperbolic identity.
blocks.subject: Mathematics I

blocks.text: Answer: cosh²x−sinh²x=1.
blocks.subject: Mathematics I

blocks.text: 5. What is the logarithm of a complex number in polar form?
blocks.subject: Mathematics I

blocks.text: Answer: If z=r(cosθ+i sinθ), then ln z=ln r+i(θ+2kπ), where k is an integer; the complex logarithm is multi-valued.
blocks.subject: Mathematics I

blocks.text: 5-MARK QUESTIONS
blocks.subject: Mathematics I

blocks.text: 1. Explain hyperbolic functions.
blocks.subject: Mathematics I

blocks.text: Answer: Hyperbolic sine and cosine are defined using exponentials: sinh x=(e^x−e^(−x))/2 and cosh x=(e^x+e^(−x))/2. Then tanh x=sinh x/cosh x. They satisfy cosh²x−sinh²x=1. Their inverse functions reverse the corresponding hyperbolic functions on appropriate domains.
blocks.subject: Mathematics I

blocks.text: 2. Explain why complex logarithms are multi-valued.
blocks.subject: Mathematics I

blocks.text: Answer: A non-zero complex number can be represented as z=r(cosθ+i sinθ), but its argument can be θ+2kπ for any integer k. Therefore ln z=ln r+i(θ+2kπ), giving infinitely many values. A chosen branch selects one argument range for a single-valued definition.
blocks.subject: Mathematics I

blocks.text: 10-MARK QUESTION
blocks.subject: Mathematics I

blocks.text: Explain the series expansions of sine and cosine and describe the role of radians.
blocks.subject: Mathematics I

blocks.text: Answer: The Maclaurin expansion of sin x is x−x³/3!+x⁵/5!−... and cos x is 1−x²/2!+x⁴/4!−.... These expansions are written with x in radians. They are obtained from successive derivatives at zero. Explain the alternating signs and show how a finite number of terms approximates function values for small x. The official syllabus also includes expansions of powers and multiple angles; practise the particular identities from the textbook.
blocks.subject: Mathematics I

blocks.text: UNIT V – DIFFERENTIAL CALCULUS
blocks.subject: Mathematics I

blocks.text: 2-MARK QUESTIONS
blocks.subject: Mathematics I

blocks.text: 1. What is successive differentiation?
blocks.subject: Mathematics I

blocks.text: Answer: Successive differentiation means differentiating a function repeatedly to obtain second, third and higher derivatives.
blocks.subject: Mathematics I

blocks.text: 2. State Leibnitz's theorem.
blocks.subject: Mathematics I

blocks.text: Answer: d^n(uv)/dx^n=Σ(r=0 to n) nCr u^(r)v^(n−r).
blocks.subject: Mathematics I

blocks.text: 3. Define a Jacobian for two variables.
blocks.subject: Mathematics I

blocks.text: Answer: ∂(u,v)/∂(x,y)=|u_x u_y; v_x v_y|=u_xv_y−u_yv_x.
blocks.subject: Mathematics I

blocks.text: 4. Define curvature.
blocks.subject: Mathematics I

blocks.text: Answer: Curvature measures how rapidly a curve changes direction. For a plane curve, it is the reciprocal of the radius of curvature.
blocks.subject: Mathematics I

blocks.text: 5. State the second-derivative test for a function of two variables.
blocks.subject: Mathematics I

blocks.text: Answer: At a stationary point, D=f_xx f_yy−(f_xy)^2. If D>0 and f_xx>0 there is a local minimum; if D>0 and f_xx<0 there is a local maximum; if D<0 there is a saddle point; if D=0 the test is inconclusive.
blocks.subject: Mathematics I

blocks.text: 5-MARK QUESTIONS
blocks.subject: Mathematics I

blocks.text: 1. Explain the application of Leibnitz's theorem.
blocks.subject: Mathematics I

blocks.text: Answer: Identify u and v in the product, calculate successive derivatives of each, and substitute in the summation formula with binomial coefficients. The theorem is useful for finding the nth derivative of a product without repeatedly applying the product rule from the beginning.
blocks.subject: Mathematics I

blocks.text: 2. Explain the method for finding maxima and minima of two variables.
blocks.subject: Mathematics I

blocks.text: Answer: Find first partial derivatives f_x and f_y; solve f_x=0 and f_y=0 for stationary points. Calculate f_xx, f_yy and f_xy and form D=f_xx f_yy−(f_xy)^2. Apply the second-derivative test at each stationary point. If D=0, use another method or further analysis.
blocks.subject: Mathematics I

blocks.text: 10-MARK QUESTION
blocks.subject: Mathematics I

blocks.text: Explain Jacobians, curvature and maxima/minima of two variables.
blocks.subject: Mathematics I

blocks.text: Answer: Define the Jacobian determinant and calculate the required partial derivatives. For y=f(x), radius of curvature is ρ=[1+(y')²]^(3/2)/|y''| where the denominator is non-zero; curvature κ=1/ρ. For a function f(x,y), find stationary points by setting first partial derivatives to zero and use D=f_xx f_yy−(f_xy)^2 to classify them. Include one example and show the algebraic steps.
blocks.subject: Mathematics I

blocks.text: SUBJECT 4 – COMMUNICATIVE ENGLISH: SPEAKING SKILLS (SFCE11)
blocks.subject: Communicative English I: Speaking Skills

blocks.text: 2-MARK QUESTIONS
blocks.subject: Communicative English I: Speaking Skills

blocks.text: 1. Name the four basic language skills.
blocks.subject: Communicative English I: Speaking Skills

blocks.text: Answer: Listening, speaking, reading and writing. Listening/reading are usually receptive; speaking/writing are productive skills.
blocks.subject: Communicative English I: Speaking Skills

blocks.text: 2. What is phonetics?
blocks.subject: Communicative English I: Speaking Skills

blocks.text: Answer: Phonetics is the study of speech sounds, including how they are produced, transmitted and perceived.
blocks.subject: Communicative English I: Speaking Skills

blocks.text: 3. What is non-verbal communication?
blocks.subject: Communicative English I: Speaking Skills

blocks.text: Answer: Communication through signals other than words, such as facial expressions, gestures, posture, eye contact, appearance and voice qualities.
blocks.subject: Communicative English I: Speaking Skills

blocks.text: 4. Define intonation.
blocks.subject: Communicative English I: Speaking Skills

blocks.text: Answer: Intonation is the rise and fall of pitch in spoken language, helping express meaning, attitude and sentence type.
blocks.subject: Communicative English I: Speaking Skills

blocks.text: 5. What is a group discussion?
blocks.subject: Communicative English I: Speaking Skills

blocks.text: Answer: A group discussion is a structured exchange in which participants share ideas and views on a topic, listen to others and work towards understanding or a conclusion.
blocks.subject: Communicative English I: Speaking Skills

blocks.text: 6. What is extempore speaking?
blocks.subject: Communicative English I: Speaking Skills

blocks.text: Answer: Extempore speaking is speaking on a topic with little or no preparation, while organising ideas quickly and expressing them clearly.
blocks.subject: Communicative English I: Speaking Skills

blocks.text: 5-MARK QUESTIONS
blocks.subject: Communicative English I: Speaking Skills

blocks.text: 1. Explain the importance of non-verbal communication.
blocks.subject: Communicative English I: Speaking Skills

blocks.text: Answer: Non-verbal cues reinforce spoken messages, communicate emotions, regulate turn-taking, show attention and influence the listener's impression. Forms include facial expression, eye contact, gestures, posture, distance, appearance and vocal tone. Meaning varies with context and culture; a gesture should not be interpreted in isolation.
blocks.subject: Communicative English I: Speaking Skills

blocks.text: 2. How should a candidate prepare for an interview?
blocks.subject: Communicative English I: Speaking Skills

blocks.text: Answer: Research the organisation and job; understand the role; prepare examples of skills and experience; practise concise answers; dress appropriately; arrive on time; listen carefully; maintain suitable eye contact and posture; answer honestly; ask relevant questions when invited; and close politely.
blocks.subject: Communicative English I: Speaking Skills

blocks.text: 3. Explain the structure of an effective presentation.
blocks.subject: Communicative English I: Speaking Skills

blocks.text: Answer: Begin with a greeting and topic statement; explain the purpose and outline; develop the main points in logical order using examples or evidence; use clear transitions; summarise the main message; conclude; and invite/respond to questions. Use readable visual aids and appropriate pace and voice modulation.
blocks.subject: Communicative English I: Speaking Skills

blocks.text: 10-MARK QUESTIONS
blocks.subject: Communicative English I: Speaking Skills

blocks.text: 1. Discuss the qualities and techniques of an effective speaker.
blocks.subject: Communicative English I: Speaking Skills

blocks.text: Answer: An effective speaker knows the audience and purpose, organises ideas, chooses clear vocabulary, pronounces words intelligibly, controls pace and volume, uses suitable tone and intonation, maintains appropriate eye contact and posture, listens to feedback and clarifies misunderstandings. Practise pronunciation, stress and intonation. In formal settings, use a clear introduction, logically ordered points and a concise conclusion. Support the discussion with examples from business conversations, interviews and presentations.
blocks.subject: Communicative English I: Speaking Skills

blocks.text: 2. Explain group discussion, panel discussion and giving instructions.
blocks.subject: Communicative English I: Speaking Skills

blocks.text: Answer: A group discussion involves several participants exchanging ideas. A good participant contributes relevant points, supports them with reasons, listens, avoids interruption and helps the group reach a conclusion. A panel discussion has several speakers, usually guided by a moderator, who explore a topic from different perspectives. Effective instructions state the objective, give steps in logical order, use clear action verbs, mention warnings/conditions and check that the listener understands.
blocks.subject: Communicative English I: Speaking Skills

blocks.text: PRACTICAL SPEAKING PROMPTS WITH MODEL RESPONSE OUTLINES
blocks.subject: Communicative English I: Speaking Skills

blocks.text: 1. Introduce yourself in an interview. Answer outline: State your education/current status, relevant skills, a specific project or achievement, the role you are seeking and why your skills fit. Keep the response truthful and concise; do not memorise an exaggerated script.
blocks.subject: Communicative English I: Speaking Skills

blocks.text: 2. Give a one-minute speech on the importance of communication. Answer outline: Define communication; explain how it supports education, teamwork and problem-solving; mention listening and feedback; conclude that clear communication reduces misunderstanding and builds cooperation.
blocks.subject: Communicative English I: Speaking Skills

blocks.text: 3. Give instructions for submitting an assignment. Answer outline: State the deadline and submission location/platform; give file-format and naming requirements; list the steps; explain how to confirm submission; mention whom to contact if a problem occurs.
blocks.subject: Communicative English I: Speaking Skills

blocks.text: SUBJECT 5 – ENGLISH (SFEN11)
blocks.subject: English I

blocks.text: LITERATURE – SHORT QUESTIONS AND ANSWERS
blocks.subject: English I

blocks.text: 1. Who wrote “My Greatest Olympic Prize”?
blocks.subject: English I

blocks.text: Answer: Jesse Owens.
blocks.subject: English I

blocks.text: 2. Who wrote “If You Are Wrong Admit It”?
blocks.subject: English I

blocks.text: Answer: Dale Carnegie.
blocks.subject: English I

blocks.text: 3. Who wrote “Monday Morning”?
blocks.subject: English I

blocks.text: Answer: Mark Twain.
blocks.subject: English I

blocks.text: 4. Who wrote “The Unexpected”?
blocks.subject: English I

blocks.text: Answer: Robert Lynd.
blocks.subject: English I

blocks.text: 5. Who wrote “La Belle Dame Sans Merci”?
blocks.subject: English I

blocks.text: Answer: John Keats.
blocks.subject: English I

blocks.text: 6. Who wrote “Mrs. Packletide's Tiger”?
blocks.subject: English I

blocks.text: Answer: Saki (H. H. Munro).
blocks.subject: English I

blocks.text: 7. Who wrote “Three Questions”?
blocks.subject: English I

blocks.text: Answer: Leo Tolstoy.
blocks.subject: English I

blocks.text: 8. Who wrote “The Gift of the Magi”?
blocks.subject: English I

blocks.text: Answer: O. Henry.
blocks.subject: English I

blocks.text: 9. What is the main idea of “My Greatest Olympic Prize”?
blocks.subject: English I

blocks.text: Answer: The lesson presents sportsmanship and friendship as values more important than winning a medal. The narrator recalls the support and fair play shown by a fellow athlete during the Olympic competition. Refer to the prescribed text for the exact incident and wording.
blocks.subject: English I

blocks.text: 10. What is the central message of “The Gift of the Magi”?
blocks.subject: English I

blocks.text: Answer: The story highlights selfless love and sacrifice. The two central characters separately give up their most valued possessions to buy gifts for each other, creating an ironic but affectionate ending.
blocks.subject: English I

blocks.text: 11. What is the central idea of “Three Questions”?
blocks.subject: English I

blocks.text: Answer: The story explores the questions of the right time to act, the right people to listen to and the most important thing to do. The answers emphasise the present moment, the person with whom one is engaged and doing good.
blocks.subject: English I

blocks.text: 12. What is the literary effect of irony in “Mrs. Packletide's Tiger”?
blocks.subject: English I

blocks.text: Answer: The story uses humour and irony to expose vanity and social competition. The apparent hunting success and its hidden circumstances create a contrast between public reputation and the truth. Use the prescribed text for detailed events.
blocks.subject: English I

blocks.text: 5-MARK QUESTIONS WITH ANSWERS
blocks.subject: English I

blocks.text: 1. Write a short note on the theme of “La Belle Dame Sans Merci”.
blocks.subject: English I

blocks.text: Answer: The poem presents an encounter between a knight and a mysterious beautiful woman. The knight is left weakened and isolated, and the poem creates an atmosphere of enchantment, uncertainty and loss. Discuss the contrast between the knight's memory of the encounter and his present condition. Support the answer with images or lines from the prescribed poem.
blocks.subject: English I

blocks.text: 2. Explain the central idea of “The Night of the Scorpion”.
blocks.subject: English I

blocks.text: Answer: The poem presents a mother suffering after a scorpion sting and the anxious reactions of family members and villagers. The poem contrasts superstition, ritual responses and the mother's suffering. The mother's final response expresses selfless concern for her children. Use the exact sequence and lines from the textbook.
blocks.subject: English I

blocks.text: 3. Explain the humour in “Monday Morning”.
blocks.subject: English I

blocks.text: Answer: The lesson uses a child's reluctance to attend school and his attempts to avoid it to create humour. Exaggeration, excuses and the child's shifting attitude expose the comic gap between a child's immediate wishes and adult expectations. Support the answer with the events in the prescribed text.
blocks.subject: English I

blocks.text: 4. What lesson does “If You Are Wrong Admit It” teach?
blocks.subject: English I

blocks.text: Answer: The lesson advises people to acknowledge mistakes honestly rather than defend an incorrect position. Admission can reduce conflict, build trust and allow correction. In a long answer, explain the author's reasoning and examples from the prescribed chapter.
blocks.subject: English I

blocks.text: 10-MARK QUESTIONS WITH ANSWER FRAMEWORKS
blocks.subject: English I

blocks.text: 1. Discuss sportsmanship and friendship in “My Greatest Olympic Prize”.
blocks.subject: English I

blocks.text: Answer: Introduce Jesse Owens and the Olympic context described in the lesson. Explain the competition and the difficulty faced by the narrator. Describe how the fellow athlete's advice or support affected the event. Discuss the values of fairness, respect and friendship that emerge from the incident. Conclude that the story presents human character and sportsmanship as a greater prize than a medal. Verify names, events and details from the text.
blocks.subject: English I

blocks.text: 2. Discuss the message and ending of “The Gift of the Magi”.
blocks.subject: English I

blocks.text: Answer: Introduce the couple and their limited means. Explain that each wants to give a meaningful gift and independently sacrifices a treasured possession. Describe the irony created when the gifts no longer serve their original purpose. The ending shows that the value of the gifts lies in the love and sacrifice behind them. Conclude that the story celebrates generosity and unselfish affection.
blocks.subject: English I

blocks.text: 3. Write a critical appreciation of “La Belle Dame Sans Merci”.
blocks.subject: English I

blocks.text: Answer: Identify the poet and the ballad-like form. Explain the dramatic situation of the knight, the mysterious woman and the aftermath of the encounter. Discuss imagery of the cold landscape, the contrast between past enchantment and present desolation, and the poem's uncertain atmosphere. Refer to the stanzas and poetic devices in the prescribed text. Conclude with the themes of love, illusion and loss.
blocks.subject: English I

blocks.text: SUBJECT 6 – PROGRAMMING IN C (SUCA104)

blocks.text: UNIT I – C FUNDAMENTALS
blocks.subject: Programming in C

blocks.text: 2-MARK QUESTIONS WITH ANSWERS
blocks.subject: Programming in C

blocks.text: 1. What is an identifier?
blocks.subject: Programming in C

blocks.text: Answer: An identifier is a programmer-defined name for a variable, function, array or other program element. It must follow C naming rules and cannot be a reserved keyword.
blocks.subject: Programming in C

blocks.text: 2. What is a keyword?
blocks.subject: Programming in C

blocks.text: Answer: A keyword is a reserved word in C with a predefined meaning, such as int, if, return or while.
blocks.subject: Programming in C

blocks.text: 3. What is a variable?
blocks.subject: Programming in C

blocks.text: Answer: A variable is a named memory location used to store a value that may change during program execution.
blocks.subject: Programming in C

blocks.text: 4. What is a constant?
blocks.subject: Programming in C

blocks.text: Answer: A constant is a value that is fixed for the relevant program context and is not intended to change during execution.
blocks.subject: Programming in C

blocks.text: 5. What is an expression?
blocks.subject: Programming in C

blocks.text: Answer: An expression is a combination of operands and operators that is evaluated to produce a value.
blocks.subject: Programming in C

blocks.text: 6. What is the modulus operator?
blocks.subject: Programming in C

blocks.text: Answer: The % operator gives the remainder after integer division. For example, 17%5 is 2.
blocks.subject: Programming in C

blocks.text: 5-MARK QUESTIONS
blocks.subject: Programming in C

blocks.text: 1. Explain the basic data types in C.
blocks.subject: Programming in C

blocks.text: Answer: int represents integers; char represents character values; float represents floating-point values; and double represents floating-point values with greater precision than float. Type modifiers and derived types extend these basic forms. The exact storage sizes depend on the implementation; use sizeof where size is required.
blocks.subject: Programming in C

blocks.text: 2. Explain operator categories in C.
blocks.subject: Programming in C

blocks.text: Answer: Arithmetic operators perform numerical operations; relational operators compare values; logical operators combine conditions; assignment operators assign values; increment/decrement operators change a value by one; conditional operator selects one of two expressions; and bitwise operators operate on individual bits. Explain precedence and associativity and use parentheses for clarity.
blocks.subject: Programming in C

blocks.subject: Programming in C

blocks.subject: Programming in C

blocks.text: UNIT II – INPUT/OUTPUT AND CONTROL STRUCTURES
blocks.subject: Programming in C

blocks.text: 2-MARK QUESTIONS
blocks.subject: Programming in C

blocks.text: 1. What is the purpose of scanf()?
blocks.subject: Programming in C

blocks.text: Answer: scanf() reads formatted input from standard input and stores the values in the addresses supplied as arguments.
blocks.subject: Programming in C

blocks.text: 2. Why is the address operator & often used with scanf()?
blocks.subject: Programming in C

blocks.text: Answer: It supplies the memory address of an ordinary variable so scanf() can store the entered value there.
blocks.subject: Programming in C

blocks.text: 3. Distinguish while and do-while loops.
blocks.subject: Programming in C

blocks.text: Answer: while tests the condition before executing the body; do-while executes the body at least once and tests the condition afterwards.
blocks.subject: Programming in C

blocks.text: 4. What is a nested loop?
blocks.subject: Programming in C

blocks.text: Answer: A nested loop is a loop placed inside another loop. The inner loop can execute for each iteration of the outer loop.
blocks.subject: Programming in C

blocks.text: 5. What is the use of break?
blocks.subject: Programming in C

blocks.text: Answer: break terminates the nearest enclosing loop or switch statement.
blocks.subject: Programming in C

blocks.text: 5-MARK QUESTIONS
blocks.subject: Programming in C

blocks.text: 1. Explain if, if-else and switch statements.
blocks.subject: Programming in C

blocks.text: Answer: if executes a block when a condition is true; if-else selects between two paths; nested if statements support multiple decisions. switch selects a case based on an integral/compatible expression. break is normally used to prevent unintended fall-through. A default case handles unmatched values.
blocks.subject: Programming in C

blocks.text: 2. Compare for, while and do-while loops.
blocks.subject: Programming in C

blocks.text: Answer: for places initialisation, condition and update in one header and is commonly used when the iteration pattern is known. while tests before each iteration and is useful when repetition depends on a condition. do-while executes at least once before testing. All loops need correct initialisation, termination condition and update.
blocks.subject: Programming in C

blocks.text: UNIT III – FUNCTIONS
blocks.subject: Programming in C

blocks.text: 2-MARK QUESTIONS
blocks.subject: Programming in C

blocks.text: 1. Define a function prototype.
blocks.subject: Programming in C

blocks.text: Answer: A function prototype declares the function name, return type and parameter types before the function is called.
blocks.subject: Programming in C

blocks.text: 2. What is recursion?
blocks.subject: Programming in C

blocks.text: Answer: Recursion is a technique in which a function calls itself to solve a smaller instance of a problem.
blocks.subject: Programming in C

blocks.text: 3. What is a base case?
blocks.subject: Programming in C

blocks.text: Answer: A base case is the condition in a recursive function that stops further recursive calls.
blocks.subject: Programming in C

blocks.text: 4. What is a storage class?
blocks.subject: Programming in C

blocks.text: Answer: A storage class describes characteristics such as scope, lifetime and linkage of an identifier.
blocks.subject: Programming in C

blocks.text: 5-MARK QUESTIONS
blocks.subject: Programming in C

blocks.text: 1. Explain call by value and call by address/pointer in C.
blocks.subject: Programming in C

blocks.text: Answer: In call by value, a copy of the argument is passed, so changes to the parameter do not directly change the caller's variable. In C, passing a pointer allows a function to modify the object through the address. C does not have built-in reference parameters like C++.
blocks.subject: Programming in C

blocks.text: 2. Explain local and global variables.
blocks.subject: Programming in C

blocks.text: Answer: A local variable is declared inside a block/function and is normally accessible only within its scope. A global variable is declared outside functions and can be accessed by functions according to its linkage and declarations. Discuss lifetime and storage class as specified in the textbook.
blocks.subject: Programming in C
