blocks.text: UNIT IV – ARRAYS, STRINGS, STRUCTURES AND UNIONS
blocks.subject: Programming in C

blocks.text: 2-MARK QUESTIONS
blocks.subject: Programming in C

blocks.text: 1. Define an array.
blocks.subject: Programming in C

blocks.text: Answer: An array is a collection of elements of the same type stored under one name and accessed using indices.
blocks.subject: Programming in C

blocks.text: 2. What is the first valid index of an ordinary C array?
blocks.subject: Programming in C

blocks.text: Answer: Zero.
blocks.subject: Programming in C

blocks.text: 3. What terminates a C string?
blocks.subject: Programming in C

blocks.text: Answer: The null character '\\0'.
blocks.subject: Programming in C

blocks.text: 4. What is a structure?
blocks.subject: Programming in C

blocks.text: Answer: A structure is a user-defined data type that groups related members, which may have different data types, under one name.
blocks.subject: Programming in C

blocks.text: 5. What is a union?
blocks.subject: Programming in C

blocks.text: Answer: A union is a user-defined type whose members share the same storage area; only one member's stored value should be treated as active at a time.
blocks.subject: Programming in C

blocks.text: 6. What is a self-referential structure?
blocks.subject: Programming in C

blocks.text: Answer: It is a structure that contains a pointer to another object of the same structure type, commonly used to build linked lists.
blocks.subject: Programming in C

blocks.text: 5-MARK QUESTIONS
blocks.subject: Programming in C

blocks.text: 1. Distinguish an array and a structure.
blocks.subject: Programming in C

blocks.text: Answer: An array stores multiple elements of the same type and accesses them by index. A structure groups related fields that may have different types and accesses them by member names. Arrays represent sequences; structures represent records.
blocks.subject: Programming in C

blocks.text: 2. Distinguish structure and union.
blocks.subject: Programming in C

blocks.text: Answer: Structure members have separate storage, so multiple members can hold values simultaneously. Union members share storage; the size is sufficient for the largest member subject to alignment. Updating one union member can overwrite the representation of another.
blocks.subject: Programming in C

blocks.text: 10-MARK QUESTION WITH PROGRAM
blocks.subject: Programming in C

blocks.text: Write a C program to calculate the sum of elements in an array.
blocks.subject: Programming in C

blocks.text: Answer:
blocks.subject: Programming in C
Programming in C

blocks.text: The first loop reads n values and the second accumulates them. The program checks that n fits the array capacity.
blocks.subject: Programming in C

blocks.text: UNIT V – POINTERS AND FILE HANDLING
blocks.subject: Programming in C

blocks.text: 2-MARK QUESTIONS
blocks.subject: Programming in C

blocks.text: 1. Define a pointer.
blocks.subject: Programming in C

blocks.text: Answer: A pointer is a variable that stores the memory address of another object or function.
blocks.subject: Programming in C

blocks.text: 2. What is the address-of operator?
blocks.subject: Programming in C

blocks.text: Answer: The unary & operator obtains the address of an object.
blocks.subject: Programming in C

blocks.text: 3. What is dereferencing?
blocks.subject: Programming in C

blocks.text: Answer: Dereferencing uses the unary * operator on a valid pointer to access the object to which it points.
blocks.subject: Programming in C

blocks.text: 4. What is a NULL pointer?
blocks.subject: Programming in C

blocks.text: Answer: A null pointer is a pointer value that is guaranteed not to point to a valid object or function. It should not be dereferenced.
blocks.subject: Programming in C

blocks.text: 5. What is a file pointer?
blocks.subject: Programming in C

blocks.text: Answer: In C, FILE* is a pointer to a stream object used by standard I/O functions to perform file operations.
blocks.subject: Programming in C

blocks.text: 5-MARK QUESTIONS
blocks.subject: Programming in C

blocks.text: 1. Explain the relationship between arrays and pointers.
blocks.subject: Programming in C

blocks.text: Answer: In many expressions, an array name is converted to a pointer to its first element. Array indexing can be expressed using pointer arithmetic, such as a[i] equivalent to *(a+i). However, an array is not itself a pointer variable; arrays have fixed storage and cannot be assigned as ordinary pointer variables.
blocks.subject: Programming in C

blocks.text: 2. Explain the steps in file handling.
blocks.subject: Programming in C

blocks.text: Answer: Declare a FILE* variable; open the file with fopen(); test whether the returned pointer is NULL; read or write using suitable functions; check errors/end-of-file conditions; close the file using fclose(). Choose a mode such as read, write or append according to the task.
blocks.subject: Programming in C

blocks.text: 10-MARK PROGRAM QUESTION
blocks.subject: Programming in C

blocks.text: Write a program to copy the contents of one text file to another.
blocks.subject: Programming in C

blocks.text: Answer:
blocks.subject: Programming in C
Programming in C

blocks.text: Explanation: Open the source in read mode and destination in write mode, copy one character at a time until EOF, check errors and close both files. The write mode overwrites an existing destination file.
blocks.subject: Programming in C

blocks.text: SUBJECT 7 – PROGRAMMING IN C LAB (SUCA105)
blocks.subject: Programming in C Lab

blocks.text: UNIT-WISE PRACTICAL QUESTION AND ANSWER SET
blocks.subject: Programming in C Lab

blocks.text: 1. How do you generate sin(x) using a series?
blocks.subject: Programming in C Lab

blocks.text: Answer: Use sin x = x − x^3/3! + x^5/5! − x^7/7! + ... with x in radians. Build terms iteratively or calculate powers/factorials carefully. Stop after a prescribed number of terms or when the term magnitude is below a tolerance. Compare the result with sin(x) from math.h. Check for overflow and use a floating-point type.
blocks.subject: Programming in C Lab

blocks.text: 2. How do you generate cos(x) using a series?
blocks.subject: Programming in C Lab

blocks.text: Answer: Use cos x = 1 − x^2/2! + x^4/4! − x^6/6! + ... . The series alternates. Use radians and compare against cos(x) from math.h.
blocks.subject: Programming in C Lab

blocks.text: 3. Explain the method for counting vowels and consonants in a line.
blocks.subject: Programming in C Lab

blocks.text: Answer: Read a line into a character array; iterate until '\\0'; check whether each alphabetic character is a vowel (a,e,i,o,u in either case) or consonant; count spaces separately; count word starts when a non-space follows a space/start. Decide how punctuation and repeated spaces will be treated and state the assumption.
blocks.subject: Programming in C Lab

blocks.text: 4. Explain palindrome checking.
blocks.subject: Programming in C Lab

blocks.text: Answer: Compare the first and last characters, then move inward. If all pairs match, the string is a palindrome. If the task requires ignoring case or spaces, normalise the string first. The simplest textbook exercise may compare characters exactly.
blocks.subject: Programming in C Lab

blocks.text: 5. How is substring replacement performed?
blocks.subject: Programming in C Lab

blocks.text: Answer: Search the main string for the target substring, copy preceding characters to a result buffer, insert the replacement text, advance past the matched substring and continue. Check output-buffer capacity and overlapping matches.
blocks.subject: Programming in C Lab

blocks.text: 6. State the formulas for nPr and nCr.
blocks.subject: Programming in C Lab

blocks.text: Answer: nPr=n!/(n−r)! and nCr=n!/[r!(n−r)!], for integers 0≤r≤n. nCr = n!/[r!(n−r)!], and nCr = nC(n−r).
blocks.subject: Programming in C Lab

blocks.text: 7. Explain Euclid's algorithm for GCD.
blocks.subject: Programming in C Lab

blocks.text: Answer: Repeatedly replace (a,b) by (b,a mod b) until b=0. The non-zero value a is the GCD. Use absolute values for negative inputs where the problem permits them.
blocks.subject: Programming in C Lab

blocks.text: 8. State the minimum moves in Towers of Hanoi.
blocks.subject: Programming in C Lab

blocks.text: Answer: For n disks, the minimum number of moves is 2^n−1. The recursive method moves n−1 disks to the auxiliary peg, moves the largest disk, then moves n−1 disks to the destination.
blocks.subject: Programming in C Lab

blocks.text: 9. State the condition for matrix multiplication AB.
blocks.subject: Programming in C Lab

blocks.text: Answer: If A is m×n and B is n×p, AB is defined and the result is m×p. The number of columns of A must equal the number of rows of B.
blocks.subject: Programming in C Lab

blocks.text: 10. Compare linear search and binary search.
blocks.subject: Programming in C Lab

blocks.text: Answer: Linear search checks items one by one and works on unsorted data; its worst-case time is O(n). Binary search repeatedly halves the search interval and requires sorted data; its time is O(log n).
blocks.subject: Programming in C Lab

blocks.text: PRACTICAL PROGRAM LOGIC / PSEUDOCODE
blocks.subject: Programming in C Lab

blocks.text: A. Fibonacci recursion: Fib(n): if n<=1 return n; otherwise return Fib(n−1)+Fib(n−2). This direct recursion is easy to understand but inefficient for large n because it repeats work.
blocks.subject: Programming in C Lab

blocks.text: B. Maximum and minimum recursively: For one element, return it as both maximum and minimum. Divide the remaining array into smaller ranges, find each range's maximum/minimum and combine by max/min comparison. Follow the exact recursion format required in the manual.
blocks.subject: Programming in C Lab

blocks.text: C. Bubble sort: For each pass, compare adjacent values; swap if the left value is greater; after a pass, the largest unsorted element reaches the end. Stop after n−1 passes or early if no swaps occur.
blocks.subject: Programming in C Lab

blocks.text: D. Insertion sort: Treat the first item as sorted. For each next key, shift larger sorted items one position right and insert the key into the correct position. The sorted prefix grows by one element per pass.
blocks.subject: Programming in C Lab

blocks.text: E. Binary search: Set low=0 and high=n−1. While low<=high, calculate mid. If a[mid]==key, report found. If key<a[mid], set high=mid−1; otherwise set low=mid+1. Data must be sorted.
blocks.subject: Programming in C Lab

blocks.text: LAB VIVA QUESTIONS
blocks.subject: Programming in C Lab

blocks.text: 1. Why must the array size be checked? Answer: To prevent reading/writing outside allocated storage. 2. Why is a base case necessary in recursion? Answer: It stops the recursive calls. 3. Why is binary search unsuitable for an unsorted list? Answer: Its decision to discard half the data depends on sorted order. 4. What is a null terminator? Answer: '\\0', marking the end of a C string. 5. Why should a file be closed? Answer: To flush buffered data and release stream resources.
blocks.subject: Programming in C Lab

blocks.text: SUBJECT 8 – MATHEMATICS II (SUCA106)
blocks.subject: Mathematics II

blocks.text: UNIT I – INTEGRAL CALCULUS AND FOURIER SERIES
blocks.subject: Mathematics II

blocks.text: 2-MARK QUESTIONS
blocks.subject: Mathematics II

blocks.text: 1. What is a reduction formula?
blocks.subject: Mathematics II

blocks.text: Answer: A reduction formula expresses an integral involving a parameter n in terms of a similar integral with a smaller parameter, reducing it to a basic case.
blocks.subject: Mathematics II

blocks.text: 2. What is a Fourier series?
blocks.subject: Mathematics II

blocks.text: Answer: A Fourier series represents a periodic function as a sum of sine and cosine terms, under suitable conditions.
blocks.subject: Mathematics II

blocks.text: 3. What is a half-range sine series?
blocks.subject: Mathematics II

blocks.text: Answer: It represents a function on (0,L) using sine terms, corresponding to an odd extension to (−L,L).
blocks.subject: Mathematics II

blocks.text: 4. What is a half-range cosine series?
blocks.subject: Mathematics II

blocks.text: Answer: It represents a function on (0,L) using cosine terms, corresponding to an even extension to (−L,L).
blocks.subject: Mathematics II

blocks.text: 5-MARK QUESTIONS
blocks.subject: Mathematics II

blocks.text: 1. State the Fourier coefficients on (−π,π).
blocks.subject: Mathematics II

blocks.text: Answer: a0=(1/π)∫(−π to π)f(x)dx; an=(1/π)∫f(x)cos(nx)dx; bn=(1/π)∫f(x)sin(nx)dx. Then f(x)≈a0/2+Σ[an cos(nx)+bn sin(nx)]. Use the interval and coefficient convention specified in the textbook.
blocks.subject: Mathematics II

blocks.text: 2. Explain the difference between half-range sine and cosine expansions.
blocks.subject: Mathematics II

blocks.text: Answer: The sine expansion uses an odd extension and only sine terms; the cosine expansion uses an even extension and only cosine terms. Their coefficients are integrated over (0,L) with the corresponding basis functions. Draw or describe the parity extension and state the interval.
blocks.subject: Mathematics II

blocks.text: 10-MARK SOLVED EXAMPLE
blocks.subject: Mathematics II

blocks.text: Find the Fourier series of f(x)=x on (−π,π).
blocks.subject: Mathematics II

blocks.text: Answer: The function is odd, so a0=0 and an=0. Compute bn=(1/π)∫(−π to π)x sin(nx)dx. Since x sin(nx) is even, bn=(2/π)∫(0 to π)x sin(nx)dx. Integration by parts gives bn=2(−1)^(n+1)/n. Hence x=2Σ[n=1 to ∞] (−1)^(n+1) sin(nx)/n for −π<x<π. At discontinuity points of the periodic extension, the series converges to the midpoint of the one-sided limits.
blocks.subject: Mathematics II

blocks.text: UNIT II – ORDINARY AND PARTIAL DIFFERENTIAL EQUATIONS
blocks.subject: Mathematics II

blocks.text: 2-MARK QUESTIONS
blocks.subject: Mathematics II

blocks.text: 1. Define an ordinary differential equation.
blocks.subject: Mathematics II

blocks.text: Answer: An ODE is an equation involving an unknown function and its derivatives with respect to one independent variable.
blocks.subject: Mathematics II

blocks.text: 2. What is the complementary function?
blocks.subject: Mathematics II

blocks.text: Answer: The complementary function is the general solution of the associated homogeneous differential equation.
blocks.subject: Mathematics II

blocks.text: 3. What is a particular integral?
blocks.subject: Mathematics II

blocks.text: Answer: A particular integral is one specific solution of the non-homogeneous differential equation.
blocks.subject: Mathematics II

blocks.text: 4. Define a partial differential equation.
blocks.subject: Mathematics II

blocks.text: Answer: A PDE is an equation involving partial derivatives of an unknown function of two or more independent variables.
blocks.subject: Mathematics II

blocks.text: 5. State Lagrange's linear PDE.
blocks.subject: Mathematics II

blocks.text: Answer: Pp+Qq=R, where p=∂z/∂x and q=∂z/∂y.
blocks.subject: Mathematics II

blocks.text: 5-MARK QUESTIONS
blocks.subject: Mathematics II

blocks.text: 1. Explain the CF+PI method for a second-order linear ODE with constant coefficients.
blocks.subject: Mathematics II

blocks.text: Answer: Write the homogeneous auxiliary equation and solve it to obtain the complementary function. Then obtain a particular integral for the given right-hand side using the appropriate method. The complete solution is y=CF+PI. Show special cases for repeated roots or right-hand terms that overlap with the complementary function as required by the textbook.
blocks.subject: Mathematics II

blocks.text: 2. Explain the auxiliary equations for Lagrange's PDE.
blocks.subject: Mathematics II

blocks.text: Answer: For Pp+Qq=R, form dx/P=dy/Q=dz/R. Find two independent integrals from these relations and combine them in an arbitrary relation F(u,v)=0 to obtain the general solution, following the method in the lesson.
blocks.subject: Mathematics II

blocks.text: 10-MARK SOLVED EXAMPLE
blocks.subject: Mathematics II

blocks.text: Solve y''−3y'+2y=0.
blocks.subject: Mathematics II

blocks.text: Answer: The auxiliary equation is m²−3m+2=0=(m−1)(m−2). Roots are 1 and 2. Therefore the complementary solution is y=C1e^x+C2e^(2x). Since the right-hand side is zero, PI=0 and this is the complete solution.
blocks.subject: Mathematics II

blocks.text: UNIT III – LAPLACE TRANSFORMS
blocks.subject: Mathematics II

blocks.text: 2-MARK QUESTIONS
blocks.subject: Mathematics II

blocks.text: 1. Define the Laplace transform.
blocks.subject: Mathematics II

blocks.text: Answer: L{f(t)}=F(s)=∫(0 to ∞)e^(−st)f(t)dt, where the integral exists.
blocks.subject: Mathematics II

blocks.text: 2. State L{1} and L{t}.
blocks.subject: Mathematics II

blocks.text: Answer: L{1}=1/s and L{t}=1/s².
blocks.subject: Mathematics II

blocks.text: 3. State L{sin at} and L{cos at}.
blocks.subject: Mathematics II

blocks.text: Answer: L{sin at}=a/(s²+a²); L{cos at}=s/(s²+a²).
blocks.subject: Mathematics II

blocks.text: 4. State the first derivative property.
blocks.subject: Mathematics II

blocks.text: Answer: L{f'(t)}=sF(s)−f(0), under the usual existence conditions.
blocks.subject: Mathematics II

blocks.text: 5-MARK QUESTIONS
blocks.subject: Mathematics II

blocks.text: 1. Explain how partial fractions are used in inverse Laplace transforms.
blocks.subject: Mathematics II

blocks.text: Answer: Factor the denominator; express the rational function as a sum of simpler fractions; determine constants by equating coefficients or substitution; identify each term with a standard transform; then combine the inverse transforms. If a repeated or irreducible quadratic factor occurs, use the corresponding partial-fraction form.
blocks.subject: Mathematics II

blocks.text: 2. Explain the use of Laplace transforms to solve an initial-value ODE.
blocks.subject: Mathematics II

blocks.text: Answer: Take the transform of both sides; replace derivative transforms using the initial values; rearrange to obtain Y(s); decompose Y(s) into standard forms; take the inverse transform; and state the time-domain solution. Show how y(0) and y'(0) enter the transformed equation.
blocks.subject: Mathematics II

blocks.text: 10-MARK SOLVED EXAMPLE
blocks.subject: Mathematics II

blocks.text: Find L{3+2t+4sin 2t}.
blocks.subject: Mathematics II

blocks.text: Answer: By linearity, L{3}=3/s; L{2t}=2/s²; L{4sin2t}=4×2/(s²+4)=8/(s²+4). Therefore F(s)=3/s+2/s²+8/(s²+4).
blocks.subject: Mathematics II

blocks.text: UNIT IV – VECTOR DIFFERENTIATION
blocks.subject: Mathematics II

blocks.text: 2-MARK QUESTIONS
blocks.subject: Mathematics II

blocks.text: 1. Define gradient.
blocks.subject: Mathematics II

blocks.text: Answer: For a scalar field φ, grad φ=∇φ. It gives the direction and rate of maximum increase of the scalar field.
blocks.subject: Mathematics II

blocks.text: 2. Define divergence.
blocks.subject: Mathematics II

blocks.text: Answer: For F=Pi+Qj+Rk, div F=∇·F=∂P/∂x+∂Q/∂y+∂R/∂z.
blocks.subject: Mathematics II

blocks.text: 3. Define curl.
blocks.subject: Mathematics II

blocks.text: Answer: curl F=∇×F, a vector describing the local rotational tendency of a vector field.
blocks.subject: Mathematics II

blocks.text: 4. What is a solenoidal field?
blocks.subject: Mathematics II

blocks.text: Answer: A vector field is solenoidal if its divergence is zero.
blocks.subject: Mathematics II

blocks.text: 5. What is an irrotational field?
blocks.subject: Mathematics II

blocks.text: Answer: A vector field is irrotational if its curl is zero.
blocks.subject: Mathematics II

blocks.text: 5-MARK QUESTION
blocks.subject: Mathematics II

blocks.text: Find grad φ for φ=x²y+yz².
blocks.subject: Mathematics II

blocks.text: Answer: ∂φ/∂x=2xy; ∂φ/∂y=x²+z²; ∂φ/∂z=2yz. Therefore grad φ=2xy i+(x²+z²)j+2yz k.
blocks.subject: Mathematics II

blocks.text: 10-MARK QUESTION
blocks.subject: Mathematics II

blocks.text: Explain gradient, divergence and curl with formulas and physical meaning.
blocks.subject: Mathematics II

blocks.text: Answer: Define the del operator ∇=i∂/∂x+j∂/∂y+k∂/∂z. For a scalar field, ∇φ is its gradient. For vector field F=Pi+Qj+Rk, ∇·F is divergence and ∇×F is curl. Explain that gradient indicates steepest increase; divergence measures net outward flux density/source strength; curl measures local rotation. A field with zero divergence is solenoidal; one with zero curl is irrotational. Work one example of each.
blocks.subject: Mathematics II

blocks.text: UNIT V – VECTOR INTEGRATION
blocks.subject: Mathematics II

blocks.text: 2-MARK QUESTIONS
blocks.subject: Mathematics II

blocks.text: 1. What is a line integral?
blocks.subject: Mathematics II

blocks.text: Answer: A line integral integrates a scalar or vector field along a specified curve.
blocks.subject: Mathematics II

blocks.text: 2. What is a surface integral?
blocks.subject: Mathematics II

blocks.text: Answer: A surface integral evaluates a field over a surface, often calculating flux through that surface.
blocks.subject: Mathematics II

blocks.text: 3. State Gauss divergence theorem.
blocks.subject: Mathematics II

blocks.text: Answer: The outward flux across a closed surface equals the volume integral of the divergence over the enclosed volume: ∬S F·n dS=∭V(∇·F)dV.
blocks.subject: Mathematics II

blocks.text: 4. State Stokes' theorem.
blocks.subject: Mathematics II

blocks.text: Answer: The circulation around a closed boundary curve equals the surface integral of curl over the surface: ∮C F·dr=∬S(∇×F)·n dS.
blocks.subject: Mathematics II

blocks.text: 5. State Green's theorem.
blocks.subject: Mathematics II

blocks.text: Answer: ∮C(Pdx+Qdy)=∬R(∂Q/∂x−∂P/∂y)dA for a positively oriented simple closed curve bounding R, under suitable conditions.
blocks.subject: Mathematics II

blocks.text: 5-MARK QUESTIONS
blocks.subject: Mathematics II

blocks.text: 1. Distinguish line, surface and volume integrals.
blocks.subject: Mathematics II

blocks.text: Answer: A line integral is taken along a curve; a surface integral is taken over a two-dimensional surface; a volume integral is taken over a three-dimensional region. Mention typical interpretations such as work along a path, flux through a surface and total mass/quantity in a volume.
blocks.subject: Mathematics II

blocks.text: 2. Explain the role of orientation in Stokes' theorem.
blocks.subject: Mathematics II

blocks.text: Answer: The direction of traversal of the boundary curve must be consistent with the chosen surface normal by the right-hand rule. Reversing the boundary orientation changes the sign of the line integral. State the orientation before evaluating.
blocks.subject: Mathematics II

blocks.text: 10-MARK QUESTION
blocks.subject: Mathematics II

blocks.text: State and explain Gauss, Stokes and Green theorems.
blocks.subject: Mathematics II

blocks.text: Answer: Write each theorem with its integral formula and conditions. Gauss relates closed-surface flux to volume divergence; Stokes relates boundary circulation to surface curl; Green relates a plane line integral around a positively oriented closed curve to a double integral over its region. Explain the surface/region and orientation requirements and solve simple examples following the textbook.
blocks.subject: Mathematics II

blocks.text: SUBJECT 9 – ENGLISH (SFEN12)
blocks.subject: English II

blocks.text: LITERATURE SHORT QUESTIONS
blocks.subject: English II

blocks.text: 1. Who wrote “The Refugee”?
blocks.subject: English II

blocks.text: Answer: K. A. Abbas.
blocks.subject: English II

blocks.text: 2. Who wrote “The Lion and the Lamb”?
blocks.subject: English II

blocks.text: Answer: Leonard Clark.
blocks.subject: English II

blocks.text: 3. Who wrote “The Lady or the Tiger?”
blocks.subject: English II

blocks.text: Answer: Frank R. Stockton.
blocks.subject: English II

blocks.text: 4. Who wrote “The Sky is the Limit”?
blocks.subject: English II

blocks.text: Answer: Kalpana Chawla.
blocks.subject: English II

blocks.text: 5. Who wrote “The Solitary Reaper”?
blocks.subject: English II

blocks.text: Answer: William Wordsworth.

blocks.text: 6. Who wrote “Gift”?

blocks.text: Answer: Alice Walker.

blocks.text: 7. Who wrote “O What is that Sound”?
blocks.subject: English II

blocks.text: Answer: W. H. Auden.
blocks.subject: English II

blocks.text: 8. Who wrote “Ode to the West Wind”?
blocks.subject: English II

blocks.text: Answer: P. B. Shelley.
blocks.subject: English II

blocks.text: 9. Who wrote “The Postmaster”?
blocks.subject: English II

blocks.text: Answer: Rabindranath Tagore.
blocks.subject: English II

blocks.text: 10. Who wrote “The Model Millionaire”?
blocks.subject: English II

blocks.text: Answer: Oscar Wilde.

blocks.text: 11. Who wrote “The Dear Departed”?
blocks.subject: English II

blocks.text: Answer: Stanley Houghton.

blocks.text: 12. Who wrote “The Anniversary”?
blocks.subject: English II

blocks.text: Answer: Anton Chekhov.
blocks.subject: English II

blocks.text: 5-MARK QUESTIONS
blocks.subject: English II

blocks.text: 1. Explain the central idea of “The Solitary Reaper”.
blocks.subject: English II

blocks.text: Answer: The poem describes a solitary young woman reaping and singing in a field. The speaker is deeply moved by the song, even though he cannot fully understand its words. The music remains in his memory after he leaves. The answer should discuss the power of song, nature and memory, using the stanzas in the textbook.
blocks.subject: English II

blocks.text: 2. Explain the significance of the title “The Lady or the Tiger?”.
blocks.subject: English II

blocks.text: Answer: The title presents the choice faced by the accused person in the story: behind one door is a lady and behind the other is a tiger. The uncertainty of the final decision is central to the story's suspense. Explain how the princess's feelings influence the choice and why the ending remains ambiguous.
blocks.subject: English II

blocks.text: 3. Write a note on the central idea of “The Postmaster”.
blocks.subject: English II

blocks.text: Answer: The story explores the relationship between the postmaster and Ratan, an orphaned village girl who helps him. Their emotional attachment is unequal: Ratan forms a deep bond while the postmaster eventually leaves. The story examines loneliness, affection, separation and the pain of unfulfilled attachment. Verify the exact events in the prescribed version.
blocks.subject: English II

blocks.text: 4. Explain the dramatic conflict in “The Dear Departed”.
blocks.subject: English II

blocks.text: Answer: The play satirises family selfishness and materialism. Family members behave as though an elderly relative has died and begin discussing possessions, but the supposed death is challenged. The conflict exposes their concern for property rather than affection. Refer to the exact plot sequence and dialogue in the play.
blocks.subject: English II

blocks.text: 10-MARK QUESTIONS WITH ANSWER FRAMEWORKS
blocks.subject: English II

blocks.text: 1. Discuss the theme of aspiration and determination in “The Sky is the Limit”.
blocks.subject: English II

blocks.text: Answer: Introduce Kalpana Chawla and the lesson's focus on her journey and achievements. Describe her interest in aviation/space, education and professional path as presented in the text. Explain the qualities of ambition, persistence, discipline and courage. Conclude with the lesson's message that determination and hard work help people pursue difficult goals. Verify biography details and dates from the textbook before including them.
blocks.subject: English II

blocks.text: 2. Discuss irony and suspense in “The Lady or the Tiger?”.
blocks.subject: English II

blocks.text: Answer: Introduce the unusual justice system in the story. Explain the accused person's choice between two doors and the role of the princess, who knows what lies behind them. Discuss the emotional conflict created by love, jealousy and the possibility of losing the beloved. Explain why the ending is unresolved and how the title focuses the reader on the central dilemma. Conclude that ambiguity makes the reader consider the princess's motives and the final choice.
blocks.subject: English II

blocks.text: 3. Write a critical appreciation of “Ode to the West Wind”.
blocks.subject: English II

blocks.text: Answer: Identify Shelley and the ode form. Explain how the West Wind is presented as both destructive and preserving, carrying dead leaves and seeds. Discuss the wind's effect on earth, sky and sea, the speaker's appeal to the wind, and the wish for renewal. Mention imagery, apostrophe, symbolism and the closing idea of change/hope. Use the exact stanza references and quotations from the textbook.
blocks.subject: English II

blocks.text: 1. Frame a question: “The train leaves at six.” Ask about time.

blocks.text: 2. Change to passive voice: “The teacher corrected the papers.”

blocks.text: Answer: The papers were corrected by the teacher.

blocks.text: 3. Correct the sentence: “Neither of the boys are present.”
blocks.subject: English II

blocks.text: 4. Add a question tag: “She has finished the work, ____?”
blocks.subject: English II

blocks.text: Answer: She has finished the work, hasn't she?

blocks.text: 5. Form a noun from “decide”.
blocks.subject: English II

blocks.text: Answer: Decision.

blocks.text: SUBJECT 10 – COMMUNICATIVE ENGLISH: LISTENING SKILLS (SFCE12)
blocks.subject: Communicative English II: Listening Skills

blocks.text: 2-MARK QUESTIONS
blocks.subject: Communicative English II: Listening Skills

blocks.text: 1. Distinguish hearing and listening.
blocks.subject: Communicative English II: Listening Skills

blocks.text: Answer: Hearing is the physical reception of sound; listening is an active process of attending to, interpreting and responding to spoken information.
blocks.subject: Communicative English II: Listening Skills

blocks.text: 2. What is listening for gist?
blocks.subject: Communicative English II: Listening Skills

blocks.text: Answer: Listening for gist means identifying the overall topic or main idea without trying to remember every detail.
blocks.subject: Communicative English II: Listening Skills

blocks.text: 3. What is listening for specific information?
blocks.subject: Communicative English II: Listening Skills

blocks.text: Answer: It means listening to identify particular details such as names, numbers, dates, places or instructions.
blocks.subject: Communicative English II: Listening Skills

blocks.text: 4. State two barriers to effective listening.
blocks.subject: Communicative English II: Listening Skills

blocks.text: Answer: Distraction and prejudice. Other barriers include noise, lack of interest, language difficulty and premature judgement.
blocks.subject: Communicative English II: Listening Skills

blocks.text: 5. What is note-taking?
blocks.subject: Communicative English II: Listening Skills

blocks.text: Answer: Note-taking is recording key points from spoken information in a concise form for later recall or use.
blocks.subject: Communicative English II: Listening Skills

blocks.text: 5-MARK QUESTIONS
blocks.subject: Communicative English II: Listening Skills

blocks.text: 1. Explain the qualities of an effective listener.
blocks.subject: Communicative English II: Listening Skills

blocks.text: Answer: An effective listener pays attention, avoids unnecessary interruption, identifies the speaker's purpose, distinguishes main ideas from details, interprets tone and context, asks for clarification when necessary, and gives appropriate feedback. Good listening requires patience and an open mind.
blocks.subject: Communicative English II: Listening Skills

blocks.text: 2. How can one understand unfamiliar accents?
blocks.subject: Communicative English II: Listening Skills

blocks.text: Answer: Focus on meaning and context; listen for stressed words; identify familiar sound patterns; use surrounding information to infer unfamiliar words; practise with speakers from different backgrounds; replay recordings where possible; and ask politely for repetition or clarification.
blocks.subject: Communicative English II: Listening Skills

blocks.text: 3. Explain how to listen to an announcement.
blocks.subject: Communicative English II: Listening Skills

blocks.text: Answer: Identify who is speaking and the purpose; record the event/action, date, time and place; note names, numbers and instructions accurately; listen for changes or warnings; and confirm what action is required. Avoid writing every word.
blocks.subject: Communicative English II: Listening Skills

blocks.text: 10-MARK QUESTIONS
blocks.subject: Communicative English II: Listening Skills

blocks.text: 1. Explain the stages of effective listening and how listening supports leadership.
blocks.subject: Communicative English II: Listening Skills

blocks.text: Answer: Prepare by focusing attention; receive the message without interruption; identify key points and evidence; interpret meaning and tone; evaluate the message; respond or ask questions; and summarise the understanding. Leadership listening helps identify team concerns, build trust, reduce misunderstanding, encourage participation and support sound decisions. A leader should listen actively rather than simply wait to speak.
blocks.subject: Communicative English II: Listening Skills

blocks.text: 2. Describe a method for comprehending a story heard on audio.
blocks.subject: Communicative English II: Listening Skills

blocks.text: Answer: Identify setting, characters and situation; follow the sequence of events; note the main conflict; distinguish important from minor details; identify turning point/climax; understand the resolution; infer the theme/message; and answer analytical questions using evidence from the story. A simple note table can contain Who? Where? What happened? Why? Result? Message?
blocks.subject: Communicative English II: Listening Skills

blocks.text: SEMESTER III – EXPANDED QUESTION BANK
blocks.subject: Communicative English II: Listening Skills

blocks.text: SUBJECT 11 – PROGRAMMING IN C++ AND DATA STRUCTURES (SUCA201A + SUCA201B)
blocks.subject: Programming in C++ and Data Structures

blocks.text: UNIT I – C++ BASICS AND FUNCTIONS
blocks.subject: Programming in C++ and Data Structures

blocks.text: 2-MARK QUESTIONS
blocks.subject: Programming in C++ and Data Structures

blocks.text: 1. Define object-oriented programming.
blocks.subject: Programming in C++ and Data Structures

blocks.text: Answer: Object-oriented programming organises a program around objects that combine data and operations. Its key concepts include classes, objects, encapsulation, inheritance and polymorphism.
blocks.subject: Programming in C++ and Data Structures

blocks.text: 2. What is a token in C++?
blocks.subject: Programming in C++ and Data Structures

blocks.text: Answer: A token is the smallest meaningful unit recognised by the compiler, such as a keyword, identifier, literal, operator or punctuator.
blocks.subject: Programming in C++ and Data Structures

blocks.text: 3. What is a reference variable?
blocks.subject: Programming in C++ and Data Structures

blocks.text: Answer: A reference variable is an alias for an existing object. It is declared with &, must be initialised and refers to the same object.
blocks.subject: Programming in C++ and Data Structures

blocks.text: 4. What is an inline function?
blocks.subject: Programming in C++ and Data Structures

blocks.text: Answer: An inline function is declared using the inline keyword. The compiler may expand it at the call site, but this is not guaranteed.
blocks.subject: Programming in C++ and Data Structures

blocks.text: 5. What is a friend function?
blocks.subject: Programming in C++ and Data Structures

blocks.text: Answer: A friend function is a non-member function granted access to private/protected members of a class that declares it as a friend.
blocks.subject: Programming in C++ and Data Structures

blocks.text: 6. What is a virtual function?
blocks.subject: Programming in C++ and Data Structures

blocks.text: Answer: A virtual function can be overridden in a derived class and supports run-time polymorphism when called through a base-class pointer or reference.
blocks.subject: Programming in C++ and Data Structures

blocks.text: 5-MARK QUESTIONS
blocks.subject: Programming in C++ and Data Structures

blocks.text: 1. Distinguish procedure-oriented and object-oriented programming.
blocks.subject: Programming in C++ and Data Structures

blocks.text: Answer: Procedure-oriented programming organises the program around functions and procedures, with data often passed between functions. OOP organises the program around classes and objects that combine data and related operations. OOP supports encapsulation, inheritance and polymorphism, which can improve modularity and reuse. Use the textbook's discussion of software evolution and program structure.
blocks.subject: Programming in C++ and Data Structures

blocks.text: 2. Explain call by value and call by reference in C++.
blocks.subject: Programming in C++ and Data Structures

blocks.text: Answer: Call by value passes a copy, so changes to the parameter do not directly modify the original variable. Call by reference passes an alias to the original object, so changes through the parameter affect the caller's object. Include syntax examples: void f(int x) and void g(int &x).
blocks.subject: Programming in C++ and Data Structures

blocks.text: 3. Explain the use of manipulators.
blocks.subject: Programming in C++ and Data Structures

blocks.text: Answer: Manipulators control input/output formatting. Examples in standard C++ include endl for a newline/flush and setw for setting field width when using the appropriate header. Use the exact manipulators in the official lesson and show how formatting changes output.
blocks.subject: Programming in C++ and Data Structures

blocks.text: 10-MARK QUESTION
blocks.subject: Programming in C++ and Data Structures

blocks.text: Explain the basic concepts and benefits of OOP.
blocks.subject: Programming in C++ and Data Structures

blocks.text: Answer: Define class and object; explain encapsulation and data hiding; describe abstraction; explain inheritance as deriving new classes from existing classes; explain polymorphism as one interface supporting multiple behaviours; and describe dynamic binding/message passing. Benefits include modularity, reuse, maintainability, extensibility and easier representation of real-world entities. Distinguish compile-time and run-time behaviour where relevant.
blocks.subject: Programming in C++ and Data Structures

blocks.text: UNIT II – CLASSES, OBJECTS, CONSTRUCTORS, OVERLOADING AND INHERITANCE
blocks.subject: Programming in C++ and Data Structures

blocks.text: 2-MARK QUESTIONS
blocks.subject: Programming in C++ and Data Structures

blocks.text: 1. What is a class?
blocks.subject: Programming in C++ and Data Structures

blocks.text: Answer: A class is a user-defined type that groups data members and member functions and defines the structure/behaviour of its objects.
blocks.subject: Programming in C++ and Data Structures

blocks.text: 2. What is an object?
blocks.subject: Programming in C++ and Data Structures

blocks.text: Answer: An object is an instance of a class with its own state and access to the class's member functions.
blocks.subject: Programming in C++ and Data Structures

blocks.text: 3. Define constructor.
blocks.subject: Programming in C++ and Data Structures

blocks.text: Answer: A constructor is a special member function called when an object is initialised. It has the same name as the class and no return type.
blocks.subject: Programming in C++ and Data Structures

blocks.text: 4. Define destructor.
blocks.subject: Programming in C++ and Data Structures

blocks.text: Answer: A destructor is a special member function called when an object's lifetime ends. Its name is the class name preceded by a tilde.
blocks.subject: Programming in C++ and Data Structures

blocks.text: 5. What is function overloading?
blocks.subject: Programming in C++ and Data Structures

blocks.text: Answer: Function overloading allows multiple functions to share a name but have different parameter lists.
blocks.subject: Programming in C++ and Data Structures

blocks.text: 6. What is operator overloading?
blocks.subject: Programming in C++ and Data Structures

blocks.text: Answer: Operator overloading defines an operator's behaviour for a user-defined type, subject to C++ language rules.
blocks.subject: Programming in C++ and Data Structures

blocks.text: 7. What is inheritance?
blocks.subject: Programming in C++ and Data Structures

blocks.text: Answer: Inheritance allows a derived class to acquire accessible members/behaviour from a base class and add or modify its own behaviour.
blocks.subject: Programming in C++ and Data Structures

blocks.text: 5-MARK QUESTIONS
blocks.subject: Programming in C++ and Data Structures

blocks.text: 1. Explain default, parameterised and copy constructors.
blocks.subject: Programming in C++ and Data Structures

blocks.text: Answer: A default constructor can initialise an object without supplied arguments; a parameterised constructor accepts values to initialise members; a copy constructor initialises an object from another object of the same class. The textbook also discusses conversion constructors. Provide a short class example and show which constructor is called for each object creation.
blocks.subject: Programming in C++ and Data Structures

blocks.text: 2. Explain the forms of inheritance.
blocks.subject: Programming in C++ and Data Structures

blocks.text: Answer: Single inheritance has one base and one derived class; multilevel inheritance forms a chain; multiple inheritance has a derived class with more than one base; hierarchical inheritance has several derived classes from one base; hybrid inheritance combines forms. Draw diagrams and mention the textbook's inheritance access modes.
blocks.subject: Programming in C++ and Data Structures

blocks.text: 3. Distinguish compile-time and run-time polymorphism.
blocks.subject: Programming in C++ and Data Structures

blocks.text: Answer: Compile-time polymorphism is resolved by the compiler, commonly through function overloading and operator overloading. Run-time polymorphism uses virtual functions and overriding; the selected function depends on the dynamic type of the object when called through a base pointer/reference.
blocks.subject: Programming in C++ and Data Structures

blocks.text: 10-MARK QUESTION
blocks.subject: Programming in C++ and Data Structures

blocks.text: Explain class, object, constructors, destructors and operator overloading with a suitable program.
blocks.subject: Programming in C++ and Data Structures

blocks.text: Answer: Define a class with private data and public methods; create objects; explain data hiding; show a constructor initialising fields and a destructor's role at object lifetime end; overload a suitable operator such as + for a user-defined type; and explain each statement. Include expected output and mention that operator precedence cannot be changed by overloading.
blocks.subject: Programming in C++ and Data Structures

blocks.text: UNIT III – FILES AND BASIC DATA STRUCTURES
blocks.subject: Programming in C++ and Data Structures

blocks.text: 2-MARK QUESTIONS
blocks.subject: Programming in C++ and Data Structures

blocks.text: 1. Name the C++ file-stream classes.
blocks.subject: Programming in C++ and Data Structures

blocks.text: Answer: ifstream for input, ofstream for output and fstream for input/output.
blocks.subject: Programming in C++ and Data Structures

blocks.text: 2. What is an ordered list?
blocks.subject: Programming in C++ and Data Structures

blocks.text: Answer: An ordered list is a list whose elements are maintained according to a specified order, such as ascending or descending key value.
blocks.subject: Programming in C++ and Data Structures

blocks.text: 3. Define asymptotic notation.
blocks.subject: Programming in C++ and Data Structures

blocks.text: Answer: Asymptotic notation describes how an algorithm's time or space requirement grows with input size.
blocks.subject: Programming in C++ and Data Structures

blocks.text: 4. What is a record?
blocks.subject: Programming in C++ and Data Structures

blocks.text: Answer: A record is a group of related fields describing one entity or item.
blocks.subject: Programming in C++ and Data Structures

blocks.text: 5-MARK QUESTIONS
blocks.subject: Programming in C++ and Data Structures

blocks.text: 1. Explain the steps for file operations in C++.
blocks.subject: Programming in C++ and Data Structures

blocks.text: Answer: Declare an ifstream/ofstream/fstream object; open the file with the appropriate mode; check the stream state; read or write data; handle end-of-file or error conditions; close the file. Discuss sequential access, file pointers/updating and command-line arguments as covered in the textbook.
blocks.subject: Programming in C++ and Data Structures

blocks.text: 2. Explain Big-O, Big-Omega and Big-Theta notation.
blocks.subject: Programming in C++ and Data Structures

blocks.text: Answer: O(g(n)) gives an asymptotic upper bound; Ω(g(n)) gives a lower bound; Θ(g(n)) gives a tight bound when both upper and lower bounds apply. Common growth rates include constant, logarithmic, linear, n log n, quadratic and exponential. Compare functions by dominant terms as n becomes large.
blocks.subject: Programming in C++ and Data Structures

blocks.text: 10-MARK QUESTION
blocks.subject: Programming in C++ and Data Structures

blocks.text: Explain data structures, operations and performance analysis.
blocks.subject: Programming in C++ and Data Structures

blocks.text: Answer: Define a data structure and classify basic/primitive and composite structures. Explain traversal, searching, insertion, deletion, sorting and merging. Describe arrays and ordered lists. Introduce asymptotic notation and compare common time-complexity classes. Explain that selecting a data structure affects access, update, memory and search performance.
blocks.subject: Programming in C++ and Data Structures

blocks.text: UNIT IV – STACKS, QUEUES AND LINKED LISTS
blocks.subject: Programming in C++ and Data Structures

blocks.text: 2-MARK QUESTIONS
blocks.subject: Programming in C++ and Data Structures

blocks.text: 1. State the principle followed by a stack.
blocks.subject: Programming in C++ and Data Structures

blocks.text: Answer: LIFO – Last In, First Out.
blocks.subject: Programming in C++ and Data Structures

blocks.text: 2. Name the two basic stack operations.
blocks.subject: Programming in C++ and Data Structures

blocks.text: Answer: PUSH inserts an item; POP removes the top item.
blocks.subject: Programming in C++ and Data Structures

blocks.text: 3. State the principle followed by a queue.
blocks.subject: Programming in C++ and Data Structures

blocks.text: Answer: FIFO – First In, First Out.
blocks.subject: Programming in C++ and Data Structures

blocks.text: 4. What is a circular queue?
blocks.subject: Programming in C++ and Data Structures

blocks.text: Answer: A circular queue treats the end of an array as connected to the beginning so deleted positions can be reused.
blocks.subject: Programming in C++ and Data Structures

blocks.text: 5. What is a linked-list node?
blocks.subject: Programming in C++ and Data Structures

blocks.text: Answer: A node stores data and one or more link pointers to other nodes.
blocks.subject: Programming in C++ and Data Structures

blocks.text: 5-MARK QUESTIONS
blocks.subject: Programming in C++ and Data Structures

blocks.text: 1. Explain infix-to-postfix conversion using a stack.
blocks.subject: Programming in C++ and Data Structures

blocks.text: Answer: Scan the expression left to right. Output operands immediately. Push opening parentheses. For operators, pop higher-precedence operators (and equal-precedence operators where associativity requires) before pushing the current operator. On a closing parenthesis, pop until the matching opening parenthesis. At the end, pop remaining operators. Show the stack after each symbol and use the textbook precedence rules.
blocks.subject: Programming in C++ and Data Structures

blocks.text: 2. Compare singly and doubly linked lists.
blocks.subject: Programming in C++ and Data Structures

blocks.text: Answer: A singly linked node contains data and a next pointer; traversal normally moves forward. A doubly linked node contains previous and next pointers, allowing forward and backward traversal but requiring more memory and updates to both links. Both support dynamic insertion/deletion without shifting an entire array.
blocks.subject: Programming in C++ and Data Structures

blocks.text: 3. Explain polynomial addition using linked lists.
blocks.subject: Programming in C++ and Data Structures

blocks.text: Answer: Represent each term as coefficient, exponent and next pointer, keeping terms in descending exponent order. Compare current terms; if exponents match, add coefficients; otherwise append the higher exponent term; continue and append remaining terms. Remove zero-coefficient terms if required.
blocks.subject: Programming in C++ and Data Structures

blocks.text: 10-MARK QUESTION
blocks.subject: Programming in C++ and Data Structures

blocks.text: Explain stack and queue implementations and applications.
blocks.subject: Programming in C++ and Data Structures

blocks.text: Answer: Define LIFO and FIFO. For an array stack, maintain top; initialise top to −1; PUSH checks overflow then increments top and stores; POP checks underflow then returns and decrements. For an array queue, maintain front/rear and update them on enqueue/dequeue; discuss circular queue to reuse positions. Applications include expression conversion/evaluation, recursion, function calls, scheduling and buffering. Include diagrams and boundary conditions.
blocks.subject: Programming in C++ and Data Structures

blocks.text: UNIT V – TREES, GRAPHS AND HASHING
blocks.subject: Programming in C++ and Data Structures

blocks.text: 2-MARK QUESTIONS
blocks.subject: Programming in C++ and Data Structures

blocks.text: 1. Define a binary tree.
blocks.subject: Programming in C++ and Data Structures

blocks.text: Answer: A binary tree is a tree in which each node has at most two children, called left and right.
blocks.subject: Programming in C++ and Data Structures

blocks.text: 2. Define inorder traversal.
blocks.subject: Programming in C++ and Data Structures

blocks.text: Answer: Visit the left subtree, then the root, then the right subtree.
blocks.subject: Programming in C++ and Data Structures

blocks.text: 3. What is a graph?
blocks.subject: Programming in C++ and Data Structures

blocks.text: Answer: A graph is a non-linear data structure consisting of vertices (nodes) and edges connecting them.
blocks.subject: Programming in C++ and Data Structures

blocks.text: 4. What is hashing?
blocks.subject: Programming in C++ and Data Structures

blocks.text: Answer: Hashing maps a key to a table index using a hash function.
blocks.subject: Programming in C++ and Data Structures

blocks.text: 5. What is a collision in hashing?
blocks.subject: Programming in C++ and Data Structures

blocks.text: Answer: A collision occurs when two different keys map to the same hash-table location.
blocks.subject: Programming in C++ and Data Structures

blocks.text: 5-MARK QUESTIONS
blocks.subject: Programming in C++ and Data Structures

blocks.text: 1. Explain preorder, inorder and postorder traversals.
blocks.subject: Programming in C++ and Data Structures

blocks.text: Answer: Preorder visits Root-Left-Right; inorder visits Left-Root-Right; postorder visits Left-Right-Root. Explain recursion and trace each order on a labelled sample tree. In a binary search tree, inorder traversal returns keys in sorted order.
blocks.subject: Programming in C++ and Data Structures

blocks.text: 2. Compare DFS and BFS.
blocks.subject: Programming in C++ and Data Structures

blocks.text: Answer: DFS explores a path deeply and backtracks, commonly using recursion or a stack. BFS explores vertices level by level using a queue. Both require marking visited vertices and can be used on graph representations such as adjacency lists/matrices.
blocks.subject: Programming in C++ and Data Structures

blocks.text: 3. Explain Dijkstra's algorithm.
blocks.subject: Programming in C++ and Data Structures

blocks.text: Answer: Initialise source distance to zero and others to infinity; repeatedly select the unprocessed vertex with the smallest tentative distance; relax its outgoing edges; mark it processed; continue until all reachable vertices are processed. The standard algorithm requires non-negative edge weights.
blocks.subject: Programming in C++ and Data Structures

blocks.text: 10-MARK QUESTION
blocks.subject: Programming in C++ and Data Structures

blocks.text: Explain binary search trees, graph traversal and hashing.
blocks.subject: Programming in C++ and Data Structures

blocks.text: Answer: Define a tree and binary tree; explain BST ordering and search/insert/delete operations; describe preorder/inorder/postorder; define graph vertices and edges; explain adjacency matrix/list; describe DFS and BFS with stack/recursion and queue; define hash function and collision; describe collision handling such as chaining/open addressing only as included in the textbook; and explain Dijkstra's shortest path with a small weighted graph.
blocks.subject: Programming in C++ and Data Structures
