blocks.text: LESSON 1 – FUNDAMENTALS OF COMPUTERS
blocks.subject: Fundamentals of Digital Computers

blocks.text: 1.1 What a computer does A computer is an electronic machine that accepts data and instructions, processes the data according to the instructions, stores information and provides results. Data are raw facts. Information is data arranged or processed so that it is meaningful to a user.
blocks.subject: Fundamentals of Digital Computers

blocks.text: Illustration: A student enters marks for five subjects. The marks are data. The computer adds them, calculates the average and displays the total and average. The calculated total and average are information for the student.
blocks.subject: Fundamentals of Digital Computers

blocks.text: 1.2 Functional units
blocks.subject: Fundamentals of Digital Computers

blocks.text: INPUT UNIT → MEMORY / STORAGE ↔ CPU → OUTPUT UNIT
blocks.subject: Fundamentals of Digital Computers

blocks.text: The Central Processing Unit contains or works with three principal functional parts described in the textbook:
blocks.subject: Fundamentals of Digital Computers

blocks.text: • Control Unit (CU): obtains instructions, interprets them and coordinates the activities of the other units. It directs the sequence of operations.
blocks.subject: Fundamentals of Digital Computers

blocks.text: • Arithmetic Logic Unit (ALU): performs arithmetic operations such as addition and subtraction and logical comparisons such as greater-than or equality.
blocks.subject: Fundamentals of Digital Computers

blocks.text: • Primary Storage / Main Memory: holds instructions, input data, intermediate results and output results while processing is taking place.
blocks.subject: Fundamentals of Digital Computers

blocks.text: Input unit: receives data/programs, converts them into a form the computer can accept and supplies them for processing. Examples named in the text include keyboard, mouse, microphone, light pen, joystick and storage media.
blocks.subject: Fundamentals of Digital Computers

blocks.text: Output unit: receives the results, converts them into a human-readable or usable form and presents them through devices such as a display screen, printer or plotter.
blocks.subject: Fundamentals of Digital Computers

blocks.text: Storage: primary storage supports current processing; secondary storage keeps data and programs for later use. Do not confuse temporary working memory with long-term storage.
blocks.subject: Fundamentals of Digital Computers

blocks.text: 1.3 Characteristics of computers
blocks.subject: Fundamentals of Digital Computers

blocks.text: • Speed: computers can execute a very large number of instructions in a short time. The textbook describes speed using small time units such as milliseconds, microseconds and nanoseconds.
blocks.subject: Fundamentals of Digital Computers

blocks.text: • Accuracy: a computer follows its instructions consistently. Incorrect data, incorrect instructions or hardware/software faults can still produce incorrect results; this is often described as garbage in, garbage out.
blocks.subject: Fundamentals of Digital Computers

blocks.text: • Efficiency / diligence: repeated tasks can be carried out without human fatigue.
blocks.subject: Fundamentals of Digital Computers

blocks.text: • Storage capability: large quantities of information can be stored in compact devices and retrieved when needed.
blocks.subject: Fundamentals of Digital Computers

blocks.text: • Versatility: a computer can be used for scientific calculations, reservation systems, billing, data processing and many other tasks.
blocks.subject: Fundamentals of Digital Computers

blocks.text: 1.4 Generations of computers The generation scheme groups computer history by major changes in technology. Learn the technology, approximate period and characteristic features exactly as the textbook presents them.
blocks.subject: Fundamentals of Digital Computers

blocks.text: • First generation – vacuum tubes: large machines, high power use, heat, expensive operation and machine-language programming; punched cards/paper tape were used for input in the textbook's examples. ENIAC and UNIVAC are named examples.
blocks.subject: Fundamentals of Digital Computers

blocks.text: • Second generation – transistors: transistors replaced vacuum tubes in the main switching circuitry; systems became smaller, faster and more reliable than the first generation.
blocks.subject: Fundamentals of Digital Computers

blocks.text: • Third generation – integrated circuits: many electronic components were combined into integrated circuits, improving size, speed, reliability and cost.
blocks.subject: Fundamentals of Digital Computers

blocks.text: • Fourth generation – microprocessors: central processing functions were placed on microprocessor chips; this supported small computers and personal computers.
blocks.subject: Fundamentals of Digital Computers

blocks.text: • Fifth generation: the textbook's discussion associates later development with more advanced processing and intelligent/knowledge-oriented applications. Use the textbook's exact characterisation if a question asks for it.
blocks.subject: Fundamentals of Digital Computers

blocks.text: 1.5 Classification of computers The textbook discusses classification by type, capacity and use. Common distinctions in the lesson include:
blocks.subject: Fundamentals of Digital Computers

blocks.text: • Analog computer: works with continuously varying physical quantities.
blocks.subject: Fundamentals of Digital Computers

blocks.text: • Digital computer: works with discrete values, usually represented in binary form.
blocks.subject: Fundamentals of Digital Computers

blocks.text: • Hybrid computer: combines aspects of analog measurement and digital processing.
blocks.subject: Fundamentals of Digital Computers

blocks.text: • Microcomputer: a smaller general-purpose computer, commonly based on a microprocessor.
blocks.subject: Fundamentals of Digital Computers

blocks.text: • Minicomputer, mainframe and supercomputer: categories used to distinguish processing capacity, scale and typical workloads. Follow the textbook's descriptions rather than assuming size alone defines every modern system.
blocks.subject: Fundamentals of Digital Computers

blocks.text: 1.6 Computer languages Machine language is the binary instruction representation understood by the processor. It is hardware-dependent and difficult for people to write directly. Assembly language uses mnemonic symbols to represent machine instructions. An assembler translates the assembly program into machine code. High-level languages use more human-readable constructs. A compiler or interpreter is used to translate/execute them, depending on the language and environment.
blocks.subject: Fundamentals of Digital Computers

blocks.text: Remember:
blocks.subject: Fundamentals of Digital Computers

blocks.text: Machine code – binary instructions. Assembly – mnemonics translated by an assembler. High-level language – human-oriented program statements translated or interpreted by language software.
blocks.subject: Fundamentals of Digital Computers

blocks.text: 1.7 Operating systems An operating system is system software that manages computer resources and provides an environment for running application programs. It coordinates the user, applications and hardware.
blocks.subject: Fundamentals of Digital Computers

blocks.text: Functions to understand:
blocks.subject: Fundamentals of Digital Computers

blocks.text: • Process/CPU management – deciding which process receives processing time.
blocks.subject: Fundamentals of Digital Computers

blocks.text: • Memory management – allocating and releasing memory.
blocks.subject: Fundamentals of Digital Computers

blocks.text: • File management – organising files and folders and controlling access.
blocks.subject: Fundamentals of Digital Computers

blocks.text: • Device management – coordinating input/output devices.
blocks.subject: Fundamentals of Digital Computers

blocks.text: • User interface – allowing a person to interact with the computer.
blocks.subject: Fundamentals of Digital Computers

blocks.text: • Protection/security – controlling access to resources.
blocks.subject: Fundamentals of Digital Computers

blocks.text: The textbook lesson includes types of operating systems. Study the exact type names and descriptions given there, including batch, multiprogramming, time-sharing, real-time and other classifications that appear in the lesson.
blocks.subject: Fundamentals of Digital Computers

blocks.text: CHECK YOUR UNDERSTANDING – LESSON 1
blocks.subject: Fundamentals of Digital Computers

blocks.text: 1. Draw the functional units of a computer and explain the role of the CPU.
blocks.subject: Fundamentals of Digital Computers

blocks.text: 2. Distinguish data and information using a student-mark example.
blocks.subject: Fundamentals of Digital Computers

blocks.text: 3. Explain any five characteristics of computers.
blocks.subject: Fundamentals of Digital Computers

blocks.text: 4. Compare the five generations using technology and features.
blocks.subject: Fundamentals of Digital Computers

blocks.text: 5. Distinguish machine, assembly and high-level languages.
blocks.subject: Fundamentals of Digital Computers

blocks.text: 6. Define an operating system and explain its major functions.
blocks.subject: Fundamentals of Digital Computers

blocks.text: LESSON 2 – NUMBER SYSTEMS
blocks.subject: Fundamentals of Digital Computers

blocks.text: 2.1 Positional notation A number system has a base (radix). In a positional system, the value of a digit depends on its position relative to the radix point. For a base-b integer with digits d_n ... d_1 d_0: Value = d_n b^n + d_(n-1)b^(n-1) + ... + d_1b + d_0. Digits to the right of a radix point have negative powers of b.
blocks.subject: Fundamentals of Digital Computers

blocks.text: Four systems to memorise:
blocks.subject: Fundamentals of Digital Computers

blocks.text: Decimal – base 10; digits 0–9. Binary – base 2; digits 0 and 1. Octal – base 8; digits 0–7. Hexadecimal – base 16; digits 0–9 and A–F (A=10 ... F=15).
blocks.subject: Fundamentals of Digital Computers

blocks.text: Example B: Convert (45)_10 to binary.
blocks.subject: Fundamentals of Digital Computers

blocks.text: 45 ÷ 2 = 22 remainder 1
blocks.subject: Fundamentals of Digital Computers

blocks.text: 22 ÷ 2 = 11 remainder 0
blocks.subject: Fundamentals of Digital Computers

blocks.text: 11 ÷ 2 = 5 remainder 1
blocks.subject: Fundamentals of Digital Computers

blocks.text: 5 ÷ 2 = 2 remainder 1
blocks.subject: Fundamentals of Digital Computers

blocks.text: 2 ÷ 2 = 1 remainder 0
blocks.subject: Fundamentals of Digital Computers

blocks.text: 1 ÷ 2 = 0 remainder 1
blocks.subject: Fundamentals of Digital Computers

blocks.text: Read the remainders upward: (101101)_2.
blocks.subject: Fundamentals of Digital Computers

blocks.text: Example C: Convert (725)_8 to decimal. = 7×8^2 + 2×8 + 5 = 448 + 16 + 5 = 469.
blocks.subject: Fundamentals of Digital Computers

blocks.text: 2.3 Binary to octal and hexadecimal For binary-to-octal, group bits in sets of three from the radix point. Add leading or trailing zeros where necessary to complete a group. For binary-to-hexadecimal, group bits in sets of four. Example: (11010110)_2 = 11 010 110 when grouped in threes from the right; add leading zero: 011 010 110 = 3 2 6, so (326)_8. For hexadecimal, group as 1101 0110 = D6, so (D6)_16.
blocks.subject: Fundamentals of Digital Computers

blocks.text: 2.4 Fractions For decimal fractions to binary, repeatedly multiply the fractional part by 2. Record the integer part of each product in order, continuing until the fraction becomes zero or the required accuracy is reached. For a base-b fraction to decimal, use negative powers: e.g. (0.101)_2 = 1×2^-1 + 0×2^-2 + 1×2^-3 = 0.5 + 0.125 = 0.625.
blocks.subject: Fundamentals of Digital Computers

blocks.text: LESSON 3 – ARITHMETIC IN NUMBER SYSTEMS
blocks.subject: Fundamentals of Digital Computers

blocks.text: Binary addition rules:
blocks.subject: Fundamentals of Digital Computers

blocks.text: Worked example:
blocks.subject: Fundamentals of Digital Computers

blocks.text: Binary subtraction rules:
blocks.subject: Fundamentals of Digital Computers

blocks.text: 0−0=0; 1−0=1; 1−1=0; 0−1 requires borrowing from the next higher position. In binary, the borrowed value is 10_2 (two decimal units) in the current column.
blocks.subject: Fundamentals of Digital Computers

blocks.text: Binary multiplication uses the same shift-and-add principle as decimal multiplication, but each partial product is formed with 0 or 1.
blocks.subject: Fundamentals of Digital Computers

blocks.text: When doing any base arithmetic:
blocks.subject: Fundamentals of Digital Computers

blocks.text: 1. Align radix points and place values.
blocks.subject: Fundamentals of Digital Computers

blocks.text: 2. Add/subtract from the least significant column.
blocks.subject: Fundamentals of Digital Computers

blocks.text: 3. Carry or borrow according to the base.
blocks.subject: Fundamentals of Digital Computers

blocks.text: 4. Check the answer by conversion to decimal when time permits.
blocks.subject: Fundamentals of Digital Computers

blocks.text: LESSON 4 – COMPLEMENTS
blocks.subject: Fundamentals of Digital Computers

blocks.text: A complement is used in digital arithmetic to represent negative values and to perform subtraction using addition.
blocks.subject: Fundamentals of Digital Computers

blocks.text: For an n-digit number in base r:
blocks.subject: Fundamentals of Digital Computers

blocks.text: (r−1)'s complement: subtract each digit from r−1. r's complement: add 1 to the (r−1)'s complement for an integer representation of fixed width.
blocks.subject: Fundamentals of Digital Computers

blocks.text: Binary:
blocks.subject: Fundamentals of Digital Computers

blocks.text: 1's complement – invert each bit. 2's complement – invert each bit and add 1.
blocks.subject: Fundamentals of Digital Computers

blocks.text: Example using 8 bits: +13 = 00001101. 1's complement = 11110010. 2's complement = 11110011. The bit width must stay fixed. When adding signed 2's-complement values, discard the carry beyond the fixed word length; interpret the remaining pattern according to the signed representation used in the lesson.
blocks.subject: Fundamentals of Digital Computers

blocks.text: To subtract B from A using 2's complement:
blocks.subject: Fundamentals of Digital Computers

blocks.text: 1. Write A and B using the same number of bits.
blocks.subject: Fundamentals of Digital Computers

blocks.text: 2. Find the 2's complement of B.
blocks.subject: Fundamentals of Digital Computers

blocks.text: 3. Add it to A.
blocks.subject: Fundamentals of Digital Computers

blocks.text: 4. Keep the result width and interpret carry/sign correctly.
blocks.subject: Fundamentals of Digital Computers

blocks.text: 5. Check the result with ordinary arithmetic.
blocks.subject: Fundamentals of Digital Computers

blocks.text: LESSON 5 – CODES
blocks.subject: Fundamentals of Digital Computers

blocks.text: A code represents data using a defined pattern of bits. Do not treat every code as ordinary binary place-value notation. The textbook's code lesson should be revised for its exact code list and conversions. Concepts to distinguish:
blocks.subject: Fundamentals of Digital Computers

blocks.text: • Weighted code: each bit position has a fixed weight; a digit's value is obtained from the weighted sum.
blocks.subject: Fundamentals of Digital Computers

blocks.text: • Non-weighted code: bit positions do not represent a simple fixed positional weight.
blocks.subject: Fundamentals of Digital Computers

blocks.text: • BCD: each decimal digit is represented separately by a four-bit binary pattern. For example, decimal 59 is represented as 0101 1001 in 8421 BCD, not as the ordinary binary representation 111011.
blocks.subject: Fundamentals of Digital Computers

blocks.text: • Gray code: adjacent code words differ in one bit; this reduces ambiguity during certain transitions.
blocks.subject: Fundamentals of Digital Computers

blocks.text: • ASCII: a character code used to represent text symbols.
blocks.subject: Fundamentals of Digital Computers

blocks.text: Study the actual table and conversions given in the official code lesson. In a conversion answer, identify the code first, then show each digit/group separately.
blocks.subject: Fundamentals of Digital Computers

blocks.text: LESSON 6 – LOGIC GATES
blocks.subject: Fundamentals of Digital Computers

blocks.text: A logic gate performs a Boolean operation on one or more binary inputs and produces a binary output.
blocks.subject: Fundamentals of Digital Computers

blocks.text: NOT: Y=A'. It reverses the input. AND: Y=A·B. Output is 1 only if both inputs are 1. OR: Y=A+B. Output is 1 if at least one input is 1. NAND: Y=(AB)'. It is the complement of AND. NOR: Y=(A+B)'. It is the complement of OR. XOR: Y=A⊕B. For two inputs, output is 1 when inputs differ. XNOR: Y=(A⊕B)'. Output is 1 when inputs are equal.
blocks.subject: Fundamentals of Digital Computers

blocks.text: Truth table:
blocks.subject: Fundamentals of Digital Computers

blocks.text: A B | AND OR NAND NOR XOR XNOR
blocks.subject: Fundamentals of Digital Computers

blocks.text: Universal gates: NAND and NOR are called universal because suitable combinations of either gate can be used to implement NOT, AND and OR and therefore any Boolean function.
blocks.subject: Fundamentals of Digital Computers

blocks.text: LESSONS 7–8 – BOOLEAN ALGEBRA, LAWS AND THEOREMS
blocks.subject: Fundamentals of Digital Computers

blocks.text: Boolean algebra works with variables that can take only 0 or 1. The three basic operations are OR (+), AND (·) and NOT (').
blocks.subject: Fundamentals of Digital Computers

blocks.text: Important laws:
blocks.subject: Fundamentals of Digital Computers

blocks.text: Identity: A+0=A; A·1=A. Null: A+1=1; A·0=0. Idempotent: A+A=A; A·A=A. Complement: A+A'=1; A·A'=0. Involution: (A')'=A. Commutative: A+B=B+A; AB=BA. Associative: (A+B)+C=A+(B+C); (AB)C=A(BC). Distributive: A(B+C)=AB+AC; A+BC=(A+B)(A+C). Absorption: A+AB=A; A(A+B)=A. De Morgan: (A+B)'=A'B'; (AB)'=A'+B'.
blocks.subject: Fundamentals of Digital Computers

blocks.text: Worked simplification:
blocks.subject: Fundamentals of Digital Computers

blocks.text: F = AB + AB'
blocks.subject: Fundamentals of Digital Computers

blocks.text: Take A common: F=A(B+B')=A×1=A.
blocks.subject: Fundamentals of Digital Computers

blocks.text: Truth-table method:
blocks.subject: Fundamentals of Digital Computers

blocks.text: 1. List all possible input combinations. Two variables have 2^2=4 rows; three variables have 2^3=8 rows.
blocks.subject: Fundamentals of Digital Computers

blocks.text: 2. Evaluate the expression row by row.
blocks.subject: Fundamentals of Digital Computers

blocks.text: 3. Identify rows where output is 1 (for sum-of-products) or 0 (for product-of-sums).
blocks.subject: Fundamentals of Digital Computers

blocks.text: 4. Write the corresponding minterms or maxterms.
blocks.subject: Fundamentals of Digital Computers

blocks.text: 5. Simplify algebraically or with a map.
blocks.subject: Fundamentals of Digital Computers

blocks.text: KARNAUGH MAP METHOD
blocks.subject: Fundamentals of Digital Computers

blocks.text: A K-map is a visual method for minimising a Boolean function. Cells are arranged in Gray-code order so that adjacent cells differ in one variable.
blocks.subject: Fundamentals of Digital Computers

blocks.text: Rules:
blocks.subject: Fundamentals of Digital Computers

blocks.text: • Place 1s in cells for the required minterms (or 0s for maxterms).
blocks.subject: Fundamentals of Digital Computers

blocks.text: • Group cells in powers of two: 1, 2, 4, 8, 16 and so on.
blocks.subject: Fundamentals of Digital Computers

blocks.text: • Make groups as large as possible while covering all required cells.
blocks.subject: Fundamentals of Digital Computers

blocks.text: • A group may wrap across opposite edges.
blocks.subject: Fundamentals of Digital Computers

blocks.text: • Diagonal cells are not adjacent.
blocks.subject: Fundamentals of Digital Computers

blocks.text: • Overlapping is allowed when it helps produce larger groups.
blocks.subject: Fundamentals of Digital Computers

blocks.text: • A variable that changes within a group is eliminated; a variable that remains constant is retained.
blocks.subject: Fundamentals of Digital Computers

blocks.text: For up to five variables, follow the exact five-variable map layout used by the textbook. Practise translating a minterm list into a map before attempting large simplifications.
blocks.subject: Fundamentals of Digital Computers

blocks.text: TABULATION / McCLUSKEY METHOD
blocks.subject: Fundamentals of Digital Computers

blocks.text: 1. Write each minterm in binary using the same number of variables.
blocks.subject: Fundamentals of Digital Computers

blocks.text: 2. Group minterms by the number of 1s.
blocks.subject: Fundamentals of Digital Computers

blocks.text: 3. Compare terms in adjacent groups. Combine terms that differ in one bit by replacing that bit with a dash.
blocks.subject: Fundamentals of Digital Computers

blocks.text: 4. Mark terms that were combined.
blocks.subject: Fundamentals of Digital Computers

blocks.text: 5. Repeat until no more combinations are possible.
blocks.subject: Fundamentals of Digital Computers

blocks.text: 6. Uncombined terms are prime implicants.
blocks.subject: Fundamentals of Digital Computers

blocks.text: 7. Build a prime-implicant chart and choose essential prime implicants first, then cover remaining minterms.
blocks.subject: Fundamentals of Digital Computers

blocks.text: This method is systematic and useful when maps are large. Show combination rounds and the prime-implicant chart in an examination answer.
blocks.subject: Fundamentals of Digital Computers

blocks.text: LESSON 9 – ARITHMETIC BUILDING BLOCKS
blocks.subject: Fundamentals of Digital Computers

blocks.text: Half adder: adds two one-bit inputs A and B. Sum S=A⊕B; Carry C=AB.
blocks.subject: Fundamentals of Digital Computers

blocks.text: Truth table:
blocks.subject: Fundamentals of Digital Computers

blocks.text: A B | S C
blocks.subject: Fundamentals of Digital Computers

blocks.text: Full adder: adds A, B and carry-in Cin. S=A⊕B⊕Cin. Cout=AB + ACin + BCin. A full adder can be constructed using two half adders and an OR gate. Draw the block/logic diagram and truth table.
blocks.subject: Fundamentals of Digital Computers

blocks.text: Half subtractor: subtracts B from A. Difference D=A⊕B. Borrow Bout=A'B.
blocks.subject: Fundamentals of Digital Computers

blocks.text: Full subtractor: subtracts B and borrow-in Bin from A. Know its truth table and logic expression from the official lesson; verify the borrow output by considering all three inputs.
blocks.subject: Fundamentals of Digital Computers

blocks.text: LESSON 10 – SIMPLIFYING LOGIC CIRCUITS
blocks.subject: Fundamentals of Digital Computers

blocks.text: A logic circuit implements a Boolean expression. Simplifying the expression usually reduces the number of gates and/or inputs and can reduce cost and complexity.
blocks.subject: Fundamentals of Digital Computers

blocks.text: Procedure:
blocks.subject: Fundamentals of Digital Computers

blocks.text: 1. Derive the Boolean expression from the truth table or circuit.
blocks.subject: Fundamentals of Digital Computers

blocks.text: 2. Apply Boolean laws, K-map or tabulation.
blocks.subject: Fundamentals of Digital Computers

blocks.text: 3. Draw the simplified gate network.
blocks.subject: Fundamentals of Digital Computers

blocks.text: 4. Verify that the simplified network gives the same output for all input combinations.
blocks.subject: Fundamentals of Digital Computers

blocks.text: LESSON 11 – KARNAUGH MAP SIMPLIFICATION
blocks.subject: Fundamentals of Digital Computers

blocks.text: Before grouping, write the variables in Gray-code order. For a two-variable map, the four cells represent 00, 01, 11, 10 in an order where neighbours differ by one bit. The same Gray-code principle extends to maps with more variables.
blocks.subject: Fundamentals of Digital Computers

blocks.text: Example with three variables: if F(A,B,C)=Σm(1,3,5,7), all listed minterms have C=1. They can be grouped together, so F=C. Verify: the four rows where C=1 yield 1, and the rows where C=0 yield 0.
blocks.subject: Fundamentals of Digital Computers

blocks.text: LESSON 12 – TABULATION METHOD
blocks.subject: Fundamentals of Digital Computers

blocks.text: Keep a clear table for each iteration. A dash means that the corresponding variable has been eliminated because both bit values occurred in the combination. Never combine two terms that differ in two or more fixed bit positions. After finding prime implicants, use a chart to make sure every required minterm is covered.
blocks.subject: Fundamentals of Digital Computers

blocks.text: LESSON 13 – FLIP-FLOPS
blocks.subject: Fundamentals of Digital Computers

blocks.text: A flip-flop is a bistable sequential circuit that stores one bit. Unlike a combinational circuit, its output can depend on the previous state and clocking.
blocks.subject: Fundamentals of Digital Computers

blocks.text: RS flip-flop: has Set and Reset inputs. Set requests Q=1; Reset requests Q=0. Identify the forbidden/invalid input combination for the particular RS implementation in the textbook. JK flip-flop: a modified RS-type device. J=K=0 holds; J=1,K=0 sets; J=0,K=1 resets; J=K=1 toggles. D flip-flop: at the active clock event, the next state follows D. T flip-flop: T=0 holds; T=1 toggles.
blocks.subject: Fundamentals of Digital Computers

blocks.text: For each flip-flop, prepare: symbol, truth/characteristic table, characteristic equation, clock behaviour and one timing/state example. Be precise about whether the device is edge-triggered or level-triggered in the textbook diagram.
blocks.subject: Fundamentals of Digital Computers

blocks.text: LESSON 14 – REGISTERS AND SHIFT REGISTERS
blocks.subject: Fundamentals of Digital Computers

blocks.text: A register is a group of flip-flops used to store a multi-bit binary word. An n-bit register normally requires n storage elements. A shift register moves bits left or right in response to clock pulses. Study the four common arrangements shown in the lesson:
blocks.subject: Fundamentals of Digital Computers

blocks.text: • Serial-In Serial-Out (SISO).
blocks.subject: Fundamentals of Digital Computers

blocks.text: • Serial-In Parallel-Out (SIPO).
blocks.subject: Fundamentals of Digital Computers

blocks.text: • Parallel-In Serial-Out (PISO).
blocks.subject: Fundamentals of Digital Computers

blocks.text: • Parallel-In Parallel-Out (PIPO).
blocks.subject: Fundamentals of Digital Computers

blocks.text: Understand the data input, output arrangement, clocking and one example sequence for each.
blocks.subject: Fundamentals of Digital Computers

blocks.text: LESSON 15 – COUNTERS
blocks.subject: Fundamentals of Digital Computers

blocks.text: A counter is a sequential circuit that passes through a prescribed sequence of states when clock pulses arrive. Ripple/asynchronous counter: the output of one flip-flop drives the clock of the next stage. Changes propagate through the stages, so delay accumulates. Synchronous counter: all flip-flops receive a common clock; combinational logic determines the next state.
blocks.subject: Fundamentals of Digital Computers

blocks.text: Counter-design procedure:
blocks.subject: Fundamentals of Digital Computers

blocks.text: 1. Write the required counting sequence.
blocks.subject: Fundamentals of Digital Computers

blocks.text: 2. Determine how many distinct states are needed.
blocks.subject: Fundamentals of Digital Computers

blocks.text: 3. Select the number of flip-flops (n bits provide up to 2^n states).
blocks.subject: Fundamentals of Digital Computers

blocks.text: 4. Construct the present-state/next-state table.
blocks.subject: Fundamentals of Digital Computers

blocks.text: Decoder: takes an n-bit input and activates one of up to 2^n outputs according to the input code. It expands a coded input into an individual output line. blocks.text: Multiplexer (MUX): selects one of several inputs and routes it to one output. Selection lines determine the active input. A 4-to-1 MUX requires two selection lines. Demultiplexer (DEMUX): routes one input to one of several outputs according to the selection lines. Decoder/MUX implementation: Boolean functions can be built by connecting the appropriate minterms or selecting appropriate variables through a multiplexer. Show selection lines and data inputs clearly. ROM: Read Only Memory stores a fixed pattern of bits; logic functions can be implemented by storing the output pattern for each possible input address. PLA: Programmable Logic Array uses programmable logic structures to implement sum-of-products functions. Draw the input, AND-plane, OR-plane and output arrangement used in the textbook.

blocks.text: SUBJECT 3 – MATHEMATICS I (SUCA103)
blocks.subject: Mathematics I

blocks.text: OFFICIAL UNIT MAP
blocks.subject: Mathematics I

blocks.text: Unit I: Algebra and Numerical Methods – summation of series; operators E, Δ, ∇; difference tables; Newton-Raphson; Newton forward/backward interpolation for equal intervals; Lagrange interpolation.
blocks.subject: Mathematics I

blocks.text: Unit II: Matrices – symmetric, skew-symmetric, orthogonal, Hermitian, skew-Hermitian, unitary matrices; eigenvalues/eigenvectors; Cayley-Hamilton (without proof), verification and inverse.
blocks.subject: Mathematics I

blocks.text: Unit III: Theory of Equations – polynomial equations with real coefficients, irrational and complex roots, symmetric functions, transformations by increasing/decreasing roots by a constant, reciprocal equations, Newton approximate roots.
blocks.subject: Mathematics I

blocks.text: Unit IV: Trigonometry – expansions of powers of sine/cosine; multiple-angle expansions; power series of sin, cos and tan; hyperbolic/inverse hyperbolic functions; logarithms of complex numbers.
blocks.subject: Mathematics I

blocks.text: Unit V: Differential Calculus – successive/nth derivatives, Leibnitz theorem without proof and applications, Jacobians, curvature/radius of curvature, maxima/minima of two variables and Lagrange multipliers.
blocks.subject: Mathematics I

blocks.text: UNIT I – ALGEBRA AND NUMERICAL METHODS
blocks.subject: Mathematics I

blocks.text: A. Rational fractions and partial fractions A rational fraction is a ratio of two polynomials. It is proper when the degree of the numerator is less than the degree of the denominator; it is improper when the numerator degree is equal to or greater than the denominator degree. An improper fraction is first divided into polynomial part plus proper fraction before decomposition.
blocks.subject: Mathematics I

blocks.text: Partial fractions express a proper rational fraction as a sum of simpler fractions. The form depends on the denominator factors:
blocks.subject: Mathematics I

blocks.text: • Distinct linear factors: A/(x−a) + B/(x−b) + ...
blocks.subject: Mathematics I

blocks.text: • Repeated linear factor (x−a)^n: A1/(x−a)+A2/(x−a)^2+...+An/(x−a)^n.
blocks.subject: Mathematics I

blocks.text: • Irreducible quadratic factor: (Ax+B)/(quadratic).
blocks.subject: Mathematics I

blocks.text: Worked example:
blocks.subject: Mathematics I

blocks.text: Resolve (3x+5)/[(x+1)(x+2)]. Assume (3x+5)/[(x+1)(x+2)] = A/(x+1)+B/(x+2). Then 3x+5=A(x+2)+B(x+1). Put x=−1: 2=A, so A=2. Put x=−2: −1=−B, so B=1. Therefore the fraction = 2/(x+1)+1/(x+2). Check by recombining: [2(x+2)+(x+1)]/denominator=(3x+5)/denominator.
blocks.subject: Mathematics I

blocks.text: B. Binomial series For positive integer n, (1+x)^n terminates after n+1 terms. The general binomial expansion begins: (1+x)^n = 1 + nx + n(n−1)x²/2! + n(n−1)(n−2)x³/3! + ... For non-integer or negative n, the expansion continues as an infinite series under its convergence conditions. Use the conditions and range stated in the textbook. Worked example: Expand (1+x)^4. =1+4x+6x²+4x³+x⁴.
blocks.subject: Mathematics I

blocks.text: C. Exponential series
blocks.subject: Mathematics I

blocks.text: The standard expansion is:
blocks.subject: Mathematics I

blocks.text: e^x = 1 + x + x²/2! + x³/3! + x⁴/4! + ... For e^(ax), replace x by ax. The series is useful for approximating values and is part of the textbook's algebra lesson.
blocks.subject: Mathematics I

blocks.text: D. Logarithmic series
blocks.subject: Mathematics I

blocks.text: A standard expansion in the textbook's lesson is:
blocks.subject: Mathematics I

blocks.text: log(1+x)=x−x²/2+x³/3−x⁴/4+... for |x|<1, with the appropriate logarithm convention. Use the exact base/convention and convergence condition stated in the prescribed text.
blocks.subject: Mathematics I

blocks.text: E. Finite-difference operators
blocks.subject: Mathematics I

blocks.text: For equally spaced x values with step h:
blocks.subject: Mathematics I

blocks.text: Example table for y=x² at x=0,1,2,3:
blocks.subject: Mathematics I

blocks.text: x: 0, 1, 2, 3 y: 0, 1, 4, 9 First forward differences: 1, 3, 5. Second forward differences: 2, 2. Third differences: 0. A polynomial of degree 2 has constant second differences for equal spacing.
blocks.subject: Mathematics I

blocks.text: F. Newton-Raphson method
blocks.subject: Mathematics I

blocks.text: To approximate a root of f(x)=0:
blocks.subject: Mathematics I

blocks.text: x_(n+1)=x_n−f(x_n)/f'(x_n). Worked example: find a root of x²−2=0 beginning with x0=1.5. f(x)=x²−2; f'(x)=2x. x1=1.5−(2.25−2)/3 = 1.4166667. x2≈1.4166667−(1.4166667²−2)/(2×1.4166667)≈1.4142157. The root is approximately √2≈1.4142. Procedure: define f, differentiate, choose starting value, calculate successive approximations and stop when the required accuracy is reached. Watch for a zero/small derivative and unsuitable starting value.
blocks.subject: Mathematics I

blocks.text: G. Newton forward interpolation Used for equally spaced data when the required x is near the beginning of the table. y = y0 + uΔy0 + [u(u−1)/2!]Δ²y0 + [u(u−1)(u−2)/3!]Δ³y0 + ... where u=(x−x0)/h. Use the forward difference table. Keep the difference order and factorial terms aligned.
blocks.subject: Mathematics I

blocks.text: H. Newton backward interpolation Used for equally spaced data when the required x is near the end of the table. y = yn + u∇yn + [u(u+1)/2!]∇²yn + [u(u+1)(u+2)/3!]∇³yn + ... where u=(x−xn)/h. Use the backward difference table.
blocks.subject: Mathematics I

blocks.text: I. Lagrange interpolation For distinct data points (x0,y0),...,(xn,yn), P(x)=Σ y_i L_i(x), where L_i(x)=Π_(j≠i)(x−x_j)/(x_i−x_j). Unlike Newton's equal-interval formulae, Lagrange's method does not require equally spaced x values. Worked example for points (1,1),(2,4),(3,9): the data lie on y=x², so the interpolating polynomial is x². In an examination, show each L_i(x) term and substitution rather than simply identifying the pattern.
blocks.subject: Mathematics I

blocks.text: UNIT II – MATRICES
blocks.subject: Mathematics I

blocks.text: A matrix is a rectangular arrangement of elements in rows and columns. The order m×n means m rows and n columns. A square matrix has the same number of rows and columns.
blocks.subject: Mathematics I

blocks.text: Types:
blocks.subject: Mathematics I

blocks.text: Row matrix – one row. Column matrix – one column. Square matrix – same number of rows and columns. Diagonal matrix – non-zero entries, if any, only on the main diagonal. Identity matrix I – diagonal entries are 1 and other entries are 0. Zero matrix – every entry is 0. Symmetric – A^T=A. Skew-symmetric – A^T=−A. Orthogonal – A^T A=I, therefore A^(-1)=A^T. Hermitian – A*=A, where * is conjugate transpose. Skew-Hermitian – A*=−A. Unitary – A* A=I, therefore A^(-1)=A*.
blocks.subject: Mathematics I

blocks.text: Matrix operations Addition/subtraction require matrices of the same order; add/subtract corresponding entries. For multiplication A_(m×n)B_(n×p), the inner dimensions must match, and the result has order m×p. The entry is obtained by multiplying a row of A by a column of B and adding. Transpose interchanges rows and columns. Determinant is defined for square matrices. A matrix is invertible only if its determinant is non-zero.
blocks.subject: Mathematics I

blocks.text: Eigenvalues and eigenvectors For a square matrix A, a non-zero vector X is an eigenvector corresponding to λ when AX=λX. Rearrange (A−λI)X=0. For a non-trivial solution, det(A−λI)=0. Solve the characteristic equation for λ, then substitute each eigenvalue to obtain an eigenvector.
blocks.subject: Mathematics I

blocks.text: Worked 2×2 example:
blocks.subject: Mathematics I

blocks.text: Characteristic equation: |A−λI|=(2−λ)(3−λ)=0.
blocks.subject: Mathematics I

blocks.text: Eigenvalues: λ=2 and λ=3. For λ=2, (A−2I)X=0 gives y=0, so an eigenvector is [1,0]^T. For λ=3, x=0, so an eigenvector is [0,1]^T.
blocks.subject: Mathematics I

blocks.text: Cayley-Hamilton theorem Every square matrix satisfies its own characteristic equation. If the characteristic polynomial is p(λ), then p(A)=0. The syllabus specifies this theorem without proof but requires verification and computation of inverse.
blocks.subject: Mathematics I

blocks.text: Method:
blocks.subject: Mathematics I

blocks.text: 1. Find characteristic polynomial det(λI−A) or follow the exact sign convention in the question.
blocks.subject: Mathematics I

blocks.text: 2. Replace λ by A to obtain the matrix equation.
blocks.subject: Mathematics I

blocks.text: 3. Simplify matrix powers.
blocks.subject: Mathematics I

blocks.text: 4. To find A^(-1), multiply/rearrange the equation if det(A)≠0.
blocks.subject: Mathematics I

blocks.text: Do not mix det(A−λI) with det(λI−A) without changing signs consistently.
blocks.subject: Mathematics I

blocks.text: UNIT III – THEORY OF EQUATIONS
blocks.subject: Mathematics I

blocks.text: Polynomial equation: a_nx^n+a_(n−1)x^(n−1)+...+a0=0, with a_n≠0. A root is a value that makes the polynomial zero. If coefficients are real, non-real complex roots occur in conjugate pairs.
blocks.subject: Mathematics I

blocks.text: For a monic cubic x³+ax²+bx+c=0 with roots α, β, γ: α+β+γ=−a. αβ+βγ+γα=b. αβγ=−c. These are symmetric functions of roots. For other degrees, follow the coefficient/root relationships given in the textbook.
blocks.subject: Mathematics I

blocks.text: Transformation of roots If the new roots are increased by k or decreased by k, substitute the corresponding shifted variable in the original polynomial and expand. First write clearly what the new variable represents. Do not substitute without defining the relationship between old and new roots.
blocks.subject: Mathematics I

blocks.text: Reciprocal equations A reciprocal equation has coefficients arranged in a symmetrical or anti-symmetrical pattern. The textbook uses substitutions to reduce the degree. Identify the symmetry first, then apply the prescribed substitution and solve the reduced equation.
blocks.subject: Mathematics I

blocks.text: Approximate roots Newton's method is used as in Unit I. Show f(x), f'(x), starting value and iterations.
blocks.subject: Mathematics I

blocks.text: UNIT IV – TRIGONOMETRY
blocks.subject: Mathematics I

blocks.text: Power series:
blocks.subject: Mathematics I

blocks.text: sin x=x−x³/3!+x⁵/5!−x⁷/7!+... cos x=1−x²/2!+x⁴/4!−x⁶/6!+... tan x=x+x³/3+2x⁵/15+17x⁷/315+... (as the corresponding Maclaurin expansion; verify the exact terms required from the textbook). These expansions use x in radians.
blocks.subject: Mathematics I

blocks.text: Multiple-angle expansions The textbook asks for expansions of powers of sinθ and cosθ and powers of sinθ, cosθ and tanθ in terms of multiples of θ. Use the relevant trigonometric identities, for example: sin²θ=(1−cos2θ)/2. cos²θ=(1+cos2θ)/2. sinθ cosθ=(sin2θ)/2. Apply identities repeatedly to higher powers and follow the textbook's target form.
blocks.subject: Mathematics I

blocks.text: Hyperbolic functions:
blocks.subject: Mathematics I

blocks.text: sinh x=(e^x−e^(−x))/2. cosh x=(e^x+e^(−x))/2. tanh x=sinh x/cosh x. Identity: cosh²x−sinh²x=1. Inverse hyperbolic functions reverse the corresponding functions on their permitted domains. Learn the expressions and derivations used in the book.
blocks.subject: Mathematics I

blocks.text: Logarithm of a complex number Write z in polar form z=r(cosθ+i sinθ). A logarithm has real part ln r and an argument term i(θ+2kπ), for integer k. Therefore the complex logarithm is multi-valued unless a branch is specified. Use the branch and principal-argument convention in the textbook's examples.
blocks.subject: Mathematics I

blocks.text: UNIT V – DIFFERENTIAL CALCULUS
blocks.subject: Mathematics I

blocks.text: Successive differentiation means differentiating repeatedly: y', y'', y''' and so on. The nth derivative is d^n y/dx^n.
blocks.subject: Mathematics I

blocks.text: Useful nth derivatives:
blocks.subject: Mathematics I

blocks.text: If y=e^(ax), then y^(n)=a^n e^(ax). If y=sin(ax+b), derivatives repeat in a four-step cycle with powers of a. If y=cos(ax+b), derivatives also repeat in a four-step cycle. Use the exact standard-result table in the textbook.
blocks.subject: Mathematics I

blocks.text: Leibnitz theorem
blocks.subject: Mathematics I

blocks.text: For a product uv:
blocks.subject: Mathematics I

blocks.text: d^n(uv)/dx^n = Σ_(r=0 to n) nCr u^(r) v^(n−r). The theorem is listed without proof. Apply the binomial-coefficient pattern and compute the derivatives carefully.
blocks.subject: Mathematics I

blocks.text: Jacobian
blocks.subject: Mathematics I

blocks.text: For u=u(x,y), v=v(x,y):
blocks.subject: Mathematics I

blocks.text: ∂(u,v)/∂(x,y) = |u_x  u_y; v_x  v_y| = u_xv_y−u_yv_x.
blocks.subject: Mathematics I

blocks.text: For three variables, form the 3×3 determinant of partial derivatives.
blocks.subject: Mathematics I

blocks.text: Curvature and radius of curvature
blocks.subject: Mathematics I

blocks.text: For y=f(x), a common Cartesian formula is:
blocks.subject: Mathematics I

blocks.text: Curvature κ=1/ρ. Calculate first and second derivatives before substitution. Use the textbook's precise sign/coordinate convention.
blocks.subject: Mathematics I

blocks.text: Maxima and minima of two variables For f(x,y), stationary points satisfy f_x=0 and f_y=0. Let D=f_xx f_yy−(f_xy)². If D>0 and f_xx>0: local minimum. If D>0 and f_xx<0: local maximum. If D<0: saddle point. If D=0: test inconclusive.
blocks.subject: Mathematics I

blocks.text: Lagrange multipliers To find extrema subject to g(x,y)=0, form ∇f=λ∇g together with the constraint. Solve simultaneously and test feasible candidates according to the problem.
blocks.subject: Mathematics I

blocks.text: MATHEMATICS I – REQUIRED WRITTEN WORK
blocks.subject: Mathematics I

blocks.text: Every numerical solution should display: given data, formula, substitution, intermediate calculations and final result. Do not jump directly to the answer. Use the same number of decimal places throughout a calculation and round only at the end unless the textbook specifies otherwise.
blocks.subject: Mathematics I

blocks.text: PRACTICE PRIORITIES – MATHEMATICS I
blocks.subject: Mathematics I

blocks.text: 1. Resolve proper/improper rational fractions into partial fractions.
blocks.subject: Mathematics I

blocks.text: 2. Expand binomial, exponential and logarithmic series.
blocks.subject: Mathematics I

blocks.text: 3. Complete finite-difference tables and apply Newton interpolation.
blocks.subject: Mathematics I

blocks.text: 4. Use Newton-Raphson to approximate roots.
blocks.subject: Mathematics I

blocks.text: 5. Identify special matrix types and calculate eigenvalues/eigenvectors.
blocks.subject: Mathematics I

blocks.text: 6. Verify Cayley-Hamilton and calculate an inverse.
blocks.subject: Mathematics I

blocks.text: 7. Use symmetric functions and transformations of equations.
blocks.subject: Mathematics I

blocks.text: 8. Expand trigonometric/hyperbolic expressions and complex logarithms.
blocks.subject: Mathematics I

blocks.text: 9. Apply Leibnitz theorem and evaluate Jacobians.
blocks.subject: Mathematics I
