blocks.text: SUBJECT 4 – COMMUNICATIVE ENGLISH: SPEAKING SKILLS (SFCE11)
blocks.subject: Communicative English I: Speaking Skills

blocks.text: OFFICIAL SCHEME OF LESSONS
blocks.subject: Communicative English I: Speaking Skills

blocks.text: 1. Speaking Skills.
blocks.subject: Communicative English I: Speaking Skills

blocks.text: 2. Non-Verbal Communication.
blocks.subject: Communicative English I: Speaking Skills

blocks.text: 3. Introduction to Phonetics.
blocks.subject: Communicative English I: Speaking Skills

blocks.text: 4. Business Conversations.
blocks.subject: Communicative English I: Speaking Skills

blocks.text: 5. Speaking in Interviews.
blocks.subject: Communicative English I: Speaking Skills

blocks.text: 6. Group Discussion and Panel Discussion.
blocks.subject: Communicative English I: Speaking Skills

blocks.text: 7. Giving Instructions.
blocks.subject: Communicative English I: Speaking Skills

blocks.text: 8. Making Presentation.
blocks.subject: Communicative English I: Speaking Skills

blocks.text: 9. Hosting Events.
blocks.subject: Communicative English I: Speaking Skills

blocks.text: 10. Business Presentations.
blocks.subject: Communicative English I: Speaking Skills

blocks.text: LESSON 1 – SPEAKING SKILLS
blocks.subject: Communicative English I: Speaking Skills

blocks.text: Four language skills Listening and reading are receptive skills because the learner receives and interprets language. Speaking and writing are productive skills because the learner creates language to communicate.
blocks.subject: Communicative English I: Speaking Skills

blocks.text: Speech production has three stages:
blocks.subject: Communicative English I: Speaking Skills

blocks.text: 1. Conceptualisation: the speaker forms the idea or intention.
blocks.subject: Communicative English I: Speaking Skills

blocks.text: 2. Formulation: the idea is organised into words and grammatical structure.
blocks.subject: Communicative English I: Speaking Skills

blocks.text: 3. Articulation: the words are physically spoken using the speech organs and airflow.
blocks.subject: Communicative English I: Speaking Skills

blocks.text: Speaking is the process of expressing thoughts and feelings through spoken language. It is two-way in effective communication because a speaker also listens and responds.
blocks.subject: Communicative English I: Speaking Skills

blocks.text: Three patterns of speaking:
blocks.subject: Communicative English I: Speaking Skills

blocks.text: • Interactive: speakers alternate between speaking and listening, as in a face-to-face or telephone conversation.
blocks.subject: Communicative English I: Speaking Skills

blocks.text: • Partially interactive: one person speaks mainly to an audience, which responds at limited points, such as a question period.
blocks.subject: Communicative English I: Speaking Skills

blocks.text: • Non-interactive: a one-way delivery such as a recitation or broadcast, where immediate listener response is not part of the event.
blocks.subject: Communicative English I: Speaking Skills

blocks.text: Formal speaking occurs in professional/institutional situations. Informal speaking occurs in personal and familiar settings. A speaker should choose vocabulary, tone and sentence structure to suit the context.
blocks.subject: Communicative English I: Speaking Skills

blocks.text: Effective speaking: listen actively; think before responding; organise the message; use suitable vocabulary; pronounce clearly; speak at an appropriate pace and volume; avoid excessive fillers; and check whether the listener understood.
blocks.subject: Communicative English I: Speaking Skills

blocks.text: LESSON 2 – NON-VERBAL COMMUNICATION
blocks.subject: Communicative English I: Speaking Skills

blocks.text: Non-verbal communication conveys meaning without words or alongside spoken language. It includes facial expression, eye contact, gesture, posture, body movement, appearance, personal space and vocal features such as tone, pitch and pace.
blocks.subject: Communicative English I: Speaking Skills

blocks.text: Functions:
blocks.subject: Communicative English I: Speaking Skills

blocks.text: • Reinforcing: body language supports the spoken message.
blocks.subject: Communicative English I: Speaking Skills

blocks.text: • Replacing: a gesture can replace words (for example, a nod).
blocks.subject: Communicative English I: Speaking Skills

blocks.text: • Regulating: eye contact and gestures help manage turn-taking.
blocks.subject: Communicative English I: Speaking Skills

blocks.text: • Revealing emotion: posture or facial expression may show confidence, concern or confusion.
blocks.subject: Communicative English I: Speaking Skills

blocks.text: • Contradicting: body language can conflict with spoken words.
blocks.subject: Communicative English I: Speaking Skills

blocks.text: Good practice: maintain natural eye contact, face the audience, keep an open posture, use purposeful gestures, avoid distracting movements and respect personal space. Non-verbal meanings can vary across cultures; interpret them in context.
blocks.subject: Communicative English I: Speaking Skills

blocks.text: LESSON 3 – INTRODUCTION TO PHONETICS
blocks.subject: Communicative English I: Speaking Skills

blocks.text: Phonetics is the study of speech sounds and how they are produced, transmitted and perceived. The lesson introduces pronunciation and neutral-accent training.
blocks.subject: Communicative English I: Speaking Skills

blocks.text: Important terms:
blocks.subject: Communicative English I: Speaking Skills

blocks.text: • Vowel: speech sound produced without a major obstruction of airflow in the vocal tract.
blocks.subject: Communicative English I: Speaking Skills

blocks.text: • Consonant: sound produced with some narrowing or obstruction of airflow.
blocks.subject: Communicative English I: Speaking Skills

blocks.text: • Voicing: vibration of the vocal folds.
blocks.subject: Communicative English I: Speaking Skills

blocks.text: • Word stress: prominence given to a syllable in a word.
blocks.subject: Communicative English I: Speaking Skills

blocks.text: • Sentence stress: prominence given to important words in a sentence.
blocks.subject: Communicative English I: Speaking Skills

blocks.text: • Intonation: rise and fall of pitch in connected speech.
blocks.subject: Communicative English I: Speaking Skills

blocks.text: • Articulation: physical formation of speech sounds.
blocks.subject: Communicative English I: Speaking Skills

blocks.text: Pronunciation practice:
blocks.subject: Communicative English I: Speaking Skills

blocks.text: 1. Listen to a model pronunciation.
blocks.subject: Communicative English I: Speaking Skills

blocks.text: 2. Identify the stressed syllable/sound.
blocks.subject: Communicative English I: Speaking Skills

blocks.text: 3. Repeat slowly, then at natural speed.
blocks.subject: Communicative English I: Speaking Skills

blocks.text: 4. Record and compare your own speech.
blocks.subject: Communicative English I: Speaking Skills

blocks.text: 5. Practise difficult sound contrasts in meaningful words.
blocks.subject: Communicative English I: Speaking Skills

blocks.text: Neutral-accent training is about intelligibility and consistent pronunciation, not erasing a speaker's identity.
blocks.subject: Communicative English I: Speaking Skills

blocks.text: LESSON 4 – BUSINESS CONVERSATIONS
blocks.subject: Communicative English I: Speaking Skills

blocks.text: A business conversation is a professional exchange intended to share information, solve a problem or agree on action.
blocks.subject: Communicative English I: Speaking Skills

blocks.text: Typical structure:
blocks.subject: Communicative English I: Speaking Skills

blocks.text: 1. Greeting and polite opening.
blocks.subject: Communicative English I: Speaking Skills

blocks.text: 2. Identify the purpose.
blocks.subject: Communicative English I: Speaking Skills

blocks.text: 3. Present information clearly.
blocks.subject: Communicative English I: Speaking Skills

blocks.text: 4. Ask questions and listen to responses.
blocks.subject: Communicative English I: Speaking Skills

blocks.text: 5. Clarify facts, dates, quantities and responsibilities.
blocks.subject: Communicative English I: Speaking Skills

blocks.text: 6. Summarise the decision and next step.
blocks.subject: Communicative English I: Speaking Skills

blocks.text: 7. Close politely.
blocks.subject: Communicative English I: Speaking Skills

blocks.text: Useful language functions: requesting, offering, agreeing, disagreeing tactfully, clarifying, confirming and apologising. Avoid vague language when a precise business detail is needed.
blocks.subject: Communicative English I: Speaking Skills

blocks.text: LESSON 5 – SPEAKING IN INTERVIEWS
blocks.subject: Communicative English I: Speaking Skills

blocks.text: An interview is a structured conversation used to assess a candidate or gather information. Preparation should include understanding the role, reviewing relevant experience, preparing examples and practising clear answers.
blocks.subject: Communicative English I: Speaking Skills

blocks.text: Answer method:
blocks.subject: Communicative English I: Speaking Skills

blocks.text: • Listen to the full question.
blocks.subject: Communicative English I: Speaking Skills

blocks.text: • Identify what is being asked.
blocks.subject: Communicative English I: Speaking Skills

blocks.text: • Give a direct opening answer.
blocks.subject: Communicative English I: Speaking Skills

blocks.text: • Support it with a relevant example.
blocks.subject: Communicative English I: Speaking Skills

blocks.text: • Explain the result or lesson.
blocks.subject: Communicative English I: Speaking Skills

blocks.text: • Avoid exaggeration and unsupported claims.
blocks.subject: Communicative English I: Speaking Skills

blocks.text: A helpful supplementary structure for experience-based questions is STAR: Situation, Task, Action, Result. Use it to organise an answer, but answer the actual question rather than forcing every reply into the same template.
blocks.subject: Communicative English I: Speaking Skills

blocks.text: Interview conduct: punctuality, suitable dress, respectful greeting, attentive listening, clear speech, appropriate eye contact and a professional closing.
blocks.subject: Communicative English I: Speaking Skills

blocks.text: LESSON 6 – GROUP DISCUSSION AND PANEL DISCUSSION
blocks.subject: Communicative English I: Speaking Skills
blocks.chapter: LESSON 6 – GROUP DISCUSSION AND PANEL DISCUSSION

blocks.text: A group discussion is an exchange of ideas among several participants on a given topic. It assesses understanding, relevance, communication, listening, reasoning and cooperation.
blocks.subject: Communicative English I: Speaking Skills
blocks.chapter: LESSON 6 – GROUP DISCUSSION AND PANEL DISCUSSION

blocks.text: Good participant behaviour:
blocks.subject: Communicative English I: Speaking Skills
blocks.chapter: LESSON 6 – GROUP DISCUSSION AND PANEL DISCUSSION

blocks.text: 1. Understand the topic and frame a position.
blocks.subject: Communicative English I: Speaking Skills
blocks.chapter: LESSON 6 – GROUP DISCUSSION AND PANEL DISCUSSION

blocks.text: 2. Begin only when there is a useful point to make.
blocks.subject: Communicative English I: Speaking Skills
blocks.chapter: LESSON 6 – GROUP DISCUSSION AND PANEL DISCUSSION

blocks.text: 3. Support views with reasons/examples.
blocks.subject: Communicative English I: Speaking Skills
blocks.chapter: LESSON 6 – GROUP DISCUSSION AND PANEL DISCUSSION

blocks.text: 4. Listen and refer to earlier points.
blocks.subject: Communicative English I: Speaking Skills
blocks.chapter: LESSON 6 – GROUP DISCUSSION AND PANEL DISCUSSION

blocks.text: 5. Disagree with ideas, not people.
blocks.subject: Communicative English I: Speaking Skills
blocks.chapter: LESSON 6 – GROUP DISCUSSION AND PANEL DISCUSSION

blocks.text: 6. Do not interrupt or dominate.
blocks.subject: Communicative English I: Speaking Skills
blocks.chapter: LESSON 6 – GROUP DISCUSSION AND PANEL DISCUSSION

blocks.text: 7. Help the group stay on topic and reach a conclusion.
blocks.subject: Communicative English I: Speaking Skills
blocks.chapter: LESSON 6 – GROUP DISCUSSION AND PANEL DISCUSSION

blocks.text: A panel discussion usually involves several speakers and a moderator. The moderator introduces the topic, manages turns and may invite audience questions. A panelist should make concise contributions and respond to other panelists respectfully.
blocks.subject: Communicative English I: Speaking Skills
blocks.chapter: LESSON 6 – GROUP DISCUSSION AND PANEL DISCUSSION

blocks.text: LESSON 7 – GIVING INSTRUCTIONS
blocks.subject: Communicative English I: Speaking Skills

blocks.text: Clear instructions help another person perform a task correctly.
blocks.subject: Communicative English I: Speaking Skills

blocks.text: Structure:
blocks.subject: Communicative English I: Speaking Skills

blocks.text: 1. State the objective.
blocks.subject: Communicative English I: Speaking Skills

blocks.text: 2. Mention materials or preparation required.
blocks.subject: Communicative English I: Speaking Skills

blocks.text: 3. Give steps in a logical order.
blocks.subject: Communicative English I: Speaking Skills

blocks.text: 4. Use clear action verbs.
blocks.subject: Communicative English I: Speaking Skills

blocks.text: 5. State cautions, conditions and exceptions.
blocks.subject: Communicative English I: Speaking Skills

blocks.text: 6. Check understanding or invite questions.
blocks.subject: Communicative English I: Speaking Skills

blocks.text: Use sequence words: first, next, then, after that, finally. Use precise references such as “the second box” rather than “that thing”.
blocks.subject: Communicative English I: Speaking Skills

blocks.text: LESSON 8 – MAKING PRESENTATIONS
blocks.subject: Communicative English I: Speaking Skills

blocks.text: A presentation communicates information to an audience. It should have a clear purpose and logical structure.
blocks.subject: Communicative English I: Speaking Skills

blocks.text: Introduction: greet the audience, introduce yourself/topic, give the purpose and outline. Body: explain the main points in a logical order, using examples and appropriate visual aids. Conclusion: summarise the message, state a recommendation or final thought and signal the end. Questions: listen carefully, answer directly and admit when you do not know.
blocks.subject: Communicative English I: Speaking Skills

blocks.text: Extempore speaking: organise quickly around an opening, two or three points and a closing. Just-a-Minute speaking: stay on one topic, use a clear sequence and finish within the assigned time.
blocks.subject: Communicative English I: Speaking Skills

blocks.text: LESSON 9 – HOSTING EVENTS
blocks.subject: Communicative English I: Speaking Skills

blocks.text: The host or master of ceremonies guides an event. Typical responsibilities:
blocks.subject: Communicative English I: Speaking Skills

blocks.text: • Welcome guests and introduce the occasion.
blocks.subject: Communicative English I: Speaking Skills

blocks.text: • Introduce speakers/performers accurately.
blocks.subject: Communicative English I: Speaking Skills

blocks.text: • Announce the sequence of programme items.
blocks.subject: Communicative English I: Speaking Skills

blocks.text: • Manage transitions and timing.
blocks.subject: Communicative English I: Speaking Skills

blocks.text: • Respond calmly to delays or changes.
blocks.subject: Communicative English I: Speaking Skills

blocks.text: • Thank participants and close the event.
blocks.subject: Communicative English I: Speaking Skills

blocks.text: Use correct names, titles and pronunciation. Do not make unsupported biographical claims about a speaker.
blocks.subject: Communicative English I: Speaking Skills

blocks.text: LESSON 10 – BUSINESS PRESENTATIONS
blocks.subject: Communicative English I: Speaking Skills

blocks.text: A business presentation focuses on a decision, proposal, performance result or plan. The presenter should understand the audience's needs, use relevant evidence, separate facts from assumptions, explain the implications and give a clear recommendation.
blocks.subject: Communicative English I: Speaking Skills

blocks.text: Suggested structure: context/problem → evidence → analysis → options → recommendation → action/next step. Slides should support the speaker, not become a wall of text.
blocks.subject: Communicative English I: Speaking Skills

blocks.text: SPEAKING SKILLS – EXAM PREPARATION
blocks.subject: Communicative English I: Speaking Skills

blocks.text: 2 marks: define receptive and productive skills; define phonetics; state two forms of non-verbal communication; define group discussion; define extempore speech. 5 marks: explain stages of speech production; discuss features of effective speaking; explain forms of non-verbal communication; list interview preparation steps; explain rules of group discussion. Long answer: explain the structure of an effective presentation; discuss business conversation techniques; describe the role of a host; explain the duties of a moderator in panel discussion.
blocks.subject: Communicative English I: Speaking Skills

blocks.text: SUBJECT 5 – ENGLISH, SEMESTER I (SFEN11)
blocks.subject: English I

blocks.text: The official book is a foundation English course. The syllabus contains preparatory lessons, prose, poetry, short stories, grammar and the Sound Right section.
blocks.subject: English I

blocks.text: UNIT I – PREPARATORY LESSONS
blocks.subject: English I

blocks.text: 1. Competition Matters – Suzanne Sievert
blocks.subject: English I

blocks.text: Central idea: competition can teach children motivation, resilience and the ability to accept defeat. The author questions the practice of declaring every participant a winner when a contest has a clear result. Her pumpkin-decorating example and family race illustrate that losing can teach improvement and sportsmanship. The lesson does not argue that children should be humiliated; it argues that they can learn to face results honestly and grow from them. Exam points: sportsmanship; accepting defeat; motivation; learning from mistakes; why a real contest needs a meaningful result.
blocks.subject: English I

blocks.text: 2. A Personal Crisis May Change History – Dr. A.P.J. Abdul Kalam
blocks.subject: English I

blocks.text: Central idea: the way a person responds to a crisis can change not only individual life but wider history. The lesson connects Gandhi's experience of racial discrimination in South Africa, Mandela's struggle against apartheid and Ashoka's turn towards non-violence after the Kalinga war. It presents empathy, courage, perseverance and non-violence as responses that can transform society. Exam points: Gandhi's response to humiliation; connection between Gandhi and Mandela; Ashoka and Ahimsa; crisis as a turning point; the role of youth in addressing social and economic inequality.
blocks.subject: English I

blocks.text: 3. Why Preserve Biodiversity – Prof. D. Balasubramanian
blocks.subject: English I

blocks.text: Central idea: biodiversity deserves protection for ethical, aesthetic and practical reasons. Living species are beautiful and valuable in themselves; plants and microbes also support food, medicine and human wellbeing. Human activity such as deforestation, short-term exploitation, poverty-related pressures, anthropocentrism and policy failures can damage ecological networks. Conservation is a responsibility to future generations. Exam points: ethical/aesthetic reason; utilitarian value; biodiversity as a genetic resource; reasons for biotic degradation; human responsibility for conservation.
blocks.subject: English I

blocks.text: 4. A Call to Action – Hillary Rodham Clinton
blocks.subject: English I

blocks.text: Central idea: violence and discrimination against women are violations of human rights. The speech describes harms such as denial of food to girl children, trafficking, dowry violence, rape, domestic violence, harmful practices and denial of reproductive choice. Its central message is that women's rights are human rights and that women must have the right to speak and be heard. Exam points: examples of rights violations; public responsibility; the purpose of the address; equality, dignity and women's voice.
blocks.subject: English I

blocks.text: 5. If Only There Were More Like Him – Revathi Seshadri
blocks.subject: English I

blocks.text: Central idea: the lesson presents kindness, humanity and valuing human relationships through the Colonel's conduct. Shankar, a servant, betrays the Colonel by helping robbers, but the Colonel protects Shankar's dignity after his death and undertakes to support his son’s education. The son's later development illustrates the long-term value of compassionate action. Exam points: the Colonel's kindness; Shankar's betrayal; how the Colonel describes Shankar's death to the police; why the son's future changes; significance of the title.
blocks.subject: English I

blocks.text: UNIT II – PROSE
blocks.subject: English I

blocks.text: 1. My Greatest Olympic Prize – Jesse Owens
blocks.subject: English I

blocks.text: The autobiographical account concerns the 1936 Berlin Olympics. Jesse Owens is determined to challenge the ideology of Aryan racial superiority through athletic performance. During the long-jump trials, his first attempts are fouls. His German rival Luz Long, despite the competition and the political atmosphere, offers practical advice that helps Owens qualify. Their friendship continues during the event. Long congratulates Owens after the winning jump, demonstrating sportsmanship even under the gaze of Hitler. Owens later explains that Long's friendship was his greatest prize. Prepare the story as an account of friendship, fair play and human dignity beyond race or nationality.
blocks.subject: English I

blocks.text: 2. If You Are Wrong, Admit It – Dale Carnegie
blocks.subject: English I

blocks.text: The essay argues that admitting a mistake quickly and honestly can reduce conflict and invite cooperation. The author uses examples involving a policeman and his dog, an artist and an art editor, Harvey and his supervisor, General Lee and Picket's Charge, and the columnist Hubbard. Instead of defending an error with excuses, the person accepts responsibility. This often changes the other person's response from anger to understanding. The lesson's practical principle is not to confess falsely, but to admit genuine mistakes and resolve them constructively.
blocks.subject: English I

blocks.text: 3. Monday Morning – Mark Twain (extract from The Adventures of Tom Sawyer)
blocks.subject: English I

blocks.text: Tom Sawyer dislikes the start of the school week and tries to invent an illness so he can stay home. He first complains of an imagined toe problem, then remembers his loose tooth. His performance wakes Sid and brings Aunt Polly to the room. Aunt Polly recognises the deception and responds in a way that exposes Tom's plan. The episode uses humour to portray childish imagination, laziness about school and a mischievous relationship between Tom and his aunt.
blocks.subject: English I

blocks.text: 4. The Unexpected – Robert Lynd
blocks.subject: English I

blocks.text: The lesson celebrates unexpected pleasures in ordinary life and nature. The author suggests that an experience can be especially delightful when it arrives without being planned or demanded. The unexpected song of a bird is used as an example: its arrival at an unanticipated moment gives it a special charm. Prepare the contrast between planned enjoyment and spontaneous delight, and explain how the natural world provides gifts that cannot be scheduled.
blocks.subject: English I

blocks.text: UNIT III – POETRY
blocks.subject: English I

blocks.text: 1. Pulley or The Gift of God – George Herbert
blocks.subject: English I

blocks.text: The poem imagines God creating humanity and deciding how to distribute blessings. God gives human beings many gifts but withholds one element—rest/complete contentment—so that human beings may continue to turn towards the Creator when worldly blessings fail to satisfy. The pulley image expresses the idea that a lack of complete rest can draw humanity back to God. In an answer, explain the creation image, the gifts, the withheld rest and the spiritual message. Use the poem's own wording only if you have verified it in the text.
blocks.subject: English I

blocks.text: 2. La Belle Dame Sans Merci – John Keats
blocks.subject: English I

blocks.text: The poem is a ballad-like encounter between a knight and a mysterious beautiful woman. The knight is found pale and weakened. He recounts meeting the woman, being captivated by her, following her to an enchanted place and experiencing a dream/vision in which other pale figures warn him. He wakes alone and desolate. Themes include enchantment, desire, transience, imagination and the destructive or unsettling power of idealised love. Prepare the setting, the knight's condition, the woman’s mysterious nature, the dream and the unresolved ending.
blocks.subject: English I

blocks.text: 3. The Night of the Scorpion – Nissim Ezekiel
blocks.subject: English I

blocks.text: The poem describes a mother who is stung by a scorpion on a rainy night. Villagers gather and offer explanations, prayers and traditional remedies. The father, described as more rationalist, tries different remedies and even uses paraffin. The poem presents a community's beliefs, fear and concern. After the mother recovers, her final response focuses on gratitude that the scorpion stung her rather than her children. Themes: maternal love, village life, superstition, faith, rationalism and compassion. Do not reduce the poem to a simple claim that villagers are foolish; the poem also shows communal solidarity.
blocks.subject: English I

blocks.text: 4. The Death of the Bird – A.D. Hope
blocks.subject: English I

blocks.text: The poem presents a bird's final migration and death, using the journey to examine instinct, ageing, exhaustion, nature and mortality. The repeated journey that once connected the bird with familiar seasonal patterns becomes increasingly difficult. Prepare the bird's movement, the contrast between natural beauty and physical decline, the cause/conditions of death described in the poem, and the emotional effect of the final migration.
blocks.subject: English I

blocks.text: POETRY ANSWER FRAMEWORK
blocks.subject: English I

blocks.text: 1. Name the poet and poem.
blocks.subject: English I

blocks.text: 2. Describe the situation or speaker.
blocks.subject: English I

blocks.text: 3. Explain the central idea in your own words.
blocks.subject: English I

blocks.text: 4. Discuss the main images/symbols that appear in the prescribed poem.
blocks.subject: English I

blocks.text: 5. Explain the theme and title.
blocks.subject: English I

blocks.text: 6. Conclude with the poem's effect or message.
blocks.subject: English I

blocks.text: Do not invent quotations or poetic devices. Use only devices you can point to in the poem.
blocks.subject: English I

blocks.text: UNIT IV – SHORT STORIES
blocks.subject: English I

blocks.text: 1. Mrs. Packletide's Tiger – Saki
blocks.subject: English I

blocks.text: Mrs. Packletide wants to shoot a tiger mainly because she envies Loona Bimberton's public attention. A weak old tiger is arranged as a safe target with the help of villagers. During the shooting, the bullet hits the goat and the tiger dies from fright/heart failure according to the story's account. Miss Mebbin discovers the truth and uses it to pressure Mrs. Packletide into buying a cottage. The story satirises vanity, social rivalry, greed and the desire for publicity. Important characters: Mrs. Packletide, Miss Mebbin, Loona Bimberton and the villagers.
blocks.subject: English I

blocks.text: 2. A Snake in the Grass – R.K. Narayan
blocks.subject: English I

blocks.text: The story centres on a household disturbed by the report of a snake in the garden. The family members react with fear and send for help, while the search and conflicting claims create suspense and humour. The ending turns on what is or is not actually found and on the way people respond to rumour. In preparing this lesson, use the exact sequence and ending in the textbook rather than relying on a generic snake-story summary. Focus on character reactions, domestic setting, fear and irony.
blocks.subject: English I

blocks.text: 3. Three Questions – Leo Tolstoy
blocks.subject: English I

blocks.text: A king believes that if he knows the right time to begin an action, the right people to listen to and the most important thing to do, he will never fail. He seeks answers from wise men, but receives varied replies. A meeting with a hermit and an injured man leads him to discover that the most important time is the present, the most important person is the one with whom he is, and the most important work is to do good to that person. The lesson emphasises presence, compassion and practical kindness.
blocks.subject: English I

blocks.text: 4. The Gift of the Magi – O. Henry
blocks.subject: English I

blocks.text: A young married couple, Della and Jim, are poor but deeply devoted to each other. Della sells her beautiful hair to buy a chain for Jim's watch. Jim sells his watch to buy combs for Della's hair. Each gift becomes temporarily unusable because of the other's sacrifice, but the gifts reveal the depth of their love. The story uses irony and the idea of wise giving: the value lies in the love and sacrifice, not the usefulness or price of the object.
blocks.subject: English I

blocks.text: UNIT V – GRAMMAR
blocks.subject: English I

blocks.text: 1. Tense and aspect
blocks.subject: English I

blocks.text: Tense locates an action in time. Aspect shows how the action is viewed (for example, as simple, ongoing or completed). Present simple: I study. Present continuous: I am studying. Present perfect: I have studied. Present perfect continuous: I have been studying. Past and future forms should be practised in the same pattern. Select a tense based on the time reference and intended meaning, not by memorising one translation.
blocks.subject: English I

blocks.text: 2. Primary auxiliaries
blocks.subject: English I

blocks.text: Be, have and do function as main verbs or auxiliaries. Examples: is reading; has completed; do not agree. They help form progressive/perfect aspects, questions and negatives.
blocks.subject: English I

blocks.text: 3. Modal auxiliaries
blocks.subject: English I

blocks.text: Can, could, may, might, shall, should, will, would, must and related forms express ability, permission, possibility, obligation, advice or willingness. The modal is followed by the base form of the main verb in common constructions: She can speak; You must study.
blocks.subject: English I

blocks.text: 4. Negatives
blocks.subject: English I

blocks.text: Use the correct auxiliary + not. Examples: She is not ready; They do not play; He has not finished. When no auxiliary is present in a simple present/past statement, use do/does/did and the base form of the verb.
blocks.subject: English I

blocks.text: 5. Yes/No questions
blocks.subject: English I

blocks.text: Move the auxiliary before the subject: She is ready → Is she ready? They have arrived → Have they arrived? If there is no auxiliary, use do/does/did: He likes tea → Does he like tea?
blocks.subject: English I

blocks.text: 6. WH questions
blocks.subject: English I

blocks.text: Who, what, when, where, why, which and how request specific information. Identify the information being asked and use correct auxiliary-subject order.
blocks.subject: English I

blocks.text: 7. Tag questions
blocks.subject: English I

blocks.text: A tag is a short question added to a statement. A positive statement commonly takes a negative tag; a negative statement commonly takes a positive tag. Use the same auxiliary and a pronoun that refers to the subject. Example: She is here, isn't she? They didn't come, did they?
blocks.subject: English I

blocks.text: 8. Completing sentences and common errors
blocks.subject: English I

blocks.text: Check subject–verb agreement, tense sequence, articles, prepositions, pronoun reference, word order and countability. Read the whole sentence for meaning before selecting an answer.
blocks.subject: English I

blocks.text: 9. Synonyms and antonyms
blocks.subject: English I

blocks.text: A synonym is a word with a similar meaning; an antonym has an opposite meaning. A near-synonym may not fit every context. Use sentence meaning to select the correct word.
blocks.subject: English I

blocks.text: 10. Word classes
blocks.subject: English I

blocks.text: Noun, pronoun, verb, adjective, adverb, preposition, conjunction and interjection. The same word can belong to different classes depending on use: “fast” can be an adjective or an adverb.
blocks.subject: English I

blocks.text: SOUND RIGHT
blocks.subject: English I

blocks.text: The book includes introduction to English sounds, word stress, strong and weak forms, sentence stress, intonation and voice modulation. Practise hearing and reproducing sounds. In a written answer, define the term and give one illustrative example consistent with the textbook.
blocks.subject: English I

blocks.text: ENGLISH I – EXAM PREPARATION
blocks.subject: English I

blocks.text: 2 marks: identify the author/poet; define a word; state the central idea; define tense/aspect; frame a tag question. 5 marks: summarise a prescribed prose/story; explain the theme of a poem; write a character sketch; correct a grammar passage. Long answer: prepare structured summaries/appreciations and theme explanations for each prescribed text. Use textbook events and names accurately.
blocks.subject: English I

blocks.text: PART II – SEMESTER II DETAILED NOTEBOOK
SUBJECT 6 – PROGRAMMING IN C (SUCA104)
blocks.subject: Programming in C

blocks.text: OFFICIAL UNIT MAP
blocks.subject: Programming in C

blocks.text: Unit I: character set, identifiers, keywords, data types, constants, variables, declarations, expressions, statements, operators and library functions.
blocks.subject: Programming in C

blocks.text: Unit II: input/output, simple programs, if/if-else, while, do-while, for, nested controls, switch, break, continue, goto and comma operator.
blocks.subject: Programming in C

blocks.text: Unit III: functions, definitions, prototypes, argument passing, recursion, storage classes and multi-file programs.
blocks.subject: Programming in C

blocks.text: Unit IV: arrays, multidimensional arrays, strings, structures, user-defined types, self-referential structures, unions and bitwise operations.
blocks.subject: Programming in C

blocks.text: Unit V: pointers, pointer operations, arrays/pointers, arrays of pointers, structures/pointers and file handling.
blocks.subject: Programming in C

blocks.text: UNIT I – INTRODUCTION, DATA TYPES AND EXPRESSIONS
blocks.subject: Programming in C

blocks.text: 1. C language and program structure
blocks.subject: Programming in C

blocks.text: The textbook presents C as a general-purpose language between high-level and low-level language categories (often described as a middle-level language). It supports structured programming and gives the programmer control over data representation and operations.
blocks.subject: Programming in C

blocks.text: A simple C program:
blocks.subject: Programming in C

blocks.text: #include <stdio.h>
blocks.subject: Programming in C

blocks.text: int main(void)
blocks.subject: Programming in C

blocks.text: printf("Hello, World!\n");
blocks.subject: Programming in C

blocks.text: return 0;
blocks.subject: Programming in C

blocks.text: Explanation:
blocks.subject: Programming in C

blocks.text: • #include <stdio.h> makes standard input/output declarations available.
blocks.subject: Programming in C

blocks.text: • main is the function where execution begins in a hosted C program.
blocks.subject: Programming in C

blocks.text: • Braces enclose the function body.
blocks.subject: Programming in C

blocks.text: • printf displays output.
blocks.subject: Programming in C

blocks.text: • return 0 indicates successful completion.
blocks.subject: Programming in C

blocks.text: 2. Character set
blocks.subject: Programming in C

blocks.text: The character set includes letters, digits, white-space characters and special symbols accepted by the language. These characters are used to construct identifiers, constants, operators and statements.
blocks.subject: Programming in C

blocks.text: 3. Identifiers and keywords
blocks.subject: Programming in C

blocks.text: Identifier: programmer-defined name for an object, function or other program entity. It must follow the language's naming rules and cannot be a reserved keyword. C identifiers are case-sensitive. Keyword: a reserved word with a predefined meaning, such as int, return, if or while.
blocks.subject: Programming in C

blocks.text: 4. Data types
blocks.subject: Programming in C

blocks.text: Basic types include char, int, float and double, with modifiers such as signed, unsigned, short and long as supported by the implementation and the textbook. The type determines the kind of value and the operations that can be performed. Use sizeof or the compiler documentation only when the problem asks about size; sizes can vary by implementation.
blocks.subject: Programming in C

blocks.text: 5. Constants and variables
blocks.subject: Programming in C

blocks.text: A constant is a fixed value; a variable is a named storage location whose value may change. Examples: 25 (integer constant), 3.14 (floating constant), 'A' (character constant), "BCA" (string literal).
blocks.subject: Programming in C

blocks.text: Declaration examples:
blocks.subject: Programming in C

blocks.text: int count; float average; char grade;
blocks.subject: Programming in C

blocks.text: Initialisation:
blocks.subject: Programming in C

blocks.text: int count = 0;
blocks.subject: Programming in C

blocks.text: float price = 12.5f;
blocks.subject: Programming in C

blocks.text: 6. Expressions and operators
blocks.subject: Programming in C

blocks.text: Arithmetic: +, -, *, /, %. Relational: <, <=, >, >=, ==, !=.
blocks.subject: Programming in C

blocks.text: Logical: &&, ||, !.
blocks.subject: Programming in C

blocks.text: Assignment: = and compound assignments. Unary: ++, --, unary +/− and address/dereference operators where relevant. Conditional: condition ? expression1 : expression2. Bitwise operators are included in Unit IV.
blocks.subject: Programming in C

blocks.text: Precedence decides how operators are grouped. Use parentheses when the order might be unclear. Integer division discards the fractional part; floating-point division produces a fractional result when the operands are floating-point.
blocks.subject: Programming in C

blocks.text: Worked expression check:
blocks.subject: Programming in C

blocks.text: int a=7, b=2; 7/2 gives integer result 3. 7.0/2 gives floating result 3.5.
blocks.subject: Programming in C

blocks.text: 7. Library functions
blocks.subject: Programming in C

blocks.text: Library functions are predefined functions supplied through standard library headers. Include the appropriate header and use the correct argument/return types. Examples often used in introductory C include mathematical functions from <math.h>, character/string functions from their headers and input/output functions from <stdio.h>. Follow the exact functions taught in the book.
blocks.subject: Programming in C

blocks.text: UNIT II – INPUT/OUTPUT AND CONTROL FLOW
blocks.subject: Programming in C

blocks.text: 1. Input and output
blocks.subject: Programming in C

blocks.text: printf formats output; scanf reads formatted input. Example:
blocks.subject: Programming in C

blocks.text: int age; printf("Enter age: "); scanf("%d", &age);
blocks.subject: Programming in C

blocks.text: printf("Age = %d\n", age);
blocks.subject: Programming in C

blocks.text: The address operator & is required in scanf for ordinary variables because scanf needs the variable's address. Strings/arrays are handled differently; do not blindly add & to every argument.
blocks.subject: Programming in C

blocks.text: Common format specifiers: %d for int, %f for float in printf, %lf for double in printf contexts according to the standard formatting requirements, %c for char and %s for a null-terminated string. Match the exact format specifier rules in the prescribed C version and function.
blocks.subject: Programming in C

blocks.text: 2. if statement
blocks.subject: Programming in C

blocks.text: if (condition) { statements; } The block executes only if the condition is true (non-zero).
blocks.subject: Programming in C

blocks.text: 3. if–else
blocks.subject: Programming in C

blocks.text: if (condition) { ... } else { ... } Exactly one branch is selected. Nested if statements place one decision inside another.
blocks.subject: Programming in C

blocks.text: 4. switch
blocks.subject: Programming in C

blocks.text: switch(expression) { case constant: statements; break; default: statements; } The expression is compared with case labels. break usually prevents execution from continuing into the next case. The default branch handles unmatched values.
blocks.subject: Programming in C

blocks.text: 5. while loop
blocks.subject: Programming in C

blocks.text: Initialise control variable; while (condition) { body; update; } The condition is tested before the body, so the body may execute zero times.
blocks.subject: Programming in C

blocks.text: 6. do–while loop
blocks.subject: Programming in C

blocks.text: Do the body first, then test the condition. The body executes at least once.
blocks.subject: Programming in C

blocks.text: 7. for loop
blocks.subject: Programming in C

blocks.text: for (initialisation; condition; update) { body; } It is suitable when the loop control pattern is clear. Avoid off-by-one errors.
blocks.subject: Programming in C

blocks.text: 8. break, continue and goto
blocks.subject: Programming in C

blocks.text: break exits the nearest loop/switch. continue skips the remaining body and proceeds to the next iteration. goto transfers execution to a labelled statement; excessive use makes program flow harder to follow.
blocks.subject: Programming in C

blocks.text: 9. Comma operator
blocks.subject: Programming in C

blocks.text: The comma operator evaluates expressions from left to right and the value of the overall expression is the value of the final expression. Do not confuse it with the comma used to separate function arguments or declarations.
blocks.subject: Programming in C

blocks.text: MODEL PROGRAM – DECISION MAKING
blocks.subject: Programming in C

blocks.text: #include <stdio.h>
blocks.subject: Programming in C

blocks.text: int main(void)
blocks.subject: Programming in C

blocks.text: int n;
blocks.subject: Programming in C

blocks.text: scanf("%d", &n);
blocks.subject: Programming in C

blocks.text: printf("Even\n");
blocks.subject: Programming in C

blocks.text: else
blocks.subject: Programming in C

blocks.text: printf("Odd\n");
blocks.subject: Programming in C

blocks.text: return 0;
blocks.subject: Programming in C

blocks.text: Input 8 → Output Even. Logic: a number is even if the remainder after division by 2 is zero.
blocks.subject: Programming in C

blocks.text: MODEL PROGRAM – LOOPING
blocks.subject: Programming in C

blocks.text: #include <stdio.h>
blocks.subject: Programming in C

blocks.text: int main(void)
blocks.subject: Programming in C

blocks.text: int n, i, sum = 0;
blocks.subject: Programming in C

blocks.text: scanf("%d", &n);
blocks.subject: Programming in C

blocks.text: for (i = 1; i <= n; ++i)
blocks.subject: Programming in C

blocks.text: sum += i;
blocks.subject: Programming in C

blocks.text: printf("%d\n", sum);
blocks.subject: Programming in C

blocks.text: return 0;
blocks.subject: Programming in C

blocks.text: Input 5 → Output 15. Logic: add all integers from 1 through n.
blocks.subject: Programming in C

blocks.text: UNIT III – FUNCTIONS, RECURSION AND STORAGE CLASSES
blocks.subject: Programming in C

blocks.text: 1. Function
blocks.subject: Programming in C

blocks.text: A function is a named unit of code that performs a task. It helps divide a large program into smaller modules that can be tested and reused.
blocks.subject: Programming in C

blocks.text: Prototype:
blocks.subject: Programming in C

blocks.text: int add(int, int);
blocks.subject: Programming in C

blocks.text: Definition:
blocks.subject: Programming in C

blocks.text: int add(int a, int b)
blocks.subject: Programming in C

blocks.text: return a + b;
blocks.subject: Programming in C

blocks.text: Call:
blocks.subject: Programming in C

blocks.text: int result = add(4, 5);
blocks.subject: Programming in C

blocks.text: 2. Parameters and arguments
blocks.subject: Programming in C

blocks.text: Actual arguments are written in the function call. Formal parameters are declared in the function definition and receive the values. In C, arguments are passed by value. A function can modify the caller's data indirectly by receiving a pointer and dereferencing it.
blocks.subject: Programming in C

blocks.text: 3. Return values
blocks.subject: Programming in C

blocks.text: A non-void function returns a value of the declared type using return. A void function does not return a value. Every control path in a value-returning function should return a value.
blocks.subject: Programming in C

blocks.text: 4. Recursion
blocks.subject: Programming in C

blocks.text: A recursive function calls itself. It must have a base case and a recursive case. The recursive case should move towards the base case.
blocks.subject: Programming in C

blocks.text: Factorial:
blocks.subject: Programming in C

blocks.text: long factorial(int n)
blocks.subject: Programming in C

blocks.text: if (n <= 1) return 1;
blocks.subject: Programming in C

blocks.text: return n * factorial(n-1);
blocks.subject: Programming in C

blocks.text: For valid non-negative integer n; large factorials can overflow a fixed-width integer type.
blocks.subject: Programming in C

blocks.text: 5. Storage classes
blocks.subject: Programming in C

blocks.text: The textbook lists automatic, external, static and register variables. Learn scope, lifetime, linkage/visibility and default initialisation as explained in the lesson. A local automatic variable generally exists during block execution; a static object retains its stored value between calls; an external declaration can refer to an object defined elsewhere; register is a storage-class request to the compiler in the source model.
blocks.subject: Programming in C

blocks.text: 6. Multi-file programs
blocks.subject: Programming in C

blocks.text: A program can be divided into source and header files. Put declarations/prototypes in a header when shared, definitions in the appropriate source file, and compile/link the required files consistently. Declarations and definitions must match.
blocks.subject: Programming in C

blocks.text: UNIT IV – ARRAYS, STRINGS, STRUCTURES AND UNIONS
blocks.subject: Programming in C

blocks.text: 1. One-dimensional array
blocks.subject: Programming in C

blocks.text: An array stores a fixed sequence of elements of the same type. Indexing begins at 0.
blocks.subject: Programming in C

blocks.text: marks[0] is 70; marks[4] is 75. Never access an index outside 0 to 4.
blocks.subject: Programming in C

blocks.text: 2. Array processing
blocks.subject: Programming in C

blocks.text: Traversal: visit each element using a loop. Search: compare each element with a key. Sum/average: accumulate the elements and divide by the count. Sorting: reorder elements by a rule. Insertion/deletion in a static array may require shifting elements.
blocks.subject: Programming in C

blocks.text: 3. Multidimensional arrays
blocks.subject: Programming in C

blocks.text: An array such as int a[2][3] represents 2 rows and 3 columns. Nested loops process each row and column. The number of columns in a parameter declaration for a 2D array must be known to calculate element addresses in the usual C parameter form.
blocks.subject: Programming in C

blocks.text: 4. Strings
blocks.subject: Programming in C

blocks.text: A C string is a character array terminated by the null character '\0'. Reserve space for this terminator. Common operations include length, copy, concatenate and compare through the functions taught in the textbook. Check buffer size to avoid writing beyond the array.
blocks.subject: Programming in C

blocks.text: 5. Structures
blocks.subject: Programming in C

blocks.text: A structure groups related values that may have different types.
blocks.subject: Programming in C

blocks.text: struct Student {
blocks.subject: Programming in C

blocks.text: int roll;
blocks.subject: Programming in C

blocks.text: char name[40];
blocks.subject: Programming in C

blocks.text: float mark;
blocks.subject: Programming in C

blocks.text: struct Student s;
blocks.subject: Programming in C

blocks.text: A structure member is accessed with the dot operator for an object and the arrow operator for a pointer.
blocks.subject: Programming in C

blocks.text: 6. User-defined types
blocks.subject: Programming in C

blocks.text: The book includes user-defined types and self-referential structures. Study the precise declarations and examples. typedef can provide an alias for a type; enum provides named integral constants if covered in the lesson.
blocks.subject: Programming in C

blocks.text: 7. Self-referential structure
blocks.subject: Programming in C

blocks.text: A structure may contain a pointer to another object of the same structure type. This allows linked nodes to be built dynamically.
blocks.subject: Programming in C

blocks.text: struct Node { int data; struct Node *next; };
blocks.subject: Programming in C

blocks.text: 8. Union
blocks.subject: Programming in C

blocks.text: A union allows different members to share the same memory area. The active interpretation depends on how the program uses the member. The size is sufficient for its largest member subject to alignment. Contrast a union with a structure, where separate storage is allocated to each member.
blocks.subject: Programming in C

blocks.text: 9. Bitwise operations
blocks.subject: Programming in C

blocks.text: & bitwise AND; | bitwise OR; ^ bitwise XOR; ~ bitwise complement; << left shift; >> right shift. They operate on bits. Distinguish bitwise operators from logical operators &&, || and !.
blocks.subject: Programming in C

blocks.text: UNIT V – POINTERS AND FILE HANDLING
blocks.subject: Programming in C

blocks.text: 1. Pointer basics
blocks.subject: Programming in C

blocks.text: A pointer stores an address. Example:
blocks.subject: Programming in C

blocks.text: int x=10; int *p=&x; *p=20; /* changes x through the pointer */ The pointer must contain a valid address before dereferencing. A null pointer is not a valid object address for dereferencing.
blocks.subject: Programming in C

blocks.text: 2. Pointer arithmetic
blocks.subject: Programming in C

blocks.text: Pointer arithmetic is scaled by the size of the pointed-to type and is intended for movement within an array/object sequence and one-past-the-end position. Do not assume adding 1 means one byte for every pointer type.
blocks.subject: Programming in C

blocks.text: 3. Arrays and pointers
blocks.subject: Programming in C

blocks.text: In many expressions an array name converts to a pointer to its first element; however, an array is not the same as a pointer variable. Use a[i] or *(a+i) for an element within bounds.
blocks.subject: Programming in C

blocks.text: 4. Pointers to functions
blocks.subject: Programming in C

blocks.text: A function pointer stores the address of a function with a compatible signature. It can be used to call the function indirectly. The declaration syntax should be copied and practised from the official examples.
blocks.subject: Programming in C

blocks.text: 5. Pointers to structures
blocks.subject: Programming in C

blocks.text: If p is a pointer to a structure, p->member accesses a field. It is equivalent to (*p).member.
blocks.subject: Programming in C

blocks.text: 6. File handling
blocks.subject: Programming in C

blocks.text: Use FILE * to represent a stream in the textbook's C file-handling lessons.
blocks.subject: Programming in C

blocks.text: Typical sequence:
blocks.subject: Programming in C

blocks.text: FILE *fp = fopen("data.txt", "r");
blocks.subject: Programming in C

blocks.text: if (fp == NULL) { /* handle error */ } /* read or write */ fclose(fp); Common modes include read, write and append; understand whether an existing file is preserved or overwritten. Learn the file functions, formatted input/output, character/string operations and end-of-file approach exactly as described in the textbook. Always test whether fopen succeeded and close the file.
blocks.subject: Programming in C

blocks.text: MODEL PROGRAM – ARRAY SUM AND AVERAGE

blocks.text: C PROGRAMMING – EXAM PRACTICE
blocks.subject: Programming in C

blocks.text: 2 marks: define identifier, keyword, variable, array, string, pointer, structure, union, recursion and file pointer. 5 marks: explain operators and precedence; compare while/do-while/for; explain functions and recursion; distinguish arrays and pointers; explain structures and unions. Trace the output of short code fragments and identify syntax/logic errors.

blocks.subject: Programming in C Lab

blocks.subject: Programming in C Lab

blocks.subject: Programming in C Lab

blocks.subject: Programming in C Lab

blocks.text: • Traverse each character.
blocks.subject: Programming in C Lab

blocks.text: • Test letters for vowel/consonant.
blocks.subject: Programming in C Lab

blocks.text: • Count whitespace separately.
blocks.subject: Programming in C Lab

blocks.text: • Count words by detecting transitions from whitespace to non-whitespace.

blocks.text: GROUP III – RECURSION
blocks.subject: Programming in C Lab

blocks.text: nPr = n!/(n−r)!. nCr = n!/[r!(n−r)!].
blocks.subject: Programming in C Lab

blocks.text: GCD: Euclid's method uses gcd(a,b)=gcd(b,a mod b), with gcd(a,0)=|a|.
blocks.subject: Programming in C Lab

blocks.text: Fibonacci: each term after the first two is the sum of the previous two. Maximum/minimum: compare elements recursively or divide the sequence into smaller pieces as shown in the manual. Towers of Hanoi: move n disks from source to destination using an auxiliary peg; move n−1 to auxiliary, move largest disk, then move n−1 to destination. The minimum move count is 2^n−1. Every recursive function requires a base case.
blocks.subject: Programming in C Lab

blocks.text: GROUP IV – MATRIX MANIPULATION
blocks.subject: Programming in C Lab

blocks.text: Addition/subtraction: same order; operate elementwise. Multiplication: if A is m×n and B is n×p, the product is m×p; entry c_ij=Σ a_ik b_kj. Transpose: exchange rows and columns. Trace: sum of diagonal elements of a square matrix. Determinant: calculate using the method taught for the order in question. Inverse: exists if determinant is non-zero; verify A A^(-1)=I.
blocks.subject: Programming in C Lab

blocks.text: GROUP V – SORTING AND SEARCHING
blocks.subject: Programming in C Lab

blocks.text: Insertion sort: maintain a sorted prefix; take next key, shift larger values right and insert the key. Bubble sort: compare adjacent items and swap when out of order; repeat passes. Linear search: compare the key with each item until it is found or the list ends. Binary search: requires sorted data; compare key with the middle element and repeatedly keep the half that may contain the key.

blocks.text: UNIT I – INTEGRAL CALCULUS
blocks.subject: Mathematics II

blocks.text: Bernoulli's formula extends integration by parts. In the textbook's notation: ∫u dv = uv − u'v1 + u''v2 − u'''v3 + ... where successive derivatives of u and successive integrals of v are used. It is especially useful when repeated differentiation eventually becomes zero, as with a polynomial u.
blocks.subject: Mathematics II

blocks.text: Worked example: ∫x e^x dx. Take u=x, dv=e^x dx; then du=dx and v=e^x. ∫x e^x dx = x e^x − ∫e^x dx = xe^x−e^x+C=e^x(x−1)+C.
blocks.subject: Mathematics II

blocks.text: Reduction formula A reduction formula expresses an integral with an index/power n in terms of a similar integral with a smaller index. The syllabus identifies integrals of sin^n x, cos^n x and sin^m x cos^n x over 0 to π/2. Use the exact formulae and boundary conditions given in the textbook, then apply repeatedly until the index reaches a basic integral.
blocks.subject: Mathematics II

blocks.text: Fourier series For a function represented over a period 2π, a common form is: f(x)=a0/2+Σ_(n=1 to ∞)[a_n cos(nx)+b_n sin(nx)]. a0=(1/π)∫_(−π)^π f(x)dx. a_n=(1/π)∫_(−π)^π f(x)cos(nx)dx. b_n=(1/π)∫_(−π)^π f(x)sin(nx)dx. For a general interval (a,a+2δ), the corresponding coefficient formulae use the interval and scaling stated in the textbook. Do not use the 2π formula unchanged when the period/interval differs.
blocks.subject: Mathematics II

blocks.text: Symmetry shortcuts:
blocks.subject: Mathematics II

blocks.text: If f is even, sine coefficients vanish over a symmetric interval. If f is odd, the constant and cosine coefficients vanish over a symmetric interval. Use symmetry only after checking the function and limits.
blocks.subject: Mathematics II

blocks.text: Half-range series
blocks.subject: Mathematics II

blocks.text: For a function on (0,L):
blocks.subject: Mathematics II

blocks.text: • Half-range sine series uses sine terms and corresponds to an odd extension.
blocks.subject: Mathematics II

blocks.text: • Half-range cosine series uses cosine terms and corresponds to an even extension.
blocks.subject: Mathematics II

blocks.text: Choose the correct coefficient integrals and interval scaling from the textbook. State which extension is being used.
blocks.subject: Mathematics II

blocks.text: UNIT II – DIFFERENTIAL EQUATIONS
blocks.subject: Mathematics II

blocks.text: Ordinary differential equation (ODE) involves derivatives with respect to one independent variable. The syllabus emphasises second-order non-homogeneous equations with constant coefficients and specified exponential/trigonometric forms on the right-hand side.
blocks.subject: Mathematics II

blocks.text: For ay''+by'+cy=X(x):
blocks.subject: Mathematics II

blocks.text: 1. Form the auxiliary equation ar²+br+c=0.
blocks.subject: Mathematics II

blocks.text: 2. Solve for roots.
blocks.subject: Mathematics II

blocks.text: 3. Construct the complementary function (CF) according to distinct/repeated/complex roots.
blocks.subject: Mathematics II

blocks.text: 4. Find the particular integral (PI) for the specified X(x) using the textbook's rules.
blocks.subject: Mathematics II

blocks.text: 5. General solution y=CF+PI.
blocks.subject: Mathematics II

blocks.text: Examples of CF forms:
blocks.subject: Mathematics II

blocks.text: Distinct real roots r1,r2: C1e^(r1x)+C2e^(r2x). Repeated root r: (C1+C2x)e^(rx). Complex roots α±iβ: e^(αx)[C1 cos(βx)+C2 sin(βx)].
blocks.subject: Mathematics II

blocks.text: Partial differential equations A PDE contains partial derivatives with respect to two or more independent variables. The textbook includes formation of PDEs by eliminating arbitrary constants/functions, complete and general integrals and four standard types. Write p=∂z/∂x and q=∂z/∂y when using Lagrange's form.
blocks.subject: Mathematics II

blocks.text: Lagrange's linear equation:
blocks.subject: Mathematics II

blocks.text: Pp+Qq=R.
blocks.subject: Mathematics II

blocks.text: Auxiliary equations:
blocks.subject: Mathematics II

blocks.text: dx/P = dy/Q = dz/R. Find two independent integrals and combine them to express the general solution. Work each auxiliary equation carefully; do not assume that any two ratios can be integrated independently without justification.
blocks.subject: Mathematics II

blocks.text: UNIT III – LAPLACE TRANSFORMS
blocks.subject: Mathematics II

blocks.text: Definition:
blocks.subject: Mathematics II

blocks.text: L{f(t)}=F(s)=∫_0^∞ e^(−st)f(t)dt, when the integral exists.
blocks.subject: Mathematics II

blocks.text: Common transforms:
blocks.subject: Mathematics II

blocks.text: L{1}=1/s. L{t}=1/s². L{t^n}=n!/s^(n+1). L{e^(at)}=1/(s−a). L{sin(at)}=a/(s²+a²). L{cos(at)}=s/(s²+a²). L{sinh(at)}=a/(s²−a²). L{cosh(at)}=s/(s²−a²).
blocks.subject: Mathematics II

blocks.text: Linearity:
blocks.subject: Mathematics II

blocks.text: L{af+bg}=aF+bG.
blocks.subject: Mathematics II

blocks.text: First derivative:
blocks.subject: Mathematics II

blocks.text: Second derivative:
blocks.subject: Mathematics II

blocks.text: L{f''}=s²F(s)−sf(0)−f'(0). Use the additional properties and conditions exactly as stated in the book.
blocks.subject: Mathematics II

blocks.text: Inverse Laplace transform Find f(t) whose transform is F(s). Methods include recognising a standard form, partial fractions, completing the square and using transform properties.
blocks.subject: Mathematics II

blocks.text: Example: F(s)=1/[s(s+1)]. Partial fractions:
blocks.subject: Mathematics II

blocks.text: 1/[s(s+1)] = 1/s − 1/(s+1). Inverse transform = 1−e^(−t).
blocks.subject: Mathematics II

blocks.text: Solving an ODE by Laplace transform
blocks.subject: Mathematics II

blocks.text: 1. Transform both sides.
blocks.subject: Mathematics II

blocks.text: 2. Substitute initial conditions into derivative transforms.
blocks.subject: Mathematics II

blocks.text: 3. Solve algebraically for Y(s).
blocks.subject: Mathematics II

blocks.text: 4. Decompose Y(s) if necessary.
blocks.subject: Mathematics II

blocks.text: 5. Apply inverse transforms.
blocks.subject: Mathematics II

blocks.text: 6. Check initial conditions where practical.
blocks.subject: Mathematics II

blocks.text: UNIT IV – VECTOR DIFFERENTIATION
blocks.subject: Mathematics II

blocks.text: A scalar point function assigns one scalar to each point. A vector point function assigns a vector to each point.
blocks.subject: Mathematics II

blocks.text: Del operator in Cartesian coordinates:
blocks.subject: Mathematics II

blocks.text: Gradient of scalar φ:
blocks.subject: Mathematics II

blocks.text: grad φ=∇φ = i φ_x + j φ_y + k φ_z. It points in the direction of the greatest local increase of φ.
blocks.subject: Mathematics II

blocks.text: Divergence of F=Pi+Qj+Rk:
blocks.subject: Mathematics II

blocks.text: div F=∇·F=P_x+Q_y+R_z. If divergence is zero, the field is solenoidal.
blocks.subject: Mathematics II

blocks.text: Curl:
blocks.subject: Mathematics II

blocks.text: curl F=∇×F, evaluated by the determinant form using i,j,k and the partial derivatives. If curl is zero, the field is irrotational.
blocks.subject: Mathematics II

blocks.text: Example: F=xi+yj+zk. div F=1+1+1=3. Its curl is zero because all cross partial derivatives cancel. Therefore this field is irrotational, but not solenoidal.
blocks.subject: Mathematics II

blocks.text: Learn the vector identities in the textbook and practise expanding each side. Keep scalar and vector products distinct.
blocks.subject: Mathematics II

blocks.text: UNIT V – VECTOR INTEGRATION
blocks.subject: Mathematics II

blocks.text: Line integral: integrates a field along a curve; parametrise the path and substitute dr. Surface integral: integrates over a surface, often measuring flux through it. Volume integral: integrates over a three-dimensional region.
blocks.subject: Mathematics II

blocks.text: Gauss divergence theorem:
blocks.subject: Mathematics II

blocks.text: ∯_S F·n dS = ∭_V (∇·F)dV, for a suitable closed surface bounding volume V.
blocks.subject: Mathematics II

blocks.text: Stokes theorem:
blocks.subject: Mathematics II

blocks.text: ∮_C F·dr = ∬_S (∇×F)·n dS, where C is the positively oriented boundary of S.
blocks.subject: Mathematics II

blocks.text: Green theorem in the plane:
blocks.subject: Mathematics II

blocks.text: ∮_C(P dx+Q dy)=∬_R(Q_x−P_y)dA, for a positively oriented simple closed curve bounding R and suitable differentiability.
blocks.subject: Mathematics II

blocks.text: For theorem problems:
blocks.subject: Mathematics II

blocks.text: 1. Identify the surface/curve/region and orientation.
blocks.subject: Mathematics II

blocks.text: 2. Compute divergence/curl/partial derivatives.
blocks.subject: Mathematics II

blocks.text: 3. Evaluate the simpler integral side.
blocks.subject: Mathematics II

blocks.text: 4. State why the theorem applies.
blocks.subject: Mathematics II

blocks.text: 5. Compare both sides.

blocks.subject: English II

blocks.subject: English II

blocks.text: Unit II: Poems.

blocks.text: UNIT I – PROSE
blocks.subject: English II

blocks.text: 1. The Refugee – K.A. Abbas
blocks.subject: English II

blocks.text: The story follows Maanji, an elderly woman who had once lived comfortably in Rawalpindi before the Partition of India and Pakistan. She had a spacious home, neighbours of different communities and an ordinary, secure routine. As communal violence increases, Muslim neighbours urge her to leave for safety. The brutal killing of a tongawallah and his horse because of his religious identity convinces her that the situation has become dangerous. She moves to Bombay and lives in a single-room tenement. Although her health and living conditions change, she does not become bitter or hateful; she retains kindness and hospitality. The story explores displacement, communal violence, memory, loss, human dignity and the persistence of compassion.
blocks.subject: English II

blocks.text: 2. The Lion and the Lamb – Leonard Clark
blocks.subject: English II

blocks.text: The narrative concerns a travelling menagerie and a lion named Conqueror that escapes after a wagon accident on a difficult snowy road. The circus show continues while the town hears increasingly exaggerated reports about the escaped animal. Rumours multiply and people claim to have seen the lion in several places. The public's fear and the town's reactions create comic episodes. The lion is finally found exhausted in the Vicar's parlour. The Vicar is Reverend Lamb, creating the final humorous association of the lion lying with the lamb. Themes include rumour, public imagination, comic exaggeration and the contrast between a frightening reputation and a tired animal.
blocks.subject: English II

blocks.text: 3. The Lady or the Tiger? – Frank R. Stockton
blocks.subject: English II

blocks.text: A semi-barbaric king uses a public arena as a method of judgment. An accused person must choose between two doors: one conceals a tiger that will kill him, while the other conceals a lady whom he must marry. The king's daughter falls in love with a young man of lower social standing. When the king discovers the relationship, the young man is sent to the arena. The princess knows which door hides the tiger and which hides the lady. She signals a door to her lover, who opens it. The story ends without revealing whether the lady or tiger appears. The unresolved ending asks whether love, jealousy and possessiveness would lead the princess to save the man or condemn him.
blocks.subject: English II

blocks.text: 4. The Sky is the Limit – Kalpana Chawla
blocks.subject: English II

blocks.text: The lesson presents Kalpana Chawla's life, education, determination and space missions. Her early interest in flight develops into formal study of aeronautical/aerospace engineering. She obtains advanced education and pursues astronaut training. She participates in the STS-87 mission and later STS-107. The Columbia disaster on 1 February 2003 kills Chawla and the six other crew members. The text remembers her as an inspiration to young people and emphasises determination, perseverance, scientific ambition and the importance of the journey as well as the goal.
blocks.subject: English II

blocks.text: UNIT II – POEMS
blocks.subject: English II

blocks.text: 1. The Solitary Reaper – William Wordsworth
blocks.subject: English II

blocks.text: The speaker sees a Highland girl harvesting grain and singing alone. The song fills the valley. The speaker compares its beauty to the song of a nightingale and a cuckoo. Although he cannot understand the girl's language, he guesses that it may concern sorrow, past events or ordinary human experience. The song remains in his memory after he leaves. Prepare the poem's auditory imagery, comparisons with birds, the speaker's inability to understand the words and the lasting emotional effect.
blocks.subject: English II

blocks.text: 2. Gift – Alice Walker
blocks.subject: English II

blocks.text: The textbook's thematic introduction reads the poem in relation to the pain of a woman in love and the possessive/selfish behaviour of a male-dominated society. Prepare the speaker's situation, the emotional conflict, the idea of giving/receiving and the poem's criticism of unequal relationships. Consult the complete poem for exact images and sequence; do not add plot details not present in the prescribed text.
blocks.subject: English II

blocks.text: 3. O What is that Sound – W.H. Auden
blocks.subject: English II

blocks.text: The textbook frames this poem as a movement poem and discusses the helpless situation of a girl and the lives of soldiers. Focus on the sound approaching, the dialogue/voices, fear and uncertainty, and the way the poem builds tension. Read the complete poem to explain who speaks each line and how the mood changes.
blocks.subject: English II

blocks.text: 4. Ode to the West Wind – P.B. Shelley
blocks.subject: English II

blocks.text: The poem addresses the West Wind as a powerful force affecting earth, sky and sea. The wind destroys dead leaves and scatters seeds, drives clouds and influences the sea. The speaker wishes to share the wind's power and use it to spread his words and ideas. The poem begins with a darker or pessimistic tone but ends with hope, expressed through the idea that winter is followed by spring. Prepare the three natural domains, the speaker's request, imagery of destruction/renewal and optimistic conclusion.
blocks.subject: English II

blocks.text: UNIT III – SHORT STORIES
blocks.subject: English II

blocks.text: 1. The Fortune-Teller – Karel Capek
blocks.subject: English II

blocks.text: Mrs. Myers, a fortune-teller, makes a prediction for a young woman whom Inspector MacLeary's wife pretends to be. The prediction states that the young woman will marry a wealthy businessman, face an obstacle and travel overseas. The inspector exposes Mrs. Myers as fraudulent, and she is punished. Later, events happen in a way that makes the prediction appear true: Mrs. MacLeary leaves with a rich businessman and crosses the ocean. The story's irony is that a false fortune-teller's prediction is fulfilled despite the authorities' confidence that they have uncovered the fraud. Themes: irony, chance, fate and the limits of human judgement.
blocks.subject: English II

blocks.text: 2. The Postmaster – Rabindranath Tagore
blocks.subject: English II

blocks.text: The story concerns a postmaster posted to a rural village and Ratan, a young orphan girl who helps him. A relationship develops through daily conversation and companionship. The postmaster teaches Ratan and shares parts of his life, but when he leaves the village, Ratan is deeply affected. The postmaster attempts to compensate her and move on, while Ratan remains emotionally attached. The story explores loneliness, human connection, unequal emotional expectations, separation and the pain of abandonment. Use the exact episode sequence and ending in the textbook for a full long answer.
blocks.subject: English II

blocks.text: 3. The Model Millionaire – Oscar Wilde
blocks.subject: English II

blocks.text: Hughie Erskine is generous but not wealthy. He visits his artist friend and sees a beggar model who is actually a rich Baron posing for a painting. Hughie gives the man a coin out of sympathy. When the Baron's identity is revealed, Hughie is embarrassed, but the Baron is impressed by his generosity. The Baron later gives him a substantial gift that helps him marry. The story uses mistaken identity and irony to show that kindness matters more than outward appearance or social status.
blocks.subject: English II

blocks.text: 4. The Dying Detective – Arthur Conan Doyle
blocks.subject: English II

blocks.text: Sherlock Holmes pretends to be gravely ill in order to trap a criminal. Watson is deeply concerned and is called to attend him. Holmes behaves in a manner intended to make the criminal believe he is near death. The deception draws the culprit into revealing himself. The story's central mechanism is Holmes's calculated performance and Watson's partial ignorance of the plan. Prepare suspense, disguise, deduction and the final explanation. Check the exact criminal identity and sequence from the full textbook text.
blocks.subject: English II

blocks.text: UNIT IV – ONE-ACT PLAYS
blocks.subject: English II

blocks.text: 1. The Death Trap – Saki
blocks.subject: English II

blocks.text: The prescribed play is a short dramatic piece. Prepare its characters, setting, conflict and ending from the full text. Use the lesson's actual plot sequence and dialogue; do not replace it with a summary of another Saki story.
blocks.subject: English II

blocks.text: 2. The Dear Departed – Stanley Houghton
blocks.subject: English II

blocks.text: The play is a comedy built around family members who believe an elderly relative has died and begin to consider the belongings and financial implications. The supposed death exposes selfishness, greed and lack of affection within the family. The old man's return/appearance disrupts their calculations and reveals their true character. Prepare the family relationships, the handling of property, the irony of the title and the social criticism.
blocks.subject: English II

blocks.text: 3. The Sheriff's Kitchen – Ronald Gow
blocks.subject: English II

blocks.text: The play takes place in the Sheriff's castle. A cook and steward argue over the Sheriff's delayed dinner and the quality/responsibility of the castle staff. A messenger announces that Robin Hood has been captured. Little John and Friar Tuck enter, eat the food and use deception to rescue Robin Hood. Little John takes the sentry's appearance and eventually traps the Sheriff in the cell. The cook and steward are confused by what has happened. The play combines comic misunderstanding, disguise and clever planning. Prepare the rescue sequence and the roles of Little John, Friar Tuck, the cook and steward.
blocks.subject: English II

blocks.text: 4. The Anniversary – Anton Chekhov
blocks.subject: English II

blocks.text: The play concerns a banker preparing for a bank anniversary and a meeting with shareholders. The accountant is tired from preparing the financial report and hopes for a promised reward. The banker's wife Tatiana arrives and distracts him with stories. An old woman, Mrs. Merchutkina, enters demanding payment of her husband's wages, although the bank has no connection to the alleged employment. Her insistence creates confusion and interrupts preparations. In the final confusion, the accountant misunderstands whom the banker wants removed. The shareholders arrive to find disorder and decide to return later. The play satirises vanity, self-importance, miscommunication and workplace chaos.
blocks.subject: English II

blocks.text: LITERATURE ANSWER PREPARATION
blocks.subject: English II

blocks.text: For prose: author/context → setting → sequence of main events → character/theme → message. For poem: poet/speaker → situation → stanza-wise idea → imagery/tone → theme/title. For short story: plot → character → conflict → turning point → ending → theme/irony. For one-act play: setting → characters → dramatic conflict → dialogue/action → climax → resolution → title/social message.
blocks.subject: English II

blocks.text: Prefix – added before a root (possible → impossible). Suffix – added after a root (teach → teacher; kind → kindness). A prefix/suffix can change meaning or word class. Check spelling changes when adding affixes.

blocks.text: OFFICIAL UNIT MAP
blocks.subject: Communicative English II: Listening Skills

blocks.text: Unit 1: Introduction to Listening – active/passive listening, barriers, improving listening and identifying foreign accents.
blocks.subject: Communicative English II: Listening Skills

blocks.text: Unit 2: Listening to announcements – decoding instructions.
blocks.subject: Communicative English II: Listening Skills

blocks.text: Unit 3: Listening to lectures, speeches, news bulletins and audio-video materials; note-taking.
blocks.subject: Communicative English II: Listening Skills

blocks.text: Unit 4: Comprehending stories and answering analytical questions.
