blocks.subject: Communicative English II: Listening Skills

blocks.text: LESSON 1 – WHAT IS LISTENING?
blocks.subject: Communicative English II: Listening Skills

blocks.text: Hearing is the physical reception of sounds whether or not we pay attention. Listening is purposeful attention and interpretation. Listening involves recognising sounds, identifying words, interpreting meaning in context, understanding the speaker's purpose and responding appropriately.
blocks.subject: Communicative English II: Listening Skills

blocks.text: Purposes of listening include obtaining information, following instructions, learning, enjoying entertainment, understanding feelings and participating in conversation.
blocks.subject: Communicative English II: Listening Skills

blocks.text: Effective listening requires distinguishing similar sounds, using context, noticing tone and identifying specific information. A listener can fail because the speaker is unclear, the language is unfamiliar, attention is divided or assumptions are made without clarification.
blocks.subject: Communicative English II: Listening Skills

blocks.text: LESSON 2 – EFFECTIVE LISTENING
blocks.subject: Communicative English II: Listening Skills

blocks.text: The effective listener:
blocks.subject: Communicative English II: Listening Skills

blocks.text: 1. Gives attention to the speaker.
blocks.subject: Communicative English II: Listening Skills

blocks.text: 2. Avoids interrupting unnecessarily.
blocks.subject: Communicative English II: Listening Skills

blocks.text: 3. Identifies main ideas and supporting details.
blocks.subject: Communicative English II: Listening Skills

blocks.text: 4. Notices tone and context.
blocks.subject: Communicative English II: Listening Skills

blocks.text: 5. Distinguishes fact from opinion where relevant.
blocks.subject: Communicative English II: Listening Skills

blocks.text: 6. Asks for clarification if meaning is uncertain.
blocks.subject: Communicative English II: Listening Skills

blocks.text: 7. Summarises or confirms important instructions.
blocks.subject: Communicative English II: Listening Skills

blocks.text: Barriers include noise, distraction, lack of vocabulary, unfamiliar accent, emotional reaction, prejudice, poor organisation and premature judgement.
blocks.subject: Communicative English II: Listening Skills

blocks.text: LESSON 3 – SUB-SKILLS OF LISTENING
blocks.subject: Communicative English II: Listening Skills

blocks.text: Listening for gist: understand the main idea without noting every word. Listening for specific information: listen for a name, date, place, number or particular detail. Listening for detail: understand supporting facts and sequence. Listening for attitude/tone: infer emotion or purpose from voice and context. Predictive listening: use context/title/topic to anticipate likely information. Note-taking: write key words, abbreviations and relationships rather than attempting to copy every spoken word.
blocks.subject: Communicative English II: Listening Skills

blocks.text: LESSON 4 – IDENTIFYING FOREIGN ACCENTS
blocks.subject: Communicative English II: Listening Skills

blocks.text: Accent differences may involve vowel/consonant pronunciation, stress, intonation, speed and rhythm. The aim is comprehension, not judging a speaker. Strategies:
blocks.subject: Communicative English II: Listening Skills

blocks.text: • Listen for key stressed words.
blocks.subject: Communicative English II: Listening Skills

blocks.text: • Use the context to infer unfamiliar vocabulary.
blocks.subject: Communicative English II: Listening Skills

blocks.text: • Ask politely for repetition or clarification.
blocks.subject: Communicative English II: Listening Skills

blocks.text: • Confirm names, numbers and dates.
blocks.subject: Communicative English II: Listening Skills

blocks.text: • Practise with varied speakers and speech rates.
blocks.subject: Communicative English II: Listening Skills

blocks.text: LESSON 5 – LISTENING TO ANNOUNCEMENTS
blocks.subject: Communicative English II: Listening Skills

blocks.text: When listening to an announcement, capture:
blocks.subject: Communicative English II: Listening Skills

blocks.text: WHO is speaking; WHAT is happening; WHERE it is happening; WHEN it will happen; WHY it matters; WHAT action the listener must take. Pay special attention to changes, exceptions, warnings and repeated information. Write exact times, platform/gate numbers, dates and location names.
blocks.subject: Communicative English II: Listening Skills

blocks.text: LESSON 6 – LISTENING TO NEWS: RADIO AND TV
blocks.subject: Communicative English II: Listening Skills
blocks.chapter: LESSON 6 – LISTENING TO NEWS: RADIO AND TV

blocks.text: Identify the headline/main event, location, people involved, time, cause or background, consequence and source. Separate reported facts from commentary. News may move quickly between topics; use headings or line breaks in notes to keep stories separate.
blocks.subject: Communicative English II: Listening Skills
blocks.chapter: LESSON 6 – LISTENING TO NEWS: RADIO AND TV

blocks.text: LESSON 7 – LISTENING TO SPEECHES
blocks.subject: Communicative English II: Listening Skills

blocks.text: Listen for opening, purpose, main arguments, examples, transitions and conclusion. Identify the intended audience and persuasive techniques. Record key phrases and supporting evidence, but avoid treating every rhetorical statement as a verified fact.
blocks.subject: Communicative English II: Listening Skills

blocks.text: LESSON 8 – LISTENING TO EDUCATIONAL/ENTERTAINMENT TOOLS
blocks.subject: Communicative English II: Listening Skills

blocks.text: The lesson describes listening through educational and entertainment media. Before listening, identify the learning objective. During listening, track the sequence, important vocabulary and examples. After listening, summarise the material and answer questions about the main message.
blocks.subject: Communicative English II: Listening Skills

blocks.text: LESSON 9 – LISTENING FOR LEADERSHIP
blocks.subject: Communicative English II: Listening Skills

blocks.text: Leadership listening supports effective interpersonal communication in professional settings. It involves hearing colleagues, understanding concerns, asking useful questions, recognising constraints, summarising a decision and clarifying action/responsibility. A leader should not merely wait to speak; the listener should understand before responding.
blocks.subject: Communicative English II: Listening Skills

blocks.text: LESSON 10 – COMPREHENDING STORIES
blocks.subject: Communicative English II: Listening Skills

blocks.text: While listening to a story, identify:
blocks.subject: Communicative English II: Listening Skills

blocks.text: • Setting (time/place).
blocks.subject: Communicative English II: Listening Skills

blocks.text: • Main and supporting characters.
blocks.subject: Communicative English II: Listening Skills

blocks.text: • Opening situation.
blocks.subject: Communicative English II: Listening Skills

blocks.text: • Conflict/problem.
blocks.subject: Communicative English II: Listening Skills

blocks.text: • Important events in chronological order.
blocks.subject: Communicative English II: Listening Skills

blocks.text: • Climax/turning point.
blocks.subject: Communicative English II: Listening Skills

blocks.text: • Resolution/ending.
blocks.subject: Communicative English II: Listening Skills

blocks.text: • Theme or message.
blocks.subject: Communicative English II: Listening Skills

blocks.text: Analytical questions may ask why a character acted, what evidence supports an inference or how an event changes the story. Answer using details actually heard.
blocks.subject: Communicative English II: Listening Skills

blocks.text: LISTENING PRACTICE ROUTINE
blocks.subject: Communicative English II: Listening Skills

blocks.text: 1. Listen once for gist without writing every detail.
blocks.subject: Communicative English II: Listening Skills

blocks.text: 2. Listen again for names, numbers and sequence.
blocks.subject: Communicative English II: Listening Skills

blocks.text: 3. Compare notes with the source if a transcript is available.
blocks.subject: Communicative English II: Listening Skills

blocks.text: 4. Write a 3–5 sentence summary.
blocks.subject: Communicative English II: Listening Skills

blocks.text: 5. Answer factual and inference questions.
blocks.subject: Communicative English II: Listening Skills

blocks.text: 6. Identify one listening difficulty and practise it.
blocks.subject: Communicative English II: Listening Skills

blocks.text: LISTENING SKILLS – PRACTICE QUESTIONS
blocks.subject: Communicative English II: Listening Skills

blocks.text: 2 marks: distinguish hearing/listening; define gist listening; name two listening barriers; define note-taking. 5 marks: explain effective listening; describe sub-skills; explain how to decode announcements; list features of listening for leadership. Long answer: discuss the process of comprehending a story; explain how to listen critically to a news bulletin/speech; describe strategies for understanding unfamiliar accents.
blocks.subject: Communicative English II: Listening Skills

blocks.text: PART III – SEMESTER III DETAILED NOTEBOOK
SUBJECT 11 – PROGRAMMING IN C++ AND DATA STRUCTURES (SUCA201A + SUCA201B)
blocks.subject: Programming in C++ and Data Structures

blocks.text: The two official books are Volume I and Volume II of one Core Paper V. Volume I contains object-oriented programming and C++ topics; Volume II contains data structures and algorithms. The source scheme uses lesson numbering 1–12 in Volume I and 15–26 in Volume II. Preserve this numbering when matching a topic to the printed book.
blocks.subject: Programming in C++ and Data Structures

blocks.text: OFFICIAL UNIT MAP
blocks.subject: Programming in C++ and Data Structures

blocks.text: Unit I: C++ introduction, tokens, keywords, identifiers, variables, operators, manipulators, expressions, control structures, pointers and functions (main, prototypes, parameter passing, return values, inline, friend and virtual functions).
blocks.subject: Programming in C++ and Data Structures

blocks.text: Unit II: classes/objects, constructors/destructors, operator overloading, type conversion, function overloading, inheritance forms, pointers, virtual functions, polymorphism and console I/O.
blocks.subject: Programming in C++ and Data Structures

blocks.text: Unit III: file streams, opening/closing, EOF, file pointers, updating/error handling, command-line arguments; data structures, data types, asymptotic notation, arrays/operations and ordered lists.
blocks.subject: Programming in C++ and Data Structures

blocks.text: Unit IV: stacks, applications, infix-to-postfix, recursion, maze problems; queues, circular queues; singly and doubly linked lists; polynomial representation/addition.
blocks.subject: Programming in C++ and Data Structures

blocks.text: Unit V: trees, binary trees, forest conversion, tree operations/traversals; graphs, hashing, graph traversal, shortest path and Dijkstra's algorithm.
blocks.subject: Programming in C++ and Data Structures

blocks.text: VOLUME I – LESSON 1: INTRODUCTION TO OBJECT-ORIENTED PROGRAMMING
blocks.subject: Programming in C++ and Data Structures

blocks.text: Software systems became more complex as user requirements, data and environments changed. Procedure-oriented approaches organise programs around functions/procedures. Object-oriented programming organises software around objects that combine data with operations.
blocks.subject: Programming in C++ and Data Structures

blocks.text: Procedure-oriented organisation:
blocks.subject: Programming in C++ and Data Structures

blocks.text: Problem → divide into tasks/functions → pass data between functions → produce result. This can be effective for smaller problems, but as the system grows, data shared across many functions can become difficult to protect and maintain.
blocks.subject: Programming in C++ and Data Structures

blocks.text: Object-oriented organisation:
blocks.subject: Programming in C++ and Data Structures

blocks.text: Identify objects/entities → define classes → define data and operations → create objects → allow objects to interact. It supports modularity, reuse, extension and a representation closer to real-world entities.
blocks.subject: Programming in C++ and Data Structures

blocks.text: OOP is a programming paradigm, not merely a particular C++ syntax feature. C++ supports both procedural and object-oriented styles.
blocks.subject: Programming in C++ and Data Structures

blocks.text: VOLUME I – LESSON 2: BASIC CONCEPTS OF OOP
blocks.subject: Programming in C++ and Data Structures

blocks.text: 1. Class: a user-defined blueprint that specifies data members and member functions.
blocks.subject: Programming in C++ and Data Structures

blocks.text: 2. Object: an instance of a class with its own state and access to the class's public operations.
blocks.subject: Programming in C++ and Data Structures

blocks.text: 3. Encapsulation: combining data and operations in one unit and controlling access to internal data.
blocks.subject: Programming in C++ and Data Structures

blocks.text: 4. Data hiding: restricting direct access to internal state using access control.
blocks.subject: Programming in C++ and Data Structures

blocks.text: 5. Abstraction: exposing essential behaviour while hiding implementation detail.
blocks.subject: Programming in C++ and Data Structures

blocks.text: 6. Inheritance: deriving a new class from an existing class to reuse/extend behaviour.
blocks.subject: Programming in C++ and Data Structures

blocks.text: 7. Polymorphism: allowing the same interface or operation name to behave differently depending on the object/type.
blocks.subject: Programming in C++ and Data Structures

blocks.text: 8. Dynamic binding: selecting an overridden virtual function at run time through a base-class pointer/reference.
blocks.subject: Programming in C++ and Data Structures

blocks.text: VOLUME I – LESSON 3: INTRODUCTION TO C++
blocks.subject: Programming in C++ and Data Structures

blocks.text: C++ tokens are the smallest meaningful units recognised by the compiler:
blocks.subject: Programming in C++ and Data Structures

blocks.text: • Keywords – reserved words such as int, class, public, if, return.
blocks.subject: Programming in C++ and Data Structures

blocks.text: • Identifiers – programmer-defined names.
blocks.subject: Programming in C++ and Data Structures

blocks.text: • Literals/constants – fixed values such as 10, 3.5, 'A' and string literals.
blocks.subject: Programming in C++ and Data Structures

blocks.text: • Operators – symbols for arithmetic, comparison, logic and other operations.
blocks.subject: Programming in C++ and Data Structures

blocks.text: • Punctuators/separators – braces, parentheses, commas and semicolons.
blocks.subject: Programming in C++ and Data Structures

blocks.text: Variables and types A variable is a named object whose value may change. Common built-in types include int, char, float, double and bool. Use a type appropriate to the value and operation.
blocks.subject: Programming in C++ and Data Structures

blocks.text: C++ input/output
blocks.subject: Programming in C++ and Data Structures

blocks.text: The textbook introduces stream-based console operations:
blocks.subject: Programming in C++ and Data Structures

blocks.text: cin >> value; cout << value; The insertion operator << sends data to output; extraction operator >> reads input.
blocks.subject: Programming in C++ and Data Structures

blocks.text: Expressions combine operands and operators. Precedence and associativity determine evaluation order. Use parentheses to make intent clear.
blocks.subject: Programming in C++ and Data Structures

blocks.text: VOLUME I – LESSON 4: MANIPULATORS AND CONTROL STATEMENTS
blocks.subject: Programming in C++ and Data Structures

blocks.text: Manipulators alter the format of console output/input. The textbook demonstrates formatting operations. In common C++ usage, endl ends a line and flushes output; setw changes the field width when the appropriate header is included. Use the manipulators taught in the official lesson.
blocks.subject: Programming in C++ and Data Structures

blocks.text: Control statements:
blocks.subject: Programming in C++ and Data Structures

blocks.text: Sequence – statements execute in order. Selection – if, if-else and switch. Iteration – for, while and do-while. Jump – break, continue, return and other statements discussed in the text.
blocks.subject: Programming in C++ and Data Structures

blocks.text: Example:
blocks.subject: Programming in C++ and Data Structures

blocks.text: #include <iostream>
blocks.subject: Programming in C++ and Data Structures

blocks.text: using namespace std;
blocks.subject: Programming in C++ and Data Structures

blocks.text: int main()
blocks.subject: Programming in C++ and Data Structures
Programming in C++ and Data Structures

blocks.text: int mark;
blocks.subject: Programming in C++ and Data Structures

blocks.text: cin >> mark;
blocks.subject: Programming in C++ and Data Structures

blocks.text: if (mark >= 50) cout << "Pass\n";
blocks.subject: Programming in C++ and Data Structures

blocks.text: else cout << "Fail\n";
blocks.subject: Programming in C++ and Data Structures

blocks.text: return 0;
blocks.subject: Programming in C++ and Data Structures
Programming in C++ and Data Structures

blocks.text: VOLUME I – LESSON 5: FUNCTIONS AND FUNCTION PROTOTYPES
blocks.subject: Programming in C++ and Data Structures

blocks.text: A function is a named block that performs a defined task. The prototype tells the compiler the function name, return type and parameter types before its use.
blocks.subject: Programming in C++ and Data Structures

blocks.text: Example:
blocks.subject: Programming in C++ and Data Structures

blocks.text: int add(int, int); // prototype int add(int a, int b) // definition
blocks.subject: Programming in C++ and Data Structures
Programming in C++ and Data Structures

blocks.text: return a+b;
blocks.subject: Programming in C++ and Data Structures
Programming in C++ and Data Structures

blocks.text: Function call:
blocks.subject: Programming in C++ and Data Structures

blocks.text: int total=add(5,7);
blocks.subject: Programming in C++ and Data Structures

blocks.text: Parameter passing:
blocks.subject: Programming in C++ and Data Structures

blocks.text: • By value – function receives a copy; assigning to the parameter does not change caller's object.
blocks.subject: Programming in C++ and Data Structures

blocks.text: • By reference – parameter aliases the caller's object; changes affect the original object.
blocks.subject: Programming in C++ and Data Structures

blocks.text: • By pointer/address – function receives an address and can access the original object through dereferencing.
blocks.subject: Programming in C++ and Data Structures

blocks.text: Return value: the value sent back to the caller, matching the function's return type.
blocks.subject: Programming in C++ and Data Structures

blocks.text: Inline function: declared with inline; the compiler may substitute the body at call sites, but this is an optimisation decision.
blocks.subject: Programming in C++ and Data Structures

blocks.text: Friend function: non-member function granted access to private/protected class members by a friend declaration.
blocks.subject: Programming in C++ and Data Structures

blocks.text: Virtual function: member function designed for run-time polymorphism. It can be overridden in a derived class.
blocks.subject: Programming in C++ and Data Structures

blocks.text: VOLUME I – LESSON 6: CLASSES AND OBJECTS
blocks.subject: Programming in C++ and Data Structures

blocks.text: Syntax outline:
blocks.subject: Programming in C++ and Data Structures

blocks.text: class Student
blocks.subject: Programming in C++ and Data Structures
Programming in C++ and Data Structures

blocks.text: private:
blocks.subject: Programming in C++ and Data Structures

blocks.text: int mark;
blocks.subject: Programming in C++ and Data Structures

blocks.text: public:
blocks.subject: Programming in C++ and Data Structures

blocks.text: void setMark(int m) { mark=m; } int getMark() const { return mark; } };
blocks.subject: Programming in C++ and Data Structures

blocks.text: Student s; s.setMark(80); cout << s.getMark();
blocks.subject: Programming in C++ and Data Structures

blocks.text: Access specifiers:
blocks.subject: Programming in C++ and Data Structures

blocks.text: private – accessible within the class and permitted friends. public – accessible through the object's public interface. protected – accessible within the class and derived classes, subject to rules. In a C++ class, the default access is private; in a struct, default access is public.
blocks.subject: Programming in C++ and Data Structures

blocks.text: VOLUME I – LESSON 7: CONSTRUCTORS AND DESTRUCTORS
blocks.subject: Programming in C++ and Data Structures

blocks.text: A constructor is a special member function invoked to initialise an object. It has the same name as the class and no return type.
blocks.subject: Programming in C++ and Data Structures

blocks.text: Common forms:
blocks.subject: Programming in C++ and Data Structures

blocks.text: • Default constructor – called without arguments.
blocks.subject: Programming in C++ and Data Structures

blocks.text: • Parameterised constructor – receives initial values.
blocks.subject: Programming in C++ and Data Structures

blocks.text: • Copy constructor – initialises an object using another object of the same class.
blocks.subject: Programming in C++ and Data Structures

blocks.text: A destructor is called when the object's lifetime ends. It uses the class name preceded by ~ and has no return type or parameters. The textbook's compiler model may be older; the fundamental purpose remains object initialisation and cleanup.
blocks.subject: Programming in C++ and Data Structures

blocks.text: VOLUME I – LESSON 8: OPERATOR OVERLOADING AND TYPE CONVERSION
blocks.subject: Programming in C++ and Data Structures

blocks.text: Operator overloading defines the behaviour of an operator for a user-defined type, within the language rules. It can make operations on objects read naturally.
blocks.subject: Programming in C++ and Data Structures

blocks.text: Example outline: A Complex class may overload + to add real and imaginary parts separately. Operator overloading does not change operator precedence, associativity or number of operands. Some operators cannot be overloaded; consult the textbook's list.
blocks.subject: Programming in C++ and Data Structures

blocks.text: Type conversion Conversions may occur between basic types and class types. The text includes conversion constructors/functions and examples. When writing an answer, distinguish:
blocks.subject: Programming in C++ and Data Structures

blocks.text: • Basic type → class type.
blocks.subject: Programming in C++ and Data Structures

blocks.text: • Class type → basic type.
blocks.subject: Programming in C++ and Data Structures

blocks.text: • One class type → another class type.
blocks.subject: Programming in C++ and Data Structures

blocks.text: Explain which constructor or conversion function performs the conversion.
blocks.subject: Programming in C++ and Data Structures

blocks.text: VOLUME I – LESSON 9: INHERITANCE
blocks.subject: Programming in C++ and Data Structures

blocks.text: Inheritance lets a derived class reuse accessible members of a base class and add or modify behaviour.
blocks.subject: Programming in C++ and Data Structures

blocks.text: Types and diagrams:
blocks.subject: Programming in C++ and Data Structures

blocks.text: Single: A → B. Multilevel: A → B → C. Multiple: A + B → C. Hierarchical: A → B and A → C. Hybrid: a combination of inheritance forms.
blocks.subject: Programming in C++ and Data Structures

blocks.text: Inheritance access mode affects how base-class members are exposed through a derived class. Learn public, protected and private inheritance and their effects from the source lesson.
blocks.subject: Programming in C++ and Data Structures

blocks.text: VOLUME I – LESSON 10: POLYMORPHISM AND VIRTUAL FUNCTIONS
blocks.subject: Programming in C++ and Data Structures

blocks.text: Compile-time polymorphism includes function overloading and operator overloading. The compiler selects the relevant function based on the call and type information.
blocks.subject: Programming in C++ and Data Structures

blocks.text: Run-time polymorphism uses inheritance and virtual functions. If a base-class pointer/reference refers to a derived-class object, a virtual call can execute the derived override.
blocks.subject: Programming in C++ and Data Structures

blocks.text: Example:
blocks.subject: Programming in C++ and Data Structures

blocks.text: #include <iostream>
blocks.subject: Programming in C++ and Data Structures

blocks.text: using namespace std;
blocks.subject: Programming in C++ and Data Structures

blocks.text: class Shape { public: virtual void draw() { cout << "Shape\n"; } };
blocks.subject: Programming in C++ and Data Structures

blocks.text: class Circle : public Shape { public: void draw() override { cout << "Circle\n"; } };
blocks.subject: Programming in C++ and Data Structures

blocks.text: int main() { Circle c; Shape *p=&c; p->draw(); return 0; }
blocks.subject: Programming in C++ and Data Structures

blocks.text: Output: Circle. The virtual function call is resolved according to the actual object type.
blocks.subject: Programming in C++ and Data Structures

blocks.text: VOLUME I – LESSON 11: WORKING WITH FILES
blocks.subject: Programming in C++ and Data Structures

blocks.text: C++ stream classes used for file operations:
blocks.subject: Programming in C++ and Data Structures

blocks.text: ifstream – file input. ofstream – file output. fstream – input and output.
blocks.subject: Programming in C++ and Data Structures

blocks.text: Basic procedure:
blocks.subject: Programming in C++ and Data Structures

blocks.text: 1. Declare a stream object.
blocks.subject: Programming in C++ and Data Structures

blocks.text: 2. Open the file with a suitable mode.
blocks.subject: Programming in C++ and Data Structures

blocks.text: 3. Check whether the file opened successfully.
blocks.subject: Programming in C++ and Data Structures

blocks.text: 4. Read/write data.
blocks.subject: Programming in C++ and Data Structures

blocks.text: 5. Check EOF and errors appropriately.
blocks.subject: Programming in C++ and Data Structures

blocks.text: 6. Close the file.
blocks.subject: Programming in C++ and Data Structures

blocks.text: File modes determine whether a file is opened for reading, writing, appending or a combination. Understand whether an opening mode truncates an existing file. The official book discusses file pointers, updating files, error handling and command-line arguments.
blocks.subject: Programming in C++ and Data Structures

blocks.text: VOLUME I – LESSON 12: SEQUENTIAL I/O OPERATIONS AND ERROR HANDLING
blocks.subject: Programming in C++ and Data Structures

blocks.text: Sequential access means reading/writing records in order. A program should check file-open state, detect read/write failures, handle end-of-file correctly and close the stream. Do not use an EOF check as a substitute for checking whether a read operation succeeded; use the method taught by the textbook and test the stream state.
blocks.subject: Programming in C++ and Data Structures

blocks.text: VOLUME II – LESSON 15: INTRODUCTION TO DATA STRUCTURES
blocks.subject: Programming in C++ and Data Structures

blocks.text: Basic data organisation:
blocks.subject: Programming in C++ and Data Structures

blocks.text: Data item – one unit of data. Field – one elementary attribute value. Record – collection of fields describing one entity. File – collection of records. Key – field used to identify/locate a record; a primary key should uniquely identify a record in the file.
blocks.subject: Programming in C++ and Data Structures

blocks.text: A data structure organises data so operations can be performed efficiently. Study three aspects:
blocks.subject: Programming in C++ and Data Structures

blocks.text: 1. Logical/mathematical description.
blocks.subject: Programming in C++ and Data Structures

blocks.text: 2. Implementation in computer memory.
blocks.subject: Programming in C++ and Data Structures

blocks.text: 3. Quantitative analysis of memory and processing time.
blocks.subject: Programming in C++ and Data Structures

blocks.text: Common operations:
blocks.subject: Programming in C++ and Data Structures

blocks.text: Traversal – visit elements. Searching – find a required element. Insertion – add an element. Deletion – remove an element. Sorting – arrange in order. Merging – combine collections.
blocks.subject: Programming in C++ and Data Structures

blocks.text: VOLUME II – LESSON 16: ARRAYS, RECORDS AND POINTERS
blocks.subject: Programming in C++ and Data Structures

blocks.text: Array: elements of a common type stored in indexed positions. Access by index is efficient. Insertion/deletion in the middle may require shifting. Record: collection of fields describing an entity. Pointer: stores an address used to access data indirectly. Ordered list: maintains an order, often by key. Insertion must preserve the order; searching may exploit the order if the algorithm supports it.
blocks.subject: Programming in C++ and Data Structures

blocks.text: VOLUME II – LESSON 17: LINKED LISTS
blocks.subject: Programming in C++ and Data Structures

blocks.text: A linked list consists of nodes. A node stores data and a link to another node. Nodes are dynamically connected and need not occupy adjacent memory positions.
blocks.subject: Programming in C++ and Data Structures

blocks.text: Singly linked list:
blocks.subject: Programming in C++ and Data Structures

blocks.text: [data|next] → [data|next] → [data|NULL]
blocks.subject: Programming in C++ and Data Structures

blocks.text: Operations:
blocks.subject: Programming in C++ and Data Structures

blocks.text: • Traverse/display – follow next links until NULL.
blocks.subject: Programming in C++ and Data Structures

blocks.text: • Search – compare each node's data with key.
blocks.subject: Programming in C++ and Data Structures

blocks.text: • Insert at beginning – new node points to old head; update head.
blocks.subject: Programming in C++ and Data Structures

blocks.text: • Insert at end – locate last node and connect its next to new node.
blocks.subject: Programming in C++ and Data Structures

blocks.text: • Delete first – update head to head->next and release old node.
blocks.subject: Programming in C++ and Data Structures

blocks.text: • Delete selected – locate predecessor, bypass target and release target.
blocks.subject: Programming in C++ and Data Structures

blocks.text: Always handle empty list, first node and last node separately.
blocks.subject: Programming in C++ and Data Structures

blocks.text: VOLUME II – LESSON 18: DOUBLY LINKED LISTS
blocks.subject: Programming in C++ and Data Structures

blocks.text: Each node stores previous link, data and next link.
blocks.subject: Programming in C++ and Data Structures

blocks.text: NULL ← [prev|data|next] ⇄ [prev|data|next] → NULL
blocks.subject: Programming in C++ and Data Structures

blocks.text: It supports forward and backward traversal. Insertion/deletion requires updating both neighbouring links. When deleting the first/last node, update head/tail and handle empty-list result.
blocks.subject: Programming in C++ and Data Structures

blocks.text: VOLUME II – LESSON 19: STACKS
blocks.subject: Programming in C++ and Data Structures

blocks.text: Stack follows LIFO: last in, first out.
blocks.subject: Programming in C++ and Data Structures

blocks.text: Operations:
blocks.subject: Programming in C++ and Data Structures

blocks.text: PUSH – insert at top. POP – remove top. PEEK/TOP – examine the top without removal. Overflow – attempting to push when full. Underflow – attempting to pop when empty.
blocks.subject: Programming in C++ and Data Structures

blocks.text: Array representation uses top index. A common initial value is top=−1. Push increments top and stores item; pop reads item and decrements top.
blocks.subject: Programming in C++ and Data Structures

blocks.text: Applications: function-call handling, recursion, expression conversion/evaluation and backtracking/maze problems.
blocks.subject: Programming in C++ and Data Structures

blocks.text: Infix-to-postfix conversion Infix places operator between operands (A+B). Postfix places it after operands (AB+).
blocks.subject: Programming in C++ and Data Structures

blocks.text: Procedure:
blocks.subject: Programming in C++ and Data Structures

blocks.text: 1. Scan left to right.
blocks.subject: Programming in C++ and Data Structures

blocks.text: 2. Output operands immediately.
blocks.subject: Programming in C++ and Data Structures

blocks.text: 3. Push opening brackets.
blocks.subject: Programming in C++ and Data Structures

blocks.text: 4. For operators, compare precedence/associativity with stack top and pop as required.
blocks.subject: Programming in C++ and Data Structures

blocks.text: 5. At a closing bracket, pop until matching opening bracket.
blocks.subject: Programming in C++ and Data Structures

blocks.text: 6. At end, pop remaining operators.
blocks.subject: Programming in C++ and Data Structures

blocks.text: Example: A+B*C → ABC*+ because multiplication has higher precedence.
blocks.subject: Programming in C++ and Data Structures

blocks.text: VOLUME II – LESSON 20: QUEUES
blocks.subject: Programming in C++ and Data Structures

blocks.text: Queue follows FIFO: first in, first out. Enqueue – add at rear. Dequeue – remove from front. Front – next item to be removed. Rear – last inserted item.
blocks.subject: Programming in C++ and Data Structures

blocks.text: Array queue needs a full/empty condition and careful index updates. A circular queue treats the array as circular and reuses positions: next index=(index+1) mod N. Exact full/empty rules depend on the textbook's representation. Learn that implementation rather than combining two different conventions.
blocks.subject: Programming in C++ and Data Structures

blocks.text: Applications include scheduling, buffering and waiting-line processing.
blocks.subject: Programming in C++ and Data Structures

blocks.text: VOLUME II – LESSON 21: TREES
blocks.subject: Programming in C++ and Data Structures

blocks.text: A tree is a hierarchical, non-linear structure. Root is the top node; parent has children; child is below a parent; leaf has no children; subtree is a node plus descendants. A binary tree gives each node at most two children, left and right.
blocks.subject: Programming in C++ and Data Structures

blocks.text: Forest-to-binary-tree conversion in the syllabus uses a representation such as left-child/right-sibling. Draw the conversion exactly as the source lesson illustrates.
blocks.subject: Programming in C++ and Data Structures

blocks.text: Traversals:
blocks.subject: Programming in C++ and Data Structures

blocks.text: Preorder – Root, Left, Right (NLR). Inorder – Left, Root, Right (LNR). Postorder – Left, Right, Root (LRN). Practise on a labelled tree and write the output sequence.
blocks.subject: Programming in C++ and Data Structures

blocks.text: VOLUME II – LESSON 22: BINARY SEARCH TREE
blocks.subject: Programming in C++ and Data Structures

blocks.text: A binary search tree (BST) follows an ordering rule: keys in the left subtree are smaller than the node's key; keys in the right subtree are larger, subject to the duplicate-key rule being used. Search: compare key with current node and move left/right. Insertion: follow comparisons until an empty child link is found.
blocks.subject: Programming in C++ and Data Structures

blocks.text: Deletion:
blocks.subject: Programming in C++ and Data Structures

blocks.text: • Leaf – remove directly.
blocks.subject: Programming in C++ and Data Structures

blocks.text: • One child – link parent to the child.
blocks.subject: Programming in C++ and Data Structures

blocks.text: • Two children – replace with inorder successor/predecessor and then delete that replacement node from its original position.
blocks.subject: Programming in C++ and Data Structures

blocks.text: Inorder traversal of a BST visits keys in sorted order.
blocks.subject: Programming in C++ and Data Structures

blocks.text: VOLUME II – LESSON 23: GRAPHS
blocks.subject: Programming in C++ and Data Structures

blocks.text: A graph consists of vertices and edges. Undirected graph: edges have no direction. Directed graph: each edge has a direction. Weighted graph: edges carry weights/costs.
blocks.subject: Programming in C++ and Data Structures

blocks.text: Representations:
blocks.subject: Programming in C++ and Data Structures

blocks.text: • Adjacency matrix: matrix entry indicates whether/what weight connects two vertices.
blocks.subject: Programming in C++ and Data Structures

blocks.text: • Adjacency list: each vertex stores its neighbouring vertices.
blocks.subject: Programming in C++ and Data Structures

blocks.text: VOLUME II – LESSON 24: HASH FUNCTIONS AND SHORTEST PATH
blocks.subject: Programming in C++ and Data Structures

blocks.text: Hashing maps a key to a table index using a hash function. A collision occurs when different keys map to the same index. Collision handling may use chaining or open addressing; learn the exact methods in the book.
blocks.subject: Programming in C++ and Data Structures

blocks.text: Dijkstra's shortest-path algorithm finds shortest paths from a source in a weighted graph with non-negative edge weights.
blocks.subject: Programming in C++ and Data Structures

blocks.text: 1. Set source distance to zero and all other distances to infinity.
blocks.subject: Programming in C++ and Data Structures

blocks.text: 2. Mark vertices unprocessed.
blocks.subject: Programming in C++ and Data Structures

blocks.text: 3. Select the unprocessed vertex with the smallest tentative distance.
blocks.subject: Programming in C++ and Data Structures

blocks.text: 4. Relax its outgoing edges: if current distance + edge weight is smaller, update the neighbour.
blocks.subject: Programming in C++ and Data Structures

blocks.text: 5. Mark the vertex processed.
blocks.subject: Programming in C++ and Data Structures

blocks.text: 6. Repeat until the relevant vertices are processed or no reachable unprocessed vertex remains.
blocks.subject: Programming in C++ and Data Structures

blocks.text: Do not use standard Dijkstra on graphs with negative edge weights.
blocks.subject: Programming in C++ and Data Structures

blocks.text: VOLUME II – LESSON 25: ALGORITHMS AND PERFORMANCE PROFILES
blocks.subject: Programming in C++ and Data Structures

blocks.text: Algorithm: finite sequence of well-defined steps that solves a problem. Time complexity describes growth in execution steps as input size grows. Space complexity describes memory use.
blocks.subject: Programming in C++ and Data Structures

blocks.text: Asymptotic notation:
blocks.subject: Programming in C++ and Data Structures

blocks.text: O(f(n)) – upper bound. Ω(f(n)) – lower bound. Θ(f(n)) – tight bound.
blocks.subject: Programming in C++ and Data Structures

blocks.text: Common growth order:
blocks.subject: Programming in C++ and Data Structures

blocks.text: O(1) < O(log n) < O(n) < O(n log n) < O(n²) < O(2^n) < O(n!). Understand best, average and worst cases when covered. The time-space trade-off means an algorithm may use extra memory to reduce processing time, or vice versa.
blocks.subject: Programming in C++ and Data Structures

blocks.text: VOLUME II – LESSON 26: DIVIDE AND CONQUER
blocks.subject: Programming in C++ and Data Structures

blocks.text: Divide and conquer has three stages:
blocks.subject: Programming in C++ and Data Structures

blocks.text: Divide – split a problem into smaller subproblems. Conquer – solve each subproblem, usually recursively. Combine – combine subproblem results. Examples commonly used to explain the method include binary search, merge sort and other recursive algorithms. Use the exact examples and recurrence treatment in the official lesson.
blocks.subject: Programming in C++ and Data Structures

blocks.text: The syllabus specifically covers the 8085 MPU and asks students to understand its architecture, instruction set, programming techniques, arithmetic/logic operations, counters, time delays, stack/subroutine, code conversions, interrupts, DMA, memory and I/O interfaces.
blocks.subject: Microprocessors and its Applications

blocks.text: UNIT I / LESSONS 1–2 – INTRODUCTION AND 8085 ARCHITECTURE
blocks.subject: Microprocessors and its Applications

blocks.text: 12.1 What is a microprocessor? A microprocessor is a programmable, clock-driven, register-based electronic device. It reads binary instructions from memory, accepts binary data, processes it according to those instructions and supplies results. It performs functions similar to the CPU of a computer.
blocks.subject: Microprocessors and its Applications

blocks.text: A microprocessor-based system is commonly organised as:
blocks.subject: Microprocessors and its Applications

blocks.text: | MICROPROCESSOR |
blocks.subject: Microprocessors and its Applications

blocks.text: |  MEMORY  |             |   I/O    |
blocks.subject: Microprocessors and its Applications

blocks.text: Memory stores instructions/data. Input/output devices communicate with the external environment. The bus carries address, data and control information between system components.
blocks.subject: Microprocessors and its Applications

blocks.text: Microprocessor vs microcomputer:
blocks.subject: Microprocessors and its Applications

blocks.text: • Microprocessor: the processing component/chip.
blocks.subject: Microprocessors and its Applications

blocks.text: • Microcomputer: a complete computer system whose CPU function is performed by a microprocessor, together with memory and I/O.
blocks.subject: Microprocessors and its Applications

blocks.text: Do not use the two terms as synonyms.
blocks.subject: Microprocessors and its Applications

blocks.text: Reprogrammable systems and embedded systems:
blocks.subject: Microprocessors and its Applications

blocks.text: • Reprogrammable systems, such as personal computers, are used for general computing and data processing; users can load/change programs.
blocks.subject: Microprocessors and its Applications

blocks.text: • Embedded systems use a processor as part of a larger product, often to perform a specific task. Examples named in the textbook include copying machines, washing machines, dishwashers, dashboard controls, traffic-light controllers and automatic testing instruments.
blocks.subject: Microprocessors and its Applications

blocks.text: Binary digits and words:
blocks.subject: Microprocessors and its Applications

blocks.text: A bit is a binary digit, 0 or 1. A word is a group of bits processed by a microprocessor. An 8-bit processor handles an 8-bit word as its basic data word; a 32-bit processor has a 32-bit word.
blocks.subject: Microprocessors and its Applications

blocks.text: 12.2 8085 key facts
blocks.subject: Microprocessors and its Applications

blocks.text: The official text describes the 8085 as:
blocks.subject: Microprocessors and its Applications

blocks.text: • An 8-bit microprocessor.
blocks.subject: Microprocessors and its Applications

blocks.text: • Having an 8-bit data bus.
blocks.subject: Microprocessors and its Applications

blocks.text: • Having a 16-bit address bus.
blocks.subject: Microprocessors and its Applications

blocks.text: • A 40-pin device.
blocks.subject: Microprocessors and its Applications

blocks.text: • Operating from a single +5 V supply.
blocks.subject: Microprocessors and its Applications

blocks.text: • A 16-bit address bus can identify 2^16 = 65,536 byte locations = 64 KB of address space.
blocks.subject: Microprocessors and its Applications

blocks.text: • The textbook gives a 3 MHz single-phase clock in its description.
blocks.subject: Microprocessors and its Applications

blocks.text: Use the exact specifications stated in your edition if asked.
blocks.subject: Microprocessors and its Applications

blocks.text: 12.3 Main 8085 registers Accumulator (A): an 8-bit register used extensively in arithmetic, logical and data-processing operations. Many instructions use the accumulator implicitly.
blocks.subject: Microprocessors and its Applications

blocks.text: General-purpose registers: B, C, D, E, H and L are 8-bit registers. Selected pairs can be used as 16-bit register pairs:
blocks.subject: Microprocessors and its Applications

blocks.text: - BC
blocks.subject: Microprocessors and its Applications

blocks.text: - DE
blocks.subject: Microprocessors and its Applications

blocks.text: - HL
blocks.subject: Microprocessors and its Applications

blocks.text: The HL pair also commonly acts as a memory pointer in instructions that refer to M.
blocks.subject: Microprocessors and its Applications

blocks.text: Program Counter (PC): a 16-bit register holding the address of the next instruction to be fetched/executed. After an instruction is fetched, the PC normally advances; a jump/call/return can change it.
blocks.subject: Microprocessors and its Applications

blocks.text: Stack Pointer (SP): a 16-bit register that identifies the current top of the stack in memory. PUSH/CALL and POP/RET operations change SP.
blocks.subject: Microprocessors and its Applications

blocks.text: Flag register: records status information produced by certain arithmetic and logical operations. The five named 8085 flags are:
blocks.subject: Microprocessors and its Applications

blocks.text: • Sign (S)
blocks.subject: Microprocessors and its Applications

blocks.text: • Zero (Z)
blocks.subject: Microprocessors and its Applications

blocks.text: • Auxiliary Carry (AC)
blocks.subject: Microprocessors and its Applications

blocks.text: • Parity (P)
blocks.subject: Microprocessors and its Applications

blocks.text: • Carry (CY)
blocks.subject: Microprocessors and its Applications

blocks.text: The flags are not all affected by every instruction. Check the instruction table for the exact flag effect.
blocks.subject: Microprocessors and its Applications

blocks.text: 12.4 8085 buses Address bus: carries the address of the memory location or I/O device selected by the processor. It is normally unidirectional from processor to the addressed unit. Data bus: carries data/instructions between processor, memory and I/O; it is bidirectional. Control bus: carries control/status signals such as read and write, coordinating transfers.
blocks.subject: Microprocessors and its Applications

blocks.text: Multiplexed low-order address/data lines:
blocks.subject: Microprocessors and its Applications

blocks.text: AD7–AD0 are multiplexed. During the first part of a machine cycle they carry the low-order address; later they carry data. ALE (Address Latch Enable) indicates the address phase so an external latch can retain the low-order address. A15–A8 carry the high-order address.
blocks.subject: Microprocessors and its Applications

blocks.text: Important signals from the textbook:
blocks.subject: Microprocessors and its Applications

blocks.text: • ALE: Address Latch Enable.
blocks.subject: Microprocessors and its Applications

blocks.text: • RD: read control, active low.
blocks.subject: Microprocessors and its Applications

blocks.text: • WR: write control, active low.
blocks.subject: Microprocessors and its Applications

blocks.text: • IO/M: distinguishes memory and I/O operations.
blocks.subject: Microprocessors and its Applications

blocks.text: • S1, S0: status signals.
blocks.subject: Microprocessors and its Applications

blocks.text: • CLK(OUT): clock output.
blocks.subject: Microprocessors and its Applications

blocks.text: • SID: serial input data.
blocks.subject: Microprocessors and its Applications

blocks.text: • SOD: serial output data.
blocks.subject: Microprocessors and its Applications

blocks.text: • Reset and interrupt-related signals: initialise/control processor operation or accept interrupts.
blocks.subject: Microprocessors and its Applications

blocks.text: Study the pin diagram and signal definitions in the official book; an exam answer should include a labelled diagram, not only signal names.
blocks.subject: Microprocessors and its Applications

blocks.text: 12.5 Fetch–decode–execute cycle
blocks.subject: Microprocessors and its Applications

blocks.text: 1. The PC holds the address of the next instruction.
blocks.subject: Microprocessors and its Applications

blocks.text: 2. The processor places the address on the address bus.
blocks.subject: Microprocessors and its Applications

blocks.text: 3. Memory supplies the instruction through the data bus.
blocks.subject: Microprocessors and its Applications

blocks.text: 4. The control unit decodes the instruction.
blocks.subject: Microprocessors and its Applications

blocks.text: 5. The required data are obtained from registers/memory/I/O.
blocks.subject: Microprocessors and its Applications

blocks.text: 6. The processor performs the operation.
blocks.subject: Microprocessors and its Applications

blocks.text: 7. The result and relevant flags are updated.
blocks.subject: Microprocessors and its Applications

blocks.text: 8. The PC moves to the next instruction or to a branch address.
blocks.subject: Microprocessors and its Applications

blocks.text: This is a conceptual sequence; bus timing and machine-cycle details must be studied from the 8085 timing diagrams in the textbook.
blocks.subject: Microprocessors and its Applications

blocks.text: 12.6 Important exam diagrams to reproduce
blocks.subject: Microprocessors and its Applications

blocks.text: • 8085 architecture/block diagram.
blocks.subject: Microprocessors and its Applications

blocks.text: • 8085 pin diagram.
blocks.subject: Microprocessors and its Applications

blocks.text: • Microprocessor-based system block diagram.
blocks.subject: Microprocessors and its Applications

blocks.text: • Address/data/control bus arrangement.
blocks.subject: Microprocessors and its Applications

blocks.subject: Microprocessors and its Applications

blocks.text: UNIT II / LESSON 3 – INSTRUCTION SET AND ASSEMBLY PROGRAMMING
blocks.subject: Microprocessors and its Applications

blocks.text: 12.7 What is an instruction set? An instruction is a binary-coded command that tells a processor to perform an operation. The instruction set is the complete collection of instructions understood by that processor. Assembly language gives readable mnemonics for those operations; an assembler translates mnemonic programs to machine code.
blocks.subject: Microprocessors and its Applications

blocks.text: The textbook classifies 8085 instructions into groups. Main groups include:
blocks.subject: Microprocessors and its Applications

blocks.text: 1. Data transfer instructions.
blocks.subject: Microprocessors and its Applications

blocks.text: 2. Arithmetic instructions.
blocks.subject: Microprocessors and its Applications

blocks.text: 3. Logical instructions.
blocks.subject: Microprocessors and its Applications

blocks.text: 4. Branching/control-transfer instructions.
blocks.subject: Microprocessors and its Applications

blocks.text: 5. Machine-control instructions.
blocks.subject: Microprocessors and its Applications

blocks.text: Learn the exact detailed classification and examples from the book's instruction-set tables.
blocks.subject: Microprocessors and its Applications

blocks.text: 12.8 Addressing modes An addressing mode tells how an instruction identifies the data/operand on which it operates.
blocks.subject: Microprocessors and its Applications

blocks.text: Immediate addressing: the data is included in the instruction. Example: MVI A, 32H places the immediate byte 32H in accumulator A.
blocks.subject: Microprocessors and its Applications

blocks.text: Register addressing: operand is in a named register. Example: MOV A, B copies B into A.
blocks.subject: Microprocessors and its Applications

blocks.text: Direct addressing: the memory address is stated in the instruction. Example: LDA 2050H loads the accumulator from memory location 2050H.
blocks.subject: Microprocessors and its Applications

blocks.text: Register-indirect addressing: a register pair holds the memory address. Example: MOV A, M uses the memory location addressed by HL (M is the memory operand referenced by HL).
blocks.subject: Microprocessors and its Applications

blocks.text: Implied addressing: the operand is implied by the instruction. Example: CMA complements the accumulator; the accumulator is implicit.
blocks.subject: Microprocessors and its Applications

blocks.text: Quick comparison:
blocks.subject: Microprocessors and its Applications

blocks.text: Immediate – operand value is in instruction. Register – operand is in a register. Direct – instruction contains memory address. Register indirect – register pair contains memory address. Implied – operand is understood from the instruction.
blocks.subject: Microprocessors and its Applications

blocks.text: 12.9 Important illustrative instruction groups
blocks.subject: Microprocessors and its Applications

blocks.text: Data transfer:
blocks.subject: Microprocessors and its Applications

blocks.text: • MOV – copy data between registers/memory as permitted.
blocks.subject: Microprocessors and its Applications

blocks.text: • MVI – move immediate 8-bit data.
blocks.subject: Microprocessors and its Applications

blocks.text: • LXI – load register pair with 16-bit immediate data.
blocks.subject: Microprocessors and its Applications

blocks.text: • LDA / STA – load/store accumulator using a direct address.
blocks.subject: Microprocessors and its Applications

blocks.text: • LHLD / SHLD – load/store HL pair using a direct address.
blocks.subject: Microprocessors and its Applications

blocks.text: • LDAX / STAX – accumulator transfer using BC or DE indirectly.
blocks.subject: Microprocessors and its Applications

blocks.text: Arithmetic:
blocks.subject: Microprocessors and its Applications

blocks.text: • ADD / ADI – add register/memory operand or immediate data to accumulator.
blocks.subject: Microprocessors and its Applications

blocks.text: • SUB / SUI – subtract operand from accumulator.
blocks.subject: Microprocessors and its Applications

blocks.text: • INR / DCR – increment/decrement 8-bit register or memory operand.
blocks.subject: Microprocessors and its Applications

blocks.text: • INX / DCX – increment/decrement a register pair.
blocks.subject: Microprocessors and its Applications

blocks.text: • DAD – add a register pair to HL.
blocks.subject: Microprocessors and its Applications

blocks.text: Logical:
blocks.subject: Microprocessors and its Applications

blocks.text: • ANA / ANI – AND with accumulator.
blocks.subject: Microprocessors and its Applications

blocks.text: • ORA / ORI – OR with accumulator.
blocks.subject: Microprocessors and its Applications

blocks.text: • XRA / XRI – XOR with accumulator.
blocks.subject: Microprocessors and its Applications

blocks.text: • CMA – complement accumulator.
blocks.subject: Microprocessors and its Applications

blocks.text: • CMP / CPI – compare operand with accumulator; result affects flags without storing a subtraction result in A.
blocks.subject: Microprocessors and its Applications

blocks.text: Branching and subroutines:
blocks.subject: Microprocessors and its Applications

blocks.text: • JMP – unconditional jump.
blocks.subject: Microprocessors and its Applications

blocks.text: • JZ / JNZ – conditional jump according to Zero flag.
blocks.subject: Microprocessors and its Applications

blocks.text: • JC / JNC – conditional jump according to Carry flag.
blocks.subject: Microprocessors and its Applications

blocks.text: • CALL – call subroutine.
blocks.subject: Microprocessors and its Applications

blocks.text: • RET – return from subroutine.
blocks.subject: Microprocessors and its Applications

blocks.text: Stack/control:
blocks.subject: Microprocessors and its Applications

blocks.text: • PUSH – save a register pair on stack.
blocks.subject: Microprocessors and its Applications

blocks.text: • POP – restore a register pair from stack.
blocks.subject: Microprocessors and its Applications

blocks.text: • HLT – halt.
blocks.subject: Microprocessors and its Applications

blocks.text: • NOP – no operation.
blocks.subject: Microprocessors and its Applications

blocks.text: • EI / DI – enable/disable maskable interrupts.
blocks.subject: Microprocessors and its Applications

blocks.text: This is a learning overview. For examinations, practise the official complete table, including opcode, byte length, operation and affected flags.
blocks.subject: Microprocessors and its Applications

blocks.text: 12.10 Assembly program structure An assembly-language program consists of instructions and labels arranged in a sequence. An illustrative program often:
blocks.subject: Microprocessors and its Applications

blocks.text: 1. Loads input data or addresses.
blocks.subject: Microprocessors and its Applications

blocks.text: 2. Performs the required operation.
blocks.subject: Microprocessors and its Applications

blocks.text: 3. Stores the result.
blocks.subject: Microprocessors and its Applications

blocks.text: 4. Stops or returns control.
blocks.subject: Microprocessors and its Applications

blocks.text: The exact syntax, assembler directives and program termination style depend on the assembler used in the textbook/teaching laboratory.
blocks.subject: Microprocessors and its Applications

blocks.text: 12.11 Looping, counting and indexing
blocks.subject: Microprocessors and its Applications

blocks.text: Loop method:
blocks.subject: Microprocessors and its Applications

blocks.text: 1. Initialise a counter.
blocks.subject: Microprocessors and its Applications

blocks.text: 2. Load or access the required data.
blocks.subject: Microprocessors and its Applications

blocks.text: 3. Perform the operation.
blocks.subject: Microprocessors and its Applications

blocks.text: 4. Update the pointer/index.
blocks.subject: Microprocessors and its Applications

blocks.text: 5. Decrement or increment the counter.
blocks.subject: Microprocessors and its Applications

blocks.text: 6. Test the counter or condition.
blocks.subject: Microprocessors and its Applications

blocks.text: 7. Branch to the loop start if more work remains.
blocks.subject: Microprocessors and its Applications

blocks.text: 8. Stop when the required number of items has been processed.
blocks.subject: Microprocessors and its Applications

blocks.text: Indexing: an index or register pair is used to access successive memory locations. When processing an array of bytes, update the address consistently and make sure the initial address and number of elements match the memory layout.
blocks.subject: Microprocessors and its Applications

blocks.text: Dynamic debugging checklist:
blocks.subject: Microprocessors and its Applications

blocks.text: • Execute one instruction at a time where the monitor permits.
blocks.subject: Microprocessors and its Applications

blocks.text: • Inspect accumulator and general registers.
blocks.subject: Microprocessors and its Applications

blocks.text: • Inspect PC and SP when branches/subroutines are used.
blocks.subject: Microprocessors and its Applications

blocks.text: • Observe flags after arithmetic or comparison.
blocks.subject: Microprocessors and its Applications

blocks.text: • Inspect relevant memory addresses.
blocks.subject: Microprocessors and its Applications

blocks.text: • Confirm each jump destination.
blocks.subject: Microprocessors and its Applications

blocks.text: • Verify that counters eventually reach the termination condition.
blocks.subject: Microprocessors and its Applications

blocks.text: UNIT III / LESSONS 4–5 – ARITHMETIC, LOGIC, COUNTERS AND TIME DELAYS
blocks.subject: Microprocessors and its Applications

blocks.text: 12.12 Arithmetic and logic operations The 8085's arithmetic and logical instructions use the accumulator and selected registers/memory operands. In answers, identify the input registers, operation, destination and relevant flags.
blocks.subject: Microprocessors and its Applications

blocks.text: Addition:
blocks.subject: Microprocessors and its Applications

blocks.text: • The result is stored in the accumulator for common ADD/ADI forms.
blocks.subject: Microprocessors and its Applications

blocks.text: • Carry flag indicates carry beyond the 8-bit result.
blocks.subject: Microprocessors and its Applications

blocks.text: • Auxiliary Carry records carry between lower and upper nibbles, relevant to BCD adjustment.
blocks.subject: Microprocessors and its Applications

blocks.text: Subtraction:
blocks.subject: Microprocessors and its Applications

blocks.text: • SUB/SUI subtract the operand from accumulator.
blocks.subject: Microprocessors and its Applications

blocks.text: • Carry flag is used as the borrow indication in 8085 subtraction conventions; check flag interpretation in the textbook.
blocks.subject: Microprocessors and its Applications

blocks.text: Logical operations:
blocks.subject: Microprocessors and its Applications

blocks.text: • AND, OR and XOR are bitwise operations.
blocks.subject: Microprocessors and its Applications

blocks.text: • Complement changes each bit of the accumulator.
blocks.subject: Microprocessors and its Applications

blocks.text: • Compare sets flags based on the comparison without keeping the subtraction result in A.
blocks.subject: Microprocessors and its Applications

blocks.text: 12.13 Multi-byte addition Purpose: add numbers larger than one byte by adding corresponding bytes and propagating carry.
blocks.subject: Microprocessors and its Applications

blocks.text: Method:
blocks.subject: Microprocessors and its Applications

blocks.text: 1. Place the least-significant bytes in the designated memory/register locations.
blocks.subject: Microprocessors and its Applications

blocks.text: 2. Add the least-significant byte pair.
blocks.subject: Microprocessors and its Applications

blocks.text: 3. Store the low byte of the result.
blocks.subject: Microprocessors and its Applications

blocks.text: 4. Include the carry in the next byte addition (using the appropriate carry instruction/sequence).
blocks.subject: Microprocessors and its Applications

blocks.text: 5. Continue through every higher byte.
blocks.subject: Microprocessors and its Applications

blocks.text: 6. Store the final carry if the question requires it.
blocks.subject: Microprocessors and its Applications

blocks.text: Illustration (two 16-bit numbers):
blocks.subject: Microprocessors and its Applications

blocks.text: -------- 14 26H Low byte: 34H + F2H = 126H → store 26H, carry 1H. High byte: 12H + 01H + 01H = 14H. This demonstrates the carry propagation logic; the assembly routine must use the instruction sequence and data locations required by the problem.
blocks.subject: Microprocessors and its Applications

blocks.text: 12.14 Multi-byte subtraction
blocks.subject: Microprocessors and its Applications

blocks.text: Method:
blocks.subject: Microprocessors and its Applications

blocks.text: 1. Subtract the least-significant byte.
blocks.subject: Microprocessors and its Applications

blocks.text: 2. Store the low-byte result.
blocks.subject: Microprocessors and its Applications

blocks.text: 3. Propagate borrow to the next byte using the correct 8085 instruction sequence.
blocks.subject: Microprocessors and its Applications

blocks.text: 4. Continue until all bytes are processed.
blocks.subject: Microprocessors and its Applications

blocks.text: 5. Check final borrow and result width.
blocks.subject: Microprocessors and its Applications

blocks.text: Do not subtract each byte independently; the borrow is part of the next higher-byte calculation.
blocks.subject: Microprocessors and its Applications

blocks.text: 12.15 BCD arithmetic BCD means Binary Coded Decimal. Each decimal digit is encoded separately using four bits. In packed BCD, two decimal digits occupy one byte. Example: decimal 59 is packed BCD 0101 1001 (59H), whereas its pure binary value is 0011 1011 (3BH). BCD and binary are not interchangeable representations.
blocks.subject: Microprocessors and its Applications

blocks.text: The 8085 instruction DAA (Decimal Adjust Accumulator) is used after certain BCD additions to adjust the accumulator to a valid packed-BCD result. The exact correction conditions depend on the accumulator and Auxiliary Carry/Carry flags. Learn the official textbook's explanation and worked examples rather than assuming DAA can be applied to any arithmetic result.
blocks.subject: Microprocessors and its Applications

blocks.text: 12.16 Multiplication and division The 8085 does not provide a general single instruction for arbitrary multiplication/division in the basic instruction set. The syllabus therefore includes program techniques to perform these operations. Common logic uses repeated addition or repeated subtraction, or other routines shown in the book. For an exam program, state:
blocks.subject: Microprocessors and its Applications

blocks.text: • How inputs are stored.
blocks.subject: Microprocessors and its Applications

blocks.text: • Which register is used as counter/accumulator.
blocks.subject: Microprocessors and its Applications

blocks.text: • The loop condition.
blocks.subject: Microprocessors and its Applications

blocks.text: • How the result and remainder are stored.
blocks.subject: Microprocessors and its Applications

blocks.text: • The case when divisor is zero, if relevant.
blocks.subject: Microprocessors and its Applications

blocks.text: 12.17 Counters A counter tracks repeated events or iterations. Hexadecimal counter: advances through hexadecimal values. The wraparound depends on the number of bits used. Modulo-10 counter: cycles through ten states, commonly 0 to 9, then returns to the starting state. It is used for decimal counting. For a program-based counter, initialise, update, compare with terminal count and reset or stop at the right time.
blocks.subject: Microprocessors and its Applications

blocks.text: 12.18 Time delay A software time delay is created by executing a loop for a known number of instruction cycles. The actual delay depends on:
blocks.subject: Microprocessors and its Applications

blocks.text: • Processor clock frequency.
blocks.subject: Microprocessors and its Applications

blocks.text: • Execution time/machine cycles of each instruction.
blocks.subject: Microprocessors and its Applications

blocks.text: • Number of times each loop executes.
blocks.subject: Microprocessors and its Applications

blocks.text: • Nested loop counts.
blocks.subject: Microprocessors and its Applications

blocks.text: A generic delay design uses an outer and inner counter. The exact delay calculation must use the instruction timings supplied in the official textbook.
blocks.subject: Microprocessors and its Applications

blocks.text: 12.19 Pulse timing and flashing lights A flashing-light program repeatedly turns an output on, waits for a delay, turns the output off, waits again and repeats. The output interface and hardware wiring determine which port/bit controls the light. The textbook's timing problem should be solved with the exact I/O setup and delay loop stated in the exercise.
blocks.subject: Microprocessors and its Applications

blocks.text: UNIT IV / LESSONS 6–8 – STACKS, SUBROUTINES AND CODE CONVERSIONS
blocks.subject: Microprocessors and its Applications

blocks.text: 12.20 Stack and Stack Pointer A stack is a last-in-first-out (LIFO) storage area in memory. The 8085 uses the Stack Pointer to identify its current top. PUSH saves a register pair; POP restores it. CALL uses stack memory to preserve a return address; RET retrieves that address.
blocks.subject: Microprocessors and its Applications

blocks.text: For a stack trace, draw a table:
blocks.subject: Microprocessors and its Applications

blocks.text: Instruction | SP before | memory action | SP after.
blocks.subject: Microprocessors and its Applications

blocks.text: Check the direction in which the stack grows and the byte order exactly as described in the textbook. Do not assume stack memory is unlimited; the stack must have reserved memory space.
blocks.subject: Microprocessors and its Applications

blocks.text: 12.21 Subroutines A subroutine is a reusable sequence of instructions that performs a task. A program calls it, it executes, then returns to the instruction after the call.
blocks.subject: Microprocessors and its Applications

blocks.text: • CALL transfers control and saves the return address on the stack.
blocks.subject: Microprocessors and its Applications

blocks.text: • RET retrieves the return address and resumes the calling program.
blocks.subject: Microprocessors and its Applications

blocks.text: • Conditional CALL/RET instructions transfer control only when the specified flag condition is satisfied.
blocks.subject: Microprocessors and its Applications

blocks.text: Subroutines reduce repeated code and make programs easier to organise.
blocks.subject: Microprocessors and its Applications

blocks.text: 12.22 BCD, binary and hexadecimal conversions Binary to decimal: evaluate the weighted powers of 2. Decimal integer to binary: repeatedly divide by 2 and read remainders in reverse order. BCD to decimal: decode each 4-bit BCD digit separately. Decimal to BCD: convert each decimal digit to its 4-bit representation. Binary to hexadecimal: group binary digits in sets of four from the radix point; translate each group to 0–F. Hexadecimal to binary: replace each hex digit by its four-bit binary equivalent. BCD-to-HEX and HEX-to-BCD: use the number's numeric value and then encode in the target representation. Follow the exact routine and byte format in the textbook.
blocks.subject: Microprocessors and its Applications

blocks.text: 12.23 ASCII conversions ASCII is a character coding scheme. A numeric digit and the character representing that digit are different values. For example, the numeric value 5 is not the same as the ASCII code for character '5'. A conversion routine must identify whether the input is a numeric nibble, packed BCD or ASCII character code. The textbook includes ASCII-to-BCD and BCD-to-ASCII / binary-to-ASCII conversions. In a long answer, define the input representation and output representation before describing the program.
blocks.subject: Microprocessors and its Applications

blocks.text: 12.24 Seven-segment display A seven-segment display uses seven segments, commonly named a through g. A code selects which segments are illuminated to show a digit. The code table differs between common-anode and common-cathode configurations. Reproduce the exact table given in the official textbook and identify the hardware assumption in the answer.
blocks.subject: Microprocessors and its Applications

blocks.text: UNIT V / LESSONS 9–10 – INTERRUPTS, DMA, MEMORY AND I/O
blocks.subject: Microprocessors and its Applications

blocks.text: 12.25 Interrupt An interrupt is an event or signal that makes the processor temporarily suspend the current program sequence and execute an interrupt service routine (ISR). After servicing, the processor can return to the interrupted program.
blocks.subject: Microprocessors and its Applications

blocks.text: General interrupt sequence:
blocks.subject: Microprocessors and its Applications

blocks.text: 1. Processor completes the current instruction as required by the architecture.
blocks.subject: Microprocessors and its Applications

blocks.text: 2. It recognises an enabled/accepted interrupt.
blocks.subject: Microprocessors and its Applications

blocks.text: 3. It saves the return address/state as specified.
blocks.subject: Microprocessors and its Applications

blocks.text: 4. It transfers control to the service routine.
blocks.subject: Microprocessors and its Applications

blocks.text: 5. The ISR performs the required service and preserves/restores registers as required.
blocks.subject: Microprocessors and its Applications

blocks.text: 6. It executes the return-from-interrupt sequence and resumes the interrupted program.
blocks.subject: Microprocessors and its Applications

blocks.text: 12.26 8085 interrupt system
blocks.subject: Microprocessors and its Applications

blocks.text: The five commonly identified hardware interrupts are:
blocks.subject: Microprocessors and its Applications

blocks.text: - TRAP
blocks.subject: Microprocessors and its Applications

blocks.text: - RST 7.5
blocks.subject: Microprocessors and its Applications

blocks.text: - RST 6.5
blocks.subject: Microprocessors and its Applications

blocks.text: - RST 5.5
blocks.subject: Microprocessors and its Applications

blocks.text: - INTR
blocks.subject: Microprocessors and its Applications

blocks.text: The official text specifically includes 8085 TRAP and problems on interrupts. Learn priority, maskability, triggering, vector addresses, interrupt-enable control and acknowledgement from the book's table. TRAP is the highest-priority and non-maskable hardware interrupt in the usual 8085 classification. Do not confuse hardware interrupt requests with software RST instructions.
blocks.subject: Microprocessors and its Applications

blocks.text: 12.27 Multiple interrupts When more than one interrupt request is pending, the processor's priority/masking rules decide which request is serviced. The design must consider:
blocks.subject: Microprocessors and its Applications

blocks.text: • Priority of each request.
blocks.subject: Microprocessors and its Applications

blocks.text: • Whether the request is maskable.
blocks.subject: Microprocessors and its Applications

blocks.text: • Whether interrupts are enabled.
blocks.subject: Microprocessors and its Applications

blocks.text: • Whether another interrupt is currently being serviced.
blocks.subject: Microprocessors and its Applications

blocks.text: • How the program returns to normal execution.
blocks.subject: Microprocessors and its Applications

blocks.text: Use the official text's priority and masking diagram/table for an exam answer.
blocks.subject: Microprocessors and its Applications

blocks.text: 12.28 Direct Memory Access (DMA) DMA is a method for transferring data between an I/O device and memory with reduced continuous involvement of the CPU. A DMA controller requests control of the system bus, performs the transfer and then releases the bus. The CPU can do other work when it does not own the bus. Learn the bus request/grant signal sequence given in the textbook.
blocks.subject: Microprocessors and its Applications

blocks.text: 12.29 RAM and ROM RAM (Random Access Memory): read/write memory used for working data; ordinary RAM is volatile, so its contents are lost when power is removed. ROM (Read Only Memory): non-volatile memory used to store fixed or persistent instructions/data. For memory interfacing, learn address lines, data lines, control signals, chip-select logic and the memory map used in the official illustrations.
blocks.subject: Microprocessors and its Applications

blocks.text: 12.30 I/O interfacing Direct / isolated I/O: I/O devices use a separate I/O address space and special I/O instructions/signals. Memory-mapped I/O: I/O device registers are assigned addresses within the memory address space and accessed using memory instructions.
blocks.subject: Microprocessors and its Applications
