blocks.text: SUBJECT 13 – NUMERICAL AND STATISTICAL METHODS (SUCA203)
blocks.subject: Numerical and Statistical Methods

blocks.text: OFFICIAL UNIT MAP
blocks.subject: Numerical and Statistical Methods

blocks.text: Unit I: errors; roots of equations (graphical, bisection, false position, Newton-Raphson, secant, Muller's, Bairstow's); simultaneous linear equations (matrix inversion, Gauss elimination, Gauss-Jordan, LU decomposition, Gauss-Seidel).
blocks.subject: Numerical and Statistical Methods

blocks.text: Unit II: numerical differentiation and errors; cubic spline; numerical integration (trapezoidal, Simpson's 1/3 and 3/8, Romberg); ODE methods (Taylor, Euler, Runge-Kutta second/fourth order, predictor-corrector).
blocks.subject: Numerical and Statistical Methods

blocks.text: Unit III: sampling, frequency distributions, cumulative frequencies, grouped samples, mean/median/mode, GM/HM, range, mean deviation, variance, standard deviation and moments.
blocks.subject: Numerical and Statistical Methods

blocks.text: Unit IV: probability laws; random variables; density/distribution functions; binomial, Poisson and hypergeometric distributions; expectation.
blocks.subject: Numerical and Statistical Methods

blocks.text: Unit V: least-squares linear and nonlinear fit, polynomial fitting, correlation (Pearson, multiple, partial, rank), significance tests, chi-square, goodness of fit, contingency tables, t-test and F-test.
blocks.subject: Numerical and Statistical Methods

blocks.text: LESSON 1 – ROOTS OF EQUATIONS
blocks.subject: Numerical and Statistical Methods

blocks.text: 13.1 Meaning of a root An equation can be written as f(x)=0. A root is a value of x that makes f(x) equal to zero. A polynomial equation may have real or complex roots. A transcendental equation contains functions such as exponential or trigonometric functions and may need a numerical method.
blocks.subject: Numerical and Statistical Methods

blocks.text: 13.2 Errors in numerical computation Numerical methods often produce approximate answers. The size of the error should be understood and, where possible, estimated.
blocks.subject: Numerical and Statistical Methods

blocks.text: Absolute error = |true value − approximate value|.
blocks.subject: Numerical and Statistical Methods

blocks.text: Relative error = absolute error / |true value| (when the true value is non-zero).
blocks.subject: Numerical and Statistical Methods

blocks.text: Percentage error = relative error × 100%.
blocks.subject: Numerical and Statistical Methods

blocks.text: Rounding error occurs when a number is represented with fewer digits than its exact value. Truncation error occurs when an infinite process/series is stopped after a finite number of terms or steps. Do not round too early in a numerical calculation; retain additional digits and round the final answer to the requested accuracy.
blocks.subject: Numerical and Statistical Methods

blocks.text: 13.3 Graphical method Plot y=f(x). A point where the curve crosses the x-axis is an approximate root. A graph helps identify a starting interval; it is generally not the final high-accuracy numerical result.
blocks.subject: Numerical and Statistical Methods

blocks.text: 13.4 Bisection method Condition: f(x) is continuous on [a,b] and f(a), f(b) have opposite signs, so a root is bracketed. Midpoint: c=(a+b)/2.
blocks.subject: Numerical and Statistical Methods

blocks.text: Procedure:
blocks.subject: Numerical and Statistical Methods

blocks.text: 1. Choose a and b with opposite signs.
blocks.subject: Numerical and Statistical Methods

blocks.text: 2. Calculate c.
blocks.subject: Numerical and Statistical Methods

blocks.text: 3. Evaluate f(c).
blocks.subject: Numerical and Statistical Methods

blocks.text: 4. Keep [a,c] if f(a) and f(c) have opposite signs; otherwise keep [c,b].
blocks.subject: Numerical and Statistical Methods

blocks.text: 5. Repeat until the interval is sufficiently small or the required accuracy is achieved.
blocks.subject: Numerical and Statistical Methods

blocks.text: The method is dependable under the sign-change condition but converges relatively slowly.
blocks.subject: Numerical and Statistical Methods

blocks.text: WORKED EXAMPLE – BISECTION
blocks.subject: Numerical and Statistical Methods

blocks.text: Find a root of f(x)=x^3−x−1 in [1,2]. f(1)=−1; f(2)=5, so a root is bracketed. Iteration 1: c1=1.5; f(1.5)=3.375−1.5−1=0.875. New interval [1,1.5]. Iteration 2: c2=1.25; f(1.25)=1.953125−1.25−1=−0.296875. New interval [1.25,1.5]. Iteration 3: c3=1.375; f(1.375)=2.599609−1.375−1=0.224609. New interval [1.25,1.375]. Iteration 4: c4=1.3125; f(1.3125)≈2.260986−1.3125−1=−0.051514. New interval [1.3125,1.375]. Iteration 5: c5=1.34375; f(1.34375)≈2.4265−1.34375−1=0.0828. New interval [1.3125,1.34375]. Continue in the same way. The exact number of iterations depends on the required decimal accuracy. Always show midpoint and sign at each step.
blocks.subject: Numerical and Statistical Methods

blocks.text: 13.5 Regula Falsi / False Position The method also maintains an interval with a sign change, but chooses the point where the straight line joining (a,f(a)) and (b,f(b)) crosses the x-axis. c = [a f(b) − b f(a)] / [f(b) − f(a)]. Replace the endpoint that has the same sign as f(c); retain the sign-changing interval. It may converge faster than bisection for some functions, but can stagnate when one endpoint remains almost fixed.
blocks.subject: Numerical and Statistical Methods

blocks.text: 13.6 Fixed-point iteration
blocks.subject: Numerical and Statistical Methods

blocks.text: Rewrite f(x)=0 as x=g(x), then iterate x_(n+1)=g(x_n). The chosen rearrangement and starting value affect convergence. A useful local convergence condition is |g'(x)|<1 near the fixed point. Do not assume all rearrangements converge.
blocks.subject: Numerical and Statistical Methods

blocks.text: 13.7 Newton-Raphson method x_(n+1)=x_n−f(x_n)/f'(x_n). Steps: define f; differentiate; select x0; calculate each successive value; stop when successive values or residual meet the required tolerance. Problems can occur if f'(x) is zero/small, if the initial value is poor or if the iteration diverges.
blocks.subject: Numerical and Statistical Methods

blocks.text: WORKED EXAMPLE – NEWTON-RAPHSON
blocks.subject: Numerical and Statistical Methods

blocks.text: Solve x^2−2=0, starting x0=1.5. f(x)=x^2−2; f'(x)=2x. x1=1.5−(1.5²−2)/(3)=1.5−0.25/3=1.4166667. x2=1.4166667−(1.4166667²−2)/(2×1.4166667)≈1.4142157. x3≈1.4142136. The positive root is approximately 1.414214. Keep more digits during iterations than are displayed.
blocks.subject: Numerical and Statistical Methods

blocks.text: 13.8 Secant method x_(n+1)=x_n−f(x_n)(x_n−x_(n−1))/[f(x_n)−f(x_(n−1))]. It uses two previous approximations and does not require explicit differentiation. The denominator must not be zero.
blocks.subject: Numerical and Statistical Methods

blocks.text: 13.9 Muller's method Muller's method uses three approximations to form a quadratic interpolating polynomial. A root of that quadratic gives a new approximation. It can approximate complex roots as well as real roots. For the examination, learn the three-point interpolation procedure, correction formula and worked table from the official textbook.
blocks.subject: Numerical and Statistical Methods

blocks.text: 13.10 Bairstow's method Bairstow's method finds quadratic factors of a polynomial through iterative correction of factor parameters. It is useful for extracting conjugate complex-root pairs for real-coefficient polynomials. Learn the synthetic division/remainder setup and correction steps shown in the textbook.
blocks.subject: Numerical and Statistical Methods

blocks.text: LESSON 2 – SIMULTANEOUS LINEAR EQUATIONS
blocks.subject: Numerical and Statistical Methods

blocks.text: 13.11 Matrix inversion method Write the system as AX=B. If A is square and nonsingular, X=A^(-1)B. First calculate det(A); if it is zero, the inverse method cannot be used.
blocks.subject: Numerical and Statistical Methods

blocks.text: 13.12 Gauss elimination
blocks.subject: Numerical and Statistical Methods

blocks.text: 1. Form the augmented matrix [A|B].
blocks.subject: Numerical and Statistical Methods

blocks.text: 2. Use elementary row operations to eliminate entries below the main diagonal.
blocks.subject: Numerical and Statistical Methods

blocks.text: 3. Obtain an upper triangular system.
blocks.subject: Numerical and Statistical Methods

blocks.text: 4. Use back substitution, starting from the last equation.
blocks.subject: Numerical and Statistical Methods

blocks.text: 5. Verify the solution in the original equations.
blocks.subject: Numerical and Statistical Methods

blocks.text: 13.13 Gauss-Jordan method
blocks.subject: Numerical and Statistical Methods

blocks.text: Use elementary row operations to reduce the coefficient matrix to the identity matrix. Apply every row operation to the augmented column. When the left side is I, the right side is the solution vector. For an inverse, reduce [A|I] to [I|A^(-1)].
blocks.subject: Numerical and Statistical Methods

blocks.text: 13.14 LU decomposition Factor A as A=LU, where L is lower triangular and U is upper triangular. First solve LY=B by forward substitution, then UX=Y by backward substitution. Follow the convention for diagonal entries of L used in the textbook.
blocks.subject: Numerical and Statistical Methods

blocks.text: 13.15 Gauss-Seidel iteration Choose initial approximations. Rearrange each equation to express one variable. Update variables sequentially, using the newest available values. Repeat until the difference between successive iterations is within the specified tolerance. Diagonal dominance is a useful sufficient condition for convergence in many standard cases, but always check the system's behaviour.
blocks.subject: Numerical and Statistical Methods

blocks.text: LESSON 3 – NUMERICAL INTEGRATION
blocks.subject: Numerical and Statistical Methods

blocks.text: 13.16 Why numerical integration? When an antiderivative is difficult to obtain or only tabulated values are available, the area under a curve can be approximated by numerical rules. The interval is divided into subintervals of width h.
blocks.subject: Numerical and Statistical Methods

blocks.text: 13.17 Trapezoidal rule
blocks.subject: Numerical and Statistical Methods

blocks.text: For equally spaced x0,...,xn with y_i=f(x_i):
blocks.subject: Numerical and Statistical Methods

blocks.text: I≈(h/2)[y0+yn+2(y1+y2+...+y_(n−1))]. The end ordinates have coefficient 1; interior ordinates have coefficient 2.
blocks.subject: Numerical and Statistical Methods

blocks.text: WORKED EXAMPLE – TRAPEZOIDAL RULE
blocks.subject: Numerical and Statistical Methods

blocks.text: Approximate ∫_0^2 x² dx using h=1 and ordinates y0=0, y1=1, y2=4.
blocks.subject: Numerical and Statistical Methods

blocks.text: Exact integral is 8/3≈2.6667. The error illustrates that a numerical rule is an approximation.
blocks.subject: Numerical and Statistical Methods

blocks.text: 13.18 Simpson's 1/3 rule
blocks.subject: Numerical and Statistical Methods

blocks.text: Requires an even number of subintervals:
blocks.subject: Numerical and Statistical Methods

blocks.text: I≈(h/3)[y0+yn+4(sum of odd-index interior ordinates)+2(sum of even-index interior ordinates)]. Coefficient pattern: 1,4,2,4,2,...,4,1.
blocks.subject: Numerical and Statistical Methods

blocks.text: WORKED EXAMPLE – SIMPSON'S 1/3
blocks.subject: Numerical and Statistical Methods

blocks.text: For ∫_0^2 x² dx with h=1 and values 0,1,4 (two subintervals):
blocks.subject: Numerical and Statistical Methods

blocks.text: For a quadratic polynomial, Simpson's 1/3 gives the exact integral (apart from arithmetic/rounding).
blocks.subject: Numerical and Statistical Methods

blocks.text: 13.19 Simpson's 3/8 rule Requires the number of subintervals to be a multiple of 3: I≈(3h/8)[y0+yn+3(sum of interior ordinates whose index is not a multiple of 3)+2(sum of interior ordinates whose index is a multiple of 3)]. For four? No—this rule is applied with 3, 6, 9, ... subintervals. Pattern for 3 subintervals: 1,3,3,1.
blocks.subject: Numerical and Statistical Methods

blocks.text: 13.20 Romberg integration Romberg integration starts with trapezoidal approximations at progressively smaller step sizes and uses extrapolation to cancel leading error terms. Build the triangular Romberg table using the recurrence printed in the official lesson. A good answer explains the repeated trapezoidal estimates, refinement of h, extrapolation and final improved approximation.
blocks.subject: Numerical and Statistical Methods

blocks.subject: Numerical and Statistical Methods

blocks.text: 13.21 Numerical differentiation Approximate a derivative using function values at nearby points. Finite-difference formulas may use forward, backward or central differences. Numerical differentiation can amplify measurement and rounding errors; use the formula and error order in the textbook.
blocks.subject: Numerical and Statistical Methods
blocks.chapter: LESSON 4 – NUMERICAL DIFFERENTIATION AND ODE METHODS

blocks.text: 13.22 Cubic spline method A cubic spline represents a curve by piecewise cubic polynomials, joined at data points. The pieces are chosen to provide smooth joining conditions. Learn the boundary conditions, equations for coefficients and worked table in the official lesson; do not improvise the spline conditions.
blocks.subject: Numerical and Statistical Methods
blocks.chapter: LESSON 4 – NUMERICAL DIFFERENTIATION AND ODE METHODS

blocks.text: 13.23 Ordinary differential equation An ODE involves derivatives with respect to one independent variable, such as dy/dx=f(x,y). A numerical method estimates y at successive x values using a chosen step size h.
blocks.subject: Numerical and Statistical Methods
blocks.chapter: LESSON 4 – NUMERICAL DIFFERENTIATION AND ODE METHODS

blocks.text: 13.24 Taylor series method
blocks.subject: Numerical and Statistical Methods
blocks.chapter: LESSON 4 – NUMERICAL DIFFERENTIATION AND ODE METHODS

blocks.text: Expand about x_n:
blocks.subject: Numerical and Statistical Methods
blocks.chapter: LESSON 4 – NUMERICAL DIFFERENTIATION AND ODE METHODS

blocks.text: y(x_n+h)=y_n+h y'_n+(h²/2!)y''_n+(h³/3!)y'''_n+... Use the differential equation to obtain higher derivatives. Substitute known values and retain terms to the specified order.
blocks.subject: Numerical and Statistical Methods
blocks.chapter: LESSON 4 – NUMERICAL DIFFERENTIATION AND ODE METHODS

blocks.subject: Numerical and Statistical Methods

blocks.text: For y'=f(x,y):

blocks.text: x_(n+1)=x_n+h. y_(n+1)=y_n+h f(x_n,y_n). It uses the slope at the beginning of the interval. It is simple but often less accurate than higher-order methods for the same step size.

blocks.text: 13.26 Runge-Kutta second order The syllabus includes a second-order Runge-Kutta method. Several RK2 variants exist, so identify the version used in your textbook before answering. One common midpoint form is: k1=h f(x_n,y_n) k2=h f(x_n+h/2, y_n+k1/2) y_(n+1)=y_n+k2. Do not replace a textbook's chosen RK2 variant with another one without stating the change.
blocks.subject: Numerical and Statistical Methods
blocks.chapter: LESSON 4 – NUMERICAL DIFFERENTIATION AND ODE METHODS

blocks.text: 13.27 Runge-Kutta fourth order
blocks.subject: Numerical and Statistical Methods

blocks.text: k1=h f(x_n,y_n) k2=h f(x_n+h/2,y_n+k1/2) k3=h f(x_n+h/2,y_n+k2/2) k4=h f(x_n+h,y_n+k3) y_(n+1)=y_n+(k1+2k2+2k3+k4)/6. All k values above include the step h.

blocks.text: 13.28 Predictor-corrector methods A predictor formula estimates the next y value. A corrector formula uses the differential equation and the predicted value to improve that estimate. Some methods repeat the corrector. Learn the exact predictor and corrector pair, starting values and stopping procedure printed in the textbook.

blocks.text: 13.29 Population and sample Population: the complete set of individuals/items/measurements under study. Sample: a subset selected from the population. Sampling is used when collecting information from every population member is impractical.
blocks.subject: Numerical and Statistical Methods
blocks.chapter: LESSON 4 – NUMERICAL DIFFERENTIATION AND ODE METHODS

blocks.text: 13.30 Frequency distribution A frequency distribution groups observations into values or class intervals and records how often each occurs.
blocks.subject: Numerical and Statistical Methods
blocks.chapter: LESSON 4 – NUMERICAL DIFFERENTIATION AND ODE METHODS

blocks.text: • Class interval: the range assigned to a class.
blocks.subject: Numerical and Statistical Methods
blocks.chapter: LESSON 4 – NUMERICAL DIFFERENTIATION AND ODE METHODS

blocks.text: • Frequency f: number of observations in the class.
blocks.subject: Numerical and Statistical Methods
blocks.chapter: LESSON 4 – NUMERICAL DIFFERENTIATION AND ODE METHODS

blocks.text: • Cumulative frequency: running total of frequencies.
blocks.subject: Numerical and Statistical Methods
blocks.chapter: LESSON 4 – NUMERICAL DIFFERENTIATION AND ODE METHODS

blocks.text: • Class midpoint: (lower class boundary + upper class boundary)/2.
blocks.subject: Numerical and Statistical Methods
blocks.chapter: LESSON 4 – NUMERICAL DIFFERENTIATION AND ODE METHODS

blocks.text: Check that sum of all frequencies equals total observations N.
blocks.subject: Numerical and Statistical Methods
blocks.chapter: LESSON 4 – NUMERICAL DIFFERENTIATION AND ODE METHODS

blocks.text: 13.31 Arithmetic mean Ungrouped mean: x̄=Σx/n. Frequency mean: x̄=Σfx/Σf. For grouped continuous data, x in fx usually means class midpoint.
blocks.subject: Numerical and Statistical Methods
blocks.chapter: LESSON 4 – NUMERICAL DIFFERENTIATION AND ODE METHODS

blocks.text: 13.32 Median Median is the central observation when data are arranged in order. For an odd number n, median is the (n+1)/2-th observation. For an even number n, median is the average of the n/2-th and (n/2+1)-th observations.
blocks.subject: Numerical and Statistical Methods
blocks.chapter: LESSON 4 – NUMERICAL DIFFERENTIATION AND ODE METHODS

blocks.text: For grouped continuous data, the common formula is:
blocks.subject: Numerical and Statistical Methods
blocks.chapter: LESSON 4 – NUMERICAL DIFFERENTIATION AND ODE METHODS

blocks.text: Median=L+[(N/2−cf)/f]h, where L = lower boundary of median class; N = total frequency; cf = cumulative frequency before median class; f = median-class frequency; h = class width.
blocks.subject: Numerical and Statistical Methods
blocks.chapter: LESSON 4 – NUMERICAL DIFFERENTIATION AND ODE METHODS

blocks.text: WORKED EXAMPLE – MEAN, MEDIAN, MODE
blocks.subject: Numerical and Statistical Methods
blocks.chapter: LESSON 4 – NUMERICAL DIFFERENTIATION AND ODE METHODS

blocks.text: Data: 2, 3, 3, 5, 7. Mean=(2+3+3+5+7)/5=20/5=4. Median=middle value=3. Mode=most frequent value=3.
blocks.subject: Numerical and Statistical Methods
blocks.chapter: LESSON 4 – NUMERICAL DIFFERENTIATION AND ODE METHODS

blocks.text: 13.33 Mode Mode is the value occurring most frequently. For grouped continuous data: Mode=L+[(f1−f0)/(2f1−f0−f2)]h, where f1 is modal-class frequency, f0 preceding-class frequency and f2 succeeding-class frequency. Check the grouping and class-boundary conventions in the problem.
blocks.subject: Numerical and Statistical Methods
blocks.chapter: LESSON 4 – NUMERICAL DIFFERENTIATION AND ODE METHODS

blocks.text: 13.34 Geometric mean For positive observations: GM=(x1x2...xn)^(1/n). For frequency data: GM=antilog[Σf log(x)/N]. It is useful for multiplicative growth rates or ratios, when its conditions are appropriate.
blocks.subject: Numerical and Statistical Methods
blocks.chapter: LESSON 4 – NUMERICAL DIFFERENTIATION AND ODE METHODS

blocks.text: 13.35 Harmonic mean For non-zero observations: HM=n/Σ(1/x). For frequency data: HM=N/Σ(f/x). It is useful for averaging rates such as speed when the same distance is travelled, under the stated conditions.
blocks.subject: Numerical and Statistical Methods
blocks.chapter: LESSON 4 – NUMERICAL DIFFERENTIATION AND ODE METHODS

blocks.text: 13.36 Measures of dispersion Range = largest observation − smallest observation.
blocks.subject: Numerical and Statistical Methods
blocks.chapter: LESSON 4 – NUMERICAL DIFFERENTIATION AND ODE METHODS

blocks.text: Mean deviation about A = Σ|x−A|/n; with frequency, Σf|x−A|/N.
blocks.subject: Numerical and Statistical Methods
blocks.chapter: LESSON 4 – NUMERICAL DIFFERENTIATION AND ODE METHODS

blocks.text: Population variance: σ²=Σ(x−μ)²/N. Sample variance: s²=Σ(x−x̄)²/(n−1). Standard deviation: positive square root of variance. Coefficient of variation: CV=(SD/mean)×100%. Smaller CV indicates less relative variation when comparing suitable data sets.
blocks.subject: Numerical and Statistical Methods
blocks.chapter: LESSON 4 – NUMERICAL DIFFERENTIATION AND ODE METHODS

blocks.text: WORKED EXAMPLE – RANGE AND POPULATION STANDARD DEVIATION
blocks.subject: Numerical and Statistical Methods
blocks.chapter: LESSON 4 – NUMERICAL DIFFERENTIATION AND ODE METHODS

blocks.text: Data: 2, 4, 6. Mean μ=4. Deviations: −2, 0, 2. Squared deviations: 4, 0, 4. Population variance=(4+0+4)/3=8/3. Population SD=√(8/3)≈1.633. Range=6−2=4. If the data are treated as a sample, use denominator n−1=2 instead; state the convention.
blocks.subject: Numerical and Statistical Methods
blocks.chapter: LESSON 4 – NUMERICAL DIFFERENTIATION AND ODE METHODS

blocks.text: 13.37 Moments Moments describe aspects of a distribution. The r-th raw moment about origin is μ′r=Σfx^r/N. The r-th central moment is μr=Σf(x−x̄)^r/N. The first central moment is zero. Higher moments help describe spread, skewness and peakedness. Use the notation/normalisation prescribed in the textbook.
blocks.subject: Numerical and Statistical Methods
blocks.chapter: LESSON 4 – NUMERICAL DIFFERENTIATION AND ODE METHODS

blocks.text: 13.39 Probability basics For equally likely outcomes, P(A)=favourable outcomes/total outcomes.
blocks.subject: Numerical and Statistical Methods
blocks.chapter: LESSON 4 – NUMERICAL DIFFERENTIATION AND ODE METHODS

blocks.subject: Numerical and Statistical Methods
blocks.chapter: LESSON 4 – NUMERICAL DIFFERENTIATION AND ODE METHODS

blocks.text: Complement law: P(A′)=1−P(A).
blocks.subject: Numerical and Statistical Methods
blocks.chapter: LESSON 4 – NUMERICAL DIFFERENTIATION AND ODE METHODS

blocks.text: 13.40 Addition law
blocks.subject: Numerical and Statistical Methods
blocks.chapter: LESSON 4 – NUMERICAL DIFFERENTIATION AND ODE METHODS

blocks.text: P(A∪B)=P(A)+P(B)−P(A∩B).
blocks.subject: Numerical and Statistical Methods
blocks.chapter: LESSON 4 – NUMERICAL DIFFERENTIATION AND ODE METHODS

blocks.text: If A and B are mutually exclusive, P(A∩B)=0, so P(A∪B)=P(A)+P(B).
blocks.subject: Numerical and Statistical Methods
blocks.chapter: LESSON 4 – NUMERICAL DIFFERENTIATION AND ODE METHODS

blocks.text: 13.41 Conditional probability P(A|B)=P(A∩B)/P(B), provided P(B)>0. It means probability of A after knowing B has occurred.
blocks.subject: Numerical and Statistical Methods
blocks.chapter: LESSON 4 – NUMERICAL DIFFERENTIATION AND ODE METHODS

blocks.text: 13.42 Multiplication law and independence
blocks.subject: Numerical and Statistical Methods
blocks.chapter: LESSON 4 – NUMERICAL DIFFERENTIATION AND ODE METHODS

blocks.text: P(A∩B)=P(A|B)P(B).
blocks.subject: Numerical and Statistical Methods
blocks.chapter: LESSON 4 – NUMERICAL DIFFERENTIATION AND ODE METHODS

blocks.text: If A and B are independent, P(A∩B)=P(A)P(B). Do not confuse independence with mutual exclusiveness.
blocks.subject: Numerical and Statistical Methods
blocks.chapter: LESSON 4 – NUMERICAL DIFFERENTIATION AND ODE METHODS

blocks.text: 13.43 Random variable and distributions A random variable assigns a numerical value to each outcome of a random experiment.
blocks.subject: Numerical and Statistical Methods
blocks.chapter: LESSON 4 – NUMERICAL DIFFERENTIATION AND ODE METHODS

blocks.text: • Discrete random variable: takes countable values.
blocks.subject: Numerical and Statistical Methods
blocks.chapter: LESSON 4 – NUMERICAL DIFFERENTIATION AND ODE METHODS

blocks.text: • Continuous random variable: may take any value in an interval.
blocks.subject: Numerical and Statistical Methods
blocks.chapter: LESSON 4 – NUMERICAL DIFFERENTIATION AND ODE METHODS

blocks.text: A probability mass function gives P(X=x) for discrete X. A probability density function describes a continuous variable; probabilities are areas/integrals over intervals. The cumulative distribution function is F(x)=P(X≤x).
blocks.subject: Numerical and Statistical Methods
blocks.chapter: LESSON 4 – NUMERICAL DIFFERENTIATION AND ODE METHODS

blocks.text: 13.44 Binomial distribution Conditions: fixed n independent trials; each trial has success/failure; success probability p is constant; q=1−p. P(X=x)=nCx p^x q^(n−x), x=0,...,n. Mean=np; variance=npq.
blocks.subject: Numerical and Statistical Methods
blocks.chapter: LESSON 4 – NUMERICAL DIFFERENTIATION AND ODE METHODS

blocks.subject: Numerical and Statistical Methods

blocks.text: 13.45 Poisson distribution P(X=x)=e^(−λ)λ^x/x!, x=0,1,2,... Mean=λ; variance=λ. It models counts in a fixed interval when the process assumptions of the model are suitable.

blocks.text: 13.46 Hypergeometric distribution Used when sampling without replacement from a finite population. If N is population size, K are successes, and n items are selected: P(X=x)=[K C x][(N−K) C (n−x)]/[N C n]. Use only feasible x values. Unlike binomial sampling, draws are not independent when sampling without replacement.
blocks.subject: Numerical and Statistical Methods
blocks.chapter: LESSON 4 – NUMERICAL DIFFERENTIATION AND ODE METHODS

blocks.text: 13.47 Mathematical expectation For a discrete variable, E(X)=ΣxP(X=x). E[g(X)]=Σg(x)P(X=x). Variance: Var(X)=E(X²)−[E(X)]².
blocks.subject: Numerical and Statistical Methods
blocks.chapter: LESSON 4 – NUMERICAL DIFFERENTIATION AND ODE METHODS

blocks.text: LESSONS 12–14 – CORRELATION, REGRESSION AND TESTS
blocks.subject: Numerical and Statistical Methods
blocks.chapter: LESSON 4 – NUMERICAL DIFFERENTIATION AND ODE METHODS

blocks.text: 13.48 Correlation Correlation measures the direction and strength of association between two variables. Correlation does not by itself prove causation.
blocks.subject: Numerical and Statistical Methods
blocks.chapter: LESSON 4 – NUMERICAL DIFFERENTIATION AND ODE METHODS

blocks.text: 13.49 Pearson's correlation coefficient r=[nΣxy−(Σx)(Σy)]/√{[nΣx²−(Σx)²][nΣy²−(Σy)²]}. −1≤r≤+1. Positive r: variables tend to increase together. Negative r: one tends to decrease as the other increases. r near 0 indicates weak linear association, not necessarily no relationship of any kind.
blocks.subject: Numerical and Statistical Methods
blocks.chapter: LESSON 4 – NUMERICAL DIFFERENTIATION AND ODE METHODS

blocks.text: 13.50 Rank correlation
blocks.subject: Numerical and Statistical Methods
blocks.chapter: LESSON 4 – NUMERICAL DIFFERENTIATION AND ODE METHODS

blocks.text: For Spearman's rank correlation without ties:
blocks.subject: Numerical and Statistical Methods
blocks.chapter: LESSON 4 – NUMERICAL DIFFERENTIATION AND ODE METHODS

blocks.text: ρ=1−[6Σd²/(n(n²−1))], where d is the difference between paired ranks. Use the tie correction/ranking procedure stated in the textbook when ranks are tied.
blocks.subject: Numerical and Statistical Methods
blocks.chapter: LESSON 4 – NUMERICAL DIFFERENTIATION AND ODE METHODS

blocks.text: 13.51 Regression and least squares Regression estimates one variable from another. A straight-line model is y=a+bx. Least squares chooses a and b to minimise the sum of squared residuals. Regression of y on x is different from regression of x on y. Identify the dependent variable before forming equations.
blocks.subject: Numerical and Statistical Methods
blocks.chapter: LESSON 4 – NUMERICAL DIFFERENTIATION AND ODE METHODS

blocks.text: 13.52 Nonlinear and polynomial fit The syllabus includes nonlinear fitting and fitting a polynomial. A nonlinear model may sometimes be transformed into a linear form. Polynomial fitting uses least-squares normal equations. Use the exact model and equations given in the textbook; show the table of required sums.
blocks.subject: Numerical and Statistical Methods
blocks.chapter: LESSON 4 – NUMERICAL DIFFERENTIATION AND ODE METHODS

blocks.text: 13.53 Multiple and partial correlation Multiple correlation measures association between one variable and a set of other variables. Partial correlation measures the association between two variables while holding another variable (or variables) constant. Learn formulas and interpretation from the relevant lesson.
blocks.subject: Numerical and Statistical Methods
blocks.chapter: LESSON 4 – NUMERICAL DIFFERENTIATION AND ODE METHODS

blocks.text: 13.54 Tests of significance – key terms Null hypothesis H0: statement tested. Alternative hypothesis H1: competing statement. Significance level α: tolerated probability of Type I error under the testing framework. Test statistic: numerical value calculated from sample data. Critical region: values leading to rejection of H0. p-value: probability, assuming H0 and model assumptions, of a result at least as extreme as observed. Type I error: rejecting a true H0. Type II error: failing to reject a false H0. A test does not prove H0 true; if it is not rejected, the sample has not provided sufficient evidence against it at the chosen level.
blocks.subject: Numerical and Statistical Methods
blocks.chapter: LESSON 4 – NUMERICAL DIFFERENTIATION AND ODE METHODS

blocks.text: 13.55 Chi-square test χ²=Σ(O−E)²/E, where O is observed frequency and E is expected frequency. Uses in this syllabus include goodness of fit and contingency-table analysis/independence. For an r×c independence table, df=(r−1)(c−1). Goodness-of-fit degrees of freedom depend on categories and estimated parameters; use the textbook's rule. Expected frequencies must be suitable for the approximation being used. Calculate expected values before the χ² statistic.
blocks.subject: Numerical and Statistical Methods
blocks.chapter: LESSON 4 – NUMERICAL DIFFERENTIATION AND ODE METHODS

blocks.text: 13.56 t-test The t-test is used for inference about means when population variance is unknown under the assumptions of the test.
blocks.subject: Numerical and Statistical Methods
blocks.chapter: LESSON 4 – NUMERICAL DIFFERENTIATION AND ODE METHODS

blocks.text: For a one-sample test:
blocks.subject: Numerical and Statistical Methods
blocks.chapter: LESSON 4 – NUMERICAL DIFFERENTIATION AND ODE METHODS

blocks.text: t=(x̄−μ0)/(s/√n), df=n−1. Other forms include paired and two-sample tests. Identify the question type and use the correct formula/degree-of-freedom convention from the textbook.
blocks.subject: Numerical and Statistical Methods
blocks.chapter: LESSON 4 – NUMERICAL DIFFERENTIATION AND ODE METHODS

blocks.text: 13.57 F-test An F statistic is a ratio of variance estimates, often written F=s1²/s2². Tail choice, numerator/denominator order and degrees of freedom depend on the test. Follow the exact procedure and F-table convention in the official textbook.
blocks.subject: Numerical and Statistical Methods
blocks.chapter: LESSON 4 – NUMERICAL DIFFERENTIATION AND ODE METHODS

blocks.subject: C++ Data Structures Lab

blocks.text: 14.1 STACK USING ARRAY
blocks.subject: C++ Data Structures Lab

blocks.text: Concept: Stack follows LIFO – Last In, First Out. Use an array and a top index. Initial state: top=−1.
blocks.subject: C++ Data Structures Lab

blocks.text: PUSH:
blocks.subject: C++ Data Structures Lab

blocks.text: 1. If top=capacity−1, report overflow.
blocks.subject: C++ Data Structures Lab

blocks.text: 2. Otherwise increment top.
blocks.subject: C++ Data Structures Lab

blocks.text: 3. Store new item at stack[top].
blocks.subject: C++ Data Structures Lab

blocks.text: POP:
blocks.subject: C++ Data Structures Lab

blocks.text: 1. If top=−1, report underflow.
blocks.subject: C++ Data Structures Lab

blocks.text: 2. Otherwise read stack[top].
blocks.subject: C++ Data Structures Lab

blocks.text: 3. Decrement top.
blocks.subject: C++ Data Structures Lab

blocks.text: Modern C++ illustration:
blocks.subject: C++ Data Structures Lab

blocks.text: #include <iostream>
blocks.subject: C++ Data Structures Lab

blocks.text: using namespace std;
blocks.subject: C++ Data Structures Lab

blocks.text: class ArrayStack {
blocks.subject: C++ Data Structures Lab

blocks.text: static const int CAP=100;
blocks.subject: C++ Data Structures Lab

blocks.text: int a[CAP];
blocks.subject: C++ Data Structures Lab

blocks.text: int top;
blocks.subject: C++ Data Structures Lab

blocks.text: public:
blocks.subject: C++ Data Structures Lab

blocks.text: ArrayStack():top(-1){} bool push(int x){ if(top==CAP-1) return false; a[++top]=x; return true; } bool pop(int &x){ if(top==-1) return false; x=a[top--]; return true; } };
blocks.subject: C++ Data Structures Lab

blocks.text: int main(){ ArrayStack s; int x; s.push(10); s.push(20); if(s.pop(x)) cout<<x<<'\n'; return 0; }
blocks.subject: C++ Data Structures Lab

blocks.text: Output: 20. Explanation: 20 was pushed last; therefore it is popped first.
blocks.subject: C++ Data Structures Lab

blocks.text: 14.2 STACK USING POINTERS
blocks.subject: C++ Data Structures Lab

blocks.text: Concept: Each node stores data and a link to the next node. A pointer top/start identifies the top node.
blocks.subject: C++ Data Structures Lab

blocks.text: PUSH steps:
blocks.subject: C++ Data Structures Lab

blocks.text: 1. Allocate a new node.
blocks.subject: C++ Data Structures Lab

blocks.text: 2. Store the data.
blocks.subject: C++ Data Structures Lab

blocks.text: 3. Set newNode->next to the current top.
blocks.subject: C++ Data Structures Lab

blocks.text: 4. Set top to newNode.
blocks.subject: C++ Data Structures Lab

blocks.text: POP steps:
blocks.subject: C++ Data Structures Lab

blocks.text: 1. If top is null, report underflow.
blocks.subject: C++ Data Structures Lab

blocks.text: 2. Save the current top node in a temporary pointer.
blocks.subject: C++ Data Structures Lab

blocks.text: 3. Read its data.
blocks.subject: C++ Data Structures Lab

blocks.text: 4. Move top to top->next.
blocks.subject: C++ Data Structures Lab

blocks.text: 5. Delete the old node to release memory.
blocks.subject: C++ Data Structures Lab

blocks.text: Common error: changing top before saving the old node may lose access to memory. Every allocated node must eventually be deleted.
blocks.subject: C++ Data Structures Lab

blocks.text: 14.3 QUEUE USING ARRAY
blocks.subject: C++ Data Structures Lab

blocks.text: Concept: Queue follows FIFO – First In, First Out. Maintain front and rear.
blocks.subject: C++ Data Structures Lab

blocks.text: ENQUEUE (add):
blocks.subject: C++ Data Structures Lab

blocks.text: 1. Check full condition.
blocks.subject: C++ Data Structures Lab

blocks.text: 2. Insert at rear.
blocks.subject: C++ Data Structures Lab

blocks.text: 3. Advance rear.
blocks.subject: C++ Data Structures Lab

blocks.text: DEQUEUE (delete):
blocks.subject: C++ Data Structures Lab

blocks.text: 1. Check empty condition.
blocks.subject: C++ Data Structures Lab

blocks.text: 2. Read the item at front.
blocks.subject: C++ Data Structures Lab

blocks.text: 3. Advance front.
blocks.subject: C++ Data Structures Lab

blocks.text: A simple linear queue may leave unused positions at the beginning after deletions. A circular queue reuses positions; use the implementation required in the question.
blocks.subject: C++ Data Structures Lab

blocks.text: 14.4 QUEUE USING POINTERS
blocks.subject: C++ Data Structures Lab

blocks.text: Use linked nodes with front and rear pointers.
blocks.subject: C++ Data Structures Lab

blocks.text: ENQUEUE:
blocks.subject: C++ Data Structures Lab

blocks.text: 1. Create a node with next=null.
blocks.subject: C++ Data Structures Lab

blocks.text: 2. If queue is empty, set both front and rear to the new node.
blocks.subject: C++ Data Structures Lab

blocks.text: 3. Otherwise link rear->next to the new node.
blocks.subject: C++ Data Structures Lab

blocks.text: 4. Update rear.
blocks.subject: C++ Data Structures Lab

blocks.text: DEQUEUE:
blocks.subject: C++ Data Structures Lab

blocks.text: 1. If front is null, queue is empty.
blocks.subject: C++ Data Structures Lab

blocks.text: 2. Save front node and its data.
blocks.subject: C++ Data Structures Lab

blocks.text: 3. Move front to front->next.
blocks.subject: C++ Data Structures Lab

blocks.text: 4. If front becomes null, set rear=null too.
blocks.subject: C++ Data Structures Lab

blocks.text: 5. Delete the removed node.
blocks.subject: C++ Data Structures Lab

blocks.text: 14.5 INFIX-TO-POSTFIX CONVERSION
blocks.subject: C++ Data Structures Lab

blocks.text: Infix: operator lies between operands, e.g. A+B*C. Postfix: operator follows operands, e.g. ABC*+. Why postfix? It can be evaluated using a stack without needing parentheses during evaluation.
blocks.subject: C++ Data Structures Lab

blocks.text: Procedure:
blocks.subject: C++ Data Structures Lab

blocks.text: 1. Scan left to right.
blocks.subject: C++ Data Structures Lab

blocks.text: 2. Send operands directly to output.
blocks.subject: C++ Data Structures Lab

blocks.text: 3. Push '(' onto operator stack.
blocks.subject: C++ Data Structures Lab

blocks.text: 4. For an operator, pop higher-precedence operators (and equal-precedence operators when required by associativity) before pushing the current operator.
blocks.subject: C++ Data Structures Lab

blocks.text: 5. On ')', pop until the matching '('; discard the parentheses.
blocks.subject: C++ Data Structures Lab

blocks.text: 6. At end, pop remaining operators.
blocks.subject: C++ Data Structures Lab

blocks.text: Example: A+B*C → ABC*+ because multiplication has higher precedence than addition. Example: (A+B)*C → AB+C*. In the examination, show the stack after each scanned symbol. Follow the precedence and associativity table from the textbook.
blocks.subject: C++ Data Structures Lab

blocks.text: 14.6 POSTFIX EVALUATION
blocks.subject: C++ Data Structures Lab

blocks.text: Method:
blocks.subject: C++ Data Structures Lab

blocks.text: 1. Scan tokens from left to right.
blocks.subject: C++ Data Structures Lab

blocks.text: 2. Push each operand.
blocks.subject: C++ Data Structures Lab

blocks.text: 3. When an operator appears, pop the required operands.
blocks.subject: C++ Data Structures Lab

blocks.text: 4. Apply the operation in the correct order.
blocks.subject: C++ Data Structures Lab

blocks.text: 5. Push the result.
blocks.subject: C++ Data Structures Lab

blocks.text: 6. At the end, one result should remain.
blocks.subject: C++ Data Structures Lab

blocks.text: For subtraction and division, the first value popped is normally the right operand b, and the next popped value is the left operand a; calculate a−b or a/b. Example: postfix 23+5*. Push 2; push 3; + gives 5; push 5; * gives 25. Result = 25.
blocks.subject: C++ Data Structures Lab

blocks.text: 14.7 POLYNOMIAL ADDITION USING ARRAYS
blocks.subject: C++ Data Structures Lab

blocks.text: Represent every term as a coefficient and exponent. Example: 4x^3+2x+5 can be represented as (4,3), (2,1), (5,0).
blocks.subject: C++ Data Structures Lab

blocks.text: Algorithm:
blocks.subject: C++ Data Structures Lab

blocks.text: 1. Store terms in descending exponent order.
blocks.subject: C++ Data Structures Lab

blocks.text: 2. Compare current exponents of the two polynomial arrays.
blocks.subject: C++ Data Structures Lab

blocks.text: 3. If equal, add coefficients and store the resulting term (unless coefficient is zero if the implementation omits zero terms).
blocks.subject: C++ Data Structures Lab

blocks.text: 4. If one exponent is higher, copy that term to the result.
blocks.subject: C++ Data Structures Lab

blocks.text: 5. Advance the corresponding index.
blocks.subject: C++ Data Structures Lab

blocks.text: 6. Append any remaining terms.
blocks.subject: C++ Data Structures Lab

blocks.text: 14.8 POLYNOMIAL ADDITION AND MULTIPLICATION USING POINTERS
blocks.subject: C++ Data Structures Lab

blocks.text: Addition follows the same exponent-comparison method, but each term is a linked node.
blocks.subject: C++ Data Structures Lab

blocks.text: Multiplication:
blocks.subject: C++ Data Structures Lab

blocks.text: 1. For every term in polynomial A, multiply it with every term in polynomial B.
blocks.subject: C++ Data Structures Lab

blocks.text: 2. Multiply coefficients.
blocks.subject: C++ Data Structures Lab

blocks.text: 3. Add exponents.
blocks.subject: C++ Data Structures Lab

blocks.text: 4. Insert the product term into the result in exponent order.
blocks.subject: C++ Data Structures Lab

blocks.text: 5. If a term with that exponent already exists, add coefficients.
blocks.subject: C++ Data Structures Lab

blocks.text: 6. Remove or ignore terms with zero coefficient as per the program design.
blocks.subject: C++ Data Structures Lab

blocks.text: Example: (2x+1)(x+3)=2x²+7x+3. The product terms are 2x·x=2x²; 2x·3=6x; 1·x=x; 1·3=3; combine 6x+x=7x.
blocks.subject: C++ Data Structures Lab

blocks.text: 14.9 DOUBLY LINKED LIST
blocks.subject: C++ Data Structures Lab

blocks.text: Each node contains prev, data and next pointers.
blocks.subject: C++ Data Structures Lab

blocks.text: NULL <- [prev | data | next] <-> [prev | data | next] -> NULL
blocks.subject: C++ Data Structures Lab

blocks.text: Insertion at beginning:
blocks.subject: C++ Data Structures Lab

blocks.text: 1. Allocate a new node.
blocks.subject: C++ Data Structures Lab

blocks.text: 2. Set its prev=null.
blocks.subject: C++ Data Structures Lab

blocks.text: 3. Set its next to old head.
blocks.subject: C++ Data Structures Lab

blocks.text: 4. If old head exists, set oldHead->prev to new node.
blocks.subject: C++ Data Structures Lab

blocks.text: 5. Set head to new node.
blocks.subject: C++ Data Structures Lab

blocks.text: Deletion at beginning:
blocks.subject: C++ Data Structures Lab

blocks.text: 1. If head is null, report empty list.
blocks.subject: C++ Data Structures Lab

blocks.text: 2. Save old head.
blocks.subject: C++ Data Structures Lab

blocks.text: 3. Move head to head->next.
blocks.subject: C++ Data Structures Lab

blocks.text: 4. If new head exists, set newHead->prev=null.
blocks.subject: C++ Data Structures Lab

blocks.text: 5. Delete old head.
blocks.subject: C++ Data Structures Lab

blocks.text: For deletion/insertion in the middle/end, update both neighbour links and handle head/tail separately.
blocks.subject: C++ Data Structures Lab

blocks.text: 14.10 BINARY TREE TRAVERSALS
blocks.subject: C++ Data Structures Lab

blocks.text: A linked binary-tree node contains data, left pointer and right pointer. Preorder (NLR): visit node, traverse left, traverse right. Inorder (LNR): traverse left, visit node, traverse right. Postorder (LRN): traverse left, traverse right, visit node.
blocks.subject: C++ Data Structures Lab

blocks.text: Example tree:
blocks.subject: C++ Data Structures Lab

blocks.text: A
blocks.subject: C++ Data Structures Lab

blocks.text: B   C
blocks.subject: C++ Data Structures Lab

blocks.text: D   E
blocks.subject: C++ Data Structures Lab

blocks.text: Preorder: A B D E C. Inorder: D B E A C. Postorder: D E B C A. Practise by writing the sequence from the diagram; do not merely memorise the letters.
blocks.subject: C++ Data Structures Lab

blocks.text: 14.11 DFS AND BFS
blocks.subject: C++ Data Structures Lab

blocks.text: Graph: set of vertices connected by edges. Depth First Search (DFS): visit a vertex, then explore an unvisited neighbour as deeply as possible before backtracking. Can use recursion or a stack. Breadth First Search (BFS): visit vertices level by level. Uses a queue. Both methods maintain a visited marker to avoid repeating vertices. For a disconnected graph, start another traversal from each unvisited vertex if the question asks to cover every component.
blocks.subject: C++ Data Structures Lab

blocks.text: SUBJECT 15 – FINANCIAL ACCOUNTING (SUCA205)
blocks.subject: Financial Accounting

blocks.text: OFFICIAL COURSE POSITION
blocks.subject: Financial Accounting

blocks.text: Second Year – Third Semester – Non-Major Elective I. The syllabus has FIVE units. The textbook's Scheme of Lessons divides the material into SIX lessons:
blocks.subject: Financial Accounting

blocks.text: 1. Accounting Framework.
blocks.subject: Financial Accounting

blocks.text: 2. Accounting Process.
blocks.subject: Financial Accounting

blocks.text: 3. Final Accounts.
blocks.subject: Financial Accounting

blocks.text: 4. Departmental Accounting.
blocks.subject: Financial Accounting

blocks.text: 5. Depreciation, Provisions and Reserves.
blocks.subject: Financial Accounting

blocks.text: 6. Single Entry System.
blocks.subject: Financial Accounting

blocks.text: Syllabus Unit I covers the first two textbook lessons. Syllabus Unit IV maps to textbook Lesson 5 (with provisions and reserves as supporting topics). Syllabus Unit V maps to Lesson 6. This numbering difference is important; answer using the syllabus unit the question refers to.
blocks.subject: Financial Accounting

blocks.text: UNIT I – ACCOUNTING FRAMEWORK AND ACCOUNTING PROCESS
blocks.subject: Financial Accounting

blocks.text: 15.1 Meaning of accounting Accounting is the process of identifying, measuring, recording, classifying, summarising and communicating economic events and their results to the users of accounting information. It is often called the language of business because it communicates the operating results and financial position of an organisation.
blocks.subject: Financial Accounting

blocks.text: The textbook gives definitions from the American Accounting Association (AAA) and the American Institute of Certified Public Accountants (AICPA). The AAA definition stresses identifying, measuring and communicating economic information for informed judgements and decisions. The AICPA definition stresses recording, classifying and summarising financial transactions in money terms and interpreting the results.
blocks.subject: Financial Accounting

blocks.text: 15.2 Scope / stages of accounting
blocks.subject: Financial Accounting

blocks.text: 1. Identification: select events having financial character.
blocks.subject: Financial Accounting

blocks.text: 2. Measurement: quantify eligible events in monetary terms.
blocks.subject: Financial Accounting

blocks.text: 3. Recording: write transactions chronologically in the Journal.
blocks.subject: Financial Accounting

blocks.text: 4. Classification: group similar items in the Ledger.
blocks.subject: Financial Accounting

blocks.text: 5. Summarising: prepare Trial Balance and financial statements.
blocks.subject: Financial Accounting

blocks.text: 6. Communication/interpretation: explain profit/loss and financial position to users.
blocks.subject: Financial Accounting

blocks.text: Flow:
blocks.subject: Financial Accounting

blocks.text: TRANSACTION → JOURNAL → LEDGER → TRIAL BALANCE → FINAL ACCOUNTS → USERS.
blocks.subject: Financial Accounting

blocks.text: An external event involves an exchange between entities, such as paying rent to a landlord. An internal event occurs within the entity, such as movement of materials from stores to production.
blocks.subject: Financial Accounting

blocks.text: 15.3 Objectives of accounting
blocks.subject: Financial Accounting

blocks.text: • Maintain systematic records and documentary evidence.
blocks.subject: Financial Accounting

blocks.text: • Ascertain profit or loss for an accounting period.
blocks.subject: Financial Accounting

blocks.text: • Show the financial position of the business.
blocks.subject: Financial Accounting

blocks.text: • Provide information for investment, credit and management decisions.
blocks.subject: Financial Accounting

blocks.text: • Support control and protection of business resources.
blocks.subject: Financial Accounting

blocks.text: 15.4 Users of accounting information Internal users include managers at different levels. External users include investors, lenders/creditors, employees, tax authorities, regulators and customers. The user group depends on the type of decision being made.
blocks.subject: Financial Accounting

blocks.text: 15.5 Book-keeping and accounting Book-keeping is mainly concerned with identifying, measuring and recording transactions and posting them to the Ledger. Accounting is broader: it includes summarising, analysing, interpreting and communicating the information. Book-keeping is part of accounting.
blocks.subject: Financial Accounting

blocks.text: 15.6 Branches of accounting Financial Accounting: prepares financial statements to show operating results and financial position. Cost Accounting: determines and controls the cost of products/services. Management Accounting: supplies information for planning, control and managerial decisions.
blocks.subject: Financial Accounting

blocks.text: 15.7 Systems of book-keeping Single Entry System: incomplete records; usually personal accounts and cash records are maintained; less systematic. Double Entry System: every transaction has two aspects; for each debit there is an equal corresponding credit. It gives a more complete record.
blocks.subject: Financial Accounting

blocks.text: 15.8 Systems of accounting Cash system: transactions are recorded when cash is received or paid. Mercantile/accrual system: transactions are recorded when amounts become due/earned/incurred, whether or not cash has moved.
blocks.subject: Financial Accounting

blocks.text: 15.9 Advantages and limitations Advantages: systematic historical records; information about assets and liabilities; profit/loss; financial position; comparison; evidence; information to users. Limitations: records only monetary events; mostly historical; estimates/judgements may affect results; price-level changes can reduce comparability; financial statements may not reveal the performance of each activity separately.
blocks.subject: Financial Accounting

blocks.text: 15.10 Accounting concepts and conventions The textbook groups them into basic assumptions, basic accounting principles and modifying principles.
blocks.subject: Financial Accounting

blocks.text: Basic assumptions:
blocks.subject: Financial Accounting

blocks.text: • Accounting Entity: business is separate from owner. Owner's capital and drawings are recorded from business viewpoint.
blocks.subject: Financial Accounting

blocks.text: • Money Measurement: only events measurable in money are recorded.
blocks.subject: Financial Accounting

blocks.text: • Going Concern/Continuity: assume the business continues unless evidence indicates otherwise.
blocks.subject: Financial Accounting

blocks.text: • Accounting Period/Periodicity: divide business life into reporting periods.
blocks.subject: Financial Accounting

blocks.text: Basic accounting principles:
blocks.subject: Financial Accounting

blocks.text: • Duality/Dual Aspect: each transaction has two effects; Assets = Liabilities + Owner's Equity.
blocks.subject: Financial Accounting

blocks.text: • Revenue Recognition/Realisation: recognise revenue when earned/realised under the textbook's stated conditions.
blocks.subject: Financial Accounting

blocks.text: • Historical Cost: record an asset at acquisition cost and necessary costs to bring it into working condition.
blocks.subject: Financial Accounting

blocks.text: • Matching: match expenses of a period with revenues of that period.
blocks.subject: Financial Accounting

blocks.text: • Full Disclosure: disclose relevant information needed for understanding statements.
blocks.subject: Financial Accounting

blocks.text: • Objectivity: use verifiable evidence and avoid personal bias.
blocks.subject: Financial Accounting

blocks.text: Modifying principles:
blocks.subject: Financial Accounting

blocks.text: • Cost-Benefit: benefits of information should justify its cost.
blocks.subject: Financial Accounting

blocks.text: • Materiality: give special attention to items significant to users.
blocks.subject: Financial Accounting

blocks.text: • Consistency: apply methods consistently and disclose changes.
blocks.subject: Financial Accounting

blocks.text: • Conservatism: provide for expected losses and avoid anticipating unrealised profit, as described in the textbook.
blocks.subject: Financial Accounting

blocks.text: • Timeliness: provide information in time for decisions.
blocks.subject: Financial Accounting

blocks.text: • Industry Practice: recognised practices may differ by industry.
blocks.subject: Financial Accounting

blocks.text: 15.11 Accounting equation Assets = Liabilities + Capital (Owner's Equity). If the owner invests cash, assets and capital increase. If a loan is taken, assets and liabilities increase. If an expense is paid, cash and capital/equity reduce through the expense.
blocks.subject: Financial Accounting

blocks.text: 15.12 Classification of accounts
blocks.subject: Financial Accounting

blocks.text: Traditional approach:
blocks.subject: Financial Accounting

blocks.text: Personal accounts – natural persons, artificial persons and representative persons. Real accounts – assets, tangible or intangible. Nominal accounts – expenses, losses, incomes and gains.
blocks.subject: Financial Accounting

blocks.text: Traditional debit-credit rules:
blocks.subject: Financial Accounting

blocks.text: Personal: Debit the receiver; Credit the giver. Real: Debit what comes in; Credit what goes out. Nominal: Debit all expenses and losses; Credit all incomes and gains.
blocks.subject: Financial Accounting

blocks.text: Accounting-equation approach:
blocks.subject: Financial Accounting

blocks.text: Assets: increase debit, decrease credit. Liabilities: decrease debit, increase credit. Capital: decrease debit, increase credit. Revenue: decrease debit, increase credit. Expenses: increase debit, decrease credit.
blocks.subject: Financial Accounting

blocks.text: Memory line: Personal – Receiver/Giver; Real – In/Out; Nominal – Expense/Loss Debit, Income/Gain Credit.
blocks.subject: Financial Accounting

blocks.text: 15.13 Journal Journal is the chronological book of original entry / Day Book. Journal columns commonly include date, particulars, ledger folio, debit amount and credit amount.
blocks.subject: Financial Accounting

blocks.text: Journalising steps:
blocks.subject: Financial Accounting

blocks.text: 1. Identify accounts affected.
blocks.subject: Financial Accounting

blocks.text: 2. Classify each account.
blocks.subject: Financial Accounting

blocks.text: 3. Apply debit/credit rule.
blocks.subject: Financial Accounting

blocks.text: 4. Enter equal debit and credit amounts.
blocks.subject: Financial Accounting

blocks.text: 5. Add a short narration.
blocks.subject: Financial Accounting

blocks.text: Illustrative journal entries:
blocks.subject: Financial Accounting

blocks.text: (a) Started business with cash Rs.50,000:
blocks.subject: Financial Accounting

blocks.text: Cash A/c Dr. 50,000 To Capital A/c 50,000
blocks.subject: Financial Accounting

blocks.text: (b) Purchased furniture for cash Rs.5,000:
blocks.subject: Financial Accounting

blocks.text: Furniture A/c Dr. 5,000 To Cash A/c 5,000
blocks.subject: Financial Accounting

blocks.text: (c) Purchased goods on credit from Ravi Rs.8,000:
blocks.subject: Financial Accounting

blocks.text: Purchases A/c Dr. 8,000 To Ravi A/c 8,000
blocks.subject: Financial Accounting

blocks.text: (d) Sold goods for cash Rs.10,000:
blocks.subject: Financial Accounting

blocks.text: Cash A/c Dr. 10,000 To Sales A/c 10,000
blocks.subject: Financial Accounting

blocks.text: (e) Paid salary Rs.2,000:
blocks.subject: Financial Accounting

blocks.text: Salary A/c Dr. 2,000 To Cash A/c 2,000 (f) Received Rs.4,900 from debtor in full settlement of Rs.5,000: Cash A/c Dr. 4,900 Discount Allowed A/c Dr. 100 To Debtor A/c 5,000
blocks.subject: Financial Accounting

blocks.text: (g) Paid creditor Rs.3,900 in full settlement of Rs.4,000:
blocks.subject: Financial Accounting

blocks.text: Creditor A/c Dr. 4,000 To Cash A/c 3,900 To Discount Received A/c 100
blocks.subject: Financial Accounting

blocks.text: Important: purchase of goods for resale goes to Purchases A/c; purchase of furniture/machinery as a fixed asset goes to the appropriate asset account.
blocks.subject: Financial Accounting

blocks.text: 15.14 Ledger Ledger is the principal book of entry / book of final entry. It groups transactions account by account. Posting transfers Journal entries to the accounts in the Ledger.
blocks.subject: Financial Accounting

blocks.text: Posting method:
blocks.subject: Financial Accounting

blocks.text: • Debit the account that was debited in the Journal.
blocks.subject: Financial Accounting

blocks.text: • Credit the account that was credited in the Journal.
blocks.subject: Financial Accounting

blocks.text: • Write the corresponding account name in particulars.
blocks.subject: Financial Accounting

blocks.text: Balancing:
blocks.subject: Financial Accounting

blocks.text: 1. Total both sides.
blocks.subject: Financial Accounting

blocks.text: 2. Find the difference.
blocks.subject: Financial Accounting

blocks.text: 3. Enter the difference as balance c/d on the smaller side.
blocks.subject: Financial Accounting

blocks.text: 4. Bring it down as balance b/d on the opposite side in the next period.
blocks.subject: Financial Accounting

blocks.text: Nominal accounts are normally transferred to Trading or Profit and Loss Account rather than carried forward as permanent balances.
blocks.subject: Financial Accounting

blocks.text: 15.15 Subsidiary books
blocks.subject: Financial Accounting

blocks.text: When transactions are numerous, special books are used:
blocks.subject: Financial Accounting

blocks.text: • Cash Book – cash/bank receipts and payments.
blocks.subject: Financial Accounting

blocks.text: • Petty Cash Book – small cash expenses.
blocks.subject: Financial Accounting

blocks.text: • Sales Book – credit sales of goods.
blocks.subject: Financial Accounting

blocks.text: • Purchases Book – credit purchases of goods.
blocks.subject: Financial Accounting

blocks.text: • Sales Returns Book – goods returned by customers.
blocks.subject: Financial Accounting

blocks.text: • Purchases Returns Book – goods returned to suppliers.
blocks.subject: Financial Accounting

blocks.text: • Bills Receivable Book – bills received.
blocks.subject: Financial Accounting

blocks.text: • Bills Payable Book – bills accepted/given.
blocks.subject: Financial Accounting

blocks.text: • Journal Proper – entries not recorded in another subsidiary book.
blocks.subject: Financial Accounting

blocks.text: 15.16 Cash Book Cash Book records receipts on the debit side and payments on the credit side. It is both a book of original entry and a ledger account for cash/bank.
blocks.subject: Financial Accounting

blocks.text: Types:
blocks.subject: Financial Accounting

blocks.text: 1. Single-column Cash Book – cash column.
blocks.subject: Financial Accounting

blocks.text: 2. Two-column Cash Book – cash and discount columns.
blocks.subject: Financial Accounting

blocks.text: 3. Three-column Cash Book – discount, cash and bank columns.
blocks.subject: Financial Accounting

blocks.text: Important items:
blocks.subject: Financial Accounting

blocks.text: • Discount allowed is recorded on the debit/receipt side; discount received is recorded on the credit/payment side, in the discount columns.
blocks.subject: Financial Accounting

blocks.text: • Cash deposited into bank: debit Bank, credit Cash; commonly marked as a contra entry.
blocks.subject: Financial Accounting

blocks.text: • Cash withdrawn from bank for office use: debit Cash, credit Bank; contra entry.
blocks.subject: Financial Accounting

blocks.text: • A contra entry affects both cash and bank columns and is identified by C in the folio/marking column in common formats.
blocks.subject: Financial Accounting

blocks.text: Do not mix discount with cash. Follow the exact format demanded by the problem.
blocks.subject: Financial Accounting

blocks.text: 15.17 Trial Balance Trial Balance is a statement of ledger balances on a particular date. Debit and credit totals should agree. Its objectives are to check arithmetical accuracy of ledger posting and provide a basis for preparing final accounts. Typical debit balances: assets, expenses, purchases, sales returns and drawings. Typical credit balances: capital, liabilities, incomes, sales and purchase returns. Agreement does not prove that every entry is correct; errors of omission, principle or compensating errors may remain undetected.
blocks.subject: Financial Accounting

blocks.text: UNIT II – FINAL ACCOUNTS OF SOLE TRADING CONCERNS
blocks.subject: Financial Accounting

blocks.text: 15.18 Purpose and components Final Accounts are prepared at the end of an accounting period to determine gross profit, net profit/loss and financial position.
blocks.subject: Financial Accounting

blocks.text: 1. Trading Account – gross profit/gross loss.
blocks.subject: Financial Accounting

blocks.text: 2. Profit and Loss Account – net profit/net loss.
blocks.subject: Financial Accounting

blocks.text: 3. Balance Sheet – assets, liabilities and capital on a particular date.
blocks.subject: Financial Accounting

blocks.text: 15.19 Trading Account Net Sales = Sales − Sales Returns. Net Purchases = Purchases − Purchase Returns. Cost of Goods Sold = Opening Stock + Net Purchases + Direct Expenses − Closing Stock. Gross Profit = Net Sales − Cost of Goods Sold.
blocks.subject: Financial Accounting

blocks.text: Debit-side items commonly include opening stock, purchases less returns, carriage inward, freight, direct wages and other direct expenses. Credit-side items include sales less returns and closing stock, as required by the format in the textbook.
blocks.subject: Financial Accounting

blocks.text: 15.20 Profit and Loss Account Gross Profit is brought down on the credit side; Gross Loss is brought down on the debit side. Indirect expenses/losses are debited; other incomes/gains are credited. Net Profit = Gross Profit + Other Incomes − Indirect Expenses.
blocks.subject: Financial Accounting

blocks.text: 15.21 Balance Sheet A Balance Sheet is a statement of assets and liabilities on a particular date; it is not an account. The textbook format places capital/liabilities on one side and assets on the other. Total sides must agree. Typical assets: land/buildings, machinery less depreciation, furniture, stock, debtors less provisions, bills receivable, cash/bank, prepaid expenses and accrued income. Typical liabilities: capital adjusted for profit/loss/drawings, creditors, bills payable, loans, bank overdraft, outstanding expenses and income received in advance.
blocks.subject: Financial Accounting

blocks.text: 15.22 Capital adjustment Closing Capital = Opening Capital + Additional Capital + Net Profit + Interest on Capital − Drawings − Net Loss − other specified deductions, with treatment according to the problem.
blocks.subject: Financial Accounting

blocks.text: 15.23 Final-account adjustments – two effects For each adjustment, identify both the effect on Trading/P&L and the effect on the Balance Sheet.
blocks.subject: Financial Accounting

blocks.text: Closing stock: show on credit side of Trading Account and asset side of Balance Sheet when the adjustment is given outside the Trial Balance. Outstanding expense: add to the expense; show as liability. Prepaid expense: deduct from expense; show as asset. Accrued/outstanding income: add to income; show as asset. Income received in advance: deduct from income; show as liability. Depreciation: debit P&L; reduce asset (or use accumulated provision method as prescribed). Bad debts: debit P&L; reduce debtors. Provision for doubtful debts: write off additional bad debts first; calculate new provision on relevant remaining debtors; compare with old provision in Trial Balance; charge/deduct the required increase or credit any decrease in P&L as prescribed. Show new provision as deduction from debtors. Provision for discount on debtors: textbook method calculates on good debtors after provision for doubtful debts; debit P&L and deduct from debtors. Provision for discount on creditors: calculate as specified; credit P&L and show as deduction from creditors in the textbook's format. Interest on capital: charge as prescribed and add to capital/creditor treatment where required. Interest on drawings: income to business; reduce proprietor's capital as shown in the solution format.
blocks.subject: Financial Accounting

blocks.text: Adjustment discipline: never record an adjustment only once if the question requires two effects. Make a separate adjustment table before preparing final accounts.
blocks.subject: Financial Accounting

blocks.text: 15.24 Worked example – Trading and P&L calculation Given: Net Sales Rs.1,00,000; Opening Stock Rs.10,000; Net Purchases Rs.60,000; Direct Wages Rs.5,000; Closing Stock Rs.15,000. COGS = 10,000 + 60,000 + 5,000 − 15,000 = Rs.60,000. Gross Profit = 1,00,000 − 60,000 = Rs.40,000.
blocks.subject: Financial Accounting

blocks.text: If indirect expenses are Rs.12,000 and other income Rs.2,000:
blocks.subject: Financial Accounting

blocks.text: Net Profit = 40,000 − 12,000 + 2,000 = Rs.30,000. This is an illustrative calculation for method practice.
blocks.subject: Financial Accounting

blocks.text: UNIT III – DEPARTMENTAL ACCOUNTING
blocks.subject: Financial Accounting

blocks.text: 15.25 Meaning and objectives When a business has more than one department, a separate Trading and Profit and Loss Account may be prepared for each department. It helps determine departmental earning capacity, compare performance, identify weak areas and support managerial decisions.
blocks.subject: Financial Accounting

blocks.text: 15.26 Direct and common expenses Direct/exclusive expenses belong to one department and are charged directly to it. Common expenses benefit more than one department; they must be allocated on a fair basis.
blocks.subject: Financial Accounting

blocks.text: 15.27 Bases of allocation in the textbook
blocks.subject: Financial Accounting

blocks.text: • Rent and rates: floor space occupied; consider value/area where relevant.
blocks.subject: Financial Accounting

blocks.text: • Repairs to plant/machinery/furniture: actual departmental repairs; otherwise value of the asset may be used.
blocks.subject: Financial Accounting

blocks.text: • Lighting: number of power points, wattage or units consumed.
blocks.subject: Financial Accounting

blocks.text: • Electricity: meter readings where available; otherwise machine usage/running hours or another relevant basis.
blocks.subject: Financial Accounting

blocks.text: • Fire insurance: stock values; premises insurance may use floor area.
blocks.subject: Financial Accounting

blocks.text: • Workmen's compensation insurance: wages.
blocks.subject: Financial Accounting

blocks.text: • Loss-of-profit policy: departmental profits of the previous period.
blocks.subject: Financial Accounting

blocks.text: • Works manager salary: time spent for each department.
blocks.subject: Financial Accounting

blocks.text: • Depreciation: value of plant/assets held by the department.
blocks.subject: Financial Accounting

blocks.text: Always use the basis stated in the question or the relevant textbook basis; do not allocate every expense using one arbitrary ratio.
blocks.subject: Financial Accounting

blocks.text: 15.28 Apportionment formula Department's share = Total common expense × Department's allocation basis / Total allocation basis for all departments. Example: expense Rs.12,000; departments A:B:C basis 2:3:1. Total parts=6.
blocks.subject: Financial Accounting

blocks.text: Check total allocation=Rs.12,000.
blocks.subject: Financial Accounting

blocks.text: 15.29 Inter-departmental transfers Where one department supplies goods to another, the supplying department is credited and receiving department debited. Transfer at cost: internal entry is at cost; no unrealised profit arises from the internal transfer price. Transfer at selling price: internal selling price includes profit. Profit included in goods still unsold at period-end is unrealised from the business viewpoint and is removed by creating stock reserve using the textbook method.
blocks.subject: Financial Accounting

blocks.text: Worked example: Cost Rs.50,000; transfer price Rs.60,000; profit Rs.10,000. If the whole lot is unsold, stock reserve = Rs.10,000. If only a portion is unsold, calculate the profit element in that portion. Be careful whether the percentage is profit on cost or profit on selling price.
blocks.subject: Financial Accounting

blocks.text: 15.30 General Profit and Loss Account The textbook's departmental example prepares a General P&L Account to consolidate departmental balances. Expenses which cannot fairly be allocated to a particular department are treated in the General P&L Account as directed by the problem. Transfer each department's net profit/loss to the General P&L Account to determine overall business result.
blocks.subject: Financial Accounting

blocks.text: UNIT IV – DEPRECIATION
blocks.subject: Financial Accounting

blocks.text: 15.31 Meaning Depreciation is the gradual, permanent and continuing reduction in the value/book value of a fixed asset due to use, passage of time, obsolescence or other causes. It is charged to the accounting periods that use the asset so that profit is correctly determined.
blocks.subject: Financial Accounting

blocks.text: 15.32 Causes
blocks.subject: Financial Accounting

blocks.text: • Wear and tear due to use.
blocks.subject: Financial Accounting

blocks.text: • Passage of time / effluxion of time.
blocks.subject: Financial Accounting

blocks.text: • Obsolescence caused by new technology, inventions, fashion or legal changes.
blocks.subject: Financial Accounting

blocks.text: • Depletion or other causes described in the textbook.
blocks.subject: Financial Accounting

blocks.text: 15.33 Factors in depreciation Total cost: purchase price plus necessary transport, handling, transit insurance and installation costs needed to bring the asset into working condition, following the textbook's treatment. Useful/economic life: period or output over which the asset is expected to be used. Residual/scrap/salvage value: estimated value at end of useful life, less disposal costs if applicable.
blocks.subject: Financial Accounting

blocks.text: 15.34 Straight Line Method (SLM) / Fixed Instalment Method Annual Depreciation = (Original Cost − Residual Value) / Useful Life. Rate = (Annual Depreciation / Original Cost) × 100. The same amount is charged each full year if estimates do not change.
blocks.subject: Financial Accounting

blocks.text: Worked example:
blocks.subject: Financial Accounting

blocks.text: Cost Rs.25,000; residual value Rs.5,000; useful life 10 years. Annual depreciation=(25,000−5,000)/10=Rs.2,000. Rate=2,000/25,000×100=8% per year. Book value after 3 years=25,000−(2,000×3)=Rs.19,000.
blocks.subject: Financial Accounting

blocks.text: 15.35 Diminishing Balance / Written Down Value (WDV) Method Depreciation is charged at a fixed rate on the opening written-down value rather than original cost. Depreciation = Opening WDV × Rate/100. Closing WDV = Opening WDV − Depreciation.
blocks.subject: Financial Accounting

blocks.text: Worked example:
blocks.subject: Financial Accounting

blocks.text: Cost Rs.25,000; rate 10%. Year 1: dep. 2,500; closing WDV 22,500. Year 2: dep. 2,250; closing WDV 20,250. Year 3: dep. 2,025; closing WDV 18,225. The annual amount reduces because the base reduces.
blocks.subject: Financial Accounting

blocks.text: 15.36 Part-year depreciation and disposal If an asset is acquired/sold during the year, calculate depreciation for the actual period (months) when required. Example: Cost Rs.15,000, SLM rate 10%, held for 6 months: depreciation=15,000×10%×6/12=Rs.750. At disposal, compare sale proceeds with book value at disposal date: Profit on sale=Sale proceeds−Book value. A negative result is loss. Follow the prescribed Asset/Machinery Account format and include depreciation up to the sale date.
blocks.subject: Financial Accounting

blocks.text: 15.37 SLM and WDV comparison SLM: base is original cost; full-year amount is normally equal; formula uses cost less residual value divided by useful life. WDV: base is opening written-down value; full-year amount reduces over time; formula uses opening WDV multiplied by fixed percentage.
blocks.subject: Financial Accounting

blocks.text: 15.38 Provisions and reserves – textbook supporting topic Provision: charge against profit for a known liability or expected loss whose amount/timing may be uncertain. Reserve: appropriation of profit retained to strengthen the financial position or provide for a purpose. Main distinction: a provision is a charge against profit; reserve is an appropriation of profit. The textbook discusses their purpose, creation and presentation. Study the exact comparison in Lesson 5.
blocks.subject: Financial Accounting

blocks.text: UNIT V – SINGLE ENTRY SYSTEM
blocks.subject: Financial Accounting

blocks.text: 15.39 Meaning and features Single Entry System is an incomplete method of maintaining accounts. It is not a uniform, complete double-entry system. Personal accounts and a cash book are commonly maintained, while nominal accounts and many real accounts may be omitted.
blocks.subject: Financial Accounting

blocks.text: Features:
blocks.subject: Financial Accounting

blocks.text: • Incomplete records and absence of uniform rules.
blocks.subject: Financial Accounting

blocks.text: • Personal accounts and cash records usually available.
blocks.subject: Financial Accounting

blocks.text: • Many nominal/real accounts absent.
blocks.subject: Financial Accounting

blocks.text: • Personal and business transactions may be mixed.
blocks.subject: Financial Accounting

blocks.text: • Supporting vouchers, invoices and other records may be needed to reconstruct information.
blocks.subject: Financial Accounting

blocks.text: 15.40 Defects
blocks.subject: Financial Accounting

blocks.text: • Records are incomplete.
blocks.subject: Financial Accounting

blocks.text: • Trial Balance generally cannot be prepared.
blocks.subject: Financial Accounting

blocks.text: • Profit/loss cannot reliably be calculated from missing income and expense accounts.
blocks.subject: Financial Accounting

blocks.text: • Financial position is harder to establish.
blocks.subject: Financial Accounting

blocks.text: • Errors/fraud may be difficult to detect.
blocks.subject: Financial Accounting

blocks.text: • Comparison, planning, financing and valuation may be difficult.
blocks.subject: Financial Accounting

blocks.text: 15.41 Single Entry vs Double Entry Double Entry: records both aspects systematically; personal, real and nominal accounts are maintained; Trial Balance and Final Accounts can normally be prepared. Single Entry: records are incomplete; Trial Balance is generally unavailable; profit/loss may need to be estimated from capital/net worth changes.
blocks.subject: Financial Accounting

blocks.text: 15.42 Statement of Affairs / Net Worth Method – numerical scope The Statement of Affairs resembles a Balance Sheet. Assets are listed on one side and outside liabilities on the other; the difference gives capital/net worth. Opening Capital = Opening Assets − Opening Outside Liabilities. Closing Capital = Closing Assets − Closing Outside Liabilities.
blocks.subject: Financial Accounting

blocks.text: Profit formula:
blocks.subject: Financial Accounting

blocks.text: Profit = Closing Capital + Drawings − Additional Capital − Opening Capital. A positive result is profit; a negative result is loss.
blocks.subject: Financial Accounting

blocks.text: Worked example:
blocks.subject: Financial Accounting

blocks.text: Opening Capital Rs.1,20,000. Closing assets Rs.2,10,000; closing outside liabilities Rs.60,000. Closing Capital=2,10,000−60,000=Rs.1,50,000. Drawings Rs.20,000; additional capital introduced Rs.10,000. Profit=1,50,000+20,000−10,000−1,20,000=Rs.40,000.
blocks.subject: Financial Accounting

blocks.text: Why add drawings? Drawings reduce closing capital but are not a business loss; add them back to calculate the profit earned. Why deduct additional capital? It increases capital but is not earned profit; deduct it. Adjust closing assets/liabilities for depreciation, bad debts, provisions and other items given in the question. Include all supplied assets/liabilities and do not omit cash, bank, stock, debtors, creditors, machinery or outstanding items.
blocks.subject: Financial Accounting

blocks.text: 15.43 Conversion Method The textbook also explains conversion of incomplete records into a more complete double-entry system using available records and supporting documents. However, the printed syllabus states: “Problems on Statement of Affairs method only.” Therefore understand the concept of conversion method, but prioritise numerical problem practice using Statement of Affairs unless official exam instructions state otherwise.
blocks.subject: Financial Accounting

blocks.text: FINANCIAL ACCOUNTING – COMMON MISTAKES
blocks.subject: Financial Accounting

blocks.text: • Debit purchases for goods bought for resale, not for purchase of fixed assets.
blocks.subject: Financial Accounting

blocks.text: • Do not forget the equal credit when recording a journal entry.
blocks.subject: Financial Accounting

blocks.text: • In the Ledger, post to both accounts affected.
blocks.subject: Financial Accounting

blocks.text: • Agreement of Trial Balance does not prove all transactions are correct.
blocks.subject: Financial Accounting

blocks.text: • Do not confuse sales returns with purchases returns.
blocks.subject: Financial Accounting

blocks.text: • In final accounts, show both effects of every adjustment.
blocks.subject: Financial Accounting

blocks.text: • Calculate closing stock and provisions on the proper base.
blocks.subject: Financial Accounting

blocks.text: • Use the correct expense allocation basis for each department.
blocks.subject: Financial Accounting

blocks.text: • Remove unrealised internal profit from unsold transferred stock.
blocks.subject: Financial Accounting

blocks.text: • Do not calculate WDV depreciation on original cost each year.
blocks.subject: Financial Accounting

blocks.text: • In Statement of Affairs profit, add drawings and deduct additional capital.
blocks.subject: Financial Accounting

blocks.text: • The syllabus specifies Statement of Affairs problems only for numerical questions on Single Entry.
blocks.subject: Financial Accounting

blocks.text: FINANCIAL ACCOUNTING – FINAL FORMULA SHEET
blocks.subject: Financial Accounting

blocks.text: Assets = Liabilities + Capital. Net Sales = Sales − Sales Returns. Net Purchases = Purchases − Purchase Returns. COGS = Opening Stock + Net Purchases + Direct Expenses − Closing Stock. Gross Profit = Net Sales − COGS. Net Profit = Gross Profit + Other Income − Indirect Expenses. Department share = Common expense × Department basis / Total basis. SLM depreciation = (Cost − Residual Value) / Useful Life. WDV depreciation = Opening WDV × Rate/100. Opening Capital = Opening Assets − Opening Outside Liabilities. Closing Capital = Closing Assets − Closing Outside Liabilities. Profit = Closing Capital + Drawings − Additional Capital − Opening Capital.
blocks.subject: Financial Accounting

• Give the main definition without looking.
• Explain the concept in simple words.
• Reproduce the important formula/diagram/program.
• Answer a short question.
• Structure a five-mark answer.
• Attempt a long answer or problem independently.
• Identify and correct a mistake from a previous attempt.
3. DAILY STUDY METHOD
For a six-hour study day:
• Session A – 90 minutes: learn one new topic.
• Session B – 90 minutes: solve examples/programs from that topic.
• Session C – 60 minutes: write short/long answers from memory.
• Session D – 60 minutes: second subject or lab exercise.
• Session E – 30 minutes: revise yesterday's topic.
• Session F – 30 minutes: quiz and error notebook.
If fewer hours are available, shorten the blocks but do not remove the daily recall test.
4. SPACED REVISION

Same day: close the book and write the definition/formula. Next day: explain the topic aloud and answer two questions. After three days: solve a fresh problem or write a fresh answer. After seven days: take a short test. Before the exam: revise marked errors, formula sheets, key diagrams and programs.
5. EXAM ANSWER STRUCTURE

2 marks: one correct definition/direct answer plus one key feature, formula or example. 5 marks: definition, four or five relevant points, and a diagram/table/example where useful. 10 marks: short introduction, headings, detailed explanation, labelled diagram/formula/algorithm/example, and a relevant conclusion. Avoid unrelated padding. Answer exactly what is asked.
6. MATHEMATICS SOLUTION PRESENTATION
1. Write what is given.
2. State what must be found.
3. Write the formula/theorem.
4. Substitute values.
5. Show all important calculation steps.
6. Keep sufficient digits during calculation.
7. State the final answer clearly and round only as requested.
8. Check units, signs and reasonableness.
7. PROGRAMMING ANSWER PRESENTATION
1. State the problem/aim.
2. List input and output.
3. Write the logic/algorithm.
4. Write the complete program.
5. Explain important statements.
6. Give sample input/output.
7. Test boundary cases and invalid input.
8. Compile on the environment prescribed by the practical centre.
8. ERROR NOTEBOOK FORMAT
For every mistake record:
Date | Subject | Topic | What I wrote/did | Correct method | Why I made the mistake | Retest date.

Mistakes to track include forgotten definitions, wrong formulas, wrong signs, skipped calculations, incorrect program syntax, array boundary errors, unclear literary summaries and failure to answer the actual question.
9. WEEKLY PERFORMANCE SCORE
Use this self-rating for every unit:

0 – Not started. 1 – Read once, cannot explain. 2 – Understands some of it with notes. 3 – Can explain with notes and solve a guided example. 4 – Can answer most questions without notes. 5 – Can independently solve/write under time pressure. Aim for 4–5 before treating a unit as exam-ready. This is a study target, not an official University pass criterion.
10. MOCK EXAM METHOD
• Use the actual paper pattern when an official question paper or pattern is available.
• Attempt questions without answers first.
• Follow the time limit.
• Award marks only for correct points/steps.
• Record marks by section and question type.
• Rewrite weak answers after reviewing the deductions.
Do not invent previous-year questions. Label model questions as practice questions only.

I will not measure preparation by pages read. I will measure it by questions answered, problems solved, programs compiled, diagrams reproduced and concepts recalled without help.
